text:
DRN-3703519
The complaint
Mr D has complained that British Friendly Society Limited unfairly declined his claim. 
What happened
Mr D bought an income protection insurance policy in 2020, underwritten by British Friendly, 
which pays a benefit if he is unable to work due to illness or injury. 
Mr D is a driver and injured his back in 2021. He made a claim which British Friendly 
declined as it said Mr D’s condition was pre-existing and so it was excluded from cover. 
Unhappy, Mr D complained to British Friendly and said the injury wasn’t pre-existing. He also 
said he was suffering from mental health problems which were preventing him from working. 
British Friendly maintained its decline but told Mr D that he wouldn’t have to return any of the 
benefit it had paid, amounting to over £2,000, which it had paid whilst it was assessing his 
claim. 
Mr D referred his complaint to this Service. 
Our investigator looked into the complaint but didn’t think British Friendly had done anything 
wrong. 
Mr D disagreed and in summary said his GP had provided medical evidence to show that his 
back problems were a new issue and not related to his previous back problems. And in 
addition, his mental health issues were serious and ongoing and preventing him from 
working.
And so the case has been passed to me for a final decision. 
What I’ve decided – and why
I’ve considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint.
Having done so, I don’t think this complaint should be upheld and largely for the same 
reasons as already explained by our investigator.
The relevant rules and industry guidelines say an insurer should handle claims promptly and 
fairly. And shouldn’t unreasonably reject a claim. 
The policy definition of incapacity is:
“This means that you are totally unable to carry out your occupation due to physical 
or mental illness or injury resulting in a complete or partial loss of income.”
The policy terms confirm benefit will not be paid for:
“any pre-existing conditions for which you have received consultation, treatment 

and/or medication, or asked advice on or had symptoms of (whether or not 
diagnosed) during the 3 years immediately before policy inception.” 
British Friendly requested and reviewed Mr D’s medical records which showed that he had 
suffered from lower back pain previously and within the 3 years before he took the policy out. 
So based on the above policy terms, Mr D’s claim wasn’t eligible as he was suffering from a 
pre-existing condition. 
I’ve considered the following key evidence:

Mr D said his condition wasn’t pre-existing and his doctor had confirmed that the 
lower back pain was different to his previous injury. The GP records were reviewed 
by British Friendly’s chief medical officer (CMO) who compared the back pain to the 
previously noted injury. He concluded the recent back pain was pre-existing based 
on the similar location of pain, the way the injury happened and symptoms. He didn’t 
think this was a new problem. 

In addition, Mr D says he is suffering from mental health problems. This was also 
considered by the CMO who said Mr D was feeling down and depressed but he 
wasn’t keen on medication and would prefer talking therapies. The CMO said there 
was an element of work-related stress but back pain was the main factor keeping him 
off work. And symptoms of low mood didn’t meet the criteria of a serious mental 
illness. Mr D wasn’t taking medication and his symptoms weren’t affecting his 
functional ability. 

Having considered the CMO’s opinion, I’m not satisfied the medical evidence 
provided meets the definition of incapacity for a mental health illness as I would 
expect to see reference to how Mr D’s mental illness was preventing him from doing 
his job. In relation to the back pain, I’m persuaded by the CMO’s opinion that this is a 
pre-existing condition taking into account his description of the back pain and a 
previous similar injury. 

Mr D says British Friendly confirmed it would arrange a mental health assessment for 
him but then failed to do this. The CMO reviewed Mr D’s records and didn’t think 
there was sufficient evidence of a serious mental illness. In addition, when declining 
the claim, British Friendly confirmed they would discuss whether an assessment 
could be arranged but didn’t guarantee that this would happen. So I don’t think British 
Friendly failed to complete an assessment when it should have. I’m satisfied it 
properly considered Mr D’s mental health claim by requesting and reviewing medical 
evidence and referring it to its CMO.

British Friendly paid Mr D over £2,000 worth of benefit whilst it was assessing his 
claim. As his claim was ultimately declined, it initially asked Mr D to pay this back. 
However, it has since confirmed it won’t ask Mr D to return the benefit which I think is 
more than reasonable. 
As British Friendly has paid Mr D some benefit and has confirmed it won’t ask him to re-pay 
this, I think it has acted reasonably and has gone above and beyond what it is expected to 
do and outside the policy terms and conditions. So I won’t be asking it to do anything more. 
My final decision
For the reasons set out above, I don’t uphold this complaint. 
Under the rules of the Financial Ombudsman Service, I’m required to ask Mr D to accept or 

reject my decision before 15 February 2023.
 
Shamaila Hussain
Ombudsman

any pre-existing conditions for which you have received consultation, treatment and/or medication, or asked advice on or had symptoms of (whether or not diagnosed) during the 3 years immediately before policy inception.

text:
DRN-3713987
The complaint
Ms B complains because Aviva Insurance Limited has refused to pay a claim under her 
private medical insurance policy. 
What happened
Ms B holds a private medical insurance policy, provided by Aviva. The policy was 
underwritten on a ‘continued medical exclusions’ basis and Ms B’s policy schedule with 
Aviva says the following: 
‘Medical Exclusions 
Any recognised related conditions or complications including any recognised 
complications of treatment(s) arising from: 
… 
Dizzy spells.’ 
In October 2021, Ms B made a claim under her policy with Aviva for investigations into dizzy 
spells. Aviva said the claim wasn’t covered because of the above exclusion on Ms B’s policy. 
Ms B complained to Aviva and provided further medical evidence. Aviva reviewed the 
evidence but maintained its decision to decline the claim. Unhappy, Ms B brought the matter 
to the attention of our service. 
One of our Investigators looked into what had happened and said she didn’t think Aviva’s 
decision to decline the claim was incorrect. Ms B didn’t agree with our Investigator’s 
conclusions, so the complaint was referred to me. 
I made my provisional decision about Ms B’s complaint in August 2022. In it, I said:
‘Industry rules set out by the regulator (the Financial Conduct Authority) say that insurers 
must handle claims fairly and shouldn’t unreasonably reject a claim. I’ve taken these rules 
into account when making my provisional decision about Ms B’s complaint. 
Our Investigator, in reaching her findings, quoted the exclusion relating to dizzy spells which 
applied to a previous private medical insurance policy held by Ms B with a different insurer. 
That exclusion isn’t relevant to Ms B’s claim. What is relevant is the exclusion which I’ve 
quoted above, which applies to Ms B’s contract with Aviva under which she made this claim. 
The exclusion under Ms B’s policy with Aviva means that no cover is provided for any 
conditions or complications arising from dizzy spells (amongst other things). The medical 
evidence (namely, the letter from Ms B’s consultant who I’ll refer to as ‘Dr N’, dated 27 
October 2021) says that Ms B was seen for ‘a sudden onset dizzy spell’. Dr N went on to say 
he was ‘not certain as to the cause of these dizzy spells’ and, therefore, recommended 
further investigations. Ms B was subsequently diagnosed with moderate cerebrovascular 
disease. 

I appreciate that Ms B’s dizzy spells were a symptom of the condition she was ultimately 
diagnosed with, rather than being a condition in themselves. But, on a strict application of 
the relevant policy exclusion, I don’t think Ms B’s claim is covered. 
However, my remit is to decide what I think is fair and reasonable in all the circumstances of 
a case. And, I don’t think that a strict application of the relevant policy exclusion to Ms B’s 
claim results in a fair and reasonable outcome in the circumstances. 
I’ve considered the purpose and intention of the relevant policy exclusion applied by Aviva. I 
think this is to limit Aviva’s exposure to risk by excluding claims relating to any of Ms B’s pre-
existing medical conditions – including dizzy spells. But, based on the medical evidence 
available to me, I don’t think this claim did relate to Ms B’s pre-existing dizzy spells. 
Aviva doesn’t appear to have requested Ms B’s medical records, made any enquiries about 
or given any consideration to the previous investigations that Ms B underwent for dizzy 
spells which led to the application of the exclusion of Ms B’s policy. So, I’ve considered the 
medical evidence which has been provided by Ms B on this point. 
Dr N’s letter dated 27 October 2021 says that Ms B’s: 
‘past history includes 2 episodes where she had unconscious spells but these were 
investigated thoroughly and were put down to simple faints at the time.’ 
A medical certificate from Ms B’s GP dated 6 December 2021 says: 
‘I understand [Ms B] had an exclusion on her insurance policy for dizzy spells 
following a fainting episode which was well investigated by a consultant cardiologist 
in 2018. It is of [sic] my opinion that this episode was entirely unrelated to her recent 
diagnosis…’ 
A letter from another consultant (who I’ll call ‘Dr D’) dated 5 January 2022 says: 
‘…when I first met you in 2006 you had some funny episodes after eating … where 
you actually fainted and you had another episode … and a third one afterwards. 
We investigated you thoroughly with echocardiography and Holter monitoring. Your 
echocardiogram showed a normal heart. The Holter monitor showed just a few 
ectopic beats which are of no significance. When I reviewed you in 2018 you had no 
more of these funny episodes. 
… 
…dizziness is not a diagnosis it is a symptom. In my opinion there is absolutely no 
connection between what happened to you 15 years ago and the stroke for which [Dr 
N] is treating you now. In my view this is a completely separate and new 
phenomenon.’ 
I think this medical evidence is persuasive in concluding that Ms B’s previous dizzy spells in 
2006 and/or 2018 were unrelated to the stroke which Ms B was diagnosed with in 2021. I 
don’t think the intention of the exclusion on Ms B’s policy was to exclude cover for strokes. 
So, I currently think it would be fair and reasonable for Aviva to accept Ms B’s claim.’
Ms B accepted my provisional findings and said she had nothing further to add. Aviva replied 
and commented on a number of issues – including the basis on which its policies with 

continued medical exclusions work, and information set out in a letter written by Dr N dated 
21 November 2021. However, Aviva said it appreciated why I intended to uphold Ms B’s 
complaint and that it would fully comply with any such decision.  
What I’ve decided – and why
I’ve considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint.
I’ve taken into account the additional points raised by Aviva but, as Aviva has acknowledged, 
there is no medical evidence linking Ms B’s stroke to her previous fainting episodes and 
dizzy spells. 
I therefore see no reason to change my provisional decision. 
Putting things right
Aviva Insurance Limited needs to put things right by accepting Ms B’s claim. 
Aviva Insurance Limited should add interest to Ms B’s claim payment at 8% simple per 
annum from the date of her claim until the date the settlement is paid1. 
My final decision
My final decision is that I uphold Ms B’s complaint and I direct Aviva Insurance Limited to put 
things right in the way I’ve outlined above. 
Under the rules of the Financial Ombudsman Service, I’m required to ask Ms B to accept or 
reject my decision before 21 October 2022.
 
Leah Nagle
Ombudsman
1 If Aviva Insurance Limited considers that it’s required by HM Revenue & Customs to take off income 
tax from that interest it should tell Ms B how much it has taken off. It should also give Ms B a 
certificate showing this if she asks for one, so she can reclaim the tax from HM Revenue & Customs if 
appropriate.

text:
DRN-3751160
The complaint
Mr and Mrs J complain that Admiral Insurance (Gibraltar) Limited has turned down a claim 
Mrs J made on a travel insurance policy.
As Mrs J made the claim and brought the complaint to us, I’ve referred only to her 
throughout this decision.
What happened
Mrs J took out a travel insurance policy in November 2021. In January 2022, while Mrs J 
was on holiday abroad, she learned that a close relative had sadly passed away. So Mrs J 
called Admiral, as she needed to get home and wanted to look into making a claim on her 
travel insurance policy.
The call handler told Mrs J that she could make arrangements to return to the UK and make 
a claim retrospectively. Mrs J cut short her trip and travelled back to the UK. She made a 
curtailment claim on the policy.
Admiral turned down Mrs J’s claim. It noted that Mrs J’s relative had been diagnosed with a 
serious medical condition some time before the policy had been taken out. And Mrs J’s 
relative had passed away as a result of this condition. Admiral told Mrs J that the policy 
specifically excluded claims which arose because of the pre-existing medical conditions of 
non-travelling relatives. Therefore, it concluded that Mrs J’s claim wasn’t covered by the 
policy terms.
Mrs J was unhappy with Admiral’s position, and she asked us to look into her complaint. She 
said Admiral’s call handler had told her that she’d be covered for all of her expenses, door-
to-door. She added that he hadn’t asked her whether her relative had any pre-existing 
medical conditions.
Our investigator didn’t think Mrs J’s complaint should be upheld. She felt the policy terms 
made it clear that Admiral didn’t cover claims caused by the pre-existing medical conditions 
of non-travelling relatives. And as Mrs J’s relative had been diagnosed with the condition a 
year prior to the policy being purchased, the investigator thought it’d been reasonable for 
Admiral to decline to pay the claim.
The investigator also listened to the call between Mrs J and Admiral’s call handler. She didn’t 
think the call handler had given Mrs J any guarantee that the claim would be paid. She also 
didn’t think the call handler would’ve had any reason to believe that the claim was down to a 
pre-existing medical condition.
Mrs J disagreed. In summary, she felt the onus of mentioning a pre-existing medical 
condition had to rest with the trained insurance professional, not on individuals who didn’t 
realise they’d need to make this point. She said this was even more important, given such 
calls were usually made during times of high stress and require all of the relevant information 
from an insurer. And she said that the call handler hadn’t indicated at any point that the claim 
might not be paid.

The complaint’s been passed to me to decide.
What I’ve decided – and why
I’ve considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint.
Having done so, whilst I’m sorry to disappoint Mrs J, I think it was fair for Admiral to turn 
down her claim and I’ll explain why.
First, I’d like to offer my sincere condolences to Mr and Mrs J for their loss. I don’t doubt 
what an upsetting time this has been for them. I’d also like to reassure Mrs J that I’ve 
carefully considered all she’s said and sent us when reaching my decision.
The relevant regulator’s rules say that insurers must handle claims promptly and fairly. And 
that they mustn’t turn down claims unreasonably. So I’ve considered, amongst other things, 
the terms of Mrs J’s policy and the relevant claims calls, to decide whether Admiral treated 
her fairly.
Is the claim covered by the policy terms?
I’ve first considered the policy terms and conditions, as these form the basis of Mrs J’s 
contract with Admiral. Page 14 of the policy sets out a ‘Medical Declaration’. This includes 
the following:
‘We will not pay any claim related to a pre-existing medical condition of other people, whose 
health may affect your decision to travel or remain overseas such as a close relative, travel 
companion, close business associate or any person you have arranged to stay with, which 
they had at the start or renewal of your policy or when you booked a trip (whichever is later).’
The definition of a pre-existing medical condition is:
‘Any disease, illness or injury that, you or any insured person (or any person your trip 
depends on) has, when arranging or renewing your policy, or when you book a trip 
(whichever is later) see Medical Declaration on page 13.’
Page 32 of the contract sets out the cover Admiral provides if a policyholder cuts short their 
trip. This includes curtailment cover if a policyholder has to cut short their trip because of the 
illness or death of a close relative. However, page 34 sets out specific events which Admiral 
has chosen to specifically exclude from curtailment cover. One of these is that it won’t pay 
any claim related to:
‘a pre-existing medical condition of other people whose health may affect your decision to 
travel or remain overseas, such as a close relative, travel companion, close business 
associate or person you have arranged to stay with, which they had at the start or renewal of 
your policy or when you booked a trip (whichever is later).’
In my view, Admiral has clearly explained in the contract what it considers a pre-existing 
condition to be and that it doesn’t cover the pre-existing conditions of close relatives. And I 
note that the Insurance Product Information Document, which sets out an at-a-glance 
summary of policy cover and important terms, also says, on page one:
‘What is not insured
Pre-existing medical conditions of non-travelling relatives or of those whose health may 

affect your decision to travel or remain overseas: this exclusion applies regardless of 
whether you were aware of the condition or not.’
There’s no dispute that Mrs J’s relative had been diagnosed with a serious illness several 
months before the policy was taken out. And it’s common ground that it was this condition 
which led to the passing of Mrs J’s relative and therefore, led to Mrs J understandably 
needing to cut short her trip. As such then, I don’t think it was unfair or unreasonable for 
Admiral to conclude that the above exclusion clause applied to the circumstances of Mrs J’s 
claim and accordingly, to turn the claim down.
The telephone calls
Like the investigator, I’ve listened carefully to the calls between Mrs J and Admiral’s call 
handler. It’s clear Mrs J strongly feels that she was given misleading information by the call 
handler and that they didn’t tell her about the pre-existing condition exclusion.
However, I don’t think that the call handler did give Mrs J unclear or misleading information. 
They explained that there was curtailment cover available on the policy and what this might 
pay out for. They also explained that Mrs J could make all the arrangements she needed to 
get back to the UK and claim retrospectively. I don’t find this was a guarantee that any claim 
would definitely be paid though or that all Mrs J’s costs would be met.
Neither do I think there was anything in the calls which ought to have put the call handler on 
notice that Mrs J’s claim might be caught by the pre-existing medical condition exclusion. So 
I wouldn’t reasonably have expected them to point this exclusion out to Mrs J at this stage in 
the claims process.
Even if I had thought the call handler had made an error though, I’d then need to go on to 
think about whether such an error had caused Mrs J to do something she wouldn’t otherwise 
have done, which had caused her to lose out. Here, that means that I’d need to be satisfied 
that Mrs J wouldn’t have curtailed her trip but for her conversation with the call handler. And 
having listened to the calls, I don’t think I could fairly find that this was the case. That’s 
because Mrs J told the call handler that due to the passing of her relative, she needed to get 
back home. So even if she’d been told upfront that potentially, her claim might not be paid, I 
still think it’s more likely than not that she’d have cut short her trip and returned to the UK.
Overall, despite my natural sympathy with Mrs J’s position, I think Admiral has treated her 
fairly. And I don’t think there are any reasonable grounds upon which I could direct it to pay 
her claim.  
My final decision
For the reasons I’ve given above, my final decision is that I don’t uphold this complaint.
Under the rules of the Financial Ombudsman Service, I’m required to ask Mrs J and Mr J to 
accept or reject my decision before 20 February 2023.
 
Lisa Barham
Ombudsman

text:
DRN-3783147
The complaint
Mr W complains that Society of Lloyd’s has turned down a claim he made on an income 
protection insurance policy,
What happened
Mr W took out a personal income protection insurance policy in 2019, through a broker. The 
policy provided cover if Mr W was unable to work due to accident or sickness. And it 
included a ‘waiting period’ (or deferred period) of 90 days. Mr W was working in two jobs – 
one full-time role from home and a separate self-employed, part-time job.
Unfortunately, on 26 April 2022, Mr W was involved in an accident and suffered fracture 
injuries. He was signed-off from his full-time job until 5 June 2022 and returned to this role 
on 6 June 2022. However, he remained unfit to return to his part-time job. Mr W made a 
claim on his income protection insurance policy.
Lloyd’s turned down Mr W’s claim. It said that Mr W had chosen a waiting period of 90 days, 
which meant he’d have needed to be medically signed-off for a continuous period of 90 days 
before benefit would be due. But as Mr W had returned to his full-time job after 40 days, 
Lloyd’s said he wasn’t entitled to any benefit under the policy for his self-employed role 
either.
Mr W was unhappy with Lloyds’ decision and he asked us to look into his complaint.
Our investigator didn’t think Mr W’s complaint should be upheld. She felt the policy terms 
made it clear that in order for a claim to be paid, a policyholder had to be unable to work for 
the duration of the waiting period. In this case, Lloyd’s considered a policyholder to be 
working if they worked more than 16 hours. As Mr W had returned to his full-time job some 
time before the policy waiting period expired, the investigator thought Lloyd’s had been 
entitled to turn down Mr W’s claim.
Mr W disagreed and so the complaint’s been passed to me to decide.
What I’ve decided – and why
I’ve considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint.
Having done so, whilst I’m sorry to disappoint Mr W, I think it was fair for Lloyd’s to turn 
down his claim and I’ll explain why.
First, it’s clear that Mr W suffered painful injuries in the accident, which left him unable to 
return to his self-employed role. I don’t doubt what a stressful time this must’ve been for Mr 
W and I do hope his recovery is progressing well.
The relevant regulator’s rules say that insurers must handle claims promptly and fairly. And 
that they mustn’t turn down claims unreasonably. So in making this decision, I’ve 
considered, amongst other things, the terms of Mr W’s policy and the circumstances of his 

claim, to decide whether Lloyd’s has treated him fairly.
I’ve first considered the policy terms and conditions, as these form the basis of Mr W’s 
contract with Lloyd’s. Mr W made a claim for incapacity due to an accident, so I think it was 
appropriate for Lloyd’s to consider the claim under section two – ‘Accident, Sickness and 
Hospitalisation Cover.’ This section of the policy provides the following cover:
‘If you are working and, after the policy transfer date, you suffer from an accident or 
sickness, including hospitalisation, one monthly benefit will be paid to you upon expiry of:
-
Your excess period (as stated on your Police Schedule); and
-
Your waiting period (as stated on your Policy Schedule).
N.B You must be unable to work for the duration of the waiting period applicable to your 
claim in order to receive your first monthly benefit payment.’
The policy states that benefit will be paid until:
‘The date you return to work.’
Lloyd’s has defined ‘waiting period’ as follows: ‘The period shown on your Policy Schedule 
in which you will need to be continuously…unable to work due to accident, sickness or 
hospitalisation…in order to be entitled to receive your monthly benefit.’
And Lloyd’s has also defined what it means by ‘work/working’. The contract says: ‘You are 
in permanent employment, a contract worker…or are self-employed or a company director 
for 16 hours or more each week in the UK.’
In my view, the policy terms make it clear that Lloyd’s will only pay accident and sickness 
benefit once a policyholder has been unable to work for the entirety of their policy waiting 
period. And that it will stop paying benefit once a policyholder has returned to work for more 
than 16 hours per week.
It's clear that Mr W did suffer painful injuries in an accident. There’s no doubt that not only 
was he signed-off from work, he was also hospitalised for a few days. But in order for 
Lloyd’s to be liable to pay benefit, Mr W needs to show that he was unable to work for the 
entirety of his waiting period. In this case, Mr W’s policy schedule shows that a waiting 
period of 90 days was selected. Broadly, as Mr W’s accident happened on 26 April 2022, a 
90-day waiting period would’ve expired on 25 July 2022.
Mr W’s employer for his full-time role completed part of his claim form. It stated that Mr W 
had returned to work on 6 June 2022, for 40 hours per week. This date was around 50 days 
before the waiting period was due to expire. As such then, it’s clear that Mr W wasn’t 
continuously unable to work for less than 16 hours per week, for a 90-day period. 
I do appreciate that Mr W was still considered medically unfit to carry out his self-employed 
role and that he’s lost income through being unable to carry out that role while he recovers. 
But I think the policy is clear enough that Lloyd’s considers that a policyholder has returned 
to work and is no longer entitled to monthly benefit if they’ve returned to work for more than 
16 hours a week. And in this case, the evidence shows that after 6 June 2022, Mr W was 
working significantly more than 16 hours per week. So I don’t think it was unfair for Lloyd’s 
to conclude that Mr W’s claim wasn’t covered.
Having considered the file, it seems Mr W was concerned about the length of the waiting 
period. It’s important to point out though that Lloyd’s didn’t sell the policy to Mr W and so, it 

wasn’t involved in selecting Mr W’s waiting period. If Mr W feels that the policy was mis-sold 
to him, he’d need to complain to the broker which sold it to him.
Overall, despite my natural sympathy with Mr W’s position, I find it was fair and reasonable 
for Lloyd’s to turn down his claim.
My final decision
For the reasons I’ve given above, my final decision is that I don’t uphold his complaint.
Under the rules of the Financial Ombudsman Service, I’m required to ask Mr W to accept or 
reject my decision before 14 February 2023.
 
Lisa Barham
Ombudsman

N.B You must be unable to work for the duration of the waiting period applicable to your claim in order to receive your first monthly benefit payment.
The period shown on your Policy Schedule in which you will need to be continuously…unable to work due to accident, sickness or hospitalisation…in order to be entitled to receive your monthly benefit.
You are in permanent employment, a contract worker…or are self-employed or a company director for 16 hours or more each week in the UK.

text:
DRN-3846116
The complaint
Mr M complains because Aviva Insurance Limited hasn’t paid a claim under his private 
medical insurance policy. 
What happened
In March 2022, Mr M bought a private medical insurance policy provided by Aviva. The 
policy was underwritten on a moratorium basis. This means there is no cover for conditions 
that a policyholder had symptoms of (amongst other things) in the five years before taking 
out the policy unless the policyholder meets certain criteria for a two-year period after the 
policy starts. 
In August 2022, Mr M made a claim under his policy arising from a diagnosis of osteoarthritis 
in his left hip. Aviva said the claim wasn’t covered because of the terms of the moratorium.
Unhappy, Mr M complained to Aviva before bringing the matter to our service. One of our 
investigators looked into what had happened and said he didn’t think Aviva had acted 
unfairly or unreasonably by declining Mr M’s claim. Mr M didn’t agree with our investigator’s 
opinion, so the complaint has been referred to me as the final stage in our process.   
What I’ve decided – and why
I’ve considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint.
Mr M has brought a separate complaint to us about the sale of his private medical insurance 
policy. Within this final decision, I’m only considering the activities which Aviva is responsible 
for (i.e., the declinature of Mr M’s claim). 
Industry rules set out by the regulator (the Financial Conduct Authority) say insurers must 
handle claims fairly and shouldn’t unreasonably reject a claim. I’ve taken these rules into 
account when making my final decision. 
I’ve read and considered all the medical evidence that has been provided. I understand that, 
in December 2021, Mr M’s hips were described by a consultant orthopaedic surgeon as 
‘mobile and appear pain free’. And it’s not in dispute that Mr M’s left hip osteoarthritis wasn’t 
diagnosed until August 2022. I think the medical evidence is very clear on this point. But this 
doesn’t automatically mean that Mr M’s claim is covered under the terms and conditions of 
his contract with Aviva. I appreciate Mr M was described as ‘surprised’ to find out the 
osteoarthritis diagnosis, and that a number of Mr M’s doctors have said his condition wasn’t 
pre-existing. But the relevant definition of ‘pre-existing’ is the one which is set out under the 
terms and conditions of Mr M’s policy, and not what Mr M’s doctors may have interpreted the 
phrase to mean.  
Mr M’s policy defines a ‘pre-existing condition’ as:
‘Any disease, illness or injury for which:


you have received medication, advice or treatment, or

you have experienced symptoms
whether the condition has been diagnosed or not before you joined the policy.’ 
The moratorium exclusion of Mr M’s policy says:
‘We do not cover treatment of any pre-existing condition, or any related condition, 
if you had:

symptoms of
…
that condition in the five years before you joined the policy.’
So, regardless of when Mr M’s osteoarthritis was diagnosed, if he had symptoms of 
osteoarthritis in the five years before buying the policy, then his claim isn’t covered. The 
medical evidence suggests that Mr M had symptoms of undiagnosed osteoarthritis during 
this time. A letter from Mr M’s consultant surgeon dated 11 August 2022 says Mr M had 
been experiencing weight-bearing issues for 15 months and it was ‘very likely that it is his 
osteoarthritic hip is causing his trouble.’ A letter from Mr M’s GP dated 18 August 2022 says 
that Mr M had been experiencing pain for 15 months and that ‘the hip is the source of pain’. 
I’m therefore satisfied, based on the available medical evidence, that Mr M had a pre-
existing condition as defined above. This means his claim isn’t covered under the terms and 
conditions of his policy, and I don’t think Aviva has acted unfairly or unreasonably by turning 
down his claim. I’m sorry to disappoint Mr M, but I won’t be directing Aviva to do anything 
further. 
My final decision
My final decision is that I don’t uphold Mr M’s complaint. 
Under the rules of the Financial Ombudsman Service, I’m required to ask Mr M to accept or 
reject my decision before 9 February 2023.
 
Leah Nagle
Ombudsman

We do not cover treatment of any pre-existing condition, or any related condition, if you had:  symptoms of … that condition in the five years before you joined the policy.
very likely that it is his osteoarthritic hip is causing his trouble.

text:
DRN-3955685
The complaint
Ms B is unhappy because she says that Albany Park Limited mis-sold her an income 
protection policy.
What happened
In January 2020 Ms B took out an income protection policy. She tried to claim on the policy 
but was told that she wasn’t covered because it was a pre-existing medical condition. So, 
she says the policy was mis-sold.
Albany Park Limited said they hadn’t mis-sold the policy and they’d explained to Ms B the 
circumstances in which any pre-existing conditions wouldn’t be covered. They didn’t uphold 
Ms B’s complaint and so she made a complaint to the Financial Ombudsman Service.
Our investigator looked into what happened and upheld Ms B’s complaint. She didn’t think it 
had been made clear to Ms B that taking painkillers would affect if she could claim on the 
policy. So, she thought Albany Park should refund the premiums.
Albany Park asked an ombudsman to review the complaint. In summary, they said it had 
been made very clear that the condition wouldn’t be covered. And, they questioned whether 
medical information from Ms B’s GP would demonstrate if she’d been receiving treatment.
In February 2023 I issued a provisional decision explaining that I wasn’t intending to uphold 
this complaint. In summary, I said:
Albany Park recommended the policy to Ms B. So, the relevant rules and industry 
guidelines say that they had a responsibility to make the sure the policy was right for 
her. And, they needed to give her information about the policy which was clear, fair 
and not misleading.
I’m not intending to uphold this complaint because:

I think Albany Park took into account Ms B’s medical condition when 
recommending the policy to her. They explained to Ms B that many insurers 
don’t cover pre-existing medical conditions at all but this policy would allow 
her claim if she’d not received treatment or experienced symptoms for a 
period of two years.

I don’t think the policy was unsuitable for Ms B just because she was taking 
painkillers and she had a pre-existing medical condition. Ms B had set out her 
budget and, as the advisor explained, most insurers don’t cover pre-existing 
conditions. And, Ms B didn’t suggest that having cover for this condition was 
particularly important to her. Overall, I think the policy offered an appropriate 
level of cover at the price Ms B wanted to pay.

During one of the calls the advisor read out the information about pre-existing 
medical conditions to Ms B. That included an explanation which, I think, made 

it sufficiently clear that if she continued to experience symptoms and take 
medication then she wouldn’t be covered. And, in any event, even if the 
information wasn’t made clear during the calls, I still wouldn’t uphold Ms B’s 
complaint for the reasons I’ll go on to explain.

The advisor highlighted the importance of checking the policy documents 
carefully when she spoke to Ms B and explained there was a cooling off 
period. Ms B was sent information about the policy after the call. The ‘key 
facts’ document says:
‘It is important that you are aware that medical conditions that are likely to 
continue to need regular or periodic treatment, medication or medical advice, 
are unlikely to ever be covered by the policy’.
So, even if I thought the advice or information provided during the calls wasn’t 
clear, I think the post-sale documentation remedied any failing. If Ms B had 
any concerns on this point it was open to her to query this with Albany Park 
and cancel within the cooling off period.

Furthermore, even if I thought the policy was mis-sold, I’d also still need to be 
persuaded that Ms B wouldn’t have taken out this particular income protection 
policy. As I’ve outlined above it’s unusual for income protection insurers to 
cover pre-existing medical conditions. If they do it usually attracts a much 
higher premium. Based on the evidence I’ve been provided with I think it’s 
unlikely Ms B would have been able to source an alternative income 
protection policy, which offered cover for her pre-existing condition, within the 
budget she quoted to the advisor.
Albany Park accepted my findings. Ms B said she was going to cancel the policy and she 
wouldn’t have taken out the policy if she’d known that she couldn’t attend a GP or take a 
painkiller. She said she’d been upfront and no one with an ounce of sense would have gone 
near such a policy. 
So, I now need to make a decision.
What I’ve decided – and why
I’ve considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint.
Ms B’s further comments haven’t changed my thoughts about the outcome of this complaint.
As I outlined in my provisional decision I’m satisfied that the sales call made it sufficiently 
clear that pre-existing medical conditions, such as the condition Ms B disclosed, would not 
be covered until she’d been symptom or treatment free for a period of two years. 
And, even if I thought it wasn’t clear from the call, I think the post-sale documentation made 
it clear that medical conditions which required regular or periodic treatment were unlikely to 
ever be covered. 
I’m sorry to disappoint Ms B, and understand she’s upset that her pre-existing condition 
wasn’t covered. But I don’t think it’s fair and reasonable to uphold this complaint for the 
reasons I’ve outlined above and in my provisional decision.

My final decision
I’m not upholding this complaint.
Under the rules of the Financial Ombudsman Service, I’m required to ask Ms B to accept or 
reject my decision before 9 March 2023.
 
Anna Wilshaw
Ombudsman
quoted_clauses: It is important that you are aware that medical conditions that are likely to continue to need regular or periodic treatment, medication or medical advice, are unlikely to ever be covered by the policy

text:
DRN-3990766
The complaint
Mr B complains about how BUPA Insurance Limited dealt with a claim against his private 
medical insurance policy.  
What happened
The details of this complaint are well known to both parties, so I won’t repeat them again 
here in full. In summary, Mr B has membership of a group, private medical insurance 
policy via his employer. He made a claim against the policy in relation to surgery on his 
foot. BUPA paid the claim in part – it didn’t pay the parts of the claim relating to 
prescribed medication and crutches, both of which were for Mr B to take home.
Mr B complains that BUPA didn’t pay his claim in full. He says that BUPA didn’t inform 
him that his medication and crutches to take home wouldn’t be covered. Mr B says that 
the relevant exclusions should have been brought to his attention when BUPA gave its 
approval for the surgery. He says that if he had known about the exclusions, he would 
have considered alternatives. Mr B wants BUPA to pay the remainder of his claim. 
One of our investigators looked at what had happened. She didn’t think that BUPA had 
acted unfairly. 
Mr B didn’t agree with the investigator and there were further exchanges between him 
and the investigator, which I won’t set out here. In summary, Mr B said that a reasonable 
person would expect prescribed drugs and crutches after his surgery, so BUPA should 
have made the exclusion clear during the pre-authorisation call, rather than expect him 
to read a lengthy policy document. He says that he made several calls to BUPA which 
shows that he was diligent about ensuring his treatment was covered. Mr B says that he 
considers the exclusions unfair. 
Mr B asked that an ombudsman consider his complaint, so it was passed to me to 
decide. 
What I’ve decided – and why
I’ve considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint.

the relevant terms and conditions 
The starting point is the terms and conditions of Mr B’s membership, the relevant parts of 
which say as follows:
‘What is not covered
[…]
Exclusion Drugs and dressings for out-patient or take-home use and complementary 
and alternative products 
We do not pay for any drugs or surgical dressings provided or prescribed for out-patient 
treatment or for you to take home with you on leaving hospital or a treatment facility.
[…]’
‘Exclusion Physical aids and devices
We do not pay for supplying or fitting physical aids and devices (eg hearing aids, spectacles, 
contact lenses, crutches, walking sticks, etc).
Exception 1: We pay for prostheses and appliances as set out in Benefits 1 and 3 in the 
section ‘Benefits’.
[…]’
has the claim been handled fairly?
The relevant rules and industry guidance say that BUPA has a responsibility to handle 
claims promptly and fairly and it shouldn’t reject a claim unreasonably. I’m not upholding                
Mr B’s complaint because I don’t think that BUPA treated him unfairly or unreasonably. I say 
that because:   

Mr B is responsible for the costs he incurs in having private treatment. However, if his 
treatment is eligible treatment, BUPA pays the costs that are covered under his  
benefits and in accordance with the terms of cover. Any costs not covered under    
Mr B’s benefits are his responsibility. BUPA wouldn’t necessarily know whether Mr B 
would be discharged with medication and crutches. Those matters are between the 
treating medics and Mr B and don’t concern BUPA.

Insurance policies aren’t designed to cover every eventuality or situation. An 
insurer will decide what risks it’s willing to cover and set these out in the terms and 
conditions. It’s not the case that cover for day surgery would automatically extend 
to prescription drugs and crutches to take home. The onus is on the consumer to 
show that the claim falls under one of the agreed areas of cover within the policy. If 
the event is covered in principle but is declined on the basis of an exclusion the 
onus shifts to the insurer to show how that exclusion applies.

I’ve set out above the relevant exclusions in this case. I don’t think that those 
exclusions are unusual or onerous such that they should have been brought 
specifically to Mr B’s attention. I think that it was sufficient for BUPA to set the 
exclusions out in the terms and conditions.  

I think the exclusions I’ve set out above are clear. The exception to the exclusion in 
relation to physical aids and devices doesn’t assist Mr B here as the benefit under 
3.2.7 relates to recognised facility charges for appliances needed as part of day 
patient treatment, not physical aids and devices to take home.  

I don’t think that it was unfair or unreasonable for BUPA to rely on the exclusions in 
this case. I’m sorry to disappoint Mr B but there are no grounds on which I can 
fairly direct BUPA to pay the remainder of his claim. 

My final decision
My final decision is that I don’t uphold Mr B’s complaint.  
Under the rules of the Financial Ombudsman Service, I’m required to ask Mr B to accept or 
reject my decision before 2 May 2023.
 
Louise Povey
Ombudsman

[…]
