text:
DRN-6505271 
 
 
The complaint 
 
Mr D is unhappy that Exeter Friendly Society Limited (Exeter) applied a new claim waiting 
period and declined to pay income protection benefit for this four-week waiting period. Mr D 
says the claim should have been continued from his previous claim. 
What happened 
In October 2023, Mr D took out an income protection policy with Exeter. The policy pays, in 
certain circumstances, a monthly benefit in the event of sickness or accident and has a 
waiting period of four weeks. 
Mr D was diagnosed with gastroenteritis and was signed off work by his GP. Mr D submitted 
a claim to Exeter for income protection benefit and the claim was accepted. The benefits 
were paid until 15 May 2025. 
Later, Mr D was signed off work from 16 May 2025, for sleep apnoea and when he submitted 
a further claim, Exeter accepted this. It applied the four-week deferred period as it was 
treated a separate claim. Mr D didn’t receive a payment for these four weeks which he didn’t 
think was fair. 
Mr D made a complaint to Exeter. It maintained its position to decline a payment for the four 
weeks as the absences were for different reasons, and the claims were therefore treated 
separately. 
Unhappy, Mr D brought his complaint to this service. Our investigator didn’t uphold the 
complaint. She didn’t think it was unreasonable for Exeter to apply a waiting period to his 
claim for the sleep apnoea.  
Mr D disagreed and asked for the complaint to be referred to an ombudsman. So, it’s been 
passed to me.  
What I’ve decided – and why 
I’ve considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint. 
Regulatory rules and industry guidelines say that insurers must handle claims fairly and 
shouldn’t unreasonably reject a claim. I’ve also taken these rules into account when looking 
at this complaint. 
 
The key issue in dispute is that Mr D believes the two conditions were linked and therefore 
the four-week waiting period shouldn’t apply on his second claim for sleep apnoea.  
 
I’ve started by looking at the policy terms and conditions. This states: 
 
‘Multiple illnesses or injuries 
 

 
 
If you’ve already started a claim and suffer another illness or injury that would 
prevent you from working, then you must inform us in the timescales detailed in 
‘When do I claim?’. 
 
We will then assess this new claim in line with the process set out in the ‘How we 
assess a claim’ section. 
 
While we can’t pay any additional benefit for this new claim, should the previous 
claim come to an end, you may be eligible for benefits for this new claim with your 
waiting period applying.’ 
 
And it further states: 
 
‘If you need to claim for a different, completely unrelated illness or injury, there is no 
time limit – you can claim again immediately and your waiting period will apply again.’ 
 
Based on the above, I think the policy makes it clear that if Mr D is off work for one reason 
and then needs to make a new claim, he may be eligible for benefits for the new claim, but 
the waiting period would be applied.  
 
The information provided shows that Mr D was off work for gastroenteritis and then for sleep 
apnoea. Exeter said under the policy terms and conditions that these would be considered 
as two separate conditions and this means that a new four-week deferred period would 
apply. 
 
I’ve looked at the medical records: 
 
• 
From 3 April 2025 – Mr D was signed off work by his GP for gastroenteritis. He was 
referred to a specialist for further investigation on 16 April 2025. GP notes state that 
Mr D had ongoing nausea, gastro symptoms and awaiting a gastroenterology review.  
• 
From 16 May 2025 – Mr D was signed off work for sleep apnoea. The GP notes first 
mention sleep apnoea on 7 May 2025 and they state that Mr D was suffering from 
sleepless nights, having nightmares and waking up with fear. He was experiencing 
constant daytime drowsiness, dizziness and extreme fatigue. Mr D was referred to a 
sleep clinic. 
 
Gastroenteritis and sleep apnoea are separate conditions, and I can’t see that they are 
linked. During the first claim for gastroenteritis, the GP notes do not show that Mr D was 
suffering from sleep apnoea. The claim was based on gastroenteritis, and the claim was 
accepted on that basis. Mr D then submitted a second claim for sleep apnoea and there’s no 
mention of this before 7 May 2025 from the GP notes provided.  
 
Exeter first informed Mr D on 2 June 2025 that it’s likely that the claim for sleep apnoea 
would be treated as a new claim and the four-week waiting period will apply. Exeter also said 
it would however write to Mr D’s GP for his medical records.  
 
I can see Mr D wrote to his GP surgery on 4 June 2025, requesting for clarification to be 
provided for his insurance company which was the subject of a claim. On 9 June 2025,  
Mr D’s GP wrote that he was aware that the physical problems Mr D originally presented 
with were likely linked to this underlying issue. I’ve considered this information. However, I’m 
more persuaded that the original notes relating to the gastroenteritis and sleep apnoea carry 
more weight. Whilst the GP provided a statement, this was on the basis of Mr D  
self-reporting that the symptoms were linked and based on the request he made to the GP. I 
can’t see any medical records that confirm this. I can only see Mr D asking the GP to provide 

 
 
clarification based on what he told the surgery. And therefore, I’m more persuaded that the 
two medical issues were separate.  
 
A sleep review was conducted in August 2025. This confirmed Mr D had symptoms of sleep 
disordered breathing and a diagnosis of Obstructive Sleep Apnoea (OSA). Therapy was 
recommended and accepted by Mr D.  
 
I realise that due to the nature of Mr D’s occupation that he should not drive if feeling 
excessively sleepy and should also inform the DVLA. And as he was signed off by his GP as 
‘not fit for work’, he couldn’t legally drive. I also understand and don’t doubt that Mr D has a 
diagnosis of OSA, and it wasn’t an isolated incident but a chronic respiratory condition. But I 
don’t think this necessarily means that Exeter shouldn’t apply the four-week waiting period to 
the claim. I say this because the fit notes provided by the GP relate to two different 
conditions. Mr D was first referred to a gastroenterology clinic and then for a sleep review, 
which show that these were two separate conditions. I note that the claim for sleep apnoea 
was accepted by Exeter, and payment was agreed following the four-week deferred period. I 
think this is fair and reasonable.  
 
Having taken everything into account, I’m satisfied that Exeter has applied the terms and 
conditions of Mr D’s policy fairly and reasonably and it wasn’t unfair to apply the four-week 
waiting period to the sleep apnoea claim. I’m sorry to disappoint Mr D, but it follows that I 
don’t require Exeter to do anything further.  
 
My final decision 
For the reason given above, I don’t uphold Mr D’s complaint about Exeter Friendly Society 
Limited.  
Under the rules of the Financial Ombudsman Service, I’m required to ask Mr D to accept or 
reject my decision before 22 September 2026. 
   
Nimisha Radia 
Ombudsman

text:
K820x#13
complaint
Mr T is unhappy with a claim he made under his critical illness policy. He says Canada Life 
Limited refused to pay him the correct level of benefit in place at the time of the claim.
background
In November 2011, Mr T joined a group scheme offered by his employer. This gave him 
critical illness cover at levels based on his annual salary. The policy was set up at a value of 
three times Mr T’s salary.
In October 2013, Mr T had shoulder pain whilst overseas. He sought advice about it, and an 
investigation including an MRI scan took place. Mr T says he wasn’t told why this was 
required.
When he came back to the UK, Mr T saw his GP. This was in early December 2013. The GP 
reviewed the results from the doctor. It was felt further tests should take place.
On 12 December 2013, Mr T was referred to a specialist. This was discussed with his GP on 
18 December 2013, with the appointment occurring two days later on 20 December 2013. 
He then saw his GP again on 30 December 2013.
In the interim, Mr T increased his policy benefit with Canada Life to five times his salary. The 
annual window to amend this benefit was open until 20 December 2013. The change came 
into effect on 1 January 2014.
Mr T had a biopsy on 7 January 2014. This showed he had a type of lymphatic cancer, 
which was diagnosed shortly after.
Mr T made a claim to Canada Life. It paid the sum assured prior to the benefit increase but it 
wouldn’t pay the difference. It said a pre-existing illness clause applies. It also told Mr T in 
July 2014 that though he’d appealed, its view hadn’t changed.
The complaint was brought to this service. Our adjudicator didn’t think the complaint should 
be upheld. She said the policy terms noted how the benefit increase isn’t payable if a 
condition exists prior to the increase date.
Mr T’s diagnosis was made after the benefit increase took effect on 1 January 2014. But, our 
adjudicator said the policy wording wasn’t based on diagnosis. Mr T’s medical records 
showed he was aware of his condition before 1 January 2014. So, she felt Canada Life had 
acted fairly and reasonably in paying the sum assured prior to the increase.
Mr T disagreed. In summary, he said:

the report from abroad only showed he had an enlarged lymph gland. Mr T thought it 
was due to travel or being tired;

his UK doctors didn’t rely on the reports from abroad; they started their own tests afresh;

it is not fair for Canada Life to rely on a report from overseas that isn’t endorsed by the 
NHS;

in fact, his doctor said that the tumour might be a fat mass, or it could be malignant (and 
this was after the policy increase);
Ref: DRN0127575

2

he was only told about the mass on 7 January 2014 and if he had known before then he 
would’ve sought treatment earlier;

his diagnosis was made after the increase came into force;

until 7 January 2014, there has been no proof of anything existing; so the increase was 
made with no knowledge of any existing conditions;

we are giving the benefit of the doubt to Canada Life, when no record says the condition 
existed.
Canada Life reiterated that the evidence confirms that an abnormality actually existed as 
early as November 2013. It could therefore not pay the increased policy benefit.
Mr T asked for the complaint to be referred to an ombudsman.
my findings
I have considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what is fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint. I’m not able to uphold this complaint. I’ll 
explain why.
Mr T’s employer extended the benefits it offered its employees in October 2013. This meant 
an employee could change from a fixed payment of three times salary for critical illness to 
other multiples. So, Mr T applied for five times salary, and the start date was 
1 January 2014.
In order for me to decide if Mr T’s claim should be met, I have looked at the group policy 
wording. This says:
“No benefit will be payable under the policy in respect of:

an insured illness (or repeat of the same insured illness) which was first diagnosed, 
treated, or which was known to have existed by the insured person, prior to entry to the 
scheme or date of inclusion of the illness in the policy if earlier…

an insured illness in respect of which any related condition... existed at any time prior to 
entry to the scheme by the insured person, unless at least two consecutive years have 
elapsed since the insured person last had symptoms of, or received treatment or advice 
in respect of such related condition."
A 'related condition' is defined in the policy as:
“any previous occurrence of an insured illness and any other medical condition which, in the 
opinion of our Medical Officer, is either directly or indirectly associated with, or is likely to 
have led to, the occurrence of that insured illness.”
A further clause sets out that when a member of the scheme is changing their level of benefit 
it will be subject to the pre-existing illnesses exclusion above. It notes “where the exclusion 
described as set out in Section 4 of the Policy Conditions refers to 'prior to entry to the 
scheme' it should be read as ‘prior to the date of increase'”.
Canada Life says Mr T’s condition was known to exist at the time he sought medical advice 
overseas.
Ref: DRN0127575

3
I understand Mr T feels that anything could be ‘pre-existing’ until the cause for a health 
problem is found. But, I need to look at his circumstances against what the policy wording 
says.
Mr T has explained that he wasn’t told anything about what has turned out to be cancer by 
the doctor overseas at the end of November. But, he has said he was told he noticed a 
growth on his lymph gland and the size was not expected at his age. It was this discovery 
that led Mr T to seek advice when he got home.
The GP’s notes dated 11 December 2013 show that there had been eight health issues 
discovered from Mr T’s scan. One of these was “possibility of thymolymphoma”. The notes 
from the follow up GP appointment of 18 December 2013 say Mr T is “aware of possible 
cancer as cause for mass seen on MRI but aware needs more information”.
Finally, at a further review on 30 December 2013, the GP notes record that:
“Mediastinal mass was found on MRI… understandably wants to know whether this is 
lymphoma or not but awaiting CT scan this Friday in first instance… Discussion about things 
– support offered re possible lymphoproliferative diagnosis.”
I accept Mr T’s point that it is unfair to assume any health issue amounts to a pre-existing 
condition. But I don’t think that’s what Canada Life has done.
Mr T says he didn’t know the condition existed; rather, it was just a possibility. I don’t doubt 
that. But, the mass was known to have existed before the change in cover, even if the cause 
for that mass wasn’t. So, I’m not of the view that because Mr T’s diagnosis came after the 
increase, that this means the exclusion can’t apply. The exclusion comes into play if the 
illness was known to be present. And the GP’s medical notes show that the mass was 
present – and it was this mass that caused Mr T’s symptoms.
I am very sorry to learn of Mr T’s illness. It is incredibly unfortunate that the symptoms of the 
illness arose before the changes took place with Mr T’s flexible benefits. But, I can only 
uphold his complaint if I think Canada Life has behaved unfairly in applying its group policy 
wording. And like our adjudicator, I don’t think it has done so in respect of Mr T’s claim.
my final decision
I do not uphold this complaint, or make any award. Under the rules of the Financial 
Ombudsman Service, I am required to ask Mr T to accept or reject my decision before 
9 November 2015.
Jo Storey
ombudsman
Ref: DRN0127575

text:
K820x#11
summary of complaint
Mrs G has complained on behalf of Mr H about the decision by Ageas Insurance Limited 
(“Ageas”) to reject a personal accident claim under his travel insurance policy, saying it was 
not made clear at the point of sale that Mr H was outside the age limit for this benefit; and 
also that the accident was not due to any pre-existing medical condition.
background to complaint
Mrs G purchased an online annual multi-trip travel insurance policy, underwritten by Ageas, 
to cover Mr H. Whilst on holiday, Mr H had a fall and was badly injured. Mrs G made a claim, 
on Mr H’s behalf, for the personal accident benefit payable for permanent disability.
Ageas rejected the claim. It stated that the personal accident benefit for permanent disability 
only covered persons aged between 18 and 65. As Mr H was outside these age parameters, 
he could not claim this benefit. 
Mrs G did not agree with Ageas. She said that the age restriction was not made clear at the 
time the policy was purchased. 
The complaint was investigated by an adjudicator. He initially concluded that Ageas had 
failed to highlight the age limitation and recommended that it should meet Mr H’s claim.
Ageas disagreed with the adjudicator. It stated that, regardless of the age restriction; the 
claim was not covered because it did not meet the policy definition for an “accidental injury”.
The adjudicator reassessed the complaint. Having done so, he considered that the 
circumstances of the accident did not meet the definition of an accidental injury detailed in 
the policy. He explained to Mrs G that he agreed with Ageas that it had no liability for the 
claim.
Mrs G did not accept the adjudicator’s assessment. She provided additional evidence 
relating to the circumstances of Mr H’s accident which resulted in his injury and permanent 
disability. In her opinion, the evidence provided by Ageas was inaccurate and unreliable.
my findings
I have considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what is fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint. Having done so, I do not uphold this 
complaint.
The issue I need to decide is whether the Ageas was reasonably entitled to reject Mr H’s 
claim. 
I have considered the complaint with the utmost sympathy since it is clear that Mr H and his 
family have suffered enormous distress and inconvenience as a result of his accident.
The personal accident section of the policy states:
“What is covered
Ref: DRN0165434

2
If during the period of insurance, you suffer an accidental injury and lose 
your sight, lose a limb, become completely disabled or die within 12 months, 
directly as a result of the accident, you or your personal representatives can 
claim one of the following amounts…
(c) Permanent Total Disability (of a person aged 18 to 65) …
Premier: £50,000”.
The definitions section of the policy provides:
“Accidental injury – Injury to you resulting directly from an accident 
involving something violent and visible. This does not include sickness 
or disease, any natural condition or the result of anything that happens 
gradually.”
Ageas has disregarded the age limitation in accordance with the adjudicator’s advice. It has 
also accepted that Mr H did not have a medical condition which he failed to declare. 
Nevertheless, it is clear from Mr H’s medical records that he had experienced similar falls 
previously and had undergone extensive investigations. These indicated that he might be 
affected by a syndrome, although no firm diagnosis had been reached.
I have taken full account of the evidence provided by Mrs G, but there is nothing to indicate 
any other cause for the accident apart from Mr H’s medical history.
Given the fact that Mr H’s treating doctors have not been able to identify a separate cause 
for the accident or even to suggest an alternative explanation, I am satisfied on a balance of 
probabilities that Mr H was affected by an ongoing illness, disease or condition which was 
the direct cause of the accident.
In my judgment, as the adjudicator explained, Ageas had sufficient evidence to support its 
conclusion that the accident was covered by the exclusion in the definition of “accidental 
injury” as a “sickness or disease, any natural condition or the result of anything that happens 
gradually”. The fact that Mr H had not received any diagnosis is not relevant given the strong 
similarity of the previous incidents to the accident that occurred on this holiday.
I have also considered Mrs G’s assertion that the policy was mis-sold. She has said that it 
was not suitable for Mr H due to the age limitation. I consider it significant that the age 
limitation applied only to some of the policy benefits, such as personal accident benefits. I 
am unable to agree with her that the failure to highlight this made the policy unsuitable for Mr 
H. in my judgment, there is nothing to indicate that the policy was inappropriate and I am 
therefore satisfied that it was sold properly.
I appreciate how disappointing Mrs G and Mr H’s other family members will find my 
conclusions and I am very sorry indeed that I am unable to give them a favourable response. 
Despite having considerable sympathy for Mr H and his family, I do not consider it would be 
either fair or reasonable to require Ageas to make payment in these circumstances.
my final decision
It is my final decision that Ageas Insurance Limited was not liable to make any payment 
under the personal accident insurance benefits section of Mr H’s travel insurance policy.
Ref: DRN0165434

3
I make no award against Ageas Insurance Limited.
Reidy Flynn
ombudsman

text:
K822x
complaint
Mr L complains that ActiveQuote mis-sold an income protection insurance policy.
background 
Mr L searched for an income protection insurance policy on a price comparison website. 
ActiveQuote says that Mr L said he wanted a benefit amount of £1,400 a month, over 
12 months.
Mr L chose a policy with insurer A. It had a benefit amount of £1,150, payable until age 65, 
with a premium of £25.42 a month.
ActiveQuote then contacted Mr L by phone. It said that it “was a free advice service and 
wanted to make sure that [Mr L] had chosen the right [policy]”. Mr L said that he’d started a 
new job the month before and was previously a student. If he was off work due to sickness, 
he would receive two weeks’ full pay and two weeks’ half pay. ActiveQuote said it would try 
to find Mr L a different policy. It then contacted him and said it had found a “better” and 
cheaper policy with insurer B that it would recommend it to Mr L. It had a benefit amount of 
£1,240, payable until age 65, with a premium of £23.15.
Mr L completed a health questionnaire. The insurer then included a number of exclusions in 
the policy relating to Mr L’s pre-existing medical conditions. Mr L queried these. But 
ActiveQuote said “…although it sounds like a lot will be excluded it is purely anything relating 
to your spine injury. So for instance if you was [sic] to break your back in a car accident you 
would get a payout because it is not relating to your pre-existing condition”. Based on that, 
Mr L decided to go ahead with the policy with insurer B.
The following month, Mr L suffered an accidental injury. He made a claim under the income 
protection insurance to insurer B. The claim was initially rejected as the insurer said it was 
related to Mr L’s pre-existing medical conditions. Mr L paid for a scan and a report from a 
doctor. The insurer then accepted that the injury wasn’t related to Mr L’s pre-existing injury. 
Insurer B then paid the claim. But the benefit amount was much less than Mr L was 
expecting. That was because the benefit amount was based on Mr L’s income over the past 
12 months. As Mr L had only been in his job for around two months, he was paid a benefit 
amount of around £200 a month.
Mr L’s employment ended three months later – as he was unable to work because of his 
injury. The claim was paid until 1 December 2016, when Mr L was declared fit to work.
Mr L complains that ActiveQuote mis-sold the policy. He says it gave him incorrect 
information about the exclusions that applied to the policy. Mr L also says that the policy 
ActiveQuote recommended wasn’t suitable for him because when he made a claim the 
benefit amount was much lower than he had been led to expect.
ActiveQuote accepted that it had given Mr L “incorrect advice” about the exclusions on the 
policy. It said the correct position was that the insurer “may consider a claim if the accident 
or sickness was not connected to the pre-existing condition”. ActiveQuote also accepted that 
it should have told Mr L that the benefit amount would be based on his taxable income in the 
12 months before any claim. It said that this ought to have been explained to Mr L as he had 
told ActiveQuote that he was a student immediately before he started his job.
Ref: DRN0193133

2
To resolve the complaint ActiveQuote offered to pay Mr L £1,638. This was made up of two 
months’ premiums, one “benefit amount” of £1,240 with interest, and £250 for the cost of the 
scan.
my provisional findings
I’ve copied my provisional findings below. But because my final decision will be published, 
I’ve taken out some personal information about Mr L.
It isn’t in dispute that ActiveQuote gave Mr L incorrect information about the exclusions on 
the policy it recommended and that it didn’t tell him that the benefit amount would be based 
on his income in the previous twelve months.
exclusions
It seems unlikely that Mr L would have been able to obtain an income protection insurance 
policy that didn’t exclude claims that related to his pre-existing medical conditions. The error 
that ActiveQuote made was not properly explaining the correct position. I can see how Mr L 
would have understood that a potentially wider range of injuries would be covered if he made 
a claim than was actually the case. But, I need to decide what Mr L would have done if 
ActiveQuote had given him the correct information.
The correct information was that the insurer would consider any claim from Mr L on the facts. 
So, for example, it was possible for him to suffer an injury to his back that was completely 
unrelated to his existing injuries. But, it was also possible for him to suffer an injury to a part 
of his body other than his back, where his pre-existing injuries would be a factor.
Mr L has explained that because of a medical condition, he has” a heightened sense of fear, 
danger and doom and envisage[s] on a daily basis that something bad may happen”. He 
says this is the reason he wanted an income protection policy. Mr L has also suffered a 
previous injury where he made a successful claim on an income protection policy. In view of 
those things, I consider it is likely that Mr L would have chosen to go ahead with a policy 
recommended by ActiveQuote if it had given him the correct information about the 
exclusions.
ActiveQuote should have taken more care to ensure that it gave Mr L correct information 
about the exclusions to his policy. But I consider it is likely that Mr L would still have gone 
ahead with the policy if it had given him the correct information. So he hasn’t lost out 
because of the incorrect information ActiveQuote gave him. It will, however, have caused 
him an unnecessary amount of disappointment and worry when he later found out the 
correct position in light of his personal circumstances as highlighted above. I have taken this 
into account in my award to reflect the trouble and upset this matter has caused Mr L.
benefit amount
ActiveQuote accepts that it knew that Mr L had only been employed for around a month 
when it gave him advice and that he was previously a student. It has also accepted that it 
didn’t properly advise Mr L that the benefit amount would therefore be limited for the first 
year or so, as it was based on Mr L’s income in the 12 months before any claim was made.
I note ActiveQuote’s points about Mr L’s level of expertise. But it was the expert here – not 
Mr L. It was reasonable for Mr L to rely on the advice that ActiveQuote had given him. The 
Ref: DRN0193133

3
fact that he has had taken out a previous income protection policy and has used a price 
comparison website to obtain different quotes does not mean that he is an expert – and to 
suggest that he is would be an unusual step for a business to take. I don’t consider it would 
be fair to say that Mr L should have identified that ActiveQuote should have recommended a 
different policy or that the policy it had recommended wasn’t suitable for him.
For the avoidance of any doubt, I’m satisfied that ActiveQuote was giving Mr L advice. The 
FCA’s Insurance Conduct of Business Sourcebook sets out what ActiveQuote should do 
when giving advice on protection policies. It says that firms should:

Take reasonable care to ensure the suitability of its advice for any customer who is 
entitled to rely upon its judgement.

Establish the customer’s demands and needs using relevant information available to the 
firm and by obtaining further relevant information from the customer.

Take reasonable care to ensure a policy is suitable for the customer’s demands and 
needs, taking into account its level of cover and cost, and relevant exclusions, excesses, 
limitations and conditions.

Inform the customer of any demands and needs that are not met.
ActiveQuote recorded Mr L’s demands and needs as

He is looking to protect his income in the event of an accident and sickness.

He was happy with the benefit of £1,240.

He was happy with the four-week wait period.

He has confirmed that the premium of £23.15 a month was affordable.
ActiveQuote has accepted that it was also aware that Mr L had only been in employment for 
around a month at the time of the sale. I consider this was a relevant piece of information 
available to ActiveQuote. It ought to have taken this into account when establishing Mr L’s 
demands and needs and recommending a policy.
ActiveQuote accepts that it should have told Mr L that the level of cover would be reduced if 
he were to make a claim soon after he took the policy out. I agree that if it was 
recommending a policy that didn’t meet Mr L’s needs, it ought to have pointed this out to 
Mr L.
I don’t consider that ActiveQuote took reasonable care in recommending the policy it did. 
The benefit amount on the policy would be limited for the first year of the policy because of 
Mr L’s employment history. ActiveQuote knew that Mr L was previously a student and had 
only been employed for a short time. It ought to have taken steps to find out more about the 
consumer’s circumstances. If it had done so it would have been able to recommend a more 
suitable policy.
Based on what ActiveQuote knew about Mr L’s circumstances it shouldn’t have 
recommended this policy. Therefore ActiveQuote has recommended an insurance policy that 
Ref: DRN0193133

4
was unsuitable for Mr L. At least it ought to have told Mr L about the limitation to the benefit 
amount.
Where a business has made a mistake, our approach is to put the consumer back in the 
position they would have been in had the mistake not occurred. So I need to decide what 
ActiveQuote would have done, if it had correctly advised Mr L.
ActiveQuote says if it hadn’t advised Mr L, he would have ended up taking the unsuitable 
policy with insurer A he had chosen through the price comparison website. I don’t agree. 
Once Mr L had accepted advice from ActiveQuote it had a duty to make sure its 
recommendations were suitable. What Mr L would have done in a non-advised sale is 
irrelevant.
Mr L was contacted by ActiveQuote after he had chosen a policy. It told him that it was 
giving him advice. ActiveQuote says its process was to tell consumers that “advice was 
available”.
From the content of the phone call I can see that Mr L was happy to receive advice. And it 
was reasonable for him to understand that he was being given advice. From the initial phone 
call it was also reasonable for Mr L to understand that if ActiveQuote didn’t find another 
policy for him it would assess whether the policy he had chosen was suitable or not.
So I don’t agree with ActiveQuote that Mr L would have taken the policy he had chosen on 
the price comparison website if it had not advised him. Bearing in mind what ActiveQuote 
has told me about its business model, it appears that it would always have contacted Mr L 
after he had chosen the policy. And Mr L would have accepted advice from it.
It follows that if ActiveQuote had acted properly it could not have recommended the policy 
with insurer A that Mr L had chosen as it was unsuitable for him. If it had no policies that 
were suitable for Mr L then it should have told Mr L this. If it had done so, I consider it 
unlikely that he would have chosen to proceed with the unsuitable policy he had chosen 
himself – especially given there were other suitable policies available.
ActiveQuote says that Mr L set the search parameters with the price comparison website for 
a benefit amount of £1,400 a month and a 12 month benefit period. But Mr L initially chose a 
policy with a benefit amount of £1,150. ActiveQuote recommended a policy with a benefit 
amount of £1,240. Mr L has shown that he previously held an income protection policy with a 
lower benefit amount. And he says he was looking for policies with a benefit amount of 
£1,000.
I consider that Mr L’s needs around the benefit amount were flexible. Even if we accept that 
he searched for a policy with a benefit amount of £1,400 – Mr L’s actions show that we was 
prepared to accept a lower benefit amount. I’ve also already found that it was likely that Mr L 
would have taken some form of income protection policy because of his medical condition 
and his previous successful claim. So if he was told that the policy he’d chosen was 
unsuitable, he’d have gone on to choose another policy that would pay the full benefit 
amount straight away if he were to make a claim.
Mr L has identified a policy with another insurer called “Breathing Space policy” as a suitable 
alternative. It doesn’t require proof of income. It provides a maximum benefit amount of £250 
a week or £13,000 a year, payable for a maximum of five years, with a premium of £31.
Ref: DRN0193133

5
ActiveQuote says it only has a selection of insurers and policies on its panel – and that 
doesn’t include the Breathing Space policy, although it does offer other policies from the 
same insurer.
ActiveQuote has identified a policy with LV that is on its panel. It says this is the policy that it 
would have recommended to Mr L if it had taken account of his circumstances. The policy 
has a benefit amount of £1,005 a month, payable for two years, with a premium of £21.35. It 
appears that Mr L would only be required to show that he was receiving some form of 
income at the time he made the claim. And ActiveQuote hasn’t pointed out any other 
features or restrictions that would mean that Mr L would receive less than £1,005 a month if 
he had taken this policy.
I’ve already found that Mr L was – reasonably – relying on the advice from ActiveQuote. So if 
it had recommended the LV policy I consider it likely that Mr L would have accepted that 
recommendation. ActiveQuote should therefore put Mr L in the position he would have been 
in had he taken that policy.
ActiveQuote should pay Mr L the difference between the benefit amount he has received 
and £1,005 a month, from the date the claim was first paid up to date of settlement, with 
interest at 8% simple per year from the date each benefit amount was paid to date of 
settlement.
It’s clear that Mr L has been caused unnecessary trouble and upset because of what 
happened and in having to pursue the complaint to this extent. His income has been 
significantly lower than it would have been had ActiveQuote recommended a suitable policy 
for him in the first place. I also recognise how difficult it must have been for him to support 
his family during this time. Mr L has also explained how he’s been affected by this matter 
and the stress it has caused him. After carefully reviewing what has happened I consider it 
would be fair for ActiveQuote to pay Mr L £900 to reflect the trouble and upset it caused him.
responses to my provisional decision
ActiveQuote said that it was happy to agree to my provisional findings to bring this matter to 
the close. It said the amount due to Mr L was £2,930.25 – and it questioned whether the 
monthly premiums should be deducted from that amount.
Mr L accepted my provisional findings – but he didn’t agree with ActiveQuote’s calculation. 
He said that he should receive £4,109 for the difference in payments, taking into account the 
payment he’d already received.
my findings
I’ve considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint. Having done so – and as both sides have 
accepted my provisional findings – I see no reason to depart from the conclusions I reached 
in my provisional decision.
I understand that ActiveQuote has been sent the evidence showing the payments made by 
insurer A to Mr L – it’s not clear if we have everything we need to calculate the redress. 
ActiveQuote should check with Mr L and/or insurer A if it feels it needs any more information. 
Ref: DRN0193133

6
Mr L has provided evidence that the claim was paid from after 11 April until 
2 December 2016.
Mr L has confirmed that he’s received £1,638 in compensation already from ActiveQuote. 
That was paid soon after Mr L received the first benefit amount – and it effectively made up 
the difference in payments for the first 67 days of the benefit period. So Mr L hasn’t been 
deprived of money during that period. Therefore ActiveQuote should only be required to pay 
interest on the difference from 18 June 2016.
my final decision
My final decision is that I uphold this complaint. ActiveQuote Limited should within 28 days of 
this decision:

Pay Mr L the difference between the total benefit amount he has received from insurer A 
and £1,005 a month from the date the claim was paid was made up to 2 December 
2106.

Pay interest on the difference in payments at 8% simple per year from the date each 
payment on or after 18 June 2016 was made up to date of settlement.

Pay Mr L £900 to reflect the trouble and upset this matter has caused him.
ActiveQuote can deduct £1,638 it has already paid to Mr L from the total amount.
Under the rules of the Financial Ombudsman Service, I’m required to ask Mr L to accept or 
reject my decision before 24 March 2017.
Ken Rose
ombudsman
Ref: DRN0193133

text:
K820x#11
complaint
Mrs A’s complaint concerns AXA PPP Healthcare Limited’s decision to decline her claim for 
investigations under her private medical insurance policy as they are linked to a pre-existing 
condition.
background
Mrs A previously held a group private medical insurance policy through her employer which 
ceased at the end of November 2013. Her current policy was taken out as a replacement 
and started on 12 December 2013.
Mrs A submitted a claim under the policy for the investigation of heavy and continuous 
premenstrual bleeding in March 2014. The claim was declined because the bleeding was 
recorded in Mrs A’s medical records as occurring as far back as September 2013, which was 
prior to the start of the policy and was therefore pre-existing as defined by the policy.
Mrs A did not agree with AXA’s conclusions and submitted her complaint to the Financial 
Ombudsman Service for further consideration.
Our adjudicator did not recommend that the complaint be upheld. She explained that Mrs A’s 
policy contained a moratorium clause which meant that pre-existing symptoms were not 
covered until two years after the start of the policy. She noted that Mrs A’s medical records 
confirmed that her symptoms had been ongoing since September 2013 and therefore fell 
outside the scope of cover.
Our adjudicator also concluded that the moratorium clause was clearly explained to Mrs A 
when the policy was taken out and noted that Mrs A was given the opportunity to take out 
continuous cover on a medical history disregarded basis, but chose not to due to the cost.
Mrs A disagreed with the adjudicator’s findings. She explained that the symptoms she had 
experienced prior to the start of the policy were not of a severity which would have led her to 
undergo investigations – if they had been she would have had them investigated under her 
previous policy. Mrs A also said that she was only without cover for 12 days and that she 
was led to believe the replacement cover she had taken was to be on the same terms as her 
existing cover.
As no agreement has been reached the matter has been referred to me to review afresh.
my findings
I have considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what is fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances. Having done so, and although I am aware that Mrs A will 
be disappointed by my decision, I do not uphold her complaint. I will explain why.
The policy that Mrs A took out in December 2013 contained the following clause:
“We will provide cover for treatment of medical conditions that arise after you join. However, 
in the first two years of cover there is no cover for the treatment of pre-existing medical 
conditions…”
The policy defines pre-existing medical condition definition as:
Ref: DRN0202159

2
“any disease, illness or injury for which:
• you have received medication, advice or treatment; or
• you have experienced symptoms;
whether the condition has been diagnosed or not in the five years before the start of your 
cover.”
I accept that Mrs A had cover before this policy commenced under which she could have 
claimed for this condition. However she did not do so as at that time as she did not consider 
the symptoms were severe. Indeed, she did not consider that she had a condition. This 
being so I can understand why she is aggrieved that her policy now does not offer cover.
Nevertheless the medical evidence demonstrates that Mrs A had experienced symptoms as 
far back as September 2013. Her GP referral to the specialist dated 3 March 2014 reports 
“an almost constant period during the previous five months … interrupted by breaks of 
approximately one week.” Although Mrs A did not consider that the change to her monthly 
cycle was abnormal for her woman of her age, I am satisfied it was a symptom of the 
condition with which she was subsequently diagnosed. Accordingly I am satisfied that her 
condition can reasonably be described as pre-existing as per the policy definition.
Mrs A suggests that if her claim is not covered by the policy then it was mis-sold to her. 
However she selected a moratorium based contract as opposed to one which covered her 
history. She said at the time of the sale that continuous cover was “far too expensive”. The 
adviser did explain the effect of the moratorium clause, and this together with the definition 
of a pre-existing condition is set out in the policy documentation. In the circumstances 
I cannot conclude that the policy was mis-sold.
my final decision
My final decision is that I do not uphold this complaint. I make no award against AXA PPP 
Healthcare Limited.
Lindsey Woloski
ombudsman
Ref: DRN0202159

text:
K820x#14
complaint
Mr M has complained that Allianz Insurance Plc has unfairly refused to pay him the total 
disablement benefit under the personal accident section of his Aon Contractor policy.
background
Mr M was involved in a road traffic accident and suffered a whiplash injury. Mr M made a 
claim on his policy and Allianz paid him temporary total disablement benefit for two years. 
He asked it to pay the lump sum benefit for total permanent disablement benefit but it said 
the medical evidence didn’t show that his permanent disablement solely arose from his 
accident. Rather it arose from a worsening of his pre-existing condition.
Mr M then brought his complaint to us. The adjudicator who investigated it didn’t think Allianz 
had done anything wrong in refusing to pay him the total permanent disablement benefit, as 
the medical evidence didn’t support this. Mr M felt that as his GP said he was permanently 
disabled, Allianz should pay this benefit. So his complaint has been passed to me to decide.
my findings
I’ve considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint.
In order to trigger the payment of the total permanent disablement lump sum benefit, Mr M 
needs to show his total and permanent disablement came about solely as a result of 
accidental bodily injury. His policy excludes any payment of this benefit, if his ‘disablement is 
contributed to by sickness or disease or any naturally occurring conditions or gradually 
operating cause’. I don’t think this type of limitation or exclusion is unusual or unfair as the 
benefit is only payable for accidental bodily injury as defined by Mr M’s policy.
Allianz initially accepted Mr M’s claim for temporary total disablement. After a year, it asked 
for Mr M to be examined by a medical consultant. That consultant said in 2016 following an 
MRI scan almost a year later, that unfortunately Mr M was suffering from the effects of 
degenerative changes in his neck and spine, which happened prior to his accident. He felt 
consequently, that Mr M’s present difficulties weren’t accident related.
In the meantime, Mr M also obtained his own medical report from a consultant. That 
consultant said in November 2015, that Mr M would have recovered from the effects of his 
whiplash around 25 months after his accident. But he felt if Mr M still had pain after that, it 
would be due to ‘his pre-existing condition of retrolisthesis of his cervical spine.’ He also felt 
at the date of his examination that Mr M had fully recovered from his accident and wasn’t in 
pain that day.
Given both of these expert’s medical reports, it’s clear to me that both doctors felt that if 
Mr M had continuing problems two years after his accident, that would be because of his 
pre-existing condition rather than the effects of his accident. So I think there’s no evidence to 
show that Mr M’s continuing problems are accident related. I do understand that Mr M’s GP 
says he can’t work presently due to the injuries from his accident. But given the expertise of 
both these specialists, and the fact they say the same thing, I think it’s more likely 
Mr M’s continuing problems are due to degenerative issues that aren’t connected to the 
injuries he sustained from his accident.
Ref: DRN0240797

2
On that basis and I appreciate this will disappoint Mr M, I don’t think Allianz did anything 
wrong in refusing to pay Mr M the permanent total disablement lump sum benefit under his 
policy.
my final decision
For the reasons I’ve discussed above, it’s my final decision that I don’t uphold this complaint.
Under the rules of the Financial Ombudsman Service, I’m required to ask Mr M to accept or 
reject my decision before 29 July 2016.
Rona Doyle
ombudsman
Ref: DRN0240797

text:
K820x#9
summary of complaint
This complaint concerns Canada Life’s decision to decline Mr Y’s claim for benefit under a 
group critical illness insurance policy. 
background to complaint
Mr Y joined his employer’s group critical illness insurance scheme in 2007. With effect from 
1 June 2011, Canada Life amended the terms of the employer’s policy so that it covered 
certain new illnesses, including “Loss of Independent Existence”, which was payable in the 
following circumstances:
“Total, permanent and irreversible disablement resulting in the inability to perform, 
even with the use of appropriate assistive devices, at least three of the following six 
‘activities of daily living’ without the direct assistance of another person”. 
The “activities of daily living” consisted of feeding/eating, dressing, bathing/grooming, 
continence, mobility and transfer (ie moving from one room to another).
Mr Y made a claim for loss of independence existence in August 2011. He said he had been 
diagnosed with diabetic neuropathy, cheiroarthropathy and osteoarthritis, and the symptoms 
of these conditions had prevented him from performing the activities of daily living without 
assistance from 1 March 2011. 
Canada Life declined the claim with reference to the policy exclusion for “Pre-existing 
conditions”:
“No benefit will be payable under the Policy in respect of:

an insured illness (or a repeat of the same insured illness) which was first
diagnosed, treated, or which was known to have existed by the insured person,
prior to entry to the scheme or date of inclusion of the illness in the Policy if later”.
Mr Y said he was not diagnosed with diabetic neuropathy until July 2011, or with 
cheiroarthropathy and osteoarthritis until November 2011. He also sent an amended claim 
form, stating he had been unable to independently perform the activities since August 2011.
DRN0315643

2
Canada Life agreed to assess the claim. However, the medical evidence it obtained did not, 
in its opinion, show that the loss of independent existence requirements had been met. 
Mr Y’s medical records also showed he had suffered with type 1 diabetes since childhood. 
Canada Life said his diabetic neuropathy, was clearly related to his diabetes and so it was 
entitled to decline the claim on the grounds that any disability was caused by a pre-existing 
condition. The relevant policy term said:
“No benefit will be payable under the Policy in respect of:

an insured illness in respect of which any related condition (as defined on page 
11 of this Policy and further detailed in this section) existed at any time prior to 
entry to the scheme by the insured person, unless at least two consecutive years 
have elapsed since the person last:
- had symptoms of; or
- received treatment or advice in respect of such related condition”. 
Mr Y was unhappy with this outcome and referred the matter to our service. Our adjudicator 
did not recommend that it should be upheld. She was not persuaded that the qualifying 
criteria for loss of independent existence had been met. She was also satisfied that Canada 
Life was entitled to categorise Mr Y’s diabetes as a pre-existing condition related to his 
diabetic neuropathy, which in turn was the cause of any disability. 
Mr Y did not accept the adjudicator’s assessment of the complaint. In summary, he said:

he was not diagnosed with diabetic neuropathy until July 2011, which was after the 
policy was amended to include loss of independent existence

diabetes should not be treated as a “related” pre-existing condition as it is not 
specifically listed in the policy, and the Association of British Insurers (“ABI”) requires 
insurers to provide exhaustive lists of covered / excluded illnesses

Canada Life cannot rely on the “related condition” clause, as he had been a member 
of the scheme for more than two years without any symptoms of diabetic neuropathy 
or osteoarthritis 

the available medical evidence confirms that he is unable to independently perform 
the activities of daily living due to osteoarthritis

there are no ongoing treatment options available to him, so Canada Life should 
accept his disabilities are permanent and irreversible 
my findings
I have considered everything that Mr Y and Canada Life have provided, in order to decide 
upon a fair and reasonable outcome to this dispute. 
The main issue for me to decide is whether it was reasonable for Canada Life to decline 
Mr Y’s claim for critical illness benefit. Having carefully considered the available evidence, I 
am satisfied Canada Life’s decision was fair and reasonable. I will explain why. 

3
Although diabetic neuropathy was not diagnosed until July 2011, after the policy changed to 
cover loss of independent existence, the available medical evidence – and Mr Y’s initial 
claim forms in August 2011 – indicated that he first sought treatment for symptoms of his 
illnesses in March 2011. This was before loss of independent existence cover was added to 
the policy. Despite this, Canada Life agreed to assess the claim on the basis of Mr Y’s later 
claim that the symptoms began in August 2011. 
In my judgement, Canada Life was entitled to classify Mr Y’s longstanding diabetes as 
“related” to his diabetic neuropathy and cheiroarthropathy. It is not disputed that there is a 
clear link between these conditions. The policy defined “Related condition” as:
“any medical condition which, in the opinion of our Medical Officer(s), is:

either directly or indirectly associated with; or

is likely to have led to 
the occurrence of an insured illness”. 
On 7 December 2011, Mr Y’s treating Consultant Physician wrote a letter confirming that:
“Mr (Y) has had Type 1 diabetes for 46 years and is currently managed on a 
continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion device. Throughout the entire time of his 
diabetes he has strived to achieve next to perfect glycaemic control however due to 
its duration is now suffering from significant diabetic neuropathy.”
The same Consultant confirmed the following on 26 January 2012:
“You have also seen Rheumatologists who agree you have also got 
cheiroarthropathy which is a diabetes related condition…”  
In my view, this shows that Mr Y’s diabetic neuropathy and cheiroarthropathy can 
reasonably be described as being “directly or indirectly associated with” his diabetes. It 
appears that his diabetes “is likely to have led to” these two conditions. 
  
I note Mr Y says that diabetes is not listed specifically in the policy as an excluded condition.  
The policy says that illnesses which are “related” to pre-existing medical conditions will not 
be covered unless “…at least two consecutive years have elapsed since the person 
last…had symptoms of…or received treatment or advice in respect of such related 
condition”. Therefore, in order for Canada Life to consider a claim for loss of independent 
existence due to diabetic neuropathy, it would need to be shown that Mr Y had received no 
treatment for (or suffered no symptoms of) diabetes for two consecutive years since he 
joined the scheme in 2007. 
Following her meeting with Mr Y on 21 November 2011, the nurse instructed by Canada Life 
confirmed that his diabetes had been controlled by insulin for almost 50 years; and the mode 
of insulin delivery had changed to a “continuous pump” ten years previously. Taking this into 
account, I do not consider that two consecutive years elapsed between 2007 and 2011 when 
Mr Y did not receive any treatment for diabetes. 

4
Overall, therefore, I am satisfied Mr Y is unable to claim for loss of independent existence 
arising from his diabetic neuropathy or cheiroarthropathy due to the “related” pre-existing 
condition clause.    
I note Mr Y has mentioned ABI guidelines on critical illness policies. Those guidelines do not 
prevent Canada Life from excluding conditions where the insured person was suffering with 
the insured condition, or a related one, before the policy started. I think the policy terms are 
clear that Canada Life will exclude conditions from cover where the insured person has 
suffered from them, or related conditions, before cover starts.
To my mind, the weight of the evidence suggests that Mr Y’s disabling symptoms were 
caused by a combination of his osteoarthritis, diabetic neuropathy and cheiroarthropathy. 
The report of Mr Y’s occupational therapist dated 13 August 2012 stated that his diabetic 
neuropathy caused “…pain on minimal exertion; constant burning in his legs; and sensory 
changes with reduced dexterity in his hands”. This report also said his cheiroarthropathy 
prevented him from being able to fully straighten his fingers or produce an efficient grip in his 
right (non-dominant) hand. Furthermore, the occupational therapist’s most recent report in 
January 2013 confirmed that Mr Y has “neuropathic pain in his hands and feet from diabetic 
neuropathy”.  
However, even if I were to accept that Mr Y’s disabling symptoms were caused by 
osteoarthritis alone, the occupational therapist’s report in January 2013 suggested he was 
able to perform four of the six activities of daily living (feeding/eating, continence, mobility 
and transfer) with the use of assistive devices – a number of which have been provided to 
Mr Y and fitted to his property.   
I accept Mr Y’s osteoarthritis may be permanent and irreversible, as required by the policy in 
order for loss of independent existence benefit to be payable. However, the policy also 
states that the claimant must be totally unable to independently perform at least three of the 
six activities of daily living “even with the use of appropriate assistive devices”. On the basis 
of the available medical evidence, I am not satisfied this requirement has been satisfied yet.  
In all the circumstances, I consider that Canada Life’s decision to decline the claim was 
made in accordance with the terms and conditions of the policy, and was neither unfair nor 
unreasonable. However, if Mr Y’s condition should deteriorate to the extent that he is unable 
to independently perform three of the six activities of daily living due to osteoarthritis alone, 
he can, of course, make a new claim to Canada Life for its consideration. 
my decision
My final decision is that I do not uphold this complaint. I make no award against Canada Life.
Greg Barham
ombudsman
