text:
K821x#15
complaint
Mr H complains that Unum Ltd refused a claim made under his employer’s group income 
protection scheme. 
background
Mr H is a member’s of his employer’s group income protection scheme. The aim of this was 
to pay benefit after a waiting period of 13 weeks if Mr H couldn’t work because of illness or 
injury. 
In 2014, Mr H was diagnosed with liver cirrhosis. He continued working, but on reduced 
hours. Then in April 2015, he felt too unwell to continue and so stopped working completely. 
The policy says that if Unum isn’t notified of a claim within 90 days of the end of the waiting 
period, it has no liability for the claim. Mr H’s employer notified Unum of the claim, but did so 
a few days outside of the 90 days notification period. Because of this, Unum thinks it has 
been prejudiced and has been unable to assess the claim properly. It declined the claim for 
this reason. But in any event, it didn’t think the available evidence supported that Mr H was 
unable to continue working in April 2015. Unhappy with this, Mr H brought a complaint to this 
service. 
Our adjudicator recommended the complaint be upheld. She didn’t think Unum had been 
prejudiced from assessing the claim. She thought the evidence supported that Mr H has a 
very serious illness which has reduced his life expectancy, and that his symptoms prevented 
him from doing his job. She recommended Unum accept the claim, and also pay £300 for 
the trouble and upset caused to Mr H. 
Unum didn’t agree with the adjudicator’s recommendations, so the matter’s been passed to 
me. 
my findings
I’ve considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint. 
For benefit to be payable, Mr H must be unable because of illness or injury, to carry out the 
material and substantial duties of his occupation throughout the 13 week waiting period. 
Mr H worked as a general manager in an office based role. 
Unum thinks it’s been prejudiced from assessing the claim properly, because Mr H’s 
employer notified it of the claim outside the 90 day period specified in the policy. Like the 
adjudicator, I don’t think Unum has been prejudiced as a result of this late notification. Mr H 
was under the care of his GP and a treating consultant throughout the waiting period, and 
I’m satisfied Unum was able to establish which symptoms Mr H had during this time, and 
how they impacted on his ability to work. 
I’ve therefore considered all the evidence, in order to decide whether or not Mr H was unable 
to continue his occupation from April 2015, and throughout the 13 week waiting period.
Unum says Mr H was diagnosed with his condition in 2014 and it has been unable to 
establish a medical reason for him stopping work in April 2015. It points out that tests 
Ref: DRN0906249

2
showed Mr H’s liver disease hadn’t deteriorated, and also that his treating consultant thought 
in March 2015 that Mr H’s outlook was generally very good. 
Mr H says that since being diagnosed with his condition he experiences increased fatigue 
and coughs up more blood. He also says he feels generally unwell. He explains that he 
continued working until April 2015 as he didn’t want to let his company down and kept 
working out of a sense of duty. But unfortunately he got progressively more tired and 
weaker, until he felt he couldn’t work anymore. 
I’ve looked at Mr H’s GP records and I see that in November 2014, it was noted he was 
managing to cope at work with reduced hours. In December 2014, he was generally doing 
well with his diagnosis. In January 2015, he was still doing well and was asymptomatic. But 
then in March 2015, it was noted he felt things had gone backwards over previous two 
weeks, as he had a recurrent feeling of lacking energy, and weakness. In April 2015, he 
continued to feel very tired, dizzy at times, and had difficulty coping with work and his illness. 
His GP notes continued to report that he was experiencing tiredness in May and June 2015.
Mr H’s GP referred him to Dr V, a consultant. In the referral, the GP said that after 
commencing medical treatment, Mr H’s symptoms initially improved, but he’d recently felt 
worse and had severe fatigue with exertional breathlessness, as well of flecks of blood in his 
saliva. The GP had doubled the dose of one of his medications.
In June 2015, Mr H was seen by Dr V. He said Mr H’s symptoms were of increasing 
tiredness, and noted he’d stopped work because of that. Dr V said the recent increase to his 
medication needed to be reduced again. 
In February 2016, Dr P (a consultant gastroenterologist) explained that Mr H had been 
diagnosed with liver cirrhosis, and said that the stage of liver cirrhosis and the medication 
Mr H takes will induce a degree of lethargy and also difficulties carrying out technical tasks. 
Dr P explained that liver cirrhosis is an end stage liver disease and once present, overall life 
expectancy is significantly reduced. He said Mr H’s laboratory tests were within normal 
parameters, and that his MELD (model for end stage liver disease) score estimated a 
mortality of around 6% within three months.
In May 2016, Dr M, an occupation health physician, met with Mr H. He said Mr H had initially 
reduced his hours because of tiredness, but then completely stopped work as he felt too 
unwell to continue. Dr M said Mr H experiences fatigue, lack of energy and difficulty getting 
up in the morning – and that these symptoms hadn’t changed since he stopped work. And 
that “Mr [H] suffers from a life long condition that is likely to deteriorate with time and a 
reduced life expectancy. He is not fit to return to work at present and it is highly unlikely that 
this situation will improve ever.” 
Overall, whilst I appreciate Mr H’s liver disease apparently hadn’t deteriorated when he 
stopped work, it’s still the case that he had the disease and it caused him extreme tiredness. 
Unum accepts that liver disease (and medication) can cause this fatigue, but says it is 
unclear what changed in April 2015 that meant Mr H had to stop working at this time. But I 
don’t think there necessarily needs to be evidence of a change in his condition to explain his 
extreme tiredness. His GP has said that the medication initially improved his symptoms (the 
GP notes also support this), but then he felt worse and experienced extreme fatigue and 
weakness. Because of that, he didn’t feel able to continue working anymore.  
Ref: DRN0906249

3
Mr H’s symptoms have been accepted by all his medical practitioners. I can’t see that Unum 
has asked any of Mr H’s treating specialists if his symptoms prevented him from working, 
which is unfortunate. But taking into account all the evidence, I think that on balance, it is 
likely Mr H’s extreme tiredness would have prevented him from carrying out the material and 
substantial duties of his role (when he stopped work in April 2015, and throughout the 13 
week waiting period). Because of this, I think Unum should’ve accepted the claim. 
I agree with the adjudicator that Mr H has been caused inconvenience by Unum’s decision to 
decline his claim. I think £300 compensation would be reasonable in the circumstances. 
my final decision
My final decision is that I uphold this complaint.
I require Unum Ltd to pay the claim from the end of the waiting period. Interest should be 
added at the rate of 8% simple per annum from the date each payment was due to the date 
of settlement.
If Unum Ltd considers that it’s required by HM Revenue & Customs to take off income tax 
from the interest, it should tell Mr H how much it’s taken off. It should also give Mr H a 
certificate showing this if he asks for one, so he can reclaim the tax from HM Revenue & 
Customs if appropriate. 
I also require Unum Ltd to pay Mr H £300 compensation directly.
Under the rules of the Financial Ombudsman Service, I’m required to ask Mr H to accept or 
reject my decision before 20 April 2017.
Chantelle Hurn-Ryan
ombudsman
Ref: DRN0906249
quoted_clauses: Mr [H] suffers from a life long condition that is likely to deteriorate with time and a reduced life expectancy. He is not fit to return to work at present and it is highly unlikely that this situation will improve ever.

text:
K820x#14
complaint
Mr M has complained that Unum Ltd refused to pay his claim for income protection under his 
employer’s group scheme policy.
background
Mr M was employed as a process operator by his employer L. L provided a Unum group 
income protection policy for its employees. This provided a benefit to an employee if they 
were unable to work due to illness or injury for a maximum of two years.  But first they had to 
have been unable to work for 26 weeks, commonly called the ‘waiting period’.
Mr M first became absent from work due to testicular pain on 9 February 2015. He was 
treated for that but in March 2015 Mr M’s GP issued a further medical certificate saying his 
continued absence from work was due to atrial fibrillation. After this Mr M saw his 
cardiologist, who said Mr M had been well since his visit to A&E although he still said he was 
tired. A review was planned for six months after this. Then in July 2015 Mr M had problems 
with his legs and back.
Mr M’s waiting period finished on 10 August 2015 and L submitted a claim to Unum. Unum 
said the medical evidence didn’t show that Mr M’s claim met the policy conditions so it 
refused to pay the claim. L appealed but Unum continued to believe the claim didn’t meet the 
policy conditions.
As a result, L terminated Mr M’s employment from December 2015. This meant Mr M had to 
take his pension early in order to have some income, which also meant his pension 
payments have been significantly reduced.
Mr M then brought his complaint to us. The adjudicator who investigated it thought Unum 
should pay his claim. Unum disagreed and Mr M’s complaint was passed to me to decide.
I issued a provisional decision on 5 July 2016.  I said that in order for Mr M’s claim to be 
valid, he must show that he is ‘unable by reason of his illness or injury to perform the 
material and substantive duties of his insured occupation.’ Benefit will be paid if the member 
is so incapacitated, was actively at work prior to the incapacity, hasn’t reached the terminal 
age and crucially in Mr M’s case was incapacitated throughout the entire ‘waiting period’.
It was clear Mr M’s initial problem, which caused him to first go off sick was due to an 
infection which cleared up in a couple of weeks following treatment. But I didn’t think the 
evidence from Mr M’s GP about his atrial fibrillation adequately showed that it stopped him 
from doing his job after that. This was because investigations carried out showed him to be 
normal and he wasn’t to be monitored except at six monthly intervals. It also appeared his 
GP only ordered a non-urgent cardiac referral. Additionally further tests showed Mr M’s 
cardiac function to be normal. So I didn’t think the evidence showed Mr M’s medical 
condition met the definition in the policy during the whole of the ‘waiting period’.
 As a result, I didn’t think Unum had done anything wrong in refusing to pay his claim. Unum 
agreed with my provisional decision. But Mr M did not. 
He sent me a letter from his GP. His GP explained that what I had thought was a non-urgent 
cardiac follow up was actually a routine expedite letter to bring an appointment due in 
Ref: DRN1135113

2
November forward. His GP then went on to discuss how Mr M is now, explaining that he’s 
waiting for an operation. He also enclosed a letter from his consultant, which discussed 
Mr M’s present problems, which are described as quite troublesome and also confirmed he 
needs the operation.
my findings
I’ve again considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint.
Unfortunately I don’t think this further evidence from Mr M’s GP and consultant shows or 
describes what Mr M’s condition was like during the ‘waiting period’ from February 2015 to 
August 2015. Mr M had been diagnosed with atrial fibrillation since 2012 and had worked 
with it up to February 2015.
I do appreciate that his GP explained that he was bringing an appointment forward rather 
than just asking for a routine one, but the rest of the evidence about Mr M’s atrial fibrillation 
doesn’t show it to be as troublesome to him as it is now. Crucially I don’t think it shows Mr M 
was incapacitated as defined in the policy from doing his job during the ‘waiting period’.
Mr M visited A&E in May 2015 and his cardiologist said afterwards that he had been well 
since his visit to A&E, although he could be tired. Prior to that, tests in April were normal. 
Further tests were done in August just at the end of the ‘waiting period’ were also normal. 
There is some evidence in July 2015, which mentions needing to get it under control but I 
don’t see evidence that shows Mr M was unable to do his job throughout the ‘waiting period’.
Therefore I don’t think Unum did anything wrong in refusing to pay his claim on the basis that 
the evidence doesn’t show him to have been incapacitated as defined in the policy 
throughout the ‘waiting period’.
my final decision
So whilst I do very much understand how much my decision will disappoint Mr M, it’s my 
final decision that I don’t uphold this complaint.
Under the rules of the Financial Ombudsman Service, I’m required to ask Mr M to accept or 
reject my decision before 25 August 2016.
Rona Doyle
ombudsman
Ref: DRN1135113
quoted_clauses: unable by reason of his illness or injury to perform the material and substantive duties of his insured occupation.

text:
K820x#9
summary of complaint
This complaint arises because Mr M is dissatisfied that Great Lakes Reinsurance (UK) Plc 
(“Great Lakes”) has declined his claim for permanent total disablement under a personal 
accident policy (“the policy”).
background to complaint
Mr M took out the policy in August 2007. The policy provided benefit in the event that a 
policyholder suffered death or a specified bodily injury or disability as a result of an accident. 
In September 2010, Mr M submitted a claim to Great Lakes, on the grounds that he had 
injured his back and shoulder whilst helping a work colleague lift a heavy item on 1 October 
2009 and that this had left him permanently and totally disabled .
As part of its assessment of the claim, Great Lakes made enquiries with Mr M’s employer at 
the time of the accident. It also arranged for Mr M to undergo an independent medical 
examination (“IME”) with a consultant orthopaedic surgeon. In August 2011, it declined the 
claim on the grounds that Mr M had not satisfactorily proven that he had suffered an 
accident. Instead, it was of the view that his disability was the result of a pre-existing 
degenerative condition.
Mr M appealed the decision but Great Lakes maintained its position. Mr M remained 
dissatisfied and therefore referred the matter to this service.
The adjudicator who considered the complaint was of the opinion that Mr M had not 
adequately demonstrated that he had suffered an accident resulting in bodily injury. The 
adjudicator further considered that, even if Mr M had suffered an accident, it was not the sole 
cause of his disability and thus any benefit payment would have to be reduced accordingly. 
However, given the lack of proof that an accident resulting in bodily injury had taken place, 
the adjudicator did not recommend that the complaint be upheld.
Mr M did not accept the adjudicator’s opinion. The matter has therefore been passed to me 
to review.
my findings
I have included only a brief summary of the complaint but I have considered all the available 
evidence and arguments from the outset, in order to decide what is fair and reasonable in 
the circumstances of this complaint. Having done so, and while I recognise that this will 
come as a deep disappointment to Mr M, I am not persuaded to uphold this complaint. Let 
me explain why.
The policy states:
“We will pay you the appropriate benefit if, during any period of insurance, an insured 
person sustains a bodily injury which, within 52 weeks, is the only cause of death, 
permanent total disablement, permanent disability, fractures, burns or 
hospitalisation”.
Ref: DRN1565649

2
The policy defines bodily injury as:
“A bodily injury which is the direct result of an accidental, external, violent and visible 
cause, including accidental injury as a result of being exposed to the elements. This 
does not include an injury caused by sickness, disease or any naturally occurring 
condition or process.”
It follows that if Mr M cannot demonstrate that he suffered an accident resulting in bodily 
injury, his complaint should not be upheld.
The first documentary evidence relating to Mr M’s accident is the entry, completed by Mr M, 
in his (now former) employer’s accident book dated 15 October 2009, two weeks after the 
accident had apparently taken place. Mr M did not see his general practitioner (“GP”) about 
his injury until 26 October 2009. The GP’s record of the consultation states:
“Low back pain … Picking up things at work and went 2 weeks ago”.
Mr M has continued to report to other medical specialists that his injury was as a result of the 
accident on 1 October 2009.
Mr M has explained that the reason for the delay in seeing a GP was because he had no GP 
at the time and therefore first needed to register with one. He says that he was in pain 
immediately following the accident; that he mentioned it to colleagues at the time; that he 
needed time off work; and that he has witnesses to this effect.
Mr M’s version of events, however, is disputed by his former employer. It says that Mr M did 
not say anything at the time about the accident and that the first it heard about it was on 20 
October 2009 while it was seeking to take disciplinary action against Mr M over a separate 
matter. It says it has witnesses to challenge Mr M’s account.
The medical evidence is inconclusive as to whether Mr M has suffered an accident. None of 
the medical experts who have examined Mr M has challenged his account that his 
disablement stemmed from an accident but neither has any of them said that he must have 
suffered an accident to be in his condition. For example, the consultant orthopaedic surgeon 
who carried out the IME stated:
“Had there been a major injury to the cervical or lumbar discs caused by the accident 
in October 2009, I would have expected an immediate onset of severe symptoms 
rather than a gradual progression of symptoms which appear to have taken place. 
Nonetheless, the precipitating factor for his present symptom complex (based upon the 
history that was given to me by Mr M) relates specifically to the accident in October 2009. In 
the absence of evidence to the contrary I have accepted the view that the accident precipitated 
his symptoms.”
There does appear to be a consensus that his disability is due, at least in part, to a pre-
existing medical condition. For example, in November 2010, his GP stated 
 ”I have to report that he had an MRI scan of his spine in February 2010, which did 
show evidence of degenerative disc disease in his lower thoracic and lower lumbar 
vertebrae. These changes would have taken some time to develop and I have to say that some 
of the changes would certainly have existed before October 2009.”
Ref: DRN1565649

3
I consider that there are significant differences in the accounts put forward by Mr M and his 
former employer concerning the events of 1 October 2009 and the days thereafter. In view of 
this, and the relative lack of either contemporaneous documentary evidence or medical 
evidence to support Mr M’s version of events, I do not feel able to say that, on the balance of 
probability, Mr M suffered an accident resulting in bodily injury in the way he describes.
It may be that, in view of the dispute over events, this is perhaps a matter that is better 
suited to a court of law, where witnesses can be cross examined, rather than the informal 
nature of our service. I note that Mr M is currently pursing a legal claim against his former 
employer for industrial injury arising from the alleged accident. Should Mr M succeed in his 
legal action against his former employer, he could use this as material new evidence and re-
submit his claim to Great Lakes.
I should stress that I have not upheld Mr M’s complaint on the basis that I consider he has 
not adequately demonstrated that he suffered an accident causing bodily injury. I have not 
considered beyond this whether he met the other criteria for benefit to be paid. Even if he 
were to obtain material new evidence to demonstrate that he did suffer an accident causing 
bodily injury, he would still need to demonstrate that this bodily injury was, at least partly, 
responsible for him being permanently and totally disabled from carrying out any work to 
which he was suited by means of experience, education or training. 
my decision
My final decision is that I do not uphold this complaint. I make no award against Great Lakes 
Reinsurance (UK) Plc.
David Poley
ombudsman
Ref: DRN1565649
quoted_clauses: We will pay you the appropriate benefit if, during any period of insurance, an insured person sustains a bodily injury which, within 52 weeks, is the only cause of death, permanent total disablement, permanent disability, fractures, burns or hospitalisation

A bodily injury which is the direct result of an accidental, external, violent and visible cause, including accidental injury as a result of being exposed to the elements. This does not include an injury caused by sickness, disease or any naturally occurring condition or process.
Low back pain … Picking up things at work and went 2 weeks ago

Had there been a major injury to the cervical or lumbar discs caused by the accident in October 2009, I would have expected an immediate onset of severe symptoms rather than a gradual progression of symptoms which appear to have taken place. Nonetheless, the precipitating factor for his present symptom complex (based upon the history that was given to me by Mr M) relates specifically to the accident in October 2009. In the absence of evidence to the contrary I have accepted the view that the accident precipitated his symptoms.

business: The Royal London Mutual Insurance Society Limited
text:
K820x#14
complaint
Mr Y complains that The Royal London Mutual Insurance Society Limited turned down his 
claim for benefit under his disability income benefit. 
background
Mr Y has disability income benefit, the aim of which is to pay an income after a waiting 
period of 52 weeks, if he can’t work because of illness or injury. Mr Y also has premium 
payment benefit (PPB). This covers the cost of the policy premium, after a waiting period of 
13 weeks, if he can’t work because of illness or injury. 
In September 2016, Mr Y stopped working because of stress and anxiety. In January 2018, 
he submitted claims for disability income benefit and PPB. After assessing the claims, Royal 
London thought Mr Y’s symptoms of stress were related to his specific employer. It therefore 
turned down the claims as it thought Mr Y was still able to carry out his occupation 
elsewhere. Unhappy with this, Mr Y brought a complaint to this service.
Our investigator didn’t recommend the complaint be upheld. She accepted that Mr Y was 
experiencing symptoms, but she didn’t think he’d shown these prevented him from working 
in his occupation. She therefore thought it had been reasonable for Royal London to turn 
down the claims. 
Mr Y didn’t accept our investigator’s findings, so the matter has been passed to me to 
consider. 
my findings
I’ve considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint. 
Disability benefit claim
The policy says a claim for disability benefit will be payable, after a waiting period of 52 
weeks, if Mr Y is unable to carry out the material and substantial duties of his own 
occupation because of illness or injury. 
The policy explains that ‘own occupation’ means:
“the trade, profession or type of work the life assured does for profit or pay. It is not a specific 
job with any particular employer and is irrespective of location and availability.”
I’ve therefore considered the available medical evidence in the relevant 52-week waiting 
period. 
I see that Mr Y’s GP signed him off work with a stress related problem. And when he first 
stopped work, his GP referred him for counselling. 
Mr Y has confirmed that he had counselling/therapy, however he hasn’t provided any reports 
from his treating counsellor/therapist, so I haven’t been able to take this into account. 
Ref: DRN1666733

2
In 2017, Mr Y was assessed by his employer’s occupational health physician (Dr S) on at 
least two occasions. I understand one assessment took place in May, and the other in 
October. Following the October consultation, Dr S said Mr Y had confirmed that his mental 
well-being had improved in the absence of communication from his employer (though recent 
communication from his employer had resulted in increased symptoms of generalised 
anxiety). Dr S thought that any attempt by Mr Y to return to work with his previous employer 
would likely result in a decrease in his mental well-being. 
In March 2018, the GP provided some further information. Although this was provided after 
the 52-week waiting period had ended, I’ve still taken it into account. 
The GP said Mr Y was suffering with a stress-related work problem. Royal London asked if 
Mr Y was totally unable to follow his occupation, and the date he became incapacitated, and 
the GP said ‘not known’. The GP confirmed there’d been an improvement in Mr Y’s condition 
since the onset of his incapacity. However, he didn’t know what Mr Y’s limitations and 
restrictions were. He said Mr Y didn’t require future treatment, and no other treatment or 
investigations had been suggested. And the GP didn’t know when Mr Y would be likely to be 
fit to return to work. 
Royal London also asked the GP:
“Clinically, if your patient still does not currently have the functional ability to carry out their 
own occupation, do you consider they have the ability to do an alternative job, which is 
similar in nature?”
The GP answered “yes” to this question.
Overall, I’m inclined to agree with Royal London that Mr Y hasn’t shown that he meets the 
policy requirements for a claim to be paid. I’ll explain why. 
Mr Y has remained under the care of his GP since stopping work, but the information from 
his GP isn’t particularly detailed, and doesn’t explain what his symptoms are or how these 
affect him. And since his GP thought he had the ability to do an alternative job which was 
similar in nature to his own, it’s not clear why Mr Y therefore couldn’t work in his own 
occupation with another employer. 
Mr Y wasn’t prescribed any medication to treat his symptoms and didn’t receive any referrals 
from his GP to specialists. Although he was initially referred for counselling when he first 
stopped work, Mr Y hasn’t provided any evidence relating to this.
I accept that the evidence from Dr S supports that Mr Y’s mental wellbeing would be affected 
if he were to return to work with his previous employer. However, crucially, Dr S doesn’t 
comment on Mr Y’s ability to carry out his occupation elsewhere.
Mr Y says he has a generalised anxiety disorder with significant periodic bouts of 
depression. However, the medical evidence I’ve seen from his GP is that he was 
experiencing work-related stress. That’s not to say that work-related stress can’t develop into 
a mental illness of such significance that it prevents someone from performing their 
occupation for any employer, but I don’t think there’s sufficient evidence of that here.
Ref: DRN1666733

3
When Mr Y submitted his claim form, I note he was asked what parts of his job he could 
carry out. He said “None. My illness inhibits contact with, and attendance at, my current 
employer.”
I appreciate Mr Y felt unable to work for his previous employer. However, for me to find that 
Mr Y was medically prevented from doing his own occupation with another employer, I’d 
expect to see stronger evidence of the impact Mr Y’s illness has had on him, and why this 
prevents him from working in his occupation elsewhere.
On balance, I don’t think Mr Y has shown that his symptoms prevented him from working for 
another employer. Consequently, I think it was fair for Royal London to decline Mr Y’s claim 
on the basis of the available evidence. 
PPB claim
The policy explains a claim for PPB will be payable, after a waiting period of 13 weeks, if Mr 
Y is unable to carry out the material and substantial duties of his own occupation because of 
illness or injury. Again, own occupation means the work the life assured does for profit or 
pay, and isn’t a specific job with any particular employer.
The medical information for the first 13 weeks is very limited. Although Mr Y’s GP had signed 
him off work with stress, I don’t think this alone shows that he was incapacitated to such an 
extent that he couldn’t carry out his occupation for another employer. I’m therefore satisfied it 
was reasonable for Royal London to turn down this claim.
my final decision
My final decision is that I don’t uphold this complaint. 
Under the rules of the Financial Ombudsman Service, I’m required to ask Mr Y to accept or 
reject my decision before 5 April 2020.
Chantelle Hurn-Ryan
ombudsman
Ref: DRN1666733
quoted_clauses: the trade, profession or type of work the life assured does for profit or pay. It is not a specific job with any particular employer and is irrespective of location and availability.

Clinically, if your patient still does not currently have the functional ability to carry out their own occupation, do you consider they have the ability to do an alternative job, which is similar in nature?
None. My illness inhibits contact with, and attendance at, my current employer.

text:
K820x#14
complaint
Mr and Mrs J are unhappy that Europaische Reiseversicherung AG (ERV) won’t pay their 
holiday cancellation claim under their travel insurance policy.
 
background
Mrs J took out the travel policy to cover her family during a holiday. Unfortunately before 
they were due to travel Mr J’s father passed away and so they couldn’t go on their holiday. 
Mrs J contacted ERV to make a claim for the holiday costs incurred. ERV declined the claim 
because Mr J’s father had a pre-existing medical condition prior to the policy being taken 
out. Mr and Mrs J brought their complaint to this service.  
Our investigator didn’t uphold the complaint. She felt that the policy was clear and the terms 
had been pointed out. Our investigator said Mr J’s father had passed away because of a pre-
existing condition and so ERV had applied the policy exclusion for this reasonably. 
Mr and Mrs J didn’t accept this and asked for their complaint to be passed to an ombudsman 
for a final decision.
my findings
I’ve considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint.
Travel policies generally have insurance cover for cancellation or curtailment of the holiday. 
But under this policy that cover excludes cancellation if it’s linked to a pre-existing medical 
condition that existed prior to the policy being taken out.
Within the key facts document it said:
“2. You will not be covered for any claim arising from a medical condition of someone you 
were going to stay with, a relative, a business associate, a travelling companion, or anyone 
on whose health your trip may depend if you were aware of the medical condition at the time 
your policy was issued.”
Within the policy it said:
“We will not pay any claims related directly or indirectly to Pre-existing Medical Conditions”
And
“This Policy does not cover any claim
4. Arising from a medical condition of someone You were going to stay with, a Relative, a 
Close Business Associate, a travelling companion or anyone on whose health Your trip may 
depend if You were aware of the medical condition at the time Your Policy was issued or 
Your trip was booked.”
I’m satisfied that the policy details are clear and as they were included within the key facts 
document and the policy I think they were reasonably brought to Mr and Mrs J’s attention. I 
don’t think Mr and Mrs J dispute that. Also I don’t think Mr and Mrs J dispute that the medical 
condition existed prior to the policy being taken out. Their point is the medical condition was 
Ref: DRN1837817

2
being looked after and effectively it was under control. They didn’t think the medical 
condition was relevant to their travel insurance policy.
I’ve looked at the details from the death certificate. This confirmed that Mr J’s father’s pre-
existing medical condition was noted as the cause of death. Mr J’s father had the medical 
condition, which he died from, for many years. The medical certificate confirmed Mr J’s 
father had been under the clinic and he’d been admitted to hospital in 2016. So even though 
I do understand the points made by Mr and Mrs J I’m satisfied that the cancellation was 
directly linked to his father’s pre-existing condition. As the policy exclusion is clear I can say 
that ERV acted reasonably when it declined to deal with the claim.
my final decision
I don’t uphold this complaint. 
I make no award against Europaische Reiseversicherung AG.
Under the rules of the Financial Ombudsman Service, I’m required to ask Mr and Mrs J to 
accept or reject my decision before 29 August 2017.
John Quinlan
ombudsman

text:
K820x#14
complaint
Mr B has complained about Ageas Insurance Limited’s decision not to pay a claim under his 
income protection policy.
background
The background to this complaint, and my provisional findings, were set out in my 
provisional decision dated 12 October 2016. A copy of this is attached and forms part of this 
final decision. In my provisional decision I invited both parties to let me have any further 
comments and evidence.
Mr B said he was previously off work because of problems with his other knee. He tried to 
claim on his policy but Ageas said he hadn’t been off work for long enough to be able to 
claim. He says, if Ageas had told him his knees weren’t covered because they were pre-
existing conditions, he would have cancelled the policy at that time.
my findings
I’ve reconsidered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint.
I’ve considered Mr B’s comment but I don’t think it affects my decision. As Ageas had 
decided not to pay Mr B’s claim for another reason, I don’t think it would be reasonable for 
me to say it should then have considered whether the claim was for a pre-existing condition.
my final decision
For the reasons I’ve given above and in my provisional decision, my final decision is I don’t 
uphold this complaint. I make no award against Ageas Insurance Limited.
Under the rules of the Financial Ombudsman Service, I’m required to ask Mr B to accept or 
reject my decision before 2 December 2016.
Charles Bacon
ombudsman
Ref: DRN1839354

2
copy of provisional decision
background
Mr B took out the policy in 2003. It was intended to provide him with a replacement for lost income if 
he was unable to work because of injury or illness.
In February 2016 Mr B made a claim on his policy. He’d had to have a knee replacement operation 
and had been off work as a result. Ageas said it wouldn’t pay the claim because it related to a medical 
condition from which Mr B had suffered before he took out the policy (“a pre-existing condition”). It 
went on to say that Mr B needed to show that he’d not had any symptoms or treatment for the 
condition in the two years before he made the claim and he hadn’t done this.
Mr B complained to Ageas about its decision but it didn’t change its position so he referred his 
complaint to this service. He says the knee replacement isn’t linked to the pre-existing condition.
my provisional findings
I’ve considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and reasonable in the 
circumstances of this complaint.  
I’ve seen a copy of the policy document and the relevant section says:
“What is not covered:
Injury or illness that occurs within twenty-four months of the policy start date and that is caused by a 
pre-existing condition. This will not apply after you have been free of all symptoms for a minimum of 
twenty-four consecutive months immediately following the start date of this policy or twenty-four 
consecutive months immediately preceding the claim and you have not received medical advice or 
treatment about the pre-existing condition during this time.”
Pre-existing condition is defined in the policy as:
“Any injury, illness, disease or medical condition…where in the 12 months immediately preceding 
your application for cover under this policy:
You received advice, treatment, medication or a consultation.”
I’ve seen a copy of Mr B’s medical history. This shows that he’s had problems with his knee since 
2001. He had an arthroscopy in January 2002 and further treatment in April 2002. I’m therefore 
satisfied that Mr B had received treatment for this condition in the twelve months before he applied for 
the policy and, consequently, that Ageas was entitled to treat it as a “pre-existing condition”.
It’s now necessary for me to consider whether Mr B can show that his condition comes within either of 
the exemptions to the exclusion of pre-existing conditions that are set out in the policy document. To 
do this, Mr B needs to show that he didn’t have any symptoms or treatment for his condition either in 
the twenty-four months after he took out the policy or the twenty-four months before he made his 
claim.
Mr B’s medical records show he consulted his doctor about his knee in July 2004. This was within the 
twenty-four months after he took out the policy so he doesn’t appear to come within the first 
exemption. The records also show Mr B had another arthroscopy in October 2014 which is within the 
twenty-four months before he had the knee replacement. This means he doesn’t appear to satisfy the 
requirements of the second exemption.
I’ve considered Mr B’s comment that his knee replacement wasn’t linked to his pre-existing condition. 
However, I’ve seen a copy of a certificate from his GP in connection with his claim. This says Mr B 
Ref: DRN1839354

3
was first diagnosed with the condition that caused him to be unfit for work in 2001. I’m not, therefore 
persuaded that the operation wasn’t linked to the pre-existing condition.
In all the circumstances, I currently think that Ageas dealt with Mr B’s claim in accordance with the 
terms of the policy and, consequently, that it treated him fairly and reasonably.
my provisional decision
Subject to any additional comments or evidence I get from the parties, my provisional decision is I 
wouldn’t uphold this complaint. I wouldn’t make any award against Ageas Insurance Limited.
Ref: DRN1839354

text:
K820x#14
complaint
Ms B has complained that Wesleyan Assurance Society was paying her lower benefit than it 
should after it accepted her claim under her income protection insurance policy.
background
Ms B had an income protection insurance policy. The policy would pay a weekly benefit, 
after a waiting period of 26 weeks, in the event that she was unable to work because of 
illness or injury. The policy also carried a waiver of premium benefit under which Ms B didn’t 
have to pay premiums while incapacitated.
Ms B became unable to work because of illness. She made a claim under the policy. 
Wesleyan accepted the claim. However, because Ms B was still entitled to 50% sickness 
pay from her employer at the time the waiting period ended, it explained that she wouldn’t 
receive the full amount of benefit for which she was insured.
Ms B complained to Wesleyan that in calculating her benefit, it had deducted the gross 
amount of her ongoing income from her employer; she felt it should have deducted only the 
net amount. Ms B further complained that Wesleyan hadn’t applied the waiver of premium 
benefit until she’d been incapacitated for 26 weeks; she felt it should have been applied after 
13 weeks.
Wesleyan was satisfied it had applied the terms of the policy correctly. It offered Ms B a 
proportionate refund of her premiums from April 2015 (which was the date from which it had 
evidence of her earnings) to reflect her over-insurance since then. Ms B didn’t accept the 
offer. She referred her complaint to this service. 
 
I issued a provisional decision explaining why I was minded to uphold this complaint in part.
waiver of premium benefit
I noted that the policy states:
“Premiums falling due for payment during any period for which income protection 
benefit is paid will not be payable by the Policyholder except during the first 
13 consecutive weeks of any period of incapacity.”
I thought this was clear that the waiver of premium applied only while income protection 
benefit was being paid. In Ms B’s case, this wasn’t until 26 weeks after her incapacity. The 
second part of the sentence, relating to the exception for the first 13 weeks of incapacity, 
wasn’t relevant to Ms B because she wasn’t entitled to waiver of premium benefit during 
these 13 weeks in any case. The exception was relevant only to those policyholders who 
had a waiting period of less than 13 weeks. I said I could understand how, if Ms B didn’t read 
the clause very carefully, she may have assumed she would be entitled to the waiver of 
premium benefit after 13 weeks and I thought it could have been drafted better. However, 
Wesleyan had pointed out that logically one would expect the waiver of premium benefit to 
take effect from when the policyholder started needing a replacement income, which would 
normally be the end of the waiting period. And I had no reason to think Ms B was misled into 
taking out the policy by any misunderstanding of when waiver of premium benefit would 
apply. In the circumstances, I thought it was reasonable for Wesleyan to apply the waiver of 
benefit premium only after 26 weeks.
Ref: DRN1966270

2
deduction of gross income
I noted Ms B was insured to receive £443 a week. However, the policy had a limitation on 
the amount of benefit which was payable. This was described in the policy as follows:
“The maximum income protection benefit payable under this Policy is the weekly 
equivalent of the following proportion of the Policyholder's income prior to incapacity:
75% of the first £45,000 plus 
50% of the balance
(or such higher amounts as the Company may from time to time determine)
less:
(a) the weekly equivalent of benefit secured by all other sickness and accident 
insurances on the life of the Policyholder and
(b) State benefits to which the Policyholder is entitled (but excluding any amounts 
relating to dependants) and
(c) the weekly equivalent of all ill-health or retirement pension benefits from any 
source and
(d) the weekly equivalent of any income arising from the Policyholder's ordinary 
occupation”
Wesleyan had said this meant Ms B was entitled to receive only £279 a week in benefit from 
the policy. In calculating this benefit, Wesleyan took account of the gross salary Ms B was 
continuing to receive from her employer while she was off sick.
I didn’t think Wesleyan was fair to take account of Ms B’s gross salary. The policy didn’t 
stipulate whether it was the gross or net amount to be used under a) to d) above. Wesleyan, 
however, had pointed out it was gross income which was used in determining pre-incapacity 
income and therefore thought it was fair that gross ongoing income was deducted from the 
benefit payable. However, I didn’t agree with this logic. The intention of the limitation of 
benefit clause was to make sure the policyholder wasn’t better off while incapacitated than 
they were while working. The clause had therefore already allowed for the impact of taxation 
on the consumer’s situation. By deducting Ms B’s gross ongoing income from the benefit 
which she would otherwise be eligible to receive, I thought Wesleyan was treating Ms B 
unfairly. Because she had to pay tax on that ongoing income from her employer, she would 
end up receiving less money overall than the limitation of benefit clause allowed. I thought 
Wesleyan should therefore take account of Ms B’s net ongoing income, rather than gross, 
when calculating the level of benefit she was due under the policy.
refund of premiums
I was satisfied that Wesleyan had made a fair offer of a proportionate refund based on the 
information available to it. However, in light of my decision on the use of gross ongoing 
income, I noted Wesleyan would need to reassess its offer. If it transpired that Ms B was still 
over-insured, and Ms B believed that over-insurance had existed further back than April 
2015, she would need to provide evidence of this to Wesleyan for it consider extending the 
period of refund.
I invited both parties to comment on my provisional decision.
Ref: DRN1966270

3
Both Ms B and Wesleyan have said they accept my provisional decision.
my findings
I’ve considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint.
Given that both parties accept my provisional decision, I’m satisfied that this should stand.
I note Wesleyan has said it will invite Ms B to provide evidence to show if she was over-
insured before April 2015. It mentions that in calculating whether she was over-insured it will 
use her net income rather than her gross income. To clarify, lest there is any 
misunderstanding, it is Ms B’s gross income which should be used to determine her pre-
incapacity income and hence the maximum benefit payable to her under the policy. It is 
Ms B’s net income which should be used to determine what deductions should be made 
from her benefit payments.  
my final decision
For the reasons given above, my final decision is that I uphold this complaint in part. I 
require Wesleyan Assurance Society to recalculate Ms B’s benefit taking into account her 
net, rather than gross, ongoing income and to pay her the amount she is due. It should add 
interest to this at the annual simple rate of 8%, calculated from the date each payment was 
due to the date of settlement.* It should also recalculate its offer of a proportionate refund of 
her premiums.
Under the rules of the Financial Ombudsman Service, I’m required to ask Ms B to accept or 
reject my decision before 2 March 2017.
David Poley
ombudsman
* If Wesleyan Assurance Society considers that it’s required by HM Revenue & Customs to take off 
income tax from that interest, it should tell Ms B how much it’s taken off. It should also give Ms B a 
certificate showing this if she asks for one, so she can reclaim the tax from HM Revenue & Customs if 
appropriate.
Ref: DRN1966270
quoted_clauses: Premiums falling due for payment during any period for which income protection benefit is paid will not be payable by the Policyholder except during the first 13 consecutive weeks of any period of incapacity.

text:
K821x#15
complaint
Mr T complains that Unum Ltd turned down his income protection claim. 
background
Mr T holds an income protection policy with Unum. The aim of the policy is to pay benefit, 
after a waiting period of 100 working days, if Mr T is unable to carry out his normal 
occupation because of illness or injury.
In 2017, Mr T stopped work. He made a claim under the policy, however this was turned 
down by Unum as it didn’t think he met the policy’s definition of incapacity. Unhappy with 
this, Mr T brought a complaint to this service. 
Our adjudicator recommended the complaint be upheld. He found Mr T’s GP’s evidence to 
be persuasive and thought Mr T did meet the policy definition of incapacity. He 
recommended Unum pay the claim from the date the waiting period ended, plus interest.
Unum didn’t agree with the adjudicator’s recommendations, and asked that the matter be 
referred to an ombudsman. The complaint has therefore been passed to me for 
consideration.
my findings
I’ve considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint. 
The policy defines ‘incapacity’ to mean:
“you cannot perform the material and substantial duties of your occupation because of your 
illness or injury.”
For the claim be payable, Mr T must meet the above definition from the date he stopped 
work on 30 October 2017 until the end of the waiting period on 19 March 2018. 
When Mr T stopped work in October 2017, he visited his GP and explained he’d been 
experiencing anxiety and stress for some time, and had pressures in his job. He said he 
couldn’t go into work as he was experiencing anxiety symptoms – that were ‘panic like’. 
Mr T’s GP prescribed him a low dose of antidepressant medication and signed him off work 
with stress. 
The following month, Mr T met with a psychological service for therapy. He reported 
pressure at work; not being able to sleep; feeling anxious and paranoid; worrying about 
work; and low motivation in other areas. He was put forward for computerised cognitive 
behavioural therapy (CBT). 
Throughout the following few months, Mr T continued to report to his GP that he was feeling 
anxious and stressed, as well as fatigued. His antidepressant medication was increased and 
he was continued to be signed off work with stress. Mr T also had six sessions of 
computerised CBT and four telephone therapy sessions.
Ref: DRN2111750

2
I see that shortly after the waiting period ended, Mr T’s antidepressant medication was 
increased to the maximum dose. 
Unum’s company medical officer (CMO) considered the case. He thought Mr T was 
experiencing work-related stress which he said isn’t an illness. He said there was no 
evidence of any specific functional impairment that would prevent Mr T from performing his 
occupation. Unum therefore turned down the claim.
After Unum turned down his claim, Mr T asked his GP to write a letter of support. Unum 
hasn’t placed much reliance on this letter. Its CMO says there’s no identifiable way that 
further comment can be made about the material period that’s in the past. Especially as the 
records suggest the GP was happy to provide information that was ‘supportive’ rather than 
objective. 
The GP notes do indeed say that Mr T asked for a letter of support as his income protection 
claim had been turned down. The GP commented that she would ask for another GP to write 
the letter as he had seen Mr T numerous times with his anxiety and depression. 
Whilst I appreciate there’s reference to a ‘letter of support’, that doesn’t mean the further 
comments provided by the GP should be ignored. Although the letter was written after the 
waiting period had ended, it does provide further clarification about Mr T’s health in the 
relevant period, which I think should be taken into account. 
In a letter dated 25 May 2018, the GP said:
“The sick notes have previously been stating stress since 30th October 2017 when really this 
could be better clarified as an anxiety and depressive disorder which had been building up 
prior to his consultation with me in October 2017. He was commenced on antidepressants in 
the form of citalopram to try and aid his symptoms and referred to…psychological services. 
He has had regular consultations with me during which at times his symptoms of anxiety, low 
mood, poor sleep, fatigue, poor concentration and poor motivation have persisted. All of 
these can be regarded as symptoms of anxiety and depression…I would be of the opinion 
that he is suffering with a mixed anxiety and depression disorder in association with work 
related stress, but given that he has not been at work for a number of months, stress would 
not be regarded as the sole diagnosis.”
Also in May 2018, Mr T met with a consultant occupational health physician (Dr W). Although 
this took place after the waiting period ended, I think Dr W’s comments are quite useful. 
Dr W said Mr T was still experiencing symptoms of tiredness, anxiety and altered sleep 
pattern. Dr W said those symptoms were consistent with work-related anxiety. He said one 
of the main barriers to returning to work would be the work-related stress issues. He thought 
that with more time for his treatments to stabilise and with further therapy, Mr T’s health 
condition would improve. And if his treatments were effective and his stress issues could be 
addressed, then a gradual phased return to work could take place. Dr W said Mr T’s current 
diagnosis was consistent with work-related stress, anxiety and depression.
I think this is a very finely balanced case. Unum’s CMO is a consultant psychiatrist and as a 
specialist, I would usually place the greatest weight on his opinion. However, I also have to 
take into account that the CMO has only carried out a desktop review of Mr T’s medical 
records, whereas the GP and Dr W have met Mr T. 
Ref: DRN2111750

3
Unum’s CMO says there’s been an absence of a systematic, progressive use of 
pharmacological interventions associated with psychiatric illness. He hasn’t expanded on 
that, but I assume he’s referring to the GP’s decision to only try one antidepressant 
medication. It’s not for me to comment on the GP’s recommended treatment, but given that 
the waiting period was a relatively short period of time (less than six months), it doesn’t 
seem particularly unusual that only one anti-depressant medication was prescribed to Mr T 
over that time - and I note the dose was steadily increased over that period. 
I fully appreciate Unum’s CMO’s point that workplace stress isn’t an illness. However, whilst 
the GP and Dr W accepted that Mr T was experiencing workplace stress, they both thought 
that he was also experiencing an illness – anxiety and depression. Both of them also thought 
he was unfit to work.
If Mr T were only experiencing work-related stress, then I’d expect his symptoms to improve 
the longer he was away from work. However, as his GP has pointed out, Mr T’s symptoms 
have persisted, despite him not being at work for some months. It may well have been the 
case that Mr T’s workplace stress acted as a trigger for his illness, but that doesn’t mean his 
claim should be declined because of this.  
I recognise Dr W said Mr T’s work-related stress was one of the main barriers to him 
returning to work, but it seems it wasn’t the only barrier. I’ve also taken into account that 
there wasn’t a specific problem at Mr T’s workplace that could potentially be resolved by his 
employer, thereby allowing him to return to work (which might indicate an employment issue, 
rather than a medical one). Dr W thought Mr T needed more time for his treatments to 
stabilise and further therapy before he could consider returning to work. 
Taking all of the above into consideration, I think it would be reasonable to conclude that 
Unum should accept the claim.
my final decision
My final decision is that I uphold this complaint. I require Unum Ltd to accept Mr T’s claim 
and pay benefit in accordance with the policy’s remaining terms and conditions. Interest 
should be added to these benefit payments at the annual simple rate of 8%, calculated from 
the date each payment was due to the date of settlement.* 
Under the rules of the Financial Ombudsman Service, I’m required to ask Mr T to accept or 
reject my decision before 3 June 2019.
Chantelle Hurn-Ryan
ombudsman
*If Unum considers that it’s required by HM Revenue & Customs to take off income tax from 
that interest, it should tell Mr T how much it’s taken off. It should also give Mr T a certificate 
showing this if he asks for one, so he can reclaim the tax from HM Revenue & Customs if 
appropriate. 
Ref: DRN2111750

text:
K821x#12
complaint
Mrs Q complains about the decision of BUPA insurance Limited (BUPA) to decline her claim 
for treatment costs under her private medical insurance policy.
background
Mrs Q was diagnosed with a medical condition in 1996. Her BUPA policy started in 
June 2011. In late 2011 Mrs Q noticed a significant worsening of some existing symptoms 
and had some new symptoms. She attended her GP’s surgery and was referred to a 
consultant for further investigation. 
Mrs Q contacted BUPA and asked it whether it would cover private treatment for this 
condition. BUPA sought information from Mrs Q’s GP, considered the GP’s response and 
declined to cover the treatment costs, as it believed the symptoms were likely to have been 
caused by Mrs Q’s underlying, long-term medical condition. 
Mrs Q went ahead with private treatment and her consultant provided her with a letter. The 
consultant said her new symptoms were due to a problem of recent origin and were 
unrelated to her existing medical condition. Mrs Q complained about BUPA’s decision.
Our adjudicator investigated the complaint and upheld it. He did not think the evidence was 
sufficient to show that Mrs Q’s recent medical problems were related to her existing, long-
term medical condition. He felt the consultant’s evidence strongly suggested that Mrs Q’s 
problems were new, acute and unrelated to any pre-existing medical condition. He 
recommended that BUPA should reconsider Mrs Q’s claim and pay her £100 in 
compensation for the distress and inconvenience caused. 
BUPA did not accept the adjudicator’s assessment. It said that the new symptoms could be 
a symptom of her pre-existing medical condition and that Mrs Q had not provided evidence 
to show that the condition was unrelated to her existing, chronic condition. BUPA also 
argued that, as the policy started four months prior to the claim, it believed that the 
symptoms predated the start of the policy. The GP mentioned that Mrs Q had long term mild 
symptoms and these became much more severe shortly after the policy started, but BUPA 
noted that the symptoms were present before the policy started.
The complaint has been passed to me for a final decision.
my findings
I have considered all the available evidence and arguments from the outset, in order to 
decide what is fair and reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint. 
BUPA is seeking to rely on an exclusion clause to decline what seems to be an otherwise 
valid claim. It is for BUPA to show that the exclusion applies in Mrs Q’s case. 
BUPA believes that the symptoms experienced by Mrs Q and investigated by the consultant 
are caused by a medical condition she has had since 1996 – many years before the policy 
started. It also says this condition is a chronic condition. If it was a pre-existing condition or a 
chronic condition, it would be excluded under the policy terms and conditions. BUPA 
excludes:
Ref: DRN2130708

2
-
any pre-existing condition, which is defined as “any disease, illness or injury for which 
in the seven years before your start date:

you have received medication, advice or treatment, or

you have experienced symptoms
whether the condition was diagnosed or not”.
And 
-
any chronic condition, which is defined as “a disease, illness or injury which has one 
or more of the following characteristics:

it needs ongoing or long term monitoring through consultations, 
examinations, check-ups and/or tests

it needs ongoing or long-term control or relief of symptoms

it requires rehabilitation or for you to be specially trained to cope with it 

it continues indefinitely

it has no known cure

it comes back or is likely to come back”
It is not disputed that Mrs Q’s medical condition, which she has had since 1996, is a chronic 
condition and a pre-existing medical condition. What is in dispute here is whether Mrs Q’s 
recent symptoms were caused by that medical condition. 
BUPA relies on the referral letter written by Mrs Q’s GP. The letter states that Mrs Q was 
diagnosed with the medical condition in 1996 and had suffered from certain mild symptoms 
since. It also says that these symptoms have recently become significantly worse, and that 
Mrs Q has also been experiencing new symptoms for the past three months. 
I agree with the adjudicator that this letter is not clear enough to show that Mrs Q’s current 
problem is related to her existing medical condition. Her existing symptoms were significantly 
worsened, but that is not to say that this was due to the same cause and there were wholly 
new symptoms present. 
Mrs Q, on the other hand, has provided a letter from the consultant surgeon who actually 
treated her, and therefore had specialist knowledge of her, her existing condition and her 
recent symptoms. The consultant said her new symptoms were of short duration, had 
resulted from a recent, identifiable cause, which was unrelated to her existing medical 
condition, were of recent origin and had no antecedent. He said he could not emphasise too 
strongly that this was an acute problem and that whilst treatment of the new problem would 
improve her existing long-term symptoms, this was a “happy accident”. 
I find the consultant’s evidence persuasive and I have seen little from BUPA to counter it. 
I do not consider BUPA has shown that Mrs Q’s new medical problem was most likely, 
related to her existing one, or that it was related to a chronic condition. It follows that I think 
neither exclusion has been proven. 
Turning to BUPA’s argument that the symptoms pre-date the start of the policy, there is no 
doubt that Mrs Q had existing ongoing symptoms of her existing medical condition, but the 
evidence indicates that these were unrelated to the new, acute health problem she suffered 
in December 2011. Her existing symptoms might have been made worse by this new 
condition, but the evidence is that the new condition started after the policy started. Mrs Q 
contacted BUPA in order to submit the claim in December 2011, whereas the policy started 
Ref: DRN2130708

3
in June 2011. The GP’s referral letter, dated October 2011, reports a three month history of 
the new symptoms. Consequently, and in the absence of evidence to the contrary, I accept 
that the new symptoms started no earlier than July. The fact that the treatment of the new 
condition helped ease the existing symptoms by “happy accident” is neither here nor there.
I consider that Mrs Q’s claim should be reconsidered based on the remaining terms and 
conditions of the policy, without further reference to the unproven exclusions. 
Finally, I consider that BUPA’s refusal of Mrs Q’s claim caused her unnecessary distress and 
inconvenience. I agree with our adjudicator that the sum of £100 should be paid by BUPA to 
Mrs Q in compensation.
my final decision
My final decision is that I uphold this complaint. I require BUPA Insurance Limited to 
reconsider Mrs Q’s claim in line with the remaining terms and conditions of the policy. 
I also require BUPA to pay Mrs Q £100 for the distress and inconvenience caused. 
I make no other award.
Greg Barham
ombudsman
Ref: DRN2130708

text:
K820x#14
complaint
Mr and Mrs B complain about Aviva Health UK Limited’s decision to turn down Mr B’s claim 
made under a private medical insurance policy.
background
Mr B held private medical insurance cover with another insurer and made a successful claim 
under it in early 2014 for a problem with his left knee. Mr and Mrs B’s membership of that 
policy ended and they took out a new policy with Aviva in September 2014. After doing so, 
Mr B had more problems with his left knee. He’d been diagnosed with arthritis and needed a 
partial knee replacement. Mr B made a claim to Aviva in early 2015. 
Aviva turned down the claim, saying the policy didn’t cover any illness or injury the insured 
sought medical advice about in the five years leading up to the start of the policy. Unless, 
that is, the insured went two years without tests, treatment and so forth after the policy 
started. Aviva said the evidence showed Mr B had a “significant history of degeneration” in 
the knee.
Mr and Mrs B went ahead with the surgery privately and complained to us. Our adjudicator 
didn’t recommend the complaint be upheld. He felt the evidence showed Mr B’s condition 
was likely to be pre-existing and that Aviva had fairly turned down the claim.
Mr and Mrs B appealed. They said, among other things, Mr B hadn’t been diagnosed with 
arthritis until after the policy started. His doctors mentioned degeneration but that wasn’t the 
same as arthritis. Their complaint was passed to me to consider.  
my findings
I’ve considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint.
Having done so, I’ve decided not to uphold this complaint. I’ll explain why.
The policy terms say Aviva won’t cover, among other things, treatment of any pre-existing 
medical condition if the insured had symptoms of, diagnostic tests for, treatment for or 
advice about that condition in the five years before the start of the policy. 
The terms go on to say Aviva will cover treatment of a pre-existing condition if there aren’t 
diagnostic tests for (and so on) that condition for a continuous two-year period after the start 
of the policy. This is what’s known as a moratorium clause.
So, for me to find Aviva fairly turned down the claim, I’d need to see evidence showing the 
condition Mr B claimed for was related to a condition he had and was advised about in the 
five years before September 2014. 
I believe, from the medical information, that Mr B was advised about arthritis more than once 
in that period. For example, Mr B saw his GP in October 2013 for left knee pain. The GP 
noted there was a restricted range of movement in the knee and he’d suffered with knee 
pain in the past. Mr B was having physiotherapy and his GP had prescribed medication for 
the pain.
Ref: DRN2346088

2
Mr B’s first consultant orthopaedic surgeon reported in October 2013 that he thought most of 
the left knee discomfort was “osteoarthritic in origin”. An MRI revealed “medial compartment 
degeneration” – the medial compartment being the inside of the knee – and a “medial 
meniscal tear”. 
In February 2014, the consultant said Mr B was still suffering with symptoms in the medial 
compartment. He recommended an arthroscopy but advised Mr B that would treat the tear 
but not any underlying degeneration. 
In April 2014, after the arthroscopy, the consultant said surgery revealed “fairly significant 
degeneration with a degenerative type effusion”. Despite the success of the arthroscopy, the 
consultant told Mr B he was likely to have some ongoing symptoms from the underlying 
degeneration within the knee. He advised Mr B regarding exercise and his weight.   
Mr B saw a second consultant orthopaedic surgeon in January 2015 because of significant 
pain and stiffness mainly to the inside of his left knee. The second consultant said clinical 
examination and x-rays confirmed Mr B had arthritis in his inner knee whereas the other two 
compartments within the knee appeared to be “well preserved”. He recommended a partial 
knee replacement, which is what Mr B paid to be done privately. 
In April 2015, the second consultant said Mr B had recovered well from surgery. He said “In 
the main his arthritic symptoms have all but disappeared now…”
Mr and Mrs B argue Mr B wasn’t formally diagnosed as suffering with arthritis of the inner 
knee until after the policy started. But that doesn’t mean that condition wasn’t pre-existing in 
line with the policy terms. That’s because of how the terms describe a pre-existing condition 
– it’s enough that there were symptoms experienced or advice given before a diagnosis was 
made. I believe that’s what happened in this case. 
Mr B’s first consultant mentioned arthritis and found knee degeneration in the inner knee 
before the policy started. His second consultant’s findings were consistent with the first’s, to 
the extent he found arthritis in the same part of the same knee. Fortunately, replacement of 
that part of the knee appears to have gone well for Mr B. I know that degeneration and 
arthritis aren’t always the same thing, although arthritis is a form of degeneration. In the 
circumstances, and given the absence of anything showing otherwise, I find it likely the 
arthritis Mr B suffered with after the policy started had also caused him problems before it 
started. 
It’s not that I think there was a connection between the arthritis Mr B claimed for with Aviva 
and the tear he claimed for with his previous insurer. Rather, I believe Aviva’s shown the 
arthritis – whether diagnosed or not – was something Mr B had suffered symptoms of and/or 
received advice about in the five-year period before the policy started.
I realise Mr and Mrs B have referred to some general medical studies in support of their 
claim and complaint. While I’ve looked at what they’ve said and considered it carefully, I’ve 
placed more weight on Mr B’s personal medical information and the findings of his treating 
doctors in reaching my decision. That’s because I think that’s the information most relevant 
to Mr B’s condition. 
Overall, I think it was fair for Aviva to turn down Mr B’s claim. I think it handled the claim 
appropriately. 
Ref: DRN2346088

3
my final decision
For the reasons given, I’ve decided not to uphold this complaint.
Under the rules of the Financial Ombudsman Service, I’m required to ask Mr and Mrs B to 
accept or reject my decision before 11 April 2016.
Nimish Patel
ombudsman
Ref: DRN2346088
