In the main his arthritic symptoms have all but disappeared now…

text:
K820x#14
complaint
Mr P complains that Allianz Insurance Plc turned down his claim under his pet insurance 
policy. 
background
On 14 August 2017 Mr P took out a four week free pet insurance policy with Allianz, via his 
vet, to cover his new puppy. In early September 2017 he took a ‘covered for life’ policy with 
Allianz, as a continuation of the free policy. The covered for life policy started on 
11 September 2017 (the day after the 4 weeks free cover ended). 
In October 2017 Mr P made a claim for vet treatment his puppy had received during 
September and October 2017. The vet said the diagnosis was “suspected intussuception 
[‘ITS’] secondary to parasites”. ITS is a condition where part of the bowel telescopes into 
another part of the bowel. The treatment costs were just under £1,800.
Allianz turned down the claim. It said the puppy had suffered from diarrhoea before Mr P 
took the free policy. It said this was a symptom of the claimed for condition of ITS, and that it 
pre-dated the free policy. Mr P provided a letter from his vet, supporting his claim. But Allianz 
said the clinical signs before the free policy started meant the treatment for suspected ITS 
was pre-existing, so the treatment wasn’t covered under the policy. Mr P didn’t agree it was 
pre-existing. He came to us.
When it sent us its file Allianz said Mr P had told it, when he applied for the annual policy, 
that his puppy had had “watery poo” in the first week he’d owned her. It said that it should 
have put a policy exclusion on the policy for any claims due to gastro-intestinal/digestive 
system disorders. But as Mr P had told it about the “watery poo” during the puppy’s first 
week with him it removed the exclusion. It also offered him a £1,000 contribution towards the 
ITS treatment costs. 
Our investigator ultimately didn’t uphold the complaint. He explained Allianz had spoken to 
Mr P’s vet, who accepted it was likely, on balance, that the puppy’s ITS had been linked to 
symptoms pre-dating the policy. This meant it was a pre-existing condition that wasn’t 
covered under the policy’s terms. Our investigator thought Allianz’s offer of a £1,000 
contribution was reasonable in the circumstances.  
Mr P didn’t agree with our investigator’s findings. So the complaint’s come to me for review. 
my findings
I’ve considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint. Having done so, I think Allianz has made 
a fair offer to resolve this complaint. I’ll explain why.
Mr P took out the covered for life annual policy to follow on from the free four week policy. 
This meant that the usual 14 days waiting period didn’t apply to the annual policy. In other 
words, had Mr P’s puppy had suffered the first signs or symptoms of illness or injury within 
the first 14 days of the annual policy Allianz would have covered a claim to treat the illness 
or injury. Allianz confirmed in the policy’s certificate and terms and conditions that any 
pre-existing condition wouldn’t be covered. 
Ref: DRN2443431

2
Allianz says that the puppy’s illness showed signs or symptoms before the date the free 
policy started. This means that any claim for this illness isn’t covered under the annual 
policy. So Allianz turned down Mr P’s claim under this pre-existing condition exclusion in the 
annual policy. This says that Allianz won’t pay a claim for an illness or injury that happened 
or first showed clinical signs before the pet’s cover started. This is regardless of whether or 
not it placed any exclusion on the policy for the injury/illness. 
I appreciate that Mr P disputes that his puppy’s illness began before the free policy started. 
He provided evidence from the vet who treated his puppy for the ITS. Allianz has also 
provided evidence from its consultant’s vet, together with the clinical notes from the first vet. 
More recently it’s spoken to the vet who treated the puppy for ITS, and has sent us the call 
recording which Mr P has also heard. 
I’ve considered all the available veterinary evidence, which I’ll summarise:

Mr P had taken the puppy to the vet on 13 August 2017. The clinical notes say that 
he’d had the puppy for four days at that point, and she’d been having diarrhoea up to 
ten times a day. She was otherwise well. The vet noted she had distended (swollen) 
abdomen, and suspected a “heavy worm burden”. The vet wormed the puppy. Later 
that same day Mr P rang the vet to say the puppy was lethargic and wasn’t interested 
in food, and he was advised to see if she settled but otherwise should ring the out of 
hours vet. 

The following day, 14 August 2017, Mr P took the puppy to the vet for her second 
vaccination. He said she’d seemed better, with the consistency of the faeces being 
more sludgy. He thought he’d seen a small worm, but wasn’t certain. The vet said her 
stomach was less swollen. The free insurance cover started that day.

By the next vaccination appointment on 28 August 2017 Mr P told the vet the puppy 
was a lot better, and he had no concerns at all. The vet noted the puppy still had a 
big abdomen, but otherwise seemed normal.

On 5 September 2017 Mr P took the puppy to the vet as she’d eaten acorns and had 
been sick. She’d had greenish faeces but they were OK in consistency. The vet 
noted she still had a very bloated abdomen and her spine/pelvis were more 
prominent that they should be. The vet treated the puppy for possible acorn 
poisoning. But the vet also noted that they needed to find out why she was so 
bloated, and advised an x-ray and scan if she was still vomiting in a few days’ time. 

On 18 September 2017 Mr P took the puppy to the vet concerned she still had 
diarrhoea and she’d lost weight. He said the first faeces in the morning were more of 
a paste but then became more runny through the day. She was quieter than he 
expected of a puppy and he was concerned there was something wrong with her. 
The vet said that her abdomen was still rounded, her spine was prominent and while 
she was growing she wasn’t getting any muscle mass. The vet queried infectious 
diarrhoea or congenital digestive disorder.

On 20 September 2017 Mr P took the puppy to a second vet’s practice. The second 
vet, Dr W, who treated the puppy said in an email supporting the claim that:
o
She first saw the puppy on 20 September 2017 with poor weight gain and 
diarrhoea. She saw that previous reports of diarrhoea with the puppy’s 
Ref: DRN2443431

3
previous vet appeared to have resolved with worming treatment, referring to 
the previous vet’s notes from 28 August 2017 when no diarrhoea was noted. 
Also, the note of vomiting on 5 September at the previous vet appeared to be 
secondary to the ingestion of acorns. Based on this Dr W felt there was the 
possibility that the claim for investigations into diarrhoea from 20 September 
could be completely separate from the diarrhoea that was treated 
successfully in August 2017.

Allianz’s consultant vet didn’t agree with Dr W’s clinical opinion. He said based on the 
evidence it wasn’t clear to him the ITS was due to parasitic loading. He said the 
normal cause was bowel hyperactivity due to irritable bowel issues of multiple cause 
including parasite. He added the history of hyper motility (movement through the 
digestive tract) was evident on 13 August 2017, and that the swollen abdomen had 
been noted at each visit. Allianz’s consultant vet strongly disagreed with Dr W’s 
interpretation of the previous vet’s clinical history. 

Based on this evidence, Allianz spoke with Dr W, saying its consultant vet disagreed 
with her opinion about the ITS, and thought the ITS could be linked to the 13 August 
2017 diarrhoea (which pre-dated the policy). 

Dr W said that in her clinical opinion the diarrhoea from 13 August 2017, on balance, 
could very well be linked to the ITS which was the subject of the claim. She said 
she’d had only the clinical notes from the first vet, which indicated that the diarrhoea 
had resolved. She fully accepted the diarrhoea and the ITS could be linked, and she 
also said that they might never know. But, on balance, she said she thought they 
were linked. 
I’ve considered all the evidence. This includes Mr P’s comments about Dr W’s conversation 
with Allianz. I think Allianz made a fair decision when it said Mr P’s puppy’s condition was a 
pre-existing condition under the policy terms. Allianz has done enough to show, on balance, 
the diarrhoea and distended abdomen which was seen before he took out the free four week 
policy was a sign or symptom of the ITS his puppy was later treated for. To do this Allianz 
needs to show it’s more likely than not that something happened, and I think it’s shown that. 
The puppy didn’t need to have had a diagnosis at the point the first signs or symptoms were 
seen for the condition to be pre-existing. Only that the signs and symptoms were seen and 
could have led to a claim. 
Mr P is concerned that Dr W’s opinion might have been based on the fact he’d paid her, or 
because she might want to avoid confrontation. I can’t comment on her motivation, but 
ultimately she’s given her professional clinical opinion and Allianz is entitled to rely on that. 
Dr W didn’t seem uncertain when she said the ITS could be linked to the diarrhoea which the 
puppy had suffered from before Mr P had taken the policy. She expressed the view it was 
likely, on balance, the diarrhoea and ITS were linked. 
I know Mr P has made the point that the diarrhoea did settle initially after the worming 
treatment, and the puppy was also treated after she’d swallowed acorns. But I think the 
weight of veterinary evidence is that the puppy’s symptoms started before the date he took 
out the free policy. This means it’s a pre-existing condition. And Allianz made it clear that it 
wouldn’t cover a pre-existing condition under the policy’s terms, both in the call when it sold 
the annual policy and in the policy documents it sent Mr P.
Ref: DRN2443431

4
Mr P asked Allianz to pre-authorise the claim. But it didn’t do that, and said he should send 
in the claim. I don’t think this was unreasonable, as it would need to see the vet’s notes 
before deciding whether to pay the claim. 
Allianz accepts that Mr P told it that his puppy had had “watery poo” when he took out the 
annual policy. It says it should have applied exclusions for any claim for gastro-
intestinal/digestive system issues from the policy’s start date. By mistake it failed to do this, 
so it agreed to remove this exclusion. I think it was reasonable for Allianz to remove the 
exclusions. To be clear if Mr P decided to renew his covered for life policy Allianz would not 
have been entitled to add these exclusions, because it failed to do so from the outset. But it 
was still entitled to reject the claim under the pre-existing condition policy exclusion. 
Mr P is concerned that he continued to pay the policy premiums during this dispute. But, as 
he says, Allianz continued to provide cover during this period. Allianz offered to pay £1,000 
towards the ITS treatment costs. Given my conclusions I think that’s a fair offer, so I don’t 
require it to do anything more. 
my final decision
For the reasons I’ve given my decision is that Allianz Insurance Plc has made a fair offer to 
pay Mr P £1,000 towards the ITS treatment costs. It has also fairly removed the policy 
exclusion for gastro-intestinal/digestive system disorders that it had applied. So I don’t 
require it to do anything more to resolve this complaint. 
Under the rules of the Financial Ombudsman Service, I’m required to ask Mr P to accept or 
reject my decision before 10 September 2018.
Amanda Maycock
ombudsman
Ref: DRN2443431
quoted_clauses: suspected intussuception [‘ITS’] secondary to parasites

K820x#14
complaint
Mr S complains that American International Group UK Limited acted unfairly and
unreasonably when dealing with his claim under a personal accident insurance policy. A
solicitor is helping Mr S to bring his complaint.
background 
The background to this complaint was set out in my provisional decision of 17 March 2020, 
an extract of which is attached and forms part of this final decision. So, I won’t repeat that 
information here. 
my provisional decision
In my provisional decision, I explained why I thought that AIG’s proposal to agree 
instructions for a new medical report and then reassess the claim was fair. I set out what I 
thought AIG should have regard to in reassessing Mr S’ claim. I also said that the 
compensation AIG had previously offered in relation to its handling of the complaint was fair.
responses to my provisional decision
Mr S said that he rejected my findings and that he’d pursue this elsewhere. We didn’t receive 
a response from AIG.  
my findings
I’ve reconsidered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint.
Given that neither Mr S nor AIG have provided me with anything further on the complaint, I 
see no reason to depart from the conclusions I reached in my provisional decision. 
So, for the reasons I’ve explained, I think that the offer AIG has already made in relation to 
reassessing Mr S’ claim and inviting him to choose from a list of three consultants is fair. In 
reassessing Mr S’s claim, AIG should have regard to what I said in my provisional decision. I 
also think that the compensation AIG previously offered in relation to its handling of the 
complaint is fair.  
my final decision
For the reasons set out above and in my provisional decision, my final decision is that the 
offer AIG has already made in relation to reassessing Mr S’ claim and inviting him to choose 
from a list of three consultants is fair. In reassessing Mr S’ claim it should have regard to 
what I said in my provisional decision. I think that the compensation AIG previously offered in 
relation to its handling of the complaint is fair.
Ref: DRN2764356

2

reject my decision before 21 May 2020
Louise Povey
ombudsman
Ref: DRN2764356

3
extract of provisional decision
complaint
Mr S complains that American International Group UK Limited acted unfairly and 
unreasonably when dealing with his claim under a personal accident insurance policy. A 
solicitor is helping Mr S to bring his complaint.
background
Mr S has a personal accident insurance policy, which, amongst other things, provides cover 
in the event of bodily injury as a result of an accident resulting in permanent disability.
There’s been a significant amount of detailed exchanges in this case. By way of summary, 
Mr S was in active military service and suffered a back injury in July 2015. In April 2017,
Mr S made a claim against his policy. AIG obtained two medical reports then offered Mr S
£7,800. It said that was based on the level of Mr S’ permanent disability solely due to 
the accident in July 2015, after deductions for the percentage of whole body impairment 
and pre-existing conditions.
Mr S didn’t accept that. He said that he didn’t have a pre-existing back problem and that AIG 
shouldn’t limit his claim by the “whole body percentage limitation”, He said that relevant 
limitations weren’t bought to his attention. He disputed the reliability of the medical reports 
and the independence of the consultants who prepared them. Mr S says that his claim 
should be assessed under item 17 of section B in the policy, without deduction for the 
percentage of disability or pre-existing conditions.
AIG withdrew its offer. It said that it had assessed Mr S’ claim under the wrong part of the 
policy. AIG said that as Mr S hadn’t lost the entire function of his back or spine, it needs to 
establish what percentage of function he has lost, taking into account any pre-existing or 
underlying condition. It set out a process for Mr S to be medically examined again. AIG 
offered Mr S compensation of £500 plus interest in relation to its handling of his claim.
Mr S commissioned his own medical report, which said that his injury equates to between
15% and 20% of total bodily disability. So, he says that AIG should pay him £60,000.
One of our investigators looked at what had happened. He thought that AIG had dealt with 
Mr S’ complaint fairly. The investigator said that AIG was right to assess Mr S’ claim 
against item 9 in section B of the policy – which relates to loss of the entire back or spine – 
and could adjust the amount payable taking into account pre-existing conditions. The 
investigator thought that it was reasonable for AIG to ask Mr S to visit another expert to 
progress the claim and that its compensation of £500 in relation to its claim handling was 
fair.
Mr S didn’t agree with the investigator. His solicitor said, in summary:

The limit that applies to Mr S’s claim is up to £20,000 per unit, not up to 
£7,000 per unit.

The degree of disability reduction doesn’t apply here because Mr S’ disability 
relates to his back, which is mentioned in the table of benefits in section B of 
the policy.
Ref: DRN2764356

4

The relevant parts of the policy should have been drawn to Mr S’ attention.

Mr S didn’t have any pre-existing injury to his back, so AIG can’t make a 
deduction for that.

Mr S’ claim should be assessed against item 17 in section B of the policy, 
using the benefit limit of up to £20,000 per unit and a deduction should be 
made based on the degree of Mr S’ actual injuries expressed as a percentage 
of whole body disability after a fresh medical report has been obtained.
The investigator didn’t change his view. There were further exchanges, which I won’t set 
out here. As there was no agreement between the parties, the complaint was passed to 
me, an ombudsman, to decide.
my provisional findings
I’ve considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair 
and reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint.
I’m conscious that I’ve condensed a lot of detail into a short narrative. That reflects our 
service that, wherever possible, aims to be informal. But I’m satisfied that I’ve captured 
the essence of Mr S’ complaint.
It’s clear and quite understandable that Mr S has very strong feelings about this matter. 
There’s a considerable sum at stake. Mr S and his solicitor have provided detailed 
submissions to support the complaint, which I have read and considered. However, I trust 
that Mr S will not take as a discourtesy the fact that I focus on what I consider the central 
issue, that is, whether AIG has treated him in accordance with the terms and conditions 
of his policy and fairly in dealing with his claim.
the relevant policy terms and conditions
The starting point is the terms and conditions of the policy, which say:
“What the insurance covers
If during the period of cover, you suffer bodily injury which, within two years solely and 
independently of any other cause, results in […] a permanent disability […], we will pay 
the total sum insured.”
The pricing and the benefits under the policy are determined by the number of 
units purchased. Mr S purchased 15 units, which is the maximum number 
available.
The table of benefits in the policy shows a list of injuries and how much AIG would pay 
for each injury per unit purchased. Items 9 and 17 on the list of table of benefits say:
“9     Loss of the entire back or spine (vertebral column) with no injury to the
spinal cord.                                                                                                  £7,000”
Ref: DRN2764356

5
“17   Permanent disability not otherwise listed
Please see the section headed ‘1. non-specified injuries’ […] for 
further details.
Up to £20,000”
“1. Non specified injuries
We will pay a benefit (or benefits) under item 17 of section B (permanent disabilities) for 
a permanent, total and irrecoverable loss by assessing the degree of disability suffered 
compared to those permanent disabilities specifically mentioned in that section without 
taking account of your occupation.
If the disability suffered does not relate to a specific disability or a part of the body 
mentioned in the table of benefits in section B, then we will assess the degree of disability 
suffered as a percentage of the whole body. […]”
The policy also provides for deduction for existing medical conditions as follows:
“2. Existing medical conditions
If you have an existing physical or medical condition, we will ask an independent 
medical consultant to:
i.
assess whether your existing physical or medical condition has 
contributed to your post-accident disability and, if so
ii.
assess the difference between your physical or medical condition before 
and your disability after the accident.
Any payment will be based on the difference, expressed as a percentage and applied to 
the appropriate item in the table of benefits.”
has the claim been declined unfairly?
The relevant rules and industry guidance say that AIG has a responsibility to handle 
claims promptly and fairly.
I think that AIG’s proposal to agree instructions for a new medical report and then 
reassess the claim is fair. But I think its reasoning hasn’t been clear throughout its 
handling of Mr S’ claim. So, I set out below what I think is fair in this case:

AIG didn’t give Mr S advice about the suitability of the policy. So, it was for     
Mr S to decide whether the policy met his needs. I think that AIG gave Mr S 
clear information that wasn’t misleading and I don’t think that it mis-sold the 
policy to Mr S.

This dispute is about how Mr S’ claim is assessed and how the policy is 
interpreted. I don’t think that AIG was required to draw Mr S’ attention to 
particular parts of the policy.

It’s common ground that Mr S suffered a permanent injury but he hasn’t 
suffered loss of his entire back or spine. So, Mr S’ permanent disability doesn’t 
fit into item 9 quoted above, as he has some use of his spine.
Ref: DRN2764356

6

Mr S’ claim should be assessed under item 17, as his is a permanent disability 
not listed in the table. This general section says that if there’s an injury relating 
to a body part mentioned in the list of permanent disabilities, but it’s not a total 
loss of use of that body part, AIG will consider the degree of loss of use and pay 
a percentage of what it would’ve paid if the entire body part had been lost. For 
example, if the medical evidence shows 20% loss of use of the spine, AIG will 
pay 20%.

20% of what? Mr S says that the benefit limit of up to £20,000 per unit in item 
17- the general section - is the relevant one. AIG says it’s the fixed sum of 
£7,000 per unit under item 9 - the spine section. The general section is 
different from the other section as it says “up to” £20,000 per unit, so it’s not a 
fixed sum. I think that’s because the highest amount for an injury under section 
B is £20,000 per unit, so reference to that in the general section allows AIG to 
pay up to that amount per unit where that’s the amount for that particular 
disability.

The wording of the policy links the payment for a partial loss of use of the back 
or spine to the relevant item within the table of benefits. That’s logically 
consistent, as if it’s £7,000 per unit for the loss of the entire back or spine, it’s 
not fair or reasonable to receive £20,000 per unit for less serious permanent 
disability affecting partial use of the back or spine. I think it’s fair and reasonable 
to use the fixed sum of £7,000 per unit as the basis of the calculation.

Mr S’ disability relates to a part of the body mentioned in the table of benefits, 
so it’s not appropriate to assess the degree of disability suffered as a 
percentage of the whole body. The correct assessment is the degree of 
disability compared to loss of the entire back or spine.

The policy provides that there’ll be a deduction for any pre-existing medical 
conditions. The medical report will deal with the extent of any pre-existing 
medical conditions, having regard to Mr S’ medical records.

I’m not persuaded by the argument that any previous injury occurred during the 
period of cover, so can’t be pre-existing. Under the terms of the policy, AIG is 
looking at whether any pre-existing conditions contributed to Mr S’ post 
accident disability for the claim he’s actually made. It’s irrelevant that Mr S’ 
previous injuries would be eligible for a claim in their own right, as he didn’t 
make those claims. 

I don’t think I need to deal with Mr S’ concerns about the medical reports by 
AIG’s appointed experts as AIG has said that Mr S can choose an expert from a 
list of three it suggests. I think that’s fair. That expert will effectively be a jointly 
appointed expert and should lead to the parties agreeing the issue about the 
degree of Mr S’ disability and any relevant pre-existing medical conditions. Mr S 
may choose to get his own report and it would be fair and reasonable for AIG to 
consider it.

AIG’s initial handling of Mr S’ claim was muddled. AIG is the expert here and 
we’d expect it to get this right. It has offered Mr S compensation of £500 
plus interest in relation to its handling of the complaint. I think that’s fair.
Ref: DRN2764356

7
my provisional decision
My provisional decision is that the offer AIG has already made in relation to 
reassessing Mr S’ claim and inviting him to choose from a list of three consultants is 
fair. In reassessing Mr S’ claim it should have regard to what I’ve said above. I think 
that the compensation AIG previously offered in relation to its handling of the complaint 
is fair.
Ref: DRN2764356

text:
K820x#14
complaint
Mr L complains that HSBC Life (UK) Limited turned down a claim made under his income 
protection policy. He also complains about the sale of the policy. 
background
In March 2013, Mr L took out the policy. The aim of the policy was to pay an income if he 
couldn’t work because of accident or illness.
On 14 December 2015, Mr L stopped work and later submitted a claim to HSBC. This was 
turned down, because the policy excludes any chronic illness that was suffered before the 
policy started. Mr L had stopped work because of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease 
(COPD). But as he’d been diagnosed with this before the policy was taken out, HSBC 
thought it fell within the policy exclusion. Unhappy with this, Mr L brought a complaint to this 
service. 
Our investigator recommended the complaint be partly upheld. She accepted that Mr L had 
been diagnosed with COPD before the policy started. But she thought the evidence 
supported that regardless of his COPD, Mr L couldn’t work because of depression. The 
investigator recommended HSBC reassess Mr L’s claim for depression. She also thought it 
should pay him £200 compensation for failing to do this previously. The investigator didn’t 
think the policy had been mis-sold. 
I issued my provisional decision on 11 September 2017. My provisional findings were:
“claim
The policy says:
“A claim…will not be paid if it is caused directly or indirectly from:

Any Chronic Illness from which the Life Insured knowingly suffered on 
the commencement date.”
‘Chronic illness’ is defined as:
“A disease, illness or injury which has at least one of the following characteristics:

It needs long term monitoring, consultations, check-ups, examinations 
or tests;

It continues indefinitely and has no known cure;

It comes back or is expected to come back;

It is permanent; and/or;

The Life Insured needs to be rehabilitated or specially trained to cope with 
it.”
Mr L was signed off work because of COPD. I see that shortly after Mr L stopped work, his 
GP explained that Mr L’s quality of life was severely affected by the restrictions of his COPD, 
and that his breathlessness meant he was unable to hold down his job. 
I’ve looked at Mr L’s medical notes and there are numerous appointments relating to his 
COPD going back to 2010, which was before he took out the policy. The NHS says that the 
Ref: DRN2847325

2
condition can’t be cured or reversed. I’m therefore satisfied that Mr L’s COPD was a chronic 
illness that he knowingly suffered from when the policy started.
Mr L says he was also unable to work because of eye floaters. But I haven’t seen any 
medical evidence to support that this problem was preventing him from working. I 
understand he’d had eye floaters for many years, and had been able to work despite that.
The investigator noted that Mr L also experienced anxiety and depression, and that his GP 
had said in June 2016 that he wouldn’t be fit to work because of that. The investigator 
thought that HSBC should have considered a claim from the date Mr L’s depression stopped 
him from working. 
For a claim to be payable, Mr L must satisfy the policy’s waiting period (also known as a 
‘deferred period’). The policy says the waiting period will be the later of:

13 weeks from the date of your incapacity, or

The date your employer stops paying you, or

The date your income from your employer reduces to or below the level of Statutory 
Sick Pay (SSP)
Mr L’s claim form was completed around 10 weeks after he stopped work. At that time, his 
only income was SSP. Therefore, the relevant waiting period for this claim was the first 13 
weeks of Mr L’s incapacity (14 December 2015 to 13 March 2016). That means Mr L must 
show he wasn’t able to work throughout this whole 13 week waiting period and beyond. 
I see that before Mr L stopped work in December 2015, the last reference to his anxiety and 
depression was in July 2015. At that time, his GP noted he was less anxious and feeling 
much brighter. He’d completed some counselling sessions and was doing well. The GP 
continued to prescribe antidepressants. 
There’s no further mention of Mr L’s anxiety and depression until May 2016 (two months 
after the waiting period had ended). Mr L’s GP explained it was the extent of Mr L’s 
breathlessness that was preventing him from working, but also said that he does have a co-
diagnosis of depression with anxiety, but this was “…currently responding well to medication 
and not linked to him being unable to work.”
It’s therefore apparent that Mr L’s anxiety and depression wasn’t the reason he couldn’t work 
throughout the 13 week waiting period. 
It seems the situation then changed, because in June 2016 the GP said “In addition to his 
chest problems he is also suffering from depression and anxiety and at present he wouldn’t 
be fit to work anyway because of his depression, whatever the state of his chest.” 
Whilst this supports that Mr L couldn’t work in June 2016 because of his depression, as I’ve 
said, the relevant period that HSBC needs to consider is the 13 week waiting period. 
Although the investigator thought HSBC should have started a new claim for depression 
from a later date to the one when Mr L stopped work, I disagree. That’s because the policy 
explains a claim can only be made if Mr L had been in active employment (working for at 
least 16 hours per week and receiving a wage) immediately before the illness or injury. Mr L 
wasn’t in active employment before June 2016, as he’d already stopped work due to his 
COPD.
Ref: DRN2847325

3
Although the investigator thought HSBC hadn’t considered Mr L’s depression when 
assessing his claim, I see that it addressed this in its letter declining his claim. So I’m 
satisfied that HSBC did take it into consideration, but found that Mr L’s depression hadn’t 
prevented him from working throughout the waiting period. 
I’m sorry to disappoint Mr L, but I think HSBC acted reasonably in declining his claim. 
sale of the policy
Mr L has also complained about the sale of the policy. He said the adviser told him to cancel 
his existing life insurance and critical illness cover, and take out the income protection policy. 
He thinks this was poor advice, as he may have been able to make a successful permanent 
total disability claim under that policy if it was still in force. He also says he wasn’t made 
aware that the income protection policy excluded chronic conditions.
Mr L met with the adviser in 2013 because he was purchasing a new property and wanted to 
take out a new mortgage. The adviser arranged a new mortgage for £107,120 over an 18 
year term. 
I’ve looked at the information from the time of sale, and the fact-find says that Mr L had a 
decreasing life insurance policy with critical illness. This policy was to protect Mr L’s existing 
mortgage and had a sum assured at that time of £12,475 (this would have continued to 
decrease each year). There’s no mention of the adviser recommending that Mr L cancel this 
policy. But I understand Mr L did cancel it in 2013. I assume that was because the sum 
assured of £12,475 wasn’t sufficient to cover his new mortgage. 
Mr L has questioned why the adviser didn’t recommend that he top-up this policy, given that 
he was taking out a new mortgage. 
After meeting with Mr L, the adviser recorded details of their conversation in a Financial 
Planning Report (FPR). The adviser does note in the FPR that Mr L didn’t want to review life 
insurance or critical illness, but it was strongly recommended he review these areas so the 
adviser could assess the right level of cover for him. I’m therefore satisfied the adviser 
wanted to look into Mr L’s need for life and critical illness cover, but Mr L didn’t want this.
The FPR notes that Mr L did have a need for income protection cover. The adviser recorded 
that Mr L said he would receive six months full sick pay, and then six months half pay from 
his employer. The adviser recommended Mr L take out £1,219 monthly benefit under the 
policy. This was his maximum available benefit. This would be paid after 13 weeks, or when 
his pay dropped to SSP levels, whichever was later. I see this waiting period was the only 
option under the policy. The adviser recommended Mr L use his contingency fund when he 
was receiving six months half sick pay (as presumably his half pay would still be higher than 
SSP levels).
Mr L turned down the adviser’s recommendations, and the adviser recorded that Mr L 
wanted to instead take out a monthly benefit of £500. However, I see from the policy 
schedule that the eventual monthly benefit taken out was £300. Mr L was aware this wasn’t 
the full cover he could take out, but it was noted he thought some cover was better than 
none.
I don’t know why Mr L told the adviser he would receive full sick pay for six months, followed 
by half pay for a further six months, when it seems this hasn’t been the case. But I don’t 
Ref: DRN2847325

4
think this makes a difference to the matter, given that there was only one waiting period 
available. 
Mr L says he told the adviser that he had a chest complaint, but the adviser didn’t ask any 
further questions about this. But HSBC has confirmed the application wasn’t medically 
underwritten, instead it excluded chronic conditions. 
Like the investigator, I’m satisfied that the FPR made it clear that any chronic condition Mr L 
already had would be excluded. 
Overall, I don’t find that the income protection policy was mis-sold. And I haven’t seen any 
evidence that Mr L was advised to cancel his existing life and critical illness cover.”
I invited both parties to provide me with any further comments they wished to make. 
However, neither party had any further comments. 
my findings
I’ve reconsidered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint. But as neither party has provided any 
further comments, I see no reason to change my provisional findings. 
my final decision
My final decision is that I don’t uphold this complaint.
Under the rules of the Financial Ombudsman Service, I’m required to ask Mr L to accept or 
reject my decision before 6 November 2017.
Chantelle Hurn-Ryan
ombudsman
Ref: DRN2847325

text:
K820x#14
complaint
Ms W has complained about advice she received from Private Medicine Intermediaries Ltd in 
connection with her private medical insurance policies.
background
In 2011 Ms W contacted PMI and asked if it could arrange private medical insurance for her. 
She already had private medical insurance, but she was unhappy with the price.
PMI obtained a quote for Ms W with another insurer that excluded cover for three medical 
conditions, including, “pain in left knee”. Ms W asked PMI whether the exclusions could be 
lifted. PMI contacted the insurer which said the exclusion for pain in the left knee could be 
reviewed in the following circumstances:
“If resolved with medication or rest – 12 months symptom & treatment free
If resolved with treatment other than medication or rest – 18 months symptom and treatment 
free”
PMI gave Ms W the above information and she cancelled her existing policy and took out a 
new policy with the other insurer.
In 2013 Ms W needed an operation on her left knee. She contacted the insurer and asked it 
to remove the exclusion. She told the insurer she had previously been symptom and 
treatment free for the required period. The insurer declined this request and kept the 
exclusion on the policy. Ms W had her operation on the NHS.
Ms W complained to PMI that she had been misled regarding the process for removal of the 
exclusion and that it had not assisted her in having the exclusion removed.
PMI didn’t uphold Ms W’s complaint and she referred it to this service.
our initial conclusions
Our adjudicator didn’t recommend the complaint should be upheld. He thought PMI had 
brought the exclusions and what would need to happen for them to be removed to Ms W’s 
attention. He didn’t think PMI should have done any more to have the exclusions reviewed or 
removed.
Ms W didn’t agree with our adjudicator’s conclusions. She says she only purchased the 
policy through PMI because she was misled about the review process.
my findings
I’ve considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint.
I’ve seen copies of emails between Ms W, PMI and the insurer from the time Ms W took out 
the policy. I’m satisfied that Ms W should have been aware of the exclusions on the policy 
and the criteria she needed to meet if she wanted the insurer to review them. I think PMI 
gave Ms W enough information to enable her to make an informed decision on whether to 
switch policies.
Ref: DRN3027461

2
I don’t think Ms W was misled regarding the possibility of having the exclusions removed. 
She was told that the insurer would review the exclusions if she met the criteria, not that it 
would remove them. It was the insurer who would decide if Ms W met the criteria for a 
review and whether to remove the exclusions. PMI couldn’t be held responsible for the 
insurer’s decision.
Ms W has referred to a letter she received from PMI in August 2012 that she says shows 
PMI were actively involved in reviewing the terms of her policy. I’m not satisfied this is 
correct. It seems to me that the letter is simply an invitation by PMI to investigate the 
availability of other policies at the time Ms W’s policy came up for renewal.
I’m not persuaded that it was reasonable for Ms W to expect PMI to prompt her to ask for a 
review of the exclusions. Ms W was aware of the criteria for review and only she would have 
known if and when the criteria had been met.
At the time she asked the insurer to remove the exclusion regarding her left knee, Ms W 
needed an operation on that knee. I don’t think it was reasonable for her to expect the 
insurer to remove the exclusion in those circumstances and I don’t think PMI could have 
assisted her to have it removed.
In all the circumstances, I’m satisfied that PMI treated Ms W fairly and reasonably, gave her 
the assistance she was entitled to expect and didn’t mislead her.
my final decision
For the reasons I’ve given, my final decision is I don’t uphold this complaint. I make no 
award against Private Medicine Intermediaries Ltd.
Under the rules of the Financial Ombudsman Service, I’m required to ask Ms W to accept or 
reject my decision before 12 September 2016.
Charles Bacon
ombudsman
Ref: DRN3027461

text:
K821x#15
complaint
Ms E has complained on behalf of the estate of her late father, Mr E, about the decision 
made by The Society of Lloyd’s (SoL) to refuse a claim under his personal accident policy. 
background 
Mr E had a personal accident policy that paid £60,000 on his accidental death. He had a fall 
and was admitted to hospital. Whilst in hospital, he developed an infection and sadly died. 
Following his death, Ms E made a claim on behalf of his estate for accidental death benefit. 
SoL refused the claim as it didn’t think Mr E’s accident was a significant contributing factor to 
his death. It noted that he was in poor health before he died, and thought that this was the 
reason for his death. Ms E disagreed with SoL and brought a complaint here on behalf of 
Mr E’s estate. 
I issued a provisional decision on 13 September 2016. My provisional findings were as 
follows:
The policy explains that benefit will be payable if an insured person suffers an accidental 
injury which is the sole cause of their death. 
Mr E’s death certificate lists three main causes of death – multi organ failure, sepsis and 
hospital acquired pneumonia. 
An examination of Mr E’s medical records was undertaken by an independent medical 
examiner (Dr D). Dr D was asked by SoL if Mr E’s fall and subsequent fractured hip 
contributed to his early death. He was also asked to give his opinion on the likely life 
expectancy of Mr E, given his age and state of health. 
Dr D noted that Mr E had a number of medical conditions and thought he had a life 
expectancy of 3.2 years at the time of his death. But he said “I am in no doubt that the fall, 
fractured hip, operative fixation and subsequent hospitalisation caused his [Mr E’s] 
premature death”. He went onto explain that in his opinion, Mr E’s life was shortened by 
approximately three years. 
Since the adjudicator issued her recommendations, SoL has gone back to Dr D with further 
questions. It asked him if he thinks Mr E’s death was 100% attributable to the fall and 
resultant hospital stay. It also asked him to give an opinion on the likelihood of someone 
dying as a result of the fall, if it had happened to someone in a good state of health. 
Dr D responded to say there can be no doubt that the fall and subsequent hospitalisation 
was the direct cause of Mr E’s death. But he also explained there was evidence regarding 
the effect of co-morbidities (presence of additional medical conditions), and that the 
presence of three or more co-morbidities is the strongest pre-operative risk for mortality. 
Dr D said it wasn’t possible to put a percentage figure to this, but said “one can say that the 
presence of his [Mr E’s] multiple co-morbidities had a significant impact on his post-operative 
survival.”
It’s unfortunate (although understandable) that Dr D didn’t feel able to put a percentage on 
the contribution that Mr E’s existing medical conditions had on his death. But he’s explained 
that Mr E’s pre-existing conditions had a significant impact on his post-operative survival, so 
Ref: DRN3233502

2
I do need to take this into account. However, it’s also the case that Mr E wouldn’t have died 
when he did, had he not had the fall. 
Taking into account all the information, I think a reasonable way forward would be for SoL to 
pay 50% of the claim.
I invited both parties to provide me with any further comments they wished to make.
Ms E responded with the following points:

It was unfair that SoL was able to further question Dr D after he provided his initial 
medical report. She doesn’t think I should take into account the further information 
provided by Dr D. 

Dr D made no mention of the substandard level of care Mr E received and the likely 
impact this would have on his survival chances. Ms E’s referred to evidence that she 
thinks supports that her father received substandard care from the hospital treating 
him.

She’s questioned why I awarded interest from the date of Dr D’s first report.
SoL responded to say it thought the terminology used by Dr D (i.e. the words ‘significant 
impact’) would suggest a contributory factor that is considerably more than half. It therefore 
thinks I should award a lower percentage than 50%. 
my findings
I’ve reconsidered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint. 
Whilst Ms E has asked that I only consider the information provided in Dr D’s original report, 
it wouldn’t be appropriate for me to ignore the later evidence Dr D provided. SoL was entitled 
to ask Dr D for further clarification on his report. I don’t agree with Ms E that SoL has unfairly 
influenced Dr D to alter his responses.
Dr D doesn’t say that a factor in Mr E’s death was substandard care he received from the 
treating hospital. But he does say that the fall, the fractured hip, the operation and the 
subsequent hospitalisation caused Mr E’s premature death. So it seems Dr D did think the 
hospitalisation played a part in Mr E’s death. But this doesn’t alter that Dr D later clarified 
that he also thought Mr E’s existing medical conditions had a significant impact on his post-
operative survival.
I’ve awarded interest from the date of Dr D’s first report as I think this was the first time 
information became available to support that the claim was payable. 
Unfortunately, we don’t have a medical opinion on what contribution Mr E’s existing medical 
conditions had on his death. I take SoL’s point that Dr D acknowledged they had a significant 
impact, but I don’t think it would be appropriate for me to estimate what this would be in 
percentage terms, particularly as Dr D didn’t feel able to. 
As I explained in my provisional decision, the available evidence supports that Mr E’s 
existing medical conditions did have an impact on his death, but it also supports that if it 
weren’t for the fall, he wouldn’t have died when he did. So in the absence of a medical 
Ref: DRN3233502

3
opinion about the percentage impact Mr E’s existing medical conditions had on his death, I 
remain satisfied that 50% of the claim is a reasonable outcome in these circumstances. 
my final decision
My final decision is that I uphold this complaint. I require The Society of Lloyd’s to pay 50% 
of the claim. Interest should be added at the rate of 8% simple per annum from the date of 
Mr D’s initial report to the date of settlement.
Under the rules of the Financial Ombudsman Service, I’m required to ask Ms E on behalf of 
Mr E’s estate to accept or reject my decision before 28 October 2016.
Chantelle Hurn-Ryan
ombudsman
Ref: DRN3233502
quoted_clauses: I am in no doubt that the fall, fractured hip, operative fixation and subsequent hospitalisation caused his [Mr E’s] premature death
one can say that the presence of his [Mr E’s] multiple co-morbidities had a significant impact on his post-operative survival.

text:
K820x#14
complaint
Mr S says Canada Life Limited has unfairly refused his critical illness claim. He’s also 
unhappy because it didn’t give him any terms and conditions.
background
Mr S joined the group critical illness scheme offered by his employer in 2011. The cover is 
provided to Mr S’s employer by Canada Life, via a broker.  
  
In 2015, Mr S became unwell and needed surgery. He made a claim for ‘heart attack’ on his 
policy. Canada Life didn’t think the claim was payable. But it said how, in any event, Mr S 
couldn’t have had a claim met. It said Mr S had hypertension since 2001, which was a 
‘related condition’. Canada Life’s policy excludes pre-existing conditions, and this includes 
related ones.  
Mr S was unhappy and made a complaint. Canada Life wouldn’t change its view. It did pay 
Mr S £300 as it felt it could have been clearer in the first instance, when it told him about the 
unsuccessful claim.  
Mr S brought a complaint to our service. He felt Canada Life had unfairly excluded his claim. 
He hadn’t been given any policy terms. He therefore didn’t know of the exclusion – and if 
he’d done so, he might’ve known to take cover out elsewhere. Mr S feels it’s unfair for 
insurers like Canada Life to offer cover in this way, without proper underwriting.   
Our adjudicator didn’t think Canada Life had done anything wrong. She looked at the policy 
wording and thought the exclusion did apply to Mr S.   
She also didn’t feel Canada Life was responsible for supplying the policy terms to Mr S. She 
noted that duty rested with his employer.  
Mr S didn’t agree. He felt the claim refusal was morally wrong. He’d been for annual 
medicals showing he had high blood pressure, yet nobody had made him aware of the policy 
exclusions. And he didn’t have the means to review the policy wording online, as Canada 
Life had noted he could.  
Mr S said he felt Canada Life ought to be responsible for the loss of his claim – he’d 
previously held personal critical illness cover but cancelled it after joining his employer’s 
scheme.  
The complaint has now been passed to me.  
my findings
I’ve considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint.
I was sorry to learn of Mr S’s illness. I realise it was important for him to hold critical illness 
cover, and why he’s now naturally upset to find his employer’s policy had exclusions.  
I must look at the complaint as it rests with the business it’s been brought against. That 
means the scope of this decision is limited to whether Canada Life has done anything wrong. 
Ref: DRN3401808

2
Canada Life’s relationship as an insurer is with its policyholder. That is not Mr S – that is his 
employer. Businesses (like Mr S’s employer) are able to consider what terms to offer 
members of their insurance schemes. Mr S’s policy comes with exclusions in respect of pre-
existing conditions.
The policy says:
“No benefit will be payable under the Policy in respect of:

an insured illness in respect of which any related condition (as defined on page 11 of 
this policy and further detailed in this section) existed at any time prior to entry to the 
scheme by the insured person, unless at least two consecutive years have elapsed 
since the insured person last:
o
had symptoms of; or
o
received treatment or advice in respect of such related condition.”
The policy then goes on to set out related conditions. In Mr S’s case this says:
“Heart attack
Hypertension or any disease or disorders of the heart. This will include congenital 
malformations that have been treated such as heart valve defects. Any obstructive or 
occlusive arterial disease such as arteriosclerosis, plus diabetes.” 
In the two years before he joined his employer’s scheme, Mr S received continued 
medication and medical reviews for hypertension. I also realise neither party disputes Mr S 
had hypertension. He’s told us how his employer knew this. 
I can see Mr S said he feels it would be ethical for Canada Life to pay a claim. But it’s clear 
that the exclusion would apply to him. So, I don’t find Canada Life has been unfair in 
applying the policy wording to Mr S’s circumstances. Nor do I think it ought to pay a claim on 
the basis he’s suggested. 
I realise Mr S is unhappy about how the policy has been underwritten. While I appreciate 
why that is, Canada Life is not at fault for the additional benefits an employer may or may not 
offer to its staff. Mr S was a member of his employer’s scheme; this is not something 
Canada Life can influence. It simply offers group cover to the employer as a policyholder. 
Because of the variable nature of flexible employment benefits, Canada Life doesn’t 
underwrite each member of a policyholder’s scheme separately. I know Mr S is unhappy 
about the way group policies operate. He feels he should have answered medical questions. 
But it is common practice with such policies to apply exclusions to pre-existing or related 
conditions. We aren’t a regulator, and so it’s not my role to determine the fairness of that 
practice. My role is to see if Canada Life has fairly interpreted the policy terms in respect of 
Mr S’s claim.  
Canada Life’s shown how it sent policy documentation to the broker and employer. Group 
policy information was also made available on its website. Though Mr S says he wasn’t 
shown any paperwork in the five years he paid for cover, he didn’t make a payment to 
Canada Life. That payment was taken from his salary by his employer. Canada Life hasn’t 
behaved unfairly in supplying the relevant paperwork to the employer, via its broker.
Ref: DRN3401808

3
I understand why Mr S says someone ought to take liability for the loss of his claim, and why 
he feels he was mis-sold his cover. But Canada Life isn’t responsible for what went on 
between Mr S and his employer at the time he joined the group policy. It didn’t sell him 
cover. I can’t require it, retrospectively or otherwise, to underwrite a scheme member in a 
particular way. 
my final decision
I know my decision will be a disappointment for Mr S. However, I’m not able to uphold his 
complaint, as Canada Life hasn’t behaved unreasonably in refusing his claim or offering his 
employer group cover. 
Under the rules of the Financial Ombudsman Service, I’m required to ask Mr S to accept or 
reject my decision before 28 December 2016. 
Jo Storey
ombudsman
Ref: DRN3401808

text:
K821x#15
complaint
Miss F and Mr S complain that Mr S’s travel insurance claim has been unfairly declined by 
AWP P&C SA (AWP). 
AWP uses a separate company to deal with claims on its behalf. For ease, whenever I refer 
to AWP in this decision, I’m including the acts or omissions of those claims-handlers. 
background
Miss F and Mr S had been travelling on a round-the-world trip since October 2015. In 
March 2016 they decided to add a trip to Hawaii to their plans, and booked flights scheduled 
to fly from the Philippines to Hawaii in August 2016. 
Miss F and Mr S already had insurance with a different insurer covering them for the 
countries they’d originally planned to travel to, and excluding travel to the USA. On 6 August 
2016, while they were at the airport in the Philippines waiting for their flight to Hawaii, they 
went online and took out a policy with AWP to cover their trip to the USA.
Mr S says he started to feel unwell during the second leg of their flight to Hawaii – from 
South Korea to Honolulu. He says he felt ‘under the weather’ and thought this might be due 
to the travel. Over the next day or so, Mr S says his symptoms got worse and he saw a 
doctor on 8 August 2016. He was diagnosed with the flu and prescribed some medicine.
Over the next few days Mr S says he started to feel better but then on 12 August 2016 he 
felt significantly worse. He was admitted to hospital and diagnosed with pneumonia which 
developed into empyema requiring surgery. Mr S was eventually discharged from hospital on 
27 August 2016 and was able to fly home to the UK on 16 September 2016.
Mr S tried to make a claim on his travel insurance with AWP but his claim was declined. 
AWP relied on a clause in the policy which excludes any illness occurring within the first 72 
hours of purchasing the policy. AWP considered Mr S’s claim to relate to conditions that all 
occurred within that 72-hour period. Mr S said that although he accepted he couldn’t claim 
for the flu, he considered the pneumonia to be a new condition occurring after the 72-hour 
period.
Our investigator upheld the complaint. He didn’t think AWP could rely on the 72-hour 
exclusion in respect of Mr S’s claim for the pneumonia as he didn’t think there was enough 
evidence to conclude that the pneumonia had occurred within the first 72 hours of the 
policy’s start date.
AWP disagreed. It said, amongst other things, that flu often developed into pneumonia and 
so it was likely that Mr S had pneumonia all along, particularly as he was showing some of 
the symptoms of pneumonia within the 72-hour period.
Because the parties haven’t been able to agree, the complaint has come to me for a final 
decision.        
my findings
I’ve considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint.
Ref: DRN3403862

2
AWP wishes to rely on an exclusion clause to decline Miss F and Mr S’s claim, so I’ve 
looked at what the policy says about this. When Miss F and Mr S took out the policy, they 
were sent their policy documents by email with a covering email that included the following: 
“No claim will be met resulting from a situation occurring within the first 72 hours from 
the issue of the policy…”
AWP has also provided a screenshot to show what Miss F and Mr S would’ve seen online 
when they took out the policy. They would’ve had to tick to confirm they had read the 
following statement before being able to continue to get a quote for the insurance:
“…If cover has been taken out after you have left home to commence your trip, there 
is a waiting period of 72 hours from the issue of the policy before the insurance takes 
effect. Any illness or injury occurring during this waiting period will be considered a 
Pre-existing medical condition and not covered under the terms of this policy…”
So for AWP to exclude a claim, it would have to show that the claim was for a pre-existing 
medical condition – that is, an illness occurring within the first 72 hours from the issue of the 
policy. In Mr S’s case, the relevant dates are between 6 and 9 August 2016. AWP hasn’t 
provided a definition of “occurring” within its policy terms, so when thinking about this I’ve 
given the word its ordinary, everyday meaning.
Mr S saw a doctor on 8 August 2016 and I’ve seen the detailed notes from her examination 
which led to her diagnosing Mr S with ‘Influenza A’. Indeed, I note that the doctor carried out 
a swab test as part of her diagnosis and the results of this showed that Mr S had the flu. I 
take AWP’s point that the flu and pneumonia share some common symptoms. However, I 
don’t think this in itself is enough for me to disregard both the medical opinion of the treating 
doctor and the results of a clinical test.
As Mr S was diagnosed with the flu within 72 hours of the issue of the policy, I agree that 
AWP has applied the exclusion fairly in declining this part of Mr S’s claim.
However, I don’t think it’s fair for the exclusion to apply to Mr S’s claim for pneumonia since 
there’s no persuasive evidence that this occurred (i.e. first arose or started) within the first 72 
hours.
AWP has argued that pneumonia often develops from the flu, but I don’t think this alters the 
outcome. As I’ve explained, AWP hasn’t defined “occurred” and so I don’t think it would be 
fair to give it a broader interpretation than its ordinary, everyday meaning, which I think is as 
set out in brackets in the preceding paragraph. So, in order to agree that the pneumonia was 
excluded, I’d have to be persuaded that Mr S’s pneumonia first arose or started within the 
72-hour period – not that he had another condition which later developed into pneumonia. 
The first mention of pneumonia within the medical notes I’ve seen was on 12 August 2016 – 
outside the 72-hour period. AWP has pointed out that a doctor later noted that Mr S had 
“pneumonia acquired in the Philippines” but I can see that the notes also say “Influenza A 
Philippine acquired with pneumonia”. Nonetheless, I can understand why AWP finds these 
notes significant. But I have to weigh this against the more compelling, contemporaneous 
evidence as to Mr S’s diagnosis within the 72-hour period – that is, the diagnosis by the 
doctor he saw at that time. Taking everything into account, I think it’s most likely that the 
pneumonia “occurred” outside the 72-hour period.
Ref: DRN3403862

3
AWP has questioned why Miss F and Mr S were travelling without insurance for the USA up 
until they were waiting for their flight to the USA. Miss F and Mr S have explained that 
Hawaii wasn’t part of their original plans; and I can see that their flights were booked when 
they were already travelling. With that in mind, I don’t think it’s unreasonable that they hadn’t 
included the USA in their original insurance policy, particularly as this probably would’ve 
added an extra, unnecessary expense. They’ve also explained that they’d talked about 
getting insurance for Hawaii in the days leading up to their flight, but hadn’t got round to it 
until they were at the airport where it was easier to get online. While it’s not ideal to arrange 
insurance so close to the time of long-planned travelling (not least because of the risk of 
adverse inferences being drawn), in the circumstances I find Miss F and Mr S’s explanation 
persuasive and reasonable. 
my final decision
My final decision is that I uphold this complaint. I require AWP P&C SA to do the following:

Cover Mr S’s claim for pneumonia, subject to the rest of the policy terms and 
conditions (and our statutory cap on money awards of £150,000);

Add interest (less tax properly deductible) to any sum paid, at the simple yearly rate 
of 8%, from the date the medical/repatriation costs were incurred to the date of 
settlement
If the claim exceeds £150,000, my non-binding recommendation is that AWP also pays the 
balance of the full amount – but this isn’t something that Mr S could enforce if AWP refused 
to do so. For the avoidance of doubt, the £150,000 cap doesn’t include the interest element 
of my award, which is payable on top of that sum. 
Under the rules of the Financial Ombudsman Service, I’m required to ask Miss F and Mr S to 
accept or reject my decision before 3 May 2017.
Daniela Cirignano
Ombudsman
Ref: DRN3403862
quoted_clauses: No claim will be met resulting from a situation occurring within the first 72 hours from the issue of the policy…

…If cover has been taken out after you have left home to commence your trip, there is a waiting period of 72 hours from the issue of the policy before the insurance takes effect. Any illness or injury occurring during this waiting period will be considered a Pre-existing medical condition and not covered under the terms of this policy…
Influenza A Philippine acquired with pneumonia

text:
K821x#12
complaint
This complaint is about the decision made by AXA PPP Healthcare Limited (“AXA”) to 
decline a claim under Mrs F’s private medical insurance policy. 
background
In 2011 Mrs F was admitted to a private hospital for two months. Prior to her admission, 
Mrs F’s treating consultant psychiatrist (“Dr A”) contacted AXA to advise it that he was 
recommending that Mrs F be admitted to hospital. AXA stated it would not pay for Mrs F’s 
private treatment as her policy did not cover emergency treatment that was available on the 
NHS within six weeks. Mrs F chose to cover the costs of the private treatment herself. 
Mrs F’s husband later complained to AXA on her behalf. He argued that the treatment was 
not an emergency but necessary. He pointed out that Mrs F had previously been offered 
cognitive behavioural therapy (“CBT”) on the NHS, but because of illness she had been 
unable to attend the course. However after Dr A had assessed Mrs F, it was considered that 
she required in-patient treatment at the private hospital in question.
AXA said that, as Mrs F had been admitted to the private hospital the day after being 
assessed by Dr A, this demonstrated the urgent nature of the treatment required, and the 
policy excluded emergency treatment. It further said that it did not consider it was clinically 
necessary for Mrs F to be admitted to hospital for the treatment she received. AXA said that 
because Mrs F had missed the start date of the CBT course, it believed the decision was 
made to admit her privately instead of waiting for the next available date on the NHS, and 
that the private treatment she received would have been available through the CBT course 
under the NHS. It said it was confident that Mrs F did not have a psychiatric condition that 
warranted in-patient treatment under the terms of her cover. 
Dissatisfied with this response, Mrs F referred a complaint to this service. Our adjudicator 
upheld the complaint. He noted that throughout the course of the complaint AXA had sought 
to rely on several policy exclusions, but he was not persuaded that any of them would apply 
to Mrs F’s claim. 
AXA disagreed and requested that the complaint be referred to an ombudsman. The matter 
has therefore been passed to me to consider afresh. 
my findings
I have considered all the available evidence and arguments from outset in order to decide 
what is fair and reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint. 
Throughout the course of this complaint, AXA has raised a number of reasons why it 
considers Mrs F’s treatment should not be covered. I will consider each one in turn. 
(i) 
AXA had initially said Mrs F’s treatment would not be covered as it was an emergency and 
Mrs F could obtain the treatment through the NHS within six weeks. Although it appears AXA 
Ref: DRN3545423

2
is no longer seeking to rely on this to decline the claim, for the sake of clarity, I will address 
this point.  
The policy wording states:
“There is no cover for urgent or emergency treatment or for in-patient or day-patient 
treatment that is available on the NHS within six weeks after the date on which the treatment 
should be undertaken. Therefore it is unlikely that there will be cover under this policy for 
such psychiatric treatment.”
I am not persuaded that Mrs F’s admission to the private hospital the day after being 
assessed by Dr A indicates, by itself, that her treatment was an emergency. I say this 
because private hospitals generally have the capacity to admit patients immediately, unlike 
NHS hospitals. I further note that Dr A said that Mrs F’s husband had told AXA that Mrs F’s 
admission was necessary rather than an emergency, and Dr A agreed that this was quite 
correct. 
AXA says that because Mrs F missed the start date of the CBT course under the NHS, it 
considers she was admitted privately instead of waiting for the next available admission. 
However Dr A has said the long admission list for Mrs F’s admission under the NHS was a 
saving for her, because it would not have been the most appropriate way forward. This does 
not indicate to me that Mrs F could have had the CBT course within six weeks on the NHS, 
and in any event, it seems Dr A did not consider the CBT course to be the most appropriate 
treatment for Mrs F. 
Accordingly, I am not persuaded that AXA can rely on the above exclusion to decline Mrs F’s 
claim. 
(ii)
AXA says it does not consider it was clinically necessary for Mrs F to be admitted to the 
hospital for the treatment she received, and that it was confident that Mrs F did not have a 
psychiatric condition that warranted in-patient treatment. AXA has further told this service 
that its criteria for in-patient psychiatric treatment is that the patient is a risk to themselves or 
to others. 
Dr A has provided a lengthy explanation to AXA as to why he considered it necessary for 
Mrs F to be admitted to hospital. I appreciate Mrs F’s case has been complicated because 
she has a number of physical health issues. However Dr A made it clear to AXA that he 
thought Mrs F had a psychosomatic disorder which was causing some of her physical 
problems. As a consultant psychiatrist, I consider he was best placed to decide upon the 
appropriate mental health treatment for Mrs F, and it is clear that he considered in-patient 
admission at the hospital in question to be necessary for her. 
Although AXA says the criteria for psychiatric in-patient treatment is that the patient must be 
a risk to themselves or to others, I find no mention of this within its policy terms. I am 
therefore not persuaded AXA can reasonably apply this to Mrs F’s claim. 
I am therefore satisfied that the evidence confirms Mrs F’s admission to hospital was 
necessary.
(iii)
Ref: DRN3545423

3
AXA has told this service it wishes to rely on the following policy exclusion:
“What we do not pay for:
(b) The monitoring of a medical condition.”
The word ‘monitoring’ suggests that observations are carried out, rather than actual 
treatment given. However the discharge summary from the hospital explained that Mrs F’s 
care plan included exploration for any psychological causes for her symptoms, as well as 
appropriate psychological interventions. It further explained that the psychological treatments 
Mrs F received took the form of various therapy programmes. 
I accept that with all treatment there is naturally some degree of monitoring of the patient. 
However it is clear from the evidence that Mrs F was admitted to hospital to receive 
treatment rather than simply for the monitoring of her conditions.
I am therefore not persuaded that AXA can rely on the above exclusion to decline the claim. 
(iv) 
AXA has told this service it also wishes to rely on the below policy exclusion:
“What we do not pay for:
(b) Psychiatric treatment of, or treatment which is in any way connected with, alcohol abuse, 
drug abuse or substance abuse.”
AXA has made reference to Mrs F being dependent upon morphine, and says that her 
admission to hospital was, in part, to try and reduce her dependence. 
I note that Mrs F became dependent on morphine after she was prescribed increased 
dosages of the medication to treat one of her conditions. I am not persuaded that this would 
be considered ‘drug or substance abuse’, as her dependency resulted inadvertently from 
medication that had been properly prescribed to her. 
In any event, Dr A has said “I categorically state that she was not admitted for the treatment 
of morphine dependence… Her morphine dependency in a hospital setting was seen as a 
disconnect and minor issue which was easily controlled with her agreement through a period 
of reduction and then cessation with her full cooperation which continued after discharge”.
Although I accept Mrs F’s dependency on morphine was treated during her hospital 
admission, Dr A’s evidence confirms it was not one of the reasons for the admission. 
Therefore even if it were the case that I agreed with AXA that Mrs F’s morphine dependence 
would be considered ‘drug or substance abuse’ - on a fair and reasonable basis, I would not 
be persuaded that Mrs F’s claim should be declined based on the above exclusion.  
In summary, I am not persuaded that AXA has shown that Mrs F’s claim should be declined 
under any of its policy terms. Accordingly, I consider her claim should be paid. Although AXA 
has discounted contracted rates with the private hospital in question, I note that Mrs F had to 
pay the full costs herself because of AXA’s refusal to accept her claim. I therefore consider 
AXA should reimburse Mrs F in full for her loss in this respect, regardless of the discounted 
rates it would have received, had it accepted her claim from the outset. 
Ref: DRN3545423

4
I also consider Mrs F has been caused distress and inconvenience by AXA’s handling of the 
claim. It has changed its reasoning for declining the claim throughout the course of Mrs F’s 
complaint, without properly communicating its reasoning to her. I therefore consider a 
payment of £200 would be appropriate in the circumstances. 
my final decision
For the reasons set out above, it is my final decision that this complaint should be upheld. 
I require AXA PPP Healthcare Limited to pay the claim. As Mrs F has paid the costs herself, 
she should be reimbursed in full directly, and interest awarded to the settlement amount at 
the rate of 8% interest per annum from the date she paid for the treatment to the date of 
settlement. 
In addition, I also require AXA PPP Healthcare Limited to pay £200 compensation to Mrs F.
Chantelle Hurn
ombudsman
Ref: DRN3545423

Therefore it is unlikely that there will be cover under this policy for such psychiatric treatment.
What we do not pay for: (b) The monitoring of a medical condition.
What we do not pay for: (b) Psychiatric treatment of, or treatment which is in any way connected with, alcohol abuse, drug abuse or substance abuse.

text:
K820x#14
complaint
Mr D has complained that Covea Insurance plc has still refused to pay his claim under his 
personal accident policy, having now received medical evidence.
background
Mr D originally brought a complaint to us concerning Covea’s refusal to pay his claim. The 
adjudicator recommended Covea should obtain some medical evidence to clarify whether 
the reason for Mr D’s hospital stay was because of an accident.
Covea did this and it now says the reason for his hospital admission was due to a pre-
existing condition and not as a result of an accident. Mr D has remained unhappy and 
brought a second complaint to us concerning this.
The adjudicator who investigated it didn’t think it should be upheld. She thought the medical 
evidence didn’t show that the reason for Mr D’s admission to hospital was because of an 
accident. Instead it was due to a pre-existing medical condition. Mr D didn’t agree, so his 
complaint has been passed to me to decide.
my findings
I’ve considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint.
Mr D’s policy only pays any benefit for a hospital admission if the injury he had, is because 
of an accident.  It defines an ‘accidental injury’ as follows:
‘Physical injury occurring during the period of insurance, which is solely and directly 
the result of accidental, outward, violent and visible means.’
So in order to be able to claim this benefit, Mr D has to show he had an accident, which 
caused his injury and hospital admission. Unfortunately, the medical report Covea obtained 
doesn’t say this. It says Mr D had suffered from back pain before he took out this policy and 
the reason he was admitted to hospital was due to the fact his back condition had got worse 
over time. The medical expert doesn’t think the cough or sneeze which Mr D suffered from 
his chest infection, which caused him such increased pain at the time, needing him to be 
admitted to hospital, could be considered to be an accident.
The medical expert carefully went through all of Mr D’s medical notes and records and was 
of the view that he had been suffering his back condition for quite some time. So I don’t think 
the reason Mr D was admitted to hospital was caused by an accident that’s covered by this 
policy. 
Mr D’s policy also says:
‘We will not pay any benefit which is the direct result of is contributed to by
a) Any physical, mental or medical condition of which you were aware or ought to 
have been aware which existed before cover started under this policy.’
It’s also clear to me that the medical report explains that Mr D had suffered from back 
problems for quite some time before Mr D took this policy out. The medical report goes on to 
Ref: DRN4044626

2
explain that the reason for his hospital admission was due to a gradual decline of his back 
condition which the sneeze or cough made worse all of a sudden.
So I don’t think Covea has done anything wrong in refusing to pay Mr D’s claim as its policy 
terms exclude such a claim, very clearly.
my final decision
So whilst I appreciate Mr D will be disappointed with my decision, for the reasons I’ve 
discussed above, it’s my final decision that I don’t uphold this complaint.
Under the rules of the Financial Ombudsman Service, I’m required to ask Mr D to accept or 
reject my decision before 21 March 2016.
Rona Doyle
ombudsman
Ref: DRN4044626
