We will not pay any benefit which is the direct result of is contributed to by a) Any physical, mental or medical condition of which you were aware or ought to have been aware which existed before cover started under this policy.

text:
K820x#14
complaint
Mr S complains about the sale of a ‘Business Start-up Essential Cover’ policy by HSBC 
Bank plc. 
background
In 2001, Mr S was sold the policy by an HSBC adviser. The policy paid a monthly benefit if 
he couldn’t perform three essential activities of daily life because of illness or injury. 
In 2016, Mr S stopped work because he needed an operation. He tried to make a claim 
under the policy, but this wasn’t successful as he didn’t meet the above criteria. Mr S 
complained to HSBC about the sale of the policy. He said he’d been led to believe benefit 
would be paid if he couldn’t do his occupation. 
Our adjudicator didn’t recommend the complaint be upheld. She thought Mr S had been 
made aware of how the policy worked at the time of sale.
Mr S didn’t accept our adjudicator’s findings, so the matter’s been passed to me.  
my findings
I’ve considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint. 
Mr S’s policy has an ‘activities of daily life’ definition of incapacity. That means that for a 
claim to be paid, he has to show that his illness prevents him from carrying out three 
essential activities of daily living, such as: - walking a certain distance, lifting a certain 
weight, or walking up and down a flight of stairs. 
This definition of incapacity is far more restrictive than others on the market. It’s usually 
offered to unemployed people, or people with occupations that are considered ‘high risk’ 
(such as manual occupations). I don’t think there’s anything wrong with selling a policy with 
this definition of incapacity, so long as the restrictive nature of the cover is fully explained at 
the time of sale. I’ve therefore considered the available evidence from when the policy was 
sold. 
HSBC has provided a fact-find that was completed at the time of sale. This explained that 
Mr S wanted to protect his income as he’d recently started his own business. It also said he 
wanted to take advantage of the policy in question, as it offered 50% discount off premiums 
for the first year and offered a waiting period of four weeks. 
After the initial meeting, the adviser sent Mr S a letter outlining his recommendations. This 
noted that Mr S wanted the maximum benefit of £1,000 a month, payable after a four week 
waiting period. The cover ended at age 50, and would cost just over £40 a month. The 
adviser said that Mr S thought this cover satisfied his needs and budget. The letter then said:
“This cover will provide a regular benefit to help you if you should be unable to perform three 
essential activities of daily life as a result of injury, serious illness or disability. I have 
explained to you the Abilities Tests which are part of the claims process to determine 
incapacity.”
Ref: DRN4292602

2
The adviser then explained that the cover was the most cost effective way to obtain the 
benefit, and that the type of cover was the most suitable for Mr S, as he didn’t have sufficient 
evidence of established business income to be eligible for other income protection options. 
The adviser also noted the premium (discount) offer would reduce Mr S’s outgoings in the 
first 12 months.
I’ve looked at the policy terms, and see that the maximum benefit payable can’t exceed the 
greater of 50% of earnings, or the full benefit shown in the schedule, or the ‘maximum initial 
benefit’ of £12,000.
As Mr S had only just started his company, he’d chosen to take out the ‘maximum initial 
benefit’ option, which initially provided £12,000 per annum of cover. This meant that even if 
his earnings were very low in the first few years whilst he built up his company, if he made a 
successful claim, he’d receive at least £1,000 a month, regardless of his actual earnings. 
The other income protection options referred to by the adviser would likely include the more 
comprehensive ‘own’ or ‘suited’ occupation, where benefit is payable if the insured isn’t able 
to carry out his usual occupation, or an occupation to which he’s suited by way of training, 
experience, or education. When calculating benefit payable under this type of cover, an 
insurer would normally take into account previous earnings. As Mr S had only just started his 
company and didn’t have previous evidence of earnings, the adviser presumably concluded 
that such policies were unsuitable for Mr S as he wouldn’t initially be able to claim any 
benefit under them.
I’ve seen no evidence to suggest that the adviser is wrong and that Mr S would have been 
able at the time of sale to obtain a policy which, regardless of his earnings, would have paid 
benefit if he were unable to do his job, particularly after only a four week waiting period.
Even if it turned out that such a policy was available and should have been recommended to 
Mr S, I have to ask myself whether Mr S has been disadvantaged by any wrong advice. It’s 
likely that such a policy would be more expensive than his existing policy and therefore the 
extra amount he would have had to pay in premiums since 2001 would likely be significantly 
more than what HSBC would pay for his recent claim, which I understand lasted around 
three months.
Mr S says he was led to believe the policy would pay benefit if he couldn’t carry out his 
occupation. But the evidence from the time of sale doesn’t support his recollections. Instead, 
it confirms that he was made aware benefit would be payable if he wasn’t able to perform 
three essential activities of daily life. The adviser also said in the recommendations letter that 
the ‘abilities tests’ had been explained to Mr S. If that wasn’t the case, then I’d have 
expected Mr S to question this after receiving the letter. But it seems he didn’t do so. 
Mr S says he didn’t receive a copy of the recommendations letter. I can’t now establish this. 
But it was addressed to Mr S, and Mr S hasn’t said the address was wrong.  
I see that Mr S also signed the fact-find which confirmed he’d received a copy of the policy 
brochure. This was also confirmed in the adviser’s recommendations letter. I’m satisfied the 
policy document clearly sets out the scope of cover.   
Mr S has provided a copy of a letter sent to him in 2013 by HSBC. This letter was about a 
review of his premium amount for this policy. The letter says “Your HSBC Life policy is 
Ref: DRN4292602

3
designed to replace a loss of income if the life insured is unable to work because of illness or 
injury.”
I agree this is incorrect. I imagine it’s a standard letter that’s sent out to all income protection 
policyholders, and HSBC may want to look into changing this. But the relevant information 
for me to consider is the evidence from the time of sale, as it was this information that Mr S 
would have relied upon in making his decision to take out the policy. I’m satisfied the 
evidence from the time of sale supports that the restrictive nature of the policy was explained 
to Mr S. I therefore don’t find that the policy was mis-sold.
my final decision
My final decision is that I don’t uphold this complaint.
Under the rules of the Financial Ombudsman Service, I’m required to ask Mr S to accept or 
reject my decision before 5 June 2017.
Chantelle Hurn-Ryan
ombudsman
Ref: DRN4292602
quoted_clauses: This cover will provide a regular benefit to help you if you should be unable to perform three essential activities of daily life as a result of injury, serious illness or disability. I have explained to you the Abilities Tests which are part of the claims process to determine incapacity.
Your HSBC Life policy is Ref: DRN4292602 3 designed to replace a loss of income if the life insured is unable to work because of illness or injury.

text:
K820x#14
complaint
Mrs C has complained that Collinson Insurance Brokers Ltd sent her incorrect information 
about her income protection insurance which meant she didn’t follow the correct procedure 
when she made a claim.
background
The background to this complaint, and my provisional findings, were set out in my 
provisional decision dated 27 March 2017. A copy of this is attached and forms part of this 
final decision. In my provisional decision I invited both parties to let me have any further 
comments and evidence.
Mrs C didn’t accept my provisional decision. She maintains that Collinson sent her incorrect 
documents. She doesn’t think it was fair to expect her to cross-reference the documents she 
received when she renewed the policy with documents she had received, earlier.
Collinson accepted my provisional decision.
my findings
I’ve reconsidered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint. Having done this, I don’t intend to change 
my decision.
I don’t think the document Collinson sent Mrs C when she renewed the policy in February 
2016 was “incorrect”. It was incorrectly described as a policy document in one of the 
accompanying documents. But the document clearly said it was only a summary and didn’t 
contain all the policy terms and conditions. I still think that Collinson didn’t mislead Mrs C into 
believing she didn’t have to register as unemployed before the waiting period would start.
my final decision
For the reasons given above and in my provisional decision, my final decision is I don’t 
uphold this complaint. I make no award against Collinson Insurance Brokers Ltd.
Under the rules of the Financial Ombudsman Service, I’m required to ask Mrs C to accept or 
reject my decision before 8 June 2017.
Charles Bacon
ombudsman
Ref: DRN4334097

2
copy of provisional decision
background
Mrs C has income protection insurance to cover her lost income if she becomes involuntarily 
unemployed. Collinson administers the insurance but it isn’t the insurer. Under the terms of the policy, 
benefit only becomes payable after a waiting period and Mrs C has to be registered as unemployed.
In April 2016 Mrs C was made redundant. She says she thought her waiting period was 90 days and 
she registered as unemployed in July 2016 shortly before the end of that period. However, she was 
then told the waiting period didn’t start until she registered as unemployed. Because of this she had to 
wait until October 2016 before she was paid anything under the policy.
Mrs C complained to Collinson that a document it sent her when her policy was renewed in February 
2016 led her to believe that she would be paid 90 days after she was made redundant, not 90 days 
after she registered as unemployed.
Collinson didn’t uphold Mrs C’s complaint. It said the policy wording shows the first day of her claim 
would be the first day she registered as unemployed.
Mrs C wasn’t happy with Collinson’s response and referred her complaint to this service.
our initial conclusions
Our adjudicator recommended the complaint should be upheld. She thought the document Collinson 
sent Mrs C in February 2016 was ambiguous and unclear and that Mrs C should receive one month’s 
benefit plus interest.
Neither Mrs C nor Collinson accepted our adjudicator’s recommendation. Collinson says it had sent 
Mrs C documents explaining the full terms of the policy. Mrs C says she thinks her claim should be 
backdated to the day she became unemployed and that Collinson should pay her 90 days benefit.
my provisional findings
I’ve considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and reasonable in the 
circumstances of this complaint.  
I’ve seen two kinds of documents that refer to the terms of Mrs C’s policy. The policy document 
contains the full terms and conditions of the policy. The other documents are summaries that set out 
key facts about the policy but don’t contain the full terms and conditions.
The policy document says:
“Waiting period means the number of days at the beginning of a claim…for which you are not eligible 
for any benefit”.
It also says:
“We will consider the first day of your claim to be the first day you are registered as unemployed”.
I think it’s clear from the above that the waiting period would start when Mrs C first registered as 
unemployed not when she stopped work.
The summary Collinson sent Mrs C in February 2016 says:
“If you become unemployed and are in receipt of [state benefit] for at least 30 consecutive days after 
the waiting period you will receive one month’s benefit”.
Ref: DRN4334097

3
Although the summary refers to “the waiting period”, it doesn’t say when it starts, but it does say it 
doesn’t contain the full terms and conditions. I think it’s reasonably clear from the policy document 
and the summary that, to make a claim, Mrs C would need to register as unemployed. The waiting 
period, in her case 60 days, would then start. If she received state benefit for 30 days after the waiting 
period expired she’d then get a month’s benefit under the policy.
In May 2014 there was a change in the insurer of the policy. Collinson sent Mrs C an email to inform 
about this and it attached the policy document and a summary to that email. I’m therefore satisfied it 
was reasonable for Collinson to think Mrs C would have been able to refer to the policy document if 
she needed to check what she had to do to make a claim.
When the policy came up for renewal in February 2016, Collinson sent Mrs C another email with 
various documents attached including a policy schedule that referred to “the enclosed …policy 
document”. However, the email attachments included a policy summary but not the policy document. 
The text of the email and an attached covering letter both refer to a policy summary.
I think, despite the reference in the schedule to a policy document, Mrs C ought to have realised she’d 
only received a summary which didn’t contain the full terms and conditions and that she’d need to 
refer to the policy document for them. If she couldn’t find the policy document she was sent in May 
2014 she could have asked Collinson for another copy.
Given the above, I’m not currently persuaded that Collinson gave Mrs C incorrect information in 
February 2016 that could reasonably have led her to believe that she didn’t need to register as 
unemployed before the waiting period would start.
my provisional decision
Subject to any additional comments and evidence I get from the parties, my provisional decision is I 
wouldn’t uphold this complaint.
Ref: DRN4334097

text:
K820x#13
complaint
Miss V has complained about The Society of Lloyd’s (SoL) over its handling of claims made 
under her personal accident policy. 
background
The background to this matter was set out in my provisional decision dated 27 February 
2015, a copy of which is attached and which forms part of my final decision.
Briefly, Miss V made a claim under her personal accident policy for permanent total 
disablement (“PTD”) as well as hospitalisation and convalescence benefits. SoL declined her 
claim for PTD but agreed to offer an ex-gratia payment for hospitalisation and 
convalescence. Miss V felt the PTD benefit should be payable. She also felt the amount paid 
under hospitalisation and convalescence was incorrect. She complained to us.
In my provisional decision, I explained why I considered that SoL had interpreted the terms 
of the policy correctly. I therefore thought it had acted reasonably in declining Miss V’s PTD 
claim and in making its offer in respect of her claim for hospitalisation and convalescence 
benefits.
I invited both parties to comment on my provisional decision.
Miss V has responded to say that she thinks SoL acted wrongly by telling her she was not 
entitled to any benefit when she first contacted it. She has said that this initial behaviour 
caused her to be suspicious of its later offer. She also has pointed out that, although my 
decision states she had been performing a sedentary role after her accident, she was put on 
sick leave completely in February 2013 and has been unable to return to any form of work 
since then.
SoL has not responded to the provisional decision.
my findings
I have considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what is fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint. Having done so, while I recognise it will 
come as a disappointment to Miss V, I see no reason to depart from my provisional decision. 
I note Miss V’s comments about SoL’s initial behaviour. However, I consider that its eventual 
offer in respect of her claim for hospitalisation and convalescence benefits was reasonable 
for the reasons previously stated. 
With regard to Miss V’s claim for PTD benefit, while I recognise her difficulties, the medical 
board that recommended her discharge from her occupation in April 2013 confirmed that, at 
that time, she was able to perform a sedentary role. If Miss V has more up-to-date medical 
evidence to demonstrate that her condition has deteriorated to the extent that she is now 
unable to perform any role, she should send this to SoL. On the basis of the available 
evidence, however, I still consider that it acted reasonably in declining her claim.
Ref: DRN4380213

2
my final decision
For the reasons given above and in my provisional decision, my final decision is that I do not 
uphold this complaint. I make no award against The Society of Lloyd’s.
Under the rules of the Financial Ombudsman Service, I am required to ask Miss V to accept 
or reject my decision before 8 May 2015.
David Poley
ombudsman
Ref: DRN4380213

3
COPY OF PROVISIONAL DECISION
complaint
Miss V has complained about The Society of Lloyd’s (SoL) over its handling of claims made under her 
personal accident policy. 
background
Miss V took out a personal accident policy with SoL in October 2007. Free cover was provided for the 
first six months, during which special terms applied. The full policy terms became applicable after this 
period finished, in April 2008. 
In February 2008, Miss V suffered accidents which caused permanent damage to her knees. This 
resulted in her undergoing a number of courses of treatment, including surgery. Unfortunately, in 
2013, Miss V was advised she would be medically discharged from her occupation. She therefore 
made a claim under her policy for permanent total disablement (“PTD”) as well as hospitalisation and 
convalescence benefits. 
SoL considered Miss V’s claims but explained that at the time of the accident, the policy was in the 
free cover period which did not provide any benefit for being totally and permanently unable to 
perform the policyholder’s own occupation. SoL, however, did agree that it would offer an ex-gratia 
payment for hospitalisation and convalescence. 
Miss V was unhappy with this response and raised a complaint. She felt the PTD benefit should be 
payable. She also felt the amount paid under hospitalisation and convalescence was incorrect as SoL 
had calculated these using the amount the policy offered at the time of the accident, rather than the 
time of the periods of hospitalisation. 
Our adjudicator recommended the complaint should be upheld in part. She was in agreement that the 
accidents occurred during the period the policy did not offer any provision for PTD – own occupation. 
The policy did provide cover for PTD – any occupation. The evidence, however, suggested that 
Miss V was able to perform a sedentary occupation – and indeed had been doing so. The adjudicator 
therefore considered that SoL had not acted unreasonably in declining Miss V’s claim for PTD benefit.
However, with regard to the ex-gratia offer for hospitalisation and convalescence benefits, the 
adjudicator noted that a SoL internal email had acknowledged that the policy’s Key Features 
document was not as clear as it might have been in describing the criteria for payment of 
convalescence benefit. It appeared to be in view of this that SoL had agreed to make an ex-gratia 
payment. The adjudicator considered that the documentation was ambiguous and therefore the 
payment of this benefit should have been offered to Miss V, not on an ex-gratia basis, but in 
accordance with the terms implied by the Key Features document. 
The adjudicator also felt the policy wording was ambiguous with regard to how the benefits would be 
calculated. The policy did not explain that the rate of benefit would be that which applied at the time of 
the accident. She noted that the policy was annually renewable and considered it would be a 
reasonable assumption of the policyholder that the applicable rate of benefit would be that which 
applied at the time of hospitalisation and convalescence. On this basis, she recommended that SoL 
should re-assess the amount payable, taking into account the relevant policy benefits at the time of 
each incident of hospitalisation and convalescence. 
SoL did not agree with this recommendation. It did not consider the contract to be ambiguous and 
said it had offered the ex-gratia payment simply to assist the policyholder. It also said that if each 
period of insurance was to be treated as a separate policy – and therefore the benefit should be 
payable as of the date of incidents rather than the accident – the injuries which gave rise to periods of 
hospitalisation and convalescence could be considered pre-existing and therefore not valid under the 
terms of the policy. 
Ref: DRN4380213

4
Because SoL did not agree with the adjudicator’s recommendations, the case has been passed to me 
for a fresh review.
my provisional findings
I have considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what is fair and reasonable in 
the circumstances of this complaint. Having done so, while I recognise it will come as a deep 
disappointment to Miss V, I am minded to depart significantly from the findings of the adjudicator and 
to not uphold this complaint.
I shall deal with the two parts of Miss V’s claim separately.
(i) claim for permanent total disablement
The policy in operation at the time of Miss V’s accident paid benefit in the event of an accidental injury 
“that totally prevents the Insured Person from attending to any and every occupation”. While I am 
satisfied that Miss V was eventually prevented through her injury from attending to her normal 
occupation, hence her medical discharge, she was not totally prevented from carrying out any 
occupation and, indeed, had been performing an alternative, sedentary role. I therefore consider that 
SoL acted reasonably in declining Miss V’s claim for permanent total disablement.  
(ii) claim for hospitalisation and convalescence benefit
The policy in operation at the time of Miss V’s accident defined the “hospitalisation” benefit as follows:
“In the event that the Insured Person is hospitalised due to accidental Bodily Injury during the period 
of insurance the Underwriters will pay £10 for each completed day of Hospitalisation, after the first 3 
(three) consecutive days of Hospitalisation, up to a maximum of £250 in all. Hospitalisation shall 
mean the admission of an Insured Person into a properly licensed hospital for treatment as an 
inpatient for a period in excess of 3 (three) consecutive days. The total benefit payable under this 
extension in respect of any one or more claims in respect of any one Insured Person shall not exceed 
£250 in all, in any one period of insurance.”
It defined the “convalescence” benefit as follows:
“In the event that the Insured Person is confined to home on the instructions of a Medical Practitioner 
following Hospitalisation due to accidental Bodily Injury during the period of insurance, the 
Underwriters will pay £25 for each complete week of confinement to home, after the first 14 days of 
confinement, up to a maximum of £250 in all. Hospitalisation shall mean the admission of an Insured 
Person into a properly licensed hospital for treatment as an inpatient for a period in excess of 3(three) 
consecutive days. The total benefit payable under this extension in respect of any one or more claims 
in respect of any one Insured Person shall not exceed £250 in all, in any one period of insurance.”
The policies in operation at the time of Miss V’s hospitalisation and convalescence offered higher 
rates of benefit (though required five consecutive days of inpatient treatment before either benefit was 
payable). 
I accept that the policies were not clear in explaining whether the relevant terms that were applicable 
to a claim were those that applied at the time of the accident or those that applied at the time of the 
hospitalisation or convalescence. However, I disagree with the adjudicator that the latter should 
therefore apply. This is because, as pointed out by SoL, the policies that were in operation at the time 
of Miss V’s spells of hospitalisation and convalescence, which were annually renewable policies, 
contain an exclusion clause stating:
“Pre-Existing Condition Exclusion
Ref: DRN4380213

5
Claims arising from any pre-existing defect, infirmity or condition for which you are receiving regular 
medical treatment, advice or consultation at the time of effecting this insurance or commencing a trip, 
whichever is the later” 
Therefore I consider that if one were to apply the terms of the later policies to Miss V’s claim, her 
claim would automatically fail on the basis of this exclusion. I therefore agree with SoL that, if Miss V 
is to receive any benefit, it is only the terms of the policy that was in operation at the time of her 
accident that can be applied to her claim.
With regard to the Key Features documents for the policies that followed the free period, I agree that 
these failed to describe adequately the criteria for convalescence benefit, referring only to the need 
for the policyholder to have been previously hospitalised, rather than hospitalised for five consecutive 
days. However, I consider that the policy itself is very clear on this matter. I therefore have to ask 
myself what Miss V would have done if the Key Features document had contained an adequate 
description of the criteria. For me to conclude, like the adjudicator, that SoL should have to pay the 
benefit in accordance with the terms suggested by the Key Features document, I would have to be 
persuaded not only that Miss V was misled into buying the policy on the basis of this failing in the Key 
Features document but also that she would have instead bought an alternative policy that offered 
cover in line with the terms implied by the Key Features document. I have seen no evidence to 
suggest that such an alternative policy was available, let alone that Miss V would have chosen to 
purchase it in preference to the SoL policy. I note that the policy schedules which Miss V received 
following her period of free cover clearly explained the requirement for five consecutive days of 
inpatient treatment before convalescence benefit became payable. On balance, I am not persuaded 
that the lack of clarity in the Key Features document made any material difference to Miss V’s 
decision to take out and subsequently renew her policy.
In view of the above, I consider that SoL was obliged only to consider Miss V’s claim for 
hospitalisation and convalescence benefit in accordance with the terms of the policy in operation at 
the time of her accident. It appears from the evidence it has submitted that it wrongly assessed her 
entitlement to benefit by reference to the need for five consecutive days of inpatient treatment, rather 
than three. However, since its ex-gratia offer was significantly more than the maximum amount to 
which she would have been entitled had it applied the strict terms of the policy, it appears that Miss V 
was not disadvantaged by this error. I am minded to conclude that SoL has acted reasonably in its 
handling of Miss V’s claim for hospitalisation and convalescence benefit.
my provisional decision
For the reasons given above, my provisional decision is to not uphold this complaint. I am minded to 
make no award against The Society of Lloyd’s.
Both parties now have one month to make further submissions before I issue my final decision.
David Poley
ombudsman
