text:
complaint
Miss M is unhappy that Legal & General Partnership Services Limited has declined a 
claim under her income protection policy.
Background
In November 2016 Miss M got in touch with L&G wanting to review one of her policies – a 
level term assurance policy. She’d taken out the policy several years earlier as a way of 
providing her children with a cash sum. But she’d recently realised the L&G policy she held 
had an end date – and she wanted a policy that would pay out on her death.  
In the discussion with L&G’s adviser, it turned out she had 3 policies –

the level term assurance policy – which she wanted to ‘convert’ to a whole of life policy

a decreasing term assurance policy to cover her outstanding mortgage; and

an income protection policy. The income protection policy was branded under the 
name of a different business - which I’ll call business B – but Miss M thought the policy 
may have been administered by L&G
After telephone conversations with L&G’s adviser, Miss M decided to retain the decreasing 
term assurance policy as recommended by the adviser.  She decided to replace the level term 
assurance policy and the income protection policy with new policies. 
The new income protection policy, which is the subject of this complaint, had a lower monthly 
premium but offered a higher monthly benefit. It also allowed Miss M to make a claim 30 days 
after being considered unfit to work – her previous policy had a deferred period of 90 days.
In early 2017, Miss M made a claim against the income protection policy. She’d been unable 
to work following a hip replacement operation. But L&G refused the claim. It says Miss M 
hadn’t answered the adviser’s questions about her health accurately and had she have done 
so, they wouldn’t have offered her the new policy.  
Miss M disagrees. She said she did tell L&G about her medical problems and because of that 
it should accept the claim. She says she spoke to the same adviser about all three policies.
Our investigator asked L&G to provide recordings of all the calls its adviser had with Miss M – 
two calls could be traced. Having listened to those calls, our investigator was of the opinion 
other calls had probably taken place but L&G couldn’t trace anything further.
Our investigator thought L&G hadn’t asked questions that were specific enough before 
recommending Miss M go ahead with the new income protection policy. He thought the term 
“sickness” wasn’t a term Miss M would relate to her particular health problems.  And because 
of that he thought Miss M had taken reasonable care when answering the adviser’s questions.  
Ref: DRN4478988

K820x#14
He also thought L&G’s adviser didn’t give Miss M the right advice based on the information 
it had received from her. The information he referred to was sent to L&G on Miss M’s 
application for the whole of life policy - not as a direct result of Miss M’s income protection 
policy application.
He suggested L&G consider the claim and pay the benefit that would have been available to 
Miss M under her previous income protection policy. He recommended the previous policy 
be reinstated and a payment of £400 made to Miss M to say sorry for the trouble and upset 
she’d been caused.
But he also gave Miss M the option of retaining the new policy knowing it would not 
cover her for claims for arthritis.
Miss M decided she’d like her previous policy reinstated. But L&G says it can’t do that 
because the policy was held by business B – and they can’t reinstate a policy belonging to 
a different company.
my findings
I’ve considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint.
When considering this case I’ve taken into account various rules and regulations that apply – 
in particular the Consumer Insurance (Disclosure and Representation) Act 2012 (CIDRA) 
and L&G’s obligations under industry standards (ICOBS).  
I previously issued a provisional decision on this complaint – a copy of which is attached, as 
it forms part of my reasoning here.
In summary, I didn’t uphold Miss M’s complaint because based on everything I’d seen, I 
thought it likely L&Gs adviser wouldn’t have recommended a new policy if he’d known more 
about Miss M’s medical problems. 
Following my provision decision, Miss M submitted further arguments in support of her 
complaint including testimony of her recollections of additional calls with L&G’s adviser. 
L&G, following a further search of their records, located recordings of three further calls with 
Miss M which I have considered as part of my final determination.
I’ll respond to what I consider to be Miss M’s main points following my provisional decision.

Miss M has said she didn’t think she needed to tell the adviser about any health 
problems she’d experienced over the proceeding12 months because she thought 
she’d already told him about that in a previous call.
The questions asked as part of the income protection policy discussions happened 
before the discussions about the whole of life plan.  The medical questions for the 
whole of life plan were asked in a separate, later call.
Ref: DRN4478988

4
I do understand that, as later calls also sometimes included reference to the income 
protection policy this may have impacted Miss M’s memory of the events.  

Miss M has said, the adviser told her taking out the new income protection policy 
wouldn’t involve any medical questions.
In the call, the adviser told Miss M there are just a few medical questions to go 
through – which she answers. These are the questions that include smoking habits, 
whether she’s waiting for tests or investigations and if she’s in good health.  

Miss M has said the L&G adviser told her he thought the new policy was similar to 
the policy held with business B, but that he’d check the details of the previous policy 
and call her back.  She said her previous policy was also with L&G so the adviser 
had a duty to compare the new policy to the previous policy terms. Miss M has also 
said L&G cancelled her previous policy so she’s surprised it can’t now reinstate it.
In one of the initial calls with Miss M, the adviser does say he’ll check the existing 
income protection policy. But in a later call he told Miss M, the policy is with business 
B and he can’t trace a policy using the reference number she’d given to him. He told 
her to check the terms before she decided to go ahead with the new policy. He also 
let her know she’d need to cancel the policy with business B because he couldn’t do 
so. 

Miss M’s has also said the adviser only gave her the positive aspects of the new 
policy and none of the negatives.
Having listened to all the calls I’ve received, between Miss M and the adviser, and 
considered the information sent to Miss M about the policy, I consider the adviser 
gave Miss M sufficient information for her to be able to decide whether to proceed 
with the new income protection policy. That’s because they discussed different levels 
of benefit and deferred periods, and premiums. Initially the discussion centred on a 
long term plan but Miss M thought the monthly cost was too high for her.
And from the information I’ve received, I consider the adviser made Miss M 
sufficiently aware of the limitations of the short term plan including the need to review 
the policy annually, the result of which might include changes in terms or in the 
monthly premium.

Miss M has said she’d have waited to have her surgery, which was not urgent, had 
she’d been aware of the 12 month clause.
Based on what I’ve seen, I think it’s reasonable to say the adviser made Miss M 
sufficiently aware the policy wouldn’t cover any pre-existing conditions for the first 
12 months of the policy.  
In determining the outcome of this complaint, I’ve carefully considered the two key aspects 
of this complaint – the eligibility of the claim and the suitability of the policy sold to Miss M.
Ref: DRN4478988

5
the claim
Based on all of the circumstances of this complaint, I consider L&G have correctly declined 
Miss M’s claim. The condition she’s claimed for pre-dated the policy and as a result, fell 
outside the terms of an eligible claim. 
I think L&G’s adviser had given Miss M sufficient information about the policy limitations 
before Miss M decided to switch to the new policy.  And Miss M was aware she had pre-
existing conditions because she talked about them during the whole of life policy application 
process.
Had Miss M told the adviser more about her health problems at that time, it’s possible the 
conversation between them may have resulted in Miss M retaining her existing policy, but 
given Miss M has said her surgery wasn’t urgent, I can’t necessarily conclude that Miss M 
wouldn’t have proceeded with the new plan.
the policy
From the information I’ve seen and the records of telephone conversations between Miss M 
and L&G’s adviser, I haven’t concluded the policy was unsuitable for her. Miss M’s working 
arrangements meant she most likely needed an income protection policy if she was unable 
to work.
During the discussions with L&G’s adviser, Miss M was offered a long term plan but she said 
the cost was too high. Miss M’s had said her existing policy’s benefit wasn’t sufficient for her 
needs, and the deferred period was too long; she wanted a policy that cost a similar amount 
each month, that would pay out more quickly if she was unable to work, and with a higher 
monthly benefit.  
The policy she was offered, and that she subsequently accepted, met all of those needs. I’m 
satisfied in the circumstances of this complaint, that L&G’s adviser took reasonable steps to 
ensure Miss M had appropriate information about the policy – including its benefits and 
limitations – to allow her to make an informed choice.
my final decision
I know Miss M will be disappointed by my decision, but based on everything I’ve seen and 
the individual circumstances of this complaint, I haven’t concluded Legal & General 
Partnership Services Limited should re-consider the claim, or reinstate the previous policy, 
so I won’t be asking it to do anything more.
Under the rules of the Financial Ombudsman Service, I’m required to ask Miss M to accept 
or reject my decision before 17 August 2018.
Sian Brightey
ombudsman
Ref: DRN4478988

6
COPY OF PROVISIONAL DECISION
complaint
Miss M is unhappy that Legal & General Partnership Services Limited has declined a claim 
under her income protection policy.
background
In November 2016 Miss M got in touch with L&G wanting to talk about one of her policies – a level 
term assurance policy. She’d taken out the policy several years earlier as a way of providing her 
children with a cash sum. But she’d recently realised the L&G policy she held had an end date – 
and she wanted a policy that would pay out on her death.
In the discussion with L&G’s adviser, it turned out she had 3 policies –

the level term assurance policy – which she wanted to ‘convert’ to a whole of life policy

a decreasing term assurance policy to cover her outstanding mortgage; and

an income protection policy. The income protection policy was branded under the name of 
a different business - which I’ll call business B - but was administered by L&G.
After telephone conversations with L&G’s adviser, Miss M decided to retain the decreasing term 
assurance policy as recommended by the adviser. She decided to replace the level term 
assurance policy and the income protection policy with new policies.
The new income protection policy, which is the subject of this complaint, had a lower monthly 
premium but offered a higher monthly benefit. It also allowed Miss M to make a claim 30 
days after being considered unfit to work – her previous policy had a deferred period of 90 
days.
In early 2017, Miss M made a claim against the income protection policy. She’d been unable to 
work following a hip replacement operation. But L&G refused the claim. It says Miss M hadn’t 
answered the adviser’s questions about her health accurately and had she have done so, they 
wouldn’t have offered her a new policy.
Miss M disagrees. She said she did tell L&G about her medical problems and because of that it 
should accept the claim. She says she spoke to the same adviser about all three policies.
Our investigator asked L&G to provide recordings of all the calls its adviser had with Miss M
- two calls could be traced. But having listened to those calls, our investigator was of the opinion 
other calls had probably taken place but L&G couldn’t trace anything further.
After listening to those calls, our investigator thought L&G hadn’t asked questions that were specific 
enough before recommending Miss M go ahead with the new income protection policy. He thought 
the term “sickness” wasn’t a term Miss M would relate to her particular health problems. And 
because of that he thought Miss M had taken reasonable care when answering the adviser’s 
questions.
He also thought L&G’s adviser didn’t give Miss M the right advice based on the information it had 
received from her. The information he referred to was sent to L&G on Miss M’s application for the 
whole of life policy - not as a direct result of Miss M’s income protection policy application.
He suggested L&G consider the claim and pay the benefit that would have been available to Miss M 
under her previous income protection policy. He recommended the previous policy be reinstated and 
a payment of £400 made to Miss M to say sorry for the trouble and upset she’d been caused.
Ref: DRN4478988

7
But he also gave Miss M the option of retaining the new policy knowing it would not cover her for 
claims for arthritis.
Miss M decided she’d like her previous policy reinstated. But L&G says it can’t do that because the 
policy was held by business B – and they can’t reinstate a policy belonging to a different company.
my provisional findings
I’ve considered all the evidence and arguments I’ve seen so far to decide what’s fair and reasonable 
in the circumstances of this complaint. My findings differ from what our investigator said and 
because of that I’m giving both parties an opportunity to provide further information for me to 
consider.
When considering this case, I’ve taken into account industry standards (ICOBS) and applicable law.  
In this case the Consumer Insurance Declaration (and Representation) Act 2012 (CIDRA) applies.
CIDRA applies to disclosure and ‘representations’ by a consumer to an insurer before they enter into 
or vary a consumer contract of insurance. CIDRA says it’s the consumer’s duty to take reasonable 
care not to make a ‘misrepresentation’ to the insurer in response to the insurer’s questions.  One of 
the considerations is how clear and specific the questions asked are.
If a consumer doesn’t take reasonable care in answering the insurer’s questions, the insurer can 
refuse to pay the claim or it can pay it proportionately. To do this the insurer must show that it either 
wouldn’t have covered the consumer at all or would have done so on different terms.
I’ve listened to recordings of two telephone conversations between Miss M and L&G’s adviser about 
the income protection policy – the calls took place in early November 2016. During the calls Miss M 
is asked about her smoking habits, whether she’s waiting for tests or investigations and if she’s in 
good health. She says she is in good health, isn’t waiting for tests or investigations and hasn’t 
smoked (or used nicotine products) in the last 12 months.
The adviser goes on the explain that the income protection policy doesn’t provide cover in the first 
12 months, for any disease, illness or injury for which the applicant has had consultation, 
medication, advice or treatment for in 12 months before the policy starts. He goes on to ask Miss M 
if she’s had any “sicknesses” in the last 12 months and she says she hasn’t. He explains the policy 
is “aimed at new illnesses rather than any pre-existing conditions”.
At this point, I think it would have been reasonable for Miss M to talk about the health 
problems she’d experienced in the previous 12 months.

Miss M’s medical records between November 2015 and November 2016 show regular 
visits to her GP for problems with her hip including the supply of prescription pain killers, a 
referral for physiotherapy and two requests for a referral for a steroid injection for hip pain. 
It also shows that in February 2016, Miss M was referred to an orthopaedic surgeon for 
“hip surgery”.

I’ve seen a letter from the orthopaedic surgeon dated 13 April 2016. The surgeon had 
suggested “sufficient functional loss” to warrant a hip replacement operation.

Her GP records also show visits for high blood pressure and a rapid heart rate. 
Miss M has said there were further conversations with the adviser where she talked about her 
hip problems, high blood pressure and rapid heart rate. And although L&G haven’t been able 
to provide copies of those calls, I’m satisfied further calls probably took place.
Ref: DRN4478988

8
Miss M has submitted a copy of her whole of life application form to show she did tell L&G about 
her health problems. And on the form there is reference to osteoarthritis, hypertension and rapid 
heart rate. But again, I think Miss M should have answered some of the questions more 
accurately.
For example
   when asked questions about the osteoarthritis Miss M said she hadn’t needed any time away 
from her “normal work or daily activities”. But her GP records appear to show significant 
periods of time when she was unable to work. In February 2016 there’s an entry which says 
“unfit to return to work” and “days off work – 6 weeks”. There’s a further entry in March 2016 
which says “unfit to return to work” and “Days off work – 4 weeks”.
   and when asked “do you expect to have, or are you currently waiting for, surgery or an 
operation …for this condition”, Miss M also said “no”. But at that point Miss M had already 
been seen by the orthopaedic surgeon who’d mentioned a hip replacement operation. I 
recognise Miss M’s point that she hadn’t agreed to go ahead with the surgery but I would have 
expected her to give more information about that on her application form.
   Miss M’s GP records suggest the hip problems were causing her considerable pain and 
difficulty in her daily life so I think it would have been reasonable for her to have expected to 
need an operation to resolve the problem.
I understand Miss M will have been very upset by L&G’s decision not to accept her claim under the 
income protection policy. I’m sure she expected the policy to pay out during the time she was 
unable to work. From what I’ve seen Miss M worked under contract, through an agency, and 
having held an income protection policy for several years, I’m satisfied Miss M had made a 
conscious decision to protect herself in the event she was unable to work.
But based on the information I’ve seen, I think Miss M should have told the adviser more about 
her health problems and had she done so, I’m satisfied he would not have recommended she 
switch to a new policy.
my provisional decision
My provision decision is that I don’t intend to uphold this complaint and won’t be asking L&G to do 
anything more but I will consider any further evidence submitted to me by 5 April 2018 before 
reaching a final determination.
Sian Brightey
ombudsman
Ref: DRN4478988
quoted_clauses: aimed at new illnesses rather than any pre-existing conditions
do you expect to have, or are you currently waiting for, surgery or an operation …for this condition

text:
K820x#14
complaint
Mr B complains that Aviva Insurance Limited declined his pet insurance policy claim and that 
he was mis-sold the policy. My references to Aviva include its agents
background
In August 2017 Mr B bought a pet insurance policy for his two dogs. Aviva is the insurer of 
the policy. Mr B brought the policy through a broker. He says he previously had pet 
insurance with another insurer.
In May 2018 one of Mr B’s dogs had treatment and he made a claim. Mr B’s vet said the dog 
was treated for peri-vulval dermatitis with urinary incontinence.
Aviva declined the claim. It said the evidence from Mr B’s vet showed the dog had the same 
condition in 2015, before the policy was taken out. Aviva also asked an independent vet for 
their opinion and they agreed the condition was pre-existing. The policy doesn’t cover pre-
existing medical conditions.
Mr B complained that his dog’s medical condition in May 2018 wasn't pre-existing, and he’s 
in dispute with his vet about that matter. He'd asked Aviva for the identity of the independent 
vet so he could check if they were qualified to give an opinion and independent, but it 
refused. Mr B also said when he bought the policy he was assured that as he was moving 
from one life cover policy to another the existing life cover would be the same. 
Mr B wants the claim paid, an apology that he’d been mis-sold the policy and details of the 
vet Aviva used for an opinion.
Our investigator explained that we’d need to look at Mr B’s mis-sale complaint separately. 
Also Mr B would need to raise his concerns about Aviva’s response to his subject access 
request with the Information Commissioner’s Office. 
Our investigator thought Aviva had fairly declined the claim 
Mr B doesn’t agree and wants an ombudsman’s decision. In summary he said:

in 2018 his dog was taken to his vet to be treated for an ulcerated vagina, not acute 
dermatitis and she wasn’t suffering from urinary incontinence when he took her to the 
vet. He thought the latter was caused by his vet wrongly prescribing his dog a steroid 
which was unsuitable given her ulcerative condition

his vet notes are inaccurate and don’t reflect the discussions he had with the vet

his dog has recently been diagnosed with a new medical condition which with the 
steroids and vet examination could have caused his dog’s incontinence at the 2018 
examination.
my findings
I’ve considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint.
Our investigator correctly explained that Mr B’s mis-sale complaint will need to be 
considered separately and we’ve set up a mis-sale complaint. She’s also correctly told Mr B 
Ref: DRN4565376

2
that the Information Commissioner’s Office, rather than this service, is most appropriate to 
consider his concerns about Aviva's response to his subject access request.
This decision is about whether Aviva fairly and reasonably declined Mr B’s claim, and I think 
it did. I don’t uphold the complaint about the decline of the claim. I’ll explain why.
The policy is a ‘life policy’. Like many pet insurance policies (including life policies) it doesn’t 
cover treatment for pre-existing medical conditions, and the policy is clear about that.
The policy defines pre-existing medical conditions as:
‘a) An injury that happened or an illness that first showed clinical signs before your 
pet’s cover started, or
b)An injury or illness that is the same as, or has the same diagnosis or clinical signs 
as an injury, illness or clinical sign your pet had before its cover started, or
c) An injury or illness that is caused by, relates to, or results from, an injury, incident, 
illness or clinical sign your pet had before its cover started. No matter where the 
injury, illness or clinical signs are noticed or happen in, or on, your pet’s body… ‘
Mr B says much of his vet notes are incorrect and don’t accurately represent their discussion 
or the facts. But Aviva can fairly and reasonably rely on Mr B’s vet’s evidence as accurate 
expert evidence unless the vet tells it the evidence contains an error and clarifies the correct 
position. 
In 2015, Mr B’s dog attended a vet at his usual practice. The vet notes say the dog suffered 
peri-vulval dermatitis with primary or secondary urinary leakage. A claim was made at that 
time for acute dermatitis and urinary incontinence.
In 2016, Mr B’s dog attended the same vet practice about a separate matter. The vet notes 
say the vet also looked at the vulva, which was sore and the dog’s previous history of urinary 
incontinence was noted.
In 2018, after the policy was taken out, Mr B’s dog attended the same vet practice. Mr B 
says it was the first time the particular vet treated his dog, but Aviva can still fairly take the  
vet’s opinion into account.. The vet notes say the dog had a bladder leak the week before 
(which Mr B denies) and she was suffering from dermatitis on her vulva and had primary or 
secondary urinary leakage ‘as before’. 
Mr B’s vet completed the 2018 claim form giving the name of illness as ‘reoccurrence of 
acute perineal moist dermatitis with urinary incontinence’. The vet also marked the claim 
form as ‘yes’ to the dog being treated for the condition before, and ‘yes’ to making a claim for 
the treatment before.
Mr B’s vet’s letter dated June 2016 (but I’m satisfied should read June 2018) also details the 
dog’s history of incontinence and dermatitis in 2014 and 2015 and details how the dog 
presented with the same condition in May 2018. The letter says:
‘I am of the opinion that while the incontinence came first, the peri-vulval dermatitis 
cannot be excluded from the incontinence, and is very much due, in large part to this 
incontinence problem’.
Ref: DRN4565376

3
I think the evidence from Mr B’s vet gave Aviva strong evidence that Mr B’s dog had suffered 
from urinary incontinence and dermatitis both before and after the policy started. Aviva could 
reasonably decline the 2018 claim using the pre-existing condition exclusion.
As Mr B disputed Aviva’s decline it sought the opinion of an independent vet. That vet said 
the dog had acute, ulcerative peri-vulval dermatitis before and after the policy was taken out. 
That vet agreed with Mr B’s vet that the medical condition claimed for in 2018 was pre-
existing.
Mr B disputes that Aviva can rely on the independent vet’s opinion without giving him all the 
vet’s identification information he’s asked for. Aviva has given Mr B the vet’s qualifications 
and on the evidence I have there’s no reason why it can’t rely on that vet’s opinion. But as 
I’ve said, even without the independent vet’s opinion Aviva had strong evidence from Mr B’s 
vet that his 2018 claim was for a pre-existing condition and it could decline the claim on that 
evidence alone.
Mr B says his dog has now been diagnosed with a new medical condition which may have 
been the cause of at least some of her problems in 2018. I’ve seen no vet evidence to 
confirm diagnosis of a new condition and more importantly no evidence that the 2018 claim 
was due to the new medical condition.
If Mr B can get such evidence from his vet then he should send it to Aviva who should 
reasonably assess the new evidence.
On the evidence I have Aviva fairly and reasonably declined the claim.
 
my final decision
I don’t uphold the complaint about Aviva Insurance Limited’s decline of the claim.
Under the rules of the Financial Ombudsman Service, I’m required to ask Mr B to accept or 
reject my decision before 22 November 2019.
Nicola Sisk
ombudsman
Ref: DRN4565376
quoted_clauses: reoccurrence of acute perineal moist dermatitis with urinary incontinence
I am of the opinion that while the incontinence came first, the peri-vulval dermatitis cannot be excluded from the incontinence, and is very much due, in large part to this incontinence problem

text:
K821x#12
complaint
Mr F has complained about the decision by Society of Lloyd’s (“Lloyds”) to decline a claim for 
benefit under his employer’s personal accident insurance policy.
background
Mr F had the benefit of a personal accident insurance policy through his employer. The policy, 
amongst other benefits, provided cover for temporary total disablement if accidental injury was 
sustained in the course of employment.
In December 2010, Mr F suffered a back injury whilst moving an orthopaedic bed at work. The 
pain in his back gradually worsened such that in March 2011 he became unable to work. Mr F 
underwent surgery on his back in April 2011 and was able to return to work in July 2011. Mr F 
therefore submitted a claim for benefit for the period in question.
Lloyds considered the claim but ultimately declined it on the basis that Mr F’s accident had not 
been the sole cause of his disability. Mr F appealed, citing a medical report from an independent 
surgeon dated February 2012. This stated that his injury had exacerbated an underlying pre-
existing medical condition, bringing the effects of the condition forwards by four to five years. Mr 
F felt that it would be fair to receive a proportionate payment but Lloyds maintained its position. 
Mr F therefore complained to this service.
I issued a provisional decision on this matter on 23 April 2013. In that decision, I noted that 
under the terms of the policy, a ‘bodily injury’ is defined as follows:
1.  “Bodily Injury” means identifiable physical injury which:-
(a) is sustained by the Insured Person and
(b) is caused by an Accident during the Period of Insurance and
(c) solely and independently of any other cause, except illness directly resulting from, or 
medical or surgical treatment rendered necessary by such injury, occasions the death or 
disablement of the Insured Person within twelve months from the date of the Accident.”
I also noted, however, that Lloyds had added an endorsement to the policy which states:
"This insurance does not cover death, disablement or loss arising from or aggravated by 
any illness, disability or condition of a recurring or chronic nature of the Insured Person 
for which medical advice or treatment has been given during the 12 months immediately 
prior to the inception date of this Insurance or the Insured Person's date of addition to 
this Insurance, whichever is the later."
I did not see how this endorsement could be used to exclude any claim which would not already 
be excluded by policy term 1(c) above and which partly defines bodily injury. This being the 
case, I had to ask myself why the endorsement was added. I considered that, at the very least, 
it created an ambiguity as to whether the policy was intended to cover outcomes related to pre-
existing conditions for which the insured person has received no medical advice or treatment in 
the 12 months before becoming insured. If there is ambiguity in an insurance contract, the 
general approach of the courts and of this service is that it should be interpreted in favour of the 
consumer.
Ref: DRN4585946

2
On top of this, however, I considered that where there is potential conflict between a standard 
term in a contract and a specially introduced term such as an endorsement, more weight should 
be placed on the latter because it has been specifically added. Furthermore, given that the 
endorsement in this case did not appear to exclude anything that was not already excluded by 
policy term 1(c), I concluded that the most likely reason it was added was to restrict the extent of 
the exclusion provided for by 1(c). 
Mr F’s temporary total disablement was due to a problem with his lower back. I understood that 
Mr F had not sought medical advice or treatment for his lower back problem in the 12 months 
before the policy started. On this basis, I considered that Mr F’s claim was not excluded under 
the above endorsement to the policy. Furthermore, for the reasons given above, I considered it 
would be unreasonable for Lloyds to seek to exclude the claim under policy term 1(c).
I was also satisfied that Mr F suffered an accidental bodily injury in the way in which he 
described. His reporting of the incident to his GP and other medical professionals had been 
consistent. None of the medical professionals who had examined Mr F had disputed that his 
disablement resulted, at least in part, from the accidental injury he described.
I was therefore minded to conclude that Mr F had a valid claim under the terms of his policy and 
that Lloyds should settle this claim in full, regardless of whether Mr F's accident exacerbated a 
pre-existing condition. I invited the parties to comment on this provisional decision.
Mr F responded by saying he accepted the provisional decision.
Lloyds responded by saying it did not necessarily accept that Mr F had not sought medical 
advice or treatment for his lower back problem in the 12 months before the policy started. It 
cited a hospital admission on 16 January 2010 and entries in his GP’s records for 9 November 
2009 and 30 December 2009 as evidence that Mr F may have sought advice or treatment for 
this condition during this period. It considered that it had not received Mr F’s full medical records 
and therefore asked that it be allowed to seek his full medical notes for the year prior to the start 
of the policy so that it could properly assess his eligibility for benefit. It also referred to 
correspondence that had taken place with the adjudicator during an earlier stage of this 
service’s investigation of this complaint and asked me to provide some clarification of this 
service’s approach to proportionate settlements in circumstances where an accident has been a 
contributory, rather than sole, cause of someone’s disability.
my findings
I have considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what is fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint. Having done so, I see no reason to depart 
from my provisional decision that this complaint should be upheld and that Lloyds should settle 
Mr F’s claim in full.
Lloyds questions whether Mr F may have sought advice or treatment for his lower back 
condition in the 12 months before his policy started. It says its doubt over this matter is based 
on three references in his medical records during this period.
The first reference it cites is a hospital discharge notification dated 22 January 2010 which 
states that Mr F was thought to be suffering from a spasm from acute lower back pain. 
However, Lloyds itself acknowledges that the later notes indicate that this was actually the early 
stages of appendicitis. I am therefore satisfied that I can dismiss this reference. 
Ref: DRN4585946

3
The second reference is a handwritten entry in Mr F’s GP records which Lloyds say is dated 9 
November 2009 showing that he was suffering from interscapular (shoulder blade/back) pain 
and which mentions the pain clinic. Having reviewed the file, however, and compared the GP 
entries with other information in the medical records, I am satisfied that Lloyds has read this 
wrongly and the entry is actually dated 9 November 2004. This means it is not relevant to my 
consideration of this complaint.
The third reference is an entry in Mr F’s GP records dated 30 December 2009 which mentions a 
discharge. Lloyds considers that this must be a hospital discharge and because it has no other 
details it considers that the medical records must be incomplete. It therefore has asked that it be 
allowed to seek full medical records for the 12 months before the policy started. I note, however, 
that Mr F’s GP has provided Lloyds with extensive medical records dating back over 50 years 
and which include hospital notes and letters. I am satisfied that Lloyds therefore already has all 
the medical records that are available and that there is nothing within these records to show that 
Mr F sought advice or treatment for his lower back condition in the 12 months before his policy 
started. I therefore see no reason to further delay the payment of Mr F’s claim.
Finally, Lloyds asked me to provide some clarification of this service’s approach to proportionate 
settlements in circumstances where an accident has been a contributory, rather than sole, 
cause of someone’s disability. I appreciate Lloyds’ wish for some guidance on this issue and 
have no desire to be unhelpful. Given, however, that this issue is no longer relevant to the 
outcome of this complaint, I do not consider it would be appropriate for me to address it in this 
decision.
my final decision
My final decision is that I uphold this complaint. I require Lloyds to settle Mr F’s claim in full in 
accordance with the remaining terms and conditions of the policy. I also require Lloyds to pay 
interest on this settlement at the annual rate of 8% simple from the date that benefit was 
payable under the policy to the date of settlement.
David Poley
ombudsman
Ref: DRN4585946
quoted_clauses: This insurance does not cover death, disablement or loss arising from or aggravated by any illness, disability or condition of a recurring or chronic nature of the Insured Person for which medical advice or treatment has been given during the 12 months immediately prior to the inception date of this Insurance or the Insured Person's date of addition to this Insurance, whichever is the later.

text:
K820x#14
complaint
Mr K says Canada Life Limited (‘Canada Life’) has unfairly refused his critical illness claim. 
To resolve his complaint, he wants his claim paid in full. 
background
Mr K joined his employer’s group critical illness scheme on 1 October 2016. The scheme is 
operated by Canada Life. Mr K joined as a ‘gold’ scheme member offering him a greater 
number of insured conditions than ‘silver’ cover, with a sum assured of £250,000.  
In January 2017, Mr K had to undergo surgery for heart valve replacement. He made a claim 
for critical illness benefit to Canada Life, as ‘heart valve replacement or repair’ is a listed 
condition on the policy.  
Canada Life told Mr K in March 2017 it wouldn’t pay the claim. It said prior to joining the 
scheme Mr K had suffered from endocarditis. This had caused inflammation of Mr K’s 
bicuspid aortic valve. As a result, he needed heart valve replacement. In the event of a heart 
valve claim, the policy wording excluded a number of stated related conditions – of which 
endocarditis was one. 
Further, Canada Life’s claims assessors felt the evidence showed Mr K had a bicuspid aortic 
valve before he joined the scheme, which meant the pre-existing condition applied too.   
Mr K complained. He explained how he’d been healthy right up to the point of his claim, 
having played sports and completing half-marathons. The diagnosis of a bicuspid heart valve 
was completely unexpected. He also said the policy wording made clear that the exclusion 
applied for conditions he knew about. And he didn’t know he had either condition until after 
he joined the scheme. 
Canada Life was not willing to change its view. It explained how group critical illness 
schemes worked. That meant it couldn’t underwrite Mr K at the point he joined the scheme. 
Instead, it had to determine whether he had a claim by assessing the exclusions. 
In its view, both the related conditions and pre-existing conditions exclusions applied. That 
was because Mr K had ongoing symptoms dating back to June 2016. After a period of 
months of investigation with other areas such as gastroenterology, Mr K’s heart problems 
were discovered. Canada Life maintained that the presence of both conditions invalidated 
the claim.  
It also didn’t accept Mr K ought to have had knowledge of the conditions. It explained that 
the wording actually said, “where an individual is known to have an existing condition”. The 
condition was known once Mr K reported to doctors with his symptoms in June 2016 – and 
those were symptoms of endocarditis caused by a bacterial streptococcus infection. 
So Mr K referred his complaint to this service, where it was looked at by an adjudicator. He 
explained how he believed Canada Life had disregarded guidance issued by this service 
which says consideration for pre-existing condition exclusions must include:
“the extent of the connection between the pre-existing condition and the condition 
that gave rise to the claim - and the foreseeability of this; and whether the consumer 
Ref: DRN4675569

2
could reasonably be expected to have been aware that they might have to make a 
claim as a result of the symptoms.”
Mr K noted he had not taken a day off sick since June 2016, and was working a minimum of 
10-hour days in a demanding job. He had been told many times his issues were gastric; 
notably on 23 December 2016 he was told there was no longer any evidence of infection.  
Our adjudicator said that Mr K’s medical records showed he had both conditions before 
October 2016. So she thought Canada Life had fairly refused the claim.  
Canada Life agreed with our adjudicator. But Mr K wanted an ombudsman to review the 
complaint. He noted that:

this service has issued external guidance regarding pre-existing conditions;

that guidance says we would usually not allow an insurer to reject a claim if the 
claimant did not know he or she had a pre-existing condition;

he had no idea that he had endocarditis or a bicuspid heart valve;

so, the adjudicator’s view went against our guidance;

he has no objection to exclusions on group policies;

but the exclusions do not apply to his circumstances;

the two conditions were not diagnosed until January 2017;

the policy wording also sets out that the exclusion only applies if he knew the 
condition existed;

any exclusion regarding related conditions shouldn’t apply either on the same basis;

he was not known to have any condition in October 2016;

it is wrong of our adjudicator to say the symptoms he had from June 2016 were 
debilitating;

he tried to find out the cause of these symptoms via private doctors but they were not 
debilitating;

in November 2016, he travelled to the US - despite telling his travel insurer about the 
ongoing investigations, his premiums remained the same.  
The complaint has now been passed to me.  
my findings
I’ve considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint. Having done so, I agree with the outcome 
reached by our adjudicator, although I have done so based on slightly different reasoning. I 
know that will be upsetting for Mr K, and I do appreciate how much of a shock it was to 
receive his eventual diagnoses. Overall, I am not able to instruct Canada Life to pay a claim 
and I’ll explain why that is.
It’s important for me to note that means I will not be addressing each specific separate point 
that Mr K has made to this service or Canada Life throughout the claims process. That 
doesn’t mean I haven’t taken account of everything Mr K has to say, and of all the evidence 
before me. I’ll set out below what I think are the relevant facts in this case, and the reasons 
for the outcome of my decision.  
related condition and pre-existing condition - endocarditis
Ref: DRN4675569

3
As Canada Life has explained, group critical illness schemes allow members to join at 
defined periods without prior underwriting. As such, these types of cover include policy 
exclusions and these are considered at the time a policyholder makes a claim under the 
scheme.  
In Mr K’s case, Canada Life says two policy exclusions apply. For the reasons I’ll go on to 
explain, I believe the ‘related condition’ exclusion applies to Mr K.  
The policy wording says: 
“Related Conditions Exclusion
In the first two years of joining the scheme claims cannot be made for an illness or 
surgical procedure where a related condition existed at any time before the claimant 
was first covered.
If a member suffers an insured illness or undergoes an insured procedure outside of 
the first two years that they are covered, we will not apply the related condition 
exclusion except for loss of independent existence, paralysis of limbs and terminal 
illness where the related conditions exclusions will remain applicable indefinitely.
If a member selects an increase in benefit after they have joined the scheme, the 
extra amount of benefit selected will also be subject to the two year related 
conditions exclusion from the date of the selection.
The main related conditions for each illness or surgical procedure are listed in this 
guide.
Why do we apply a Related Conditions Exclusion?
A Related Condition is any medical condition that is associated with or is likely to 
have led to the occurrence of the insured illness or surgical procedure. Where an 
individual is known to have an existing condition, say high blood pressure 
which is a known risk factor for stroke, this could lead to a claim under an 
insured condition, in this case stroke [my emphasis]. As with the [pre-existing 
conditions exclusion] PECE, the use of the related conditions exclusion allows us to 
cover groups of individuals without prior assessment of their medical history and 
lifestyle, within agreed limits.”
In addition to the claimable event of ‘heart valve replacement or repair’, Mr K could likely 
have made a claim under ‘open heart surgery’, which is also a listed critical illness. However, 
both of these contain wording for listed related conditions that include endocarditis and 
bicuspid aortic valve. I need to consider the related condition exclusion because Mr K’s claim 
falls within the two-year moratorium set out above.  
I know Mr K is especially unhappy because at the time he joined the scheme (at the first 
eligible point at which he could do so) he did not know he had either condition. I accept that 
and I agree with him. Canada Life also accepts that until he was admitted to hospital in 
January 2017, Mr K had no inclination that the cause of his symptoms was endocarditis, or 
that he was born with a bicuspid heart valve. 
Ref: DRN4675569

4
But, I think Mr K is relying on the part of the wording above (which I have written in bold) in 
isolation. The wording is an explanation of how high blood pressure ‘could’ lead to a stroke 
claim. It is illustrative – i.e., it is set out to give an example. It also is not the exclusion itself – 
the part Mr K refers to is further guidance about how group critical illness schemes work. 
The overall exclusion says “claims cannot be made for an illness or surgical procedure 
where a related condition existed at any time before the claimant was first covered”. That 
wording applies to Mr K. And, in any event, I do believe that the condition was known to Mr K 
from June 2016. Unfortunately, it had simply not been diagnosed by 1 October 2017. In my 
view, the medical evidence shows that Mr K was suffering from endocarditis from June 2016 
onwards.  
In his report to Canada Life Mr K’s GP was asked, “when were you first consulted regarding 
the condition that led to the surgical repair and at that time, how long had symptoms been 
present?” In his reply, the GP gave a date in August 2016.  
An eventual diagnosis of a condition is a distinct event. It differs from the existence of a 
condition beforehand. Upon confirmation of diagnosis from an appropriate medical 
professional, a person may be confirmed as having had that diagnosed condition for a 
specified period. That is because many conditions require a period of investigation to 
determine an ultimate diagnosis, if it’s possible to provide one. 
In Mr K’s case, the primary route taken with his investigations was that of a gastric nature. 
His symptoms had first begun overseas in June 2016, directly after Mr K had undergone 
dental work. I know Mr K was previously fit and healthy, running 8km each day as part of his 
commute. He did not resume this at any time before the diagnosis. Given his previous clear 
medical history and recent overseas visit, I can see why Mr K’s GP initially began 
investigations with suspicions of a gastroenterological origin. 
But, it is now clear that the origin of Mr K’s condition was a bacterial infection caused by his 
dental work. The type of infection Mr K had was rare, but nonetheless I understand it is the 
most common cause of subacute bacterial endocarditis. 
I have seen the letter from a cardiologist, Dr M, of 8 January 2017. Mr K was given a 
diagnosis for the symptoms he had suffered at that date. The cardiologist diagnosed “six 
month illness with streptococcus sanguis endocarditis causing aortic root abscess and 
severe aortic regurgitation”.  
In his letter to us following the adjudicator’s view Mr K confirms he “did everything 
reasonable to gain a diagnosis of my symptoms once they began”. I can see that. I realise it 
must have been concerning for Mr K to suffer from his symptoms. And I know that he was 
told these were likely gastric, even being told on 23 December 2017 that any “likely severe 
GI infection has passed”. But I hope Mr K can appreciate that the discharge from 
gastroenterology is not the relevant diagnosis. I’ve already explained why Canada Life, in 
these circumstances, is reasonably entitled to look at Mr K’s symptoms to see whether they 
were likely to have led to his the insured event, as it says in the policy wording explanation 
above. 
I agree with Canada Life that the symptoms Mr K had after his dental procedure (primarily 
fever, rigors, night sweats, chills, weight loss, lethargy, muscle pain, low haemoglobin, and 
later the confirmation of a heart murmur) were highly likely to have been caused by 
bacterial/infective endocarditis.  
Ref: DRN4675569

5
So, it is not unreasonable of Canada Life to have determined that these symptoms led to his 
diagnosis. And Mr K accepts these symptoms were present before he joined the scheme. An 
insurer is entitled to protect itself from claims where a new entrant is suffering from an 
existing illness. To apply exclusions of this nature is standard practice for group policies of 
this type. 
I therefore agree that in these circumstances, Canada Life was entitled to refuse the claim. 
And since it is not required, I’ve not gone on to consider the pre-existing condition exclusion. 
I should note though, that I do believe it would exclude Mr K for the same reasons (even 
where it includes wording that a condition is ‘known to have existed’) because Mr K’s 
symptoms existed before he joined the scheme. 
related condition and pre-existing condition - bicuspid aortic valve
I’m not going to go further and reach detailed conclusions about the presence of Mr K’s 
bicuspid valve because I don’t believe a claim is payable under either listed critical illness. I 
do note though, that this condition differs from Mr K’s ongoing symptoms that were 
eventually confirmed to be endocarditis. Though Mr K might have discovered that he had a 
bicuspid aortic valve in the future, I also understand that in many cases, a bicuspid aortic 
valve will cause no problems. This diagnosis was only made because that valve was 
affected by the infective nature of Mr K’s bacterial endocarditis. I understand, and accept 
that neither Mr K nor any medical professional knew or could reasonably have known of the 
existence of his congenital valve defect until he sadly contracted bacterial endocarditis.  
our external guidance
I know Mr K has placed great weight on our external guidance, and I appreciate the 
significance of it to him. In particular, he’s quoted a section of a guidance page which 
concerns “undiagnosed symptoms”. The guidance says even where insurers include pre-
existing conditions which were not yet diagnosed, we “generally take the view that claims 
should not be excluded where the consumer had suffered only from some undiagnosed or 
minor generalised symptoms at the start of the policy”. 
Unfortunately, the quote Mr K has relied on is not relevant for long-term group critical illness 
schemes. It explains at the top of the guidance how “long-term policies can last up to 25 
years, while short-term policies can be annual or for single trips only. This section of our 
website is principally about short-term insurance policies”. 
It does go on to say that some parts of the approach might sometimes also apply to long 
term products. But the general related and pre-existing conclusions in this case are not 
subject to the approach Mr K has quoted. That is because they are group offerings (usually 
to employees) for long-term protection as an alternative to personal critical illness policies, 
which are underwritten at outset.  
If Mr K had sought a standalone critical illness policy, he’d have been required to disclose 
his ongoing investigations. Insurers in those circumstances are unlikely to accept applicants 
who have ongoing investigations without a conclusion or diagnosis. That is because they are 
determining risk and price for insurance to cover events over a significant number of years. 
Each insurer is entitled to determine the risk it is willing to accept.  
Ref: DRN4675569

6
The guidance Mr K has mentioned is for short term (predominantly travel) health policies 
where there are many different considerations for insurers, given the nature of the insurance 
needs and the time restrictions that apply. With a long-term investigation in the background 
of a short-term insurance application, the final diagnosis could easily post-date the insured 
event. For a long-term personal protection policy like critical illness cover, an insurer will 
need to satisfy itself as to the cost and risk of offering insurance for an extensive term. 
Group schemes cannot do that from outset, so they are assessed from the point of any 
claim.  
My role here is to apply the terms of Mr K’s policy fairly to his particular circumstances, 
having regard for what’s fair and reasonable and for any wider law or regulations. Having 
done that, I do not think Canada Life has been unfair in refusing the claim under the related 
exclusion clause. 
As an aside, I note within the ‘gold’ policy wording that ‘aorta graft surgery’ does not contain 
a related condition of endocarditis. However, I’ve not made any findings about that listed 
critical illness. That’s because neither Canada Life nor Mr K has made mention of that being 
a considered claimable event during the course of their correspondence other than a brief 
reference from Canada Life in the supply of its evidence to our adjudicator. It may therefore 
be the case that one or both parties may believe it is not applicable. 
If Mr K believes that a claim ought to be considered for that condition, he’d need to inform 
Canada Life to instruct a further claims assessment on that basis. 
my final decision
I was sorry to learn Mr K was unwell and I know my decision will not be what he’d hoped for. 
I don’t uphold his complaint, nor do I make any award or direction.  
Under the rules of the Financial Ombudsman Service, I’m required to ask Mr K to accept or 
reject my decision before 23 April 2018.
Jo Storey
ombudsman
Ref: DRN4675569

the extent of the connection between the pre-existing condition and the condition that gave rise to the claim - and the foreseeability of this; and whether the consumer Ref: DRN4675569 2 could reasonably be expected to have been aware that they might have to make a claim as a result of the symptoms.
claims cannot be made for an illness or surgical procedure where a related condition existed at any time before the claimant was first covered
when were you first consulted regarding the condition that led to the surgical repair and at that time, how long had symptoms been present?
six month illness with streptococcus sanguis endocarditis causing aortic root abscess and severe aortic regurgitation
did everything reasonable to gain a diagnosis of my symptoms once they began
generally take the view that claims should not be excluded where the consumer had suffered only from some undiagnosed or minor generalised symptoms at the start of the policy

text:
K820x#14
complaint
Mr P has brought a complaint on behalf of his company about AXA Insurance UK Plc’s 
decision to refuse a personal accident claim.
background
Mr P suffered with long-standing problems with his left knee. He said that following an 
accident at work in October 2014, his knee problem worsened. And that surgery on his knee 
was needed sooner than it otherwise would have been, because of his accident. 
Mr P’s company holds an insurance policy that includes personal accident cover. He made a 
claim under that cover for disability payment as he hasn’t been able to return to work 
following his surgery in November 2014. 
AXA refused the claim as it thought Mr P’s injury was pre-existing and therefore excluded. It 
also said there was no evidence Mr P had suffered an accident. Unhappy with AXA’s 
decision, Mr P brought a complaint to this service. 
Our adjudicator didn’t uphold the complaint. He didn’t think AXA had done anything wrong in 
refusing the claim. 
Mr P disagreed with the adjudicator, so the matter has been passed to me. 
my findings
I’ve considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint.
The policy says:
“We will pay the benefits…to the insured person…if during the period of insurance they 
suffer bodily injury.” 
‘Bodily injury’ is defined as:
“A physical injury caused by an identifiable accident which within 12 months of the accident 
results in death disability or loss described under 'What is covered'.”
The policy also explains it won’t pay for:
“2. Pre-existing injury
bodily injury arising from or contributed to by any physical or mental condition which the 
insured person is or has been suffering from at any time during the two years before:
a) the start of this section or
b) commencement of cover for such insured person”
Mr P explains that on 4 October 2014 he fell over whilst at work and hurt his knees. 
I see from Mr P’s medical notes that he had problems with his left knee before the personal 
accident cover started in May 2012. I also understand he’d had a number of surgeries on his 
left knee before the fall in October 2014. 
Ref: DRN4693884

2
I therefore accept that Mr P’s left knee problems would be considered a pre-existing injury 
under the policy. But if Mr P did have an accident that accelerated the effects of his existing 
problem with his knee, then I can still consider whether it would be reasonable for AXA to 
meet a proportion of the claim.
I’ve therefore looked at the medical evidence around the time Mr P says he had the fall. 
I see that in August and September 2014, Mr P’s treating surgeon (Mr A) noted that Mr P 
was experiencing significant pain again in his left knee. Mr A thought Mr P’s knee would 
need replacing, but he wanted to find an alternative. Mr A arranged an MRI scan and after 
reviewing the results, he wrote to Mr P’s GP to explain that Mr P seemed to be developing a 
varus deformity and, rather than a total knee replacement, he thought Mr P’s severe pain 
could be relieved with an osteotomy. He wanted the GP to arrange for some leg films. 
Two weeks after Mr P says he had a fall, he attended an appointment with Mr A to review 
the results of the leg films. In this appointment, Mr A said there was a definite varus 
deformity of the left knee. Mr A confirmed he was therefore going to book Mr P for a left tibial 
osteotomy. There was no mention in Mr A’s notes of Mr P hurting his left knee in an 
accident. 
I’ve also looked at Mr P’s GP notes, and on 7 October his GP reviewed him and noted he 
was still in a lot of pain with his knee, and was scheduled to have an osteotomy, as per 
Mr A’s correspondence from September. Again, there was no mention of an accident.
Based on this evidence, it appears that Mr A had intended to carry out an osteotomy before 
Mr P says he had a fall on 4 October. 
Mr P has since provided statements from Mr A written in 2015 and 2016. Mr A says that 
Mr P had a fall in October 2014 which seemed to cause a major flare up, and because of the 
pain he was experiencing, this advanced the need for a tibial osteotomy. Mr A said that if 
Mr P hadn’t had the injury, he didn’t think he would be operating on him for some time (he 
estimated six months to two years). 
Whist I’ve taken into account Mr A’s more recent remarks about Mr P requiring an osteotomy 
sooner than he otherwise would have because of a fall, this isn’t supported by the medical 
evidence at the time. There’s no mention in the medical notes of Mr P having a fall, or this 
worsening his condition. And the evidence from Mr A in September 2014 was that an 
osteotomy would help Mr P with the pain he was experiencing at that time (not at a later 
date).
Overall, I think greater weight should be placed on the evidence from the time Mr P says he 
had the fall. This doesn’t support that the need for the osteotomy was brought forward 
because of a fall, therefore I can’t reasonably conclude that AXA should pay a proportion of 
the claim.
Ref: DRN4693884

3
my final decision
My final decision is that I don’t uphold this complaint. 
Under the rules of the Financial Ombudsman Service, I’m required to ask Mr P on behalf of 
his company to accept or reject my decision before 19 May 2016.
Chantelle Hurn-Ryan
ombudsman
Ref: DRN4693884

text:
K820x#11
summary of complaint
Mr Y’s complaint is about UK Insurance Limited (UKI) not providing private medical cover 
under his travel insurance policy when his wife became ill abroad. He is also unhappy with 
the settlement of his curtailment claim. 
background to complaint
Mr Y had travel insurance for himself and his wife (who I shall refer to as “Mrs Y”). The policy 
was part of Mr Y’s packaged bank account and was underwritten by UKI. 
During a holiday abroad, where they stayed with family, Mrs Y was admitted to hospital. UKI 
told Mr Y that, as the country where they were staying had a reciprocal health agreement 
with the UK, he was unable to elect for Mrs Y to have private medical treatment or 
rehabilitation. Mrs Y had treatment at a state hospital and no private medical fees were 
incurred. They remained with their family and UKI paid for an upgraded flight home due to 
Mrs Y’s condition.
Mr Y complained to UKI through his bank. He believed he had purchased cover for private 
medical treatment. As private medical costs were not excluded by the policy terms he said 
these should have been covered. He sought compensation for his and his wife’s distress and 
inconvenience. He also wanted to claim for curtailment.
UKI said it was its standard practice to use reciprocal health arrangements but the policy 
booklet had not been updated. It made no specific comment on the curtailment claim save to 
explain that under the policy terms it was not obliged to provide Mr and Mrs Y’s return flight 
on their preferred airline.
Mr Y referred his complaint to this service. He said he had paid for cover for private medical 
treatment that had not been provided. The bank or UKI had admitted the policy wording did 
not reflect its standard practice of using reciprocal health arrangements. He queried whether 
his complaint should be set up against UKI or the bank.
The adjudicator explained that Mr Y could raise a separate complaint against the bank for 
mis-sale of the policy but the issues Mr Y had raised were against UKI. The adjudicator did 
not recommend the complaint against UKI be upheld. He listened to the recording of the 
telephone call to upgrade the policy and found this related only to a change in age and 
length of trip, not private health cover. The policy terms did not provide private medical cover 
nor the option to include that cover. He also considered that the circumstances surrounding 
Mrs Y’s hospitalisation were not covered by the curtailment policy terms as Mr and Mrs Y 
were staying with family and there were no unused accommodation costs. 
Mr Y said that whether it was the bank’s or UKI’s fault his wife had to have state medical 
care rather than private health care and this was not stated in the policy. He said he had 
been legally advised that as the details were not specifically in the policy document they 
could not be enforced.
my findings
I have considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what is fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint. 
Ref: DRN4719361

2
Mr Y remains concerned whether this complaint should be against the bank. The adjudicator 
has correctly explained the situation in detail to Mr Y. In brief, his complaint about the policy 
terms and level of cover in the policy should be against UKI. If Mr Y wishes to complain that 
the policy was mis-sold to him by the bank he can make a separate complaint against the 
bank.
I understand that no private medical fees were incurred for Mrs Y’s condition so Mr Y has not 
suffered any actual financial loss. The issues I have to decide in this complaint are: 

whether compensation is due from UKI to Mr Y for the distress and inconvenience 
caused by Mrs Y not being covered for private medical fees, and 

whether UKI has reasonably dealt with the claim for curtailment.
For me to find that UKI should pay an award for distress and inconvenience I need to 
consider whether UKI led Mr Y to reasonably believe that the policy covered private medical 
treatment.
Mr Y has suggested he specifically purchased cover which included private medical fees as 
he insured himself for private medical care in the UK. Many travel polices do not provide 
elective private medical care and there is nothing in the policy that suggests such fees will 
be covered. There is a specific exclusion that the policy will not cover:
“any additional hospital costs arising from single or private room accommodation 
unless medically necessary”.
Arguably that is an exclusion for costs of a private room only, rather than private treatment, 
but I consider this exclusion to be clear in its intention. The absence of cover for elective 
private health care is not an unusual limitation of cover that I would expect to be specifically 
highlighted in the policy document. 
As there is no indication in the policy that private medical fees would be covered it would 
have been reasonable for Mr Y to have checked whether the policy provided such cover. 
This is particularly so as Mr Y says such cover was important to him. Mr Y did telephone UKI 
to upgrade the policy but this upgrade related to age and length of trip extension. At no point 
during the call did Mr Y request, or UKI confirm, that the policy upgrade included private 
health care. UKI wrote to Mr Y to confirm the areas that had been upgraded.
There is no evidence that UKI led Mr Y to reasonably believe that private medical fees were 
part of the policy cover. I do not consider there is any basis for me to reasonably award 
compensation against UKI for any distress and inconvenience Mr Y may have suffered due 
to the absence of such cover. As UKI informed Mr Y of the limitation of cover before he 
incurred any expenses for private care UKI did not prejudice Mr Y’s position.
As to the curtailment claim, the policy provides cover for unused travel, accommodation and 
other trip expenses paid on the bank’s specified charge card. The expenses must be prepaid 
or for which Mr Y was contracted to pay. Mr and Mrs Y were staying with family abroad as 
planned and I have seen no evidence that they had unused expenses that would be covered 
by the policy terms. On the available information UKI’s settlement of the curtailment claim 
with the upgraded return flight was reasonable.
Ref: DRN4719361

3
my final decision
My final decision is that I do not uphold Mr Y’s complaint.
I make no award against UK Insurance Limited.
Nicola Sisk
ombudsman
Ref: DRN4719361
quoted_clauses: any additional hospital costs arising from single or private room accommodation unless medically necessary

text:
K820x#11
complaint
Mrs G has complained about the decision by AIG Europe Limited to decline a claim under 
her personal accident policy for total and permanent loss of use of one hand. 
background
In May 2008, Mrs G had a fall in which she fractured her wrist.
In January 2010, she submitted a claim under her personal accident policy. AIG settled the 
claim under the “Fracture benefit” of the policy. However, it declined a claim for permanent 
disability benefit in respect of total loss of use of Mrs G’s hand because her GP had not 
confirmed, on the claim form, that permanent disability had been suffered solely as a result 
of the accident.
In September 2012, Mrs G re-submitted a claim for permanent disability benefit. AIG 
arranged or her to undergo an independent medical examination (IME) by a consultant 
orthopaedic surgeon (“Doctor B”). 
In March 2013, while waiting to assess Doctor B’s report, AIG acknowledged that there had 
been delays in assessing Mrs G’s claim and offered £100 compensation.
In May 2013, having assessed Doctor B’s report, AIG continued to decline the claim. Mrs G 
did not agree with AIG’s decision and referred the matter to this service. She also 
considered that the £100 compensation for the delays was insufficient.
Our adjudicator did not recommend that the complaint be upheld. He concluded, based upon 
the medical evidence that Mrs G’s disability was as a result of a pre-existing condition rather 
than because of the accident. He considered the compensation award for the delays to be 
reasonable.
Mrs G did not accept the adjudicator’s conclusions. She outlined the loss of functionality in 
her hand since the accident and submitted a letter in support of her case from a neighbour 
who was a former GP (“Doctor C”). The adjudicator forwarded the letter to AIG for its 
consideration but it said that its decision was unchanged as it put more weight on the 
conclusions of Mrs G’s GP and Doctor B over that of Doctor C.
The adjudicator agreed with AIG’s comments and continued to recommend that the 
complaint be not upheld. Mrs G still did not accept his recommendation. The matter has 
therefore been passed to me for determination.
my findings
I have considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what is fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint. Having done so, while I recognise it will 
come as a disappointment to Mrs G, I do not uphold this complaint. I shall explain why.
The policy states:
“The company will pay the benefit shown to an Insured Person as specified on the 
application schedule who suffers an accidental bodily injury during any period of 
insurance, which solely and independently of any other cause results within 12 
Ref: DRN4724453

2
months of the date of the accident in any of the disabilities or fractures listed and 
defined below.” 
This service takes the approach that reliance on the “sole cause” wording where disability 
results partly from an accident is unfair and that the fair and reasonable approach is to pay a 
proportionate settlement according to the extent to which the accident contributed to the 
disability. However, for benefit to be payable, Mrs G must therefore still demonstrate that the 
accident contributed to her permanent disability.
When Mrs G initially submitted her claim in January 2010, her GP completed a form which 
included the question:
“In your opinion do you think the patient will be left with a permanent disability solely 
as a result of the accident?” 
Her GP left a blank response. It was on this basis that AIG declined her claim for permanent 
loss of use of her hand.
When Mrs G re-submitted her claim in September 2012, it appears that she asked for her 
GP to complete the form again but her GP refused. The GP record states:
“long discussion as wants me to sign her hand disability is solely as a result of her 
wrist fracture, so insurance company will give her £30,000 claim advance. I cannot 
do this as she had disability in my opinion from brachial plexus injury, not wrist.”
AIG, however, agreed to send Mrs G for an IME with Doctor B to assess whether the claim 
might be payable. Doctor B’s report stated:
“It is very clear and evident from the medical record that [Mrs G] had complete loss of 
function over her left arm, and loss of sensation due to fibrosis of her brachial plexus 
due to [her previous medical condition and subsequent treatment] ...I would not have 
expected her fracture to have caused any effects on the function of her left upper 
limb … I do not believe the accident will have caused her any long-term problem or 
disability.”
In a further report, Doctor B stated:
“I have re-examined the medical record and my report again. I can confirm that [Mrs 
G’s] loss of function of her left hand and the contracture of her fingers are caused by 
her pre-existing problem and damage to the brachial plexus … and not caused by the 
index accident.”
Mrs G has submitted a letter from Doctor C in support of her case but I agree with AIG that 
this does not carry as much weight as the opinion of her GP and Doctor B. I say this 
because her GP is actively involved in Mrs G’s treatment and Doctor B is a specialist in an 
area relevant to Mrs G’s injury. Doctor C, on the other hand, is no longer a practicing 
medical professional and his opinion has been offered apparently without the benefit of 
seeing Mrs G’s full medical records. 
Overall, I do not consider that Mrs G has submitted enough medical evidence to persuade 
me that her accident has contributed to the permanent loss of use of her hand. In these 
circumstances, I consider it was reasonable of AIG to decline her claim.
Ref: DRN4724453

3
I also consider that AIG’s offer of £100 compensation for the delays in dealing with the claim 
was reasonable.
my final decision
For the reasons above, my final decision is that I do not uphold this complaint. I make no 
award against AIG Europe Limited.
David Poley
ombudsman 
Ref: DRN4724453
