long discussion as wants me to sign her hand disability is solely as a result of her wrist fracture, so insurance company will give her £30,000 claim advance. I cannot do this as she had disability in my opinion from brachial plexus injury, not wrist.

It is very clear and evident from the medical record that [Mrs G] had complete loss of function over her left arm, and loss of sensation due to fibrosis of her brachial plexus due to [her previous medical condition and subsequent treatment] ...I would not have expected her fracture to have caused any effects on the function of her left upper limb … I do not believe the accident will have caused her any long-term problem or disability.

I have re-examined the medical record and my report again. I can confirm that [Mrs G’s] loss of function of her left hand and the contracture of her fingers are caused by her pre-existing problem and damage to the brachial plexus … and not caused by the index accident.

text:
K821x#15
complaint
Mr and Mrs H complain that Union Reiseversicherung AG (‘Union’) unfairly declined their 
travel insurance claim and misled them during a telephone call to discuss the claim.
background
I issued my provisional decision on this complaint in November 2018, which forms part of 
this final decision. In it, I concluded that the policy exclusion relating to the pre-existing 
medical conditions of travelling companions was not made clear, so I didn’t think it would be 
fair for Union to decline Mr and Mrs H’s claim by relying on it.
I didn’t think the exclusion satisfied the requirement for transparency under section 68 of the 
Consumer Rights Act (CRA) 2015. I also considered that the way it was presented was 
ambiguous, such that it could give rise to different meanings. And according to section 69 of 
the CRA 2015, the meaning that is most favourable to the consumer is to prevail, which in 
this context would mean that the pre-existing conditions of travelling companions would be 
covered if it was the cause of a trip being cancelled. So I said I was minded to uphold 
Mr and Mrs H’s complaint and was intending to ask Union to meet the cancellation claim 
subject to the remaining terms of the policy.
Union responded saying they hadn’t seen any evidence that Mr and Mrs H thought they 
were covered as a result of the way the travelling companion exclusion was presented, and 
that few travel insurance policies would cover such risks. 
Mr and Mrs H had nothing further to add in response to my provisional decision.
my findings
I’ve reconsidered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint – including Union’s response. Having 
done so, I’ve decided to uphold Mr and Mrs H’s complaint for the same reasons as set out in 
my provisional decision. 
Union say they’ve seen no evidence to suggest that Mr and Mrs H thought they were 
covered, and believe that they would’ve been well aware of F’s increasing infirmity and 
simply assumed it would be covered. But regardless of whether they thought their travelling 
companion’s medical condition would’ve been covered, the point is that it had not been 
made clear that it wasn’t covered, which means that Union cannot fairly seek to rely on it. So 
if Mr and Mrs H did just simply assumed it would be covered as Union submits, this 
assumption isn’t necessarily unjustified given that the exclusion is ambiguous and is not 
transparent. And in any event, I think that Mr and Mrs H did in fact think their reasons for 
cancelling the holiday were covered.
Union say that few, if any, travel insurance policies would cover such risks, which I 
appreciate may be the case. But as the party that drafted the contract, it was for Union to 
ensure – under section 68 of the CRA 2015 – that any terms or exclusions they may want to 
rely on are transparent which, for the reasons set out in my provisional decision, I don’t 
consider this exclusion was. And where any such clause is considered to be ambiguous, the 
more favourable meaning of the term is to prevail under section 69 of the CRA 2015, 
meaning that F’s condition will be covered. So Union’s submissions do not change the 
reasoning set out in my provisional decision.
Ref: DRN4870931

2
my final decision
For the reasons given above, and in my provisional decision, I uphold Mr and Mrs H’s 
complaint. I direct Union Reiseversicherung AG to meet Mr and Mrs H’s travel insurance 
claim, subject to the remaining terms and conditions of the policy. It follows that interest 
should be added to any settlement at the simple rate of 8% a year from the date of loss (i.e. 
cancellation) to the date of payment.
Under the rules of the Financial Ombudsman Service, I’m required to ask Mr and Mrs H to 
accept or reject my decision before 13 January 2019.
Jack Ferris 
ombudsman
Ref: DRN4870931

3
COPY OF PROVISIONAL DECISION 
complaint
Mr and Mrs H complain that Union Reiseversicherung AG (‘Union’) unfairly declined their travel 
insurance claim and misled them during a telephone call to discuss the claim.
background
Mr and Mrs H took out an annual travel insurance policy with Union on 2 February 2017. They booked 
a holiday with their friends on 13 February 2017 to travel later in the year. But one of their travelling 
companions (whom I will refer to as ‘F’) informed Mr and Mrs H on 12 July 2017 that he would need to 
have an operation and would no longer be able to come.
Mr and Mrs H called Union on 13 July 2017 to discuss their options under the policy, and say they 
were advised that there would be no issues in claiming for the cost of the holiday if they wanted to 
cancel. Following this, Mr and Mrs H obtained a medical certificate from F’s GP and went ahead and 
cancelled their trip. 
Despite what Mr and Mrs H were reportedly told over the phone, Union later declined their 
cancellation claim on the basis that the further surgery F required resulted from a pre-existing medical 
condition. Union based its decision on a referral letter from F’s GP which they say shows he was 
being treated for symptoms he was experiencing as far back as October 2016 – which pre-dated the 
policy and was therefore excluded under the terms and conditions.
Mr and Mrs H contested Union’s decision to decline the claim, as they argued that F’s condition was 
not diagnosed until July 2017 and, therefore, was not pre-existing. They obtained a letter from F’s GP 
explaining that the referral back in October 2016 was not in any way related to the condition that led 
to F being unable to go on holiday – which the GP confirmed was not a problem until later in 2017, i.e. 
after the policy’s inception. 
Union considered the GP’s letter, but maintained that its decision to decline the claim was correct. Mr 
and Mrs H complained that the claim was unfairly declined, and further submit that they were misled 
during the initial call they had with Union when they discussed the claim, as they say they were given 
incorrect information and wouldn’t have cancelled the holiday if they’d been advised that F’s condition 
wouldn’t have been covered. 
Our investigator initially upheld Mr and Mrs H’s complaint, as he didn’t consider there was enough 
evidence to show that F’s condition was pre-existing – particularly in light of the letter from F’s GP 
which said the condition was a separate issue to the problem reported in October 2016. 
In response, Union pointed out that F originally had an operation in March 2017, which was soon after 
the policy had been purchased. Union says it wasn’t clear what had happened leading up to the 
operation – so it requested further medical records. Our investigator felt this was reasonable, and a 
letter was subsequently provided by F’s GP who said the March 2017 operation was not carried out 
on an emergency basis. The letter explained that F had originally seen a specialist back in 2015 when 
he was first considering the operation, but given that his symptoms were improving at that time there 
was no intervention. F was later seen in a clinic on 10 January 2017, however, as his symptoms were 
returning. He was then referred to a surgeon who proposed the surgery that was carried out in March 
2017. 
Following this new evidence, our investigator decided that he could no longer uphold Mr and Mrs H’s 
complaint because it did appear that the claim was excluded. He concluded that Union could rely on 
the exclusion as he felt it was made clear in the policy documentation and because the claim arose 
from a medical condition that was diagnosed prior to the holiday being booked. With regards to the 
phone call, the investigator explained that Union didn’t guarantee the claim would be paid. 
Mr and Mrs H disagreed, so the complaint has been passed to me.
Ref: DRN4870931

4
my provisional findings
I’ve considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and reasonable in the 
circumstances of this complaint. Having done so, I’m currently intending to uphold it. 
The relevant exclusion Union is seeking to rely on (which I will later refer to as “the travel companion 
exclusion”) states that: 
‘…we can only offer to medically screen and extend cover for existing medical conditions to our 
own policyholders so if any of the following people cause you to cancel because of a 
reoccurrence or complication of a medical condition diagnosed prior to booking, you will not be 
covered;
-
a travel companion not insured by us.’
An ‘existing medical condition’ is further defined by the policy as ‘any serious or recurring medical 
condition which has been previously diagnosed or been investigated or treated in any way, at any 
time prior to travel, even if this condition is currently considered to be stable and under control’. Union 
says that F’s condition that ultimately led to Mr and Mrs H’s holiday being cancelled was pre-existing 
and is therefore excluded under the policy terms and conditions. Having considered the evidence 
myself, I do think that F’s condition was pre-existing. So I’ve considered whether Union can fairly rely 
on the exclusion.
Exclusions relating to pre-existing conditions are generally considered to be significant in nature and, 
as such, must be clearly highlighted at the point of sale, preferably outside the strict contractual terms 
and conditions, if an insurer wants to later rely on it. This has long been regarded as good industry 
practice by both its own professional association and the regulator. The policy documentation 
provided by Union does indeed highlight the fact that any undeclared medical conditions – seemingly 
attributable to the policyholder – will not be covered, which is made clear in the policy summary and a 
number of other areas within the policy document itself. But in this case, the claim is not concerned 
with a pre-existing condition of the policyholder, but that of an uninsured travel companion. This is an 
important distinction. 
Having considered the policy documentation, I don’t think the travel companion exclusion has been 
sufficiently highlighted or brought to Mr and Mrs H’s attention at all. There is no mention in the policy 
summary, for example, of the extent to which a travelling companion’s medical conditions may be 
excluded. And it only seems to appear once within the policy documentation at page 12. But I do 
appreciate that an exclusion relating to an uninsured person’s medical conditions is arguably not a 
‘significant’ term in the same way as an exclusion for the insured person themselves, and may 
therefore not require the same level of prominence.
But as well as considering the well-established approach to significant restrictions or limitations on 
cover, it’s also my duty as an ombudsman to take account of the relevant law when considering 
whether Union can fairly rely on the exclusion.
Relevant law includes the Consumer Rights Act 2015 (‘CRA 2015’), of which section 68 sets down an 
obligation on traders (a term that would include insurers) to ‘ensure that a written term of a consumer 
contract…is transparent’ – meaning it must be ‘expressed in plain and intelligible language and is 
legible’. But in the context of the relevant documentation considered as a whole, and how it might 
reasonably be interpreted by the average consumer, I think the travel companion exclusion fails the 
requirement for transparency under section 68.
I already explained earlier that the travel companion exclusion is not mentioned in the policy summary 
or key facts document. It sets out that existing medical conditions are excluded, but it doesn’t make it 
clear whether that is in the context of the policyholder or anyone else for that matter. Turning to the 
policy document itself, the travel companion exclusion is similarly not mentioned in the section titled 
Ref: DRN4870931

5
‘Conditions and exclusions applying to your policies’. Again, it outlines that the policyholder is not 
covered for any existing medical conditions, but there is no mention of travel companions. 
The ‘pre travel policy’ summary on page three of the policy document also sets out the cover that is 
available under this section:
‘A1 – If you are unable to go on your trip:
Cover for your proportion of prepaid transport, pre booked excursions, accommodation and 
additional travel expenses that you cannot recover from any other source if you cannot travel 
due to; your, a close relative, the person you are intending to stay with, a travelling 
companion, or a business associates death, injury or illness…’
The same section then sets out the exclusions that apply to the above, where it states that cover will 
only be provided under this section of the policy if:
‘you are not claiming due to an existing medical condition of a non-travelling close relative, 
the person you are intending to stay with, or a close business associate’
So again, despite this section saying that cover is available for trips cancelled due to issues with a 
travel companion, it sets out certain categories of uninsured people where pre-existing conditions will 
not covered, but it still fails to state that pre-existing conditions of the travelling companion are also 
excluded. It then isn’t until page 12 of the policy document that the travel companion exclusion is set 
out and indicates they are, in fact, not covered.
Given that it’s relatively difficult to establish whether a travelling companion’s pre-existing conditions 
are excluded or not – and taking into account the context of the policy documentation as a whole – I 
consider that the exclusion fails the requirement for transparency under section 68 of the CRA 2015 
as it’s not presented in plain and intelligible language.
I also consider that the way the cover and relevant exclusions are presented in the policy could give 
rise to different meanings. Section 69 of the CRA 2015 deals with contract terms that may have 
different meanings, and stipulates that ‘if a term in a consumer contract…could have different 
meanings, the meaning that is most favourable to the consumer is to prevail’. This effectively codifies 
the long-established rule of contractual interpretation known by the Latin tag contra proferentem, 
whereby an unclear or ambiguous term is construed against the person who drafted it – in this case, 
Union.
As I set out earlier, the ‘pre travel policy’ summary lists certain categories of uninsured people whose 
pre-existing medical conditions will be excluded in the event of the policyholder’s holiday being 
cancelled. Similarly, there is an entire page dedicated to medical conditions on page seven of the 
policy, with a prominent section that states:
‘BE AWARE! We do not provide cover for:
Claims caused by an existing medical condition of a non-travelling close relative, a close business 
associate, person you intend to stay with or any recognised complication caused by the existing 
medical condition…’
Given that there are two separate instances in the policy where travel companions are not included 
alongside this group of other uninsured people, it creates an ambiguity that their pre-existing medical 
conditions will therefore be covered – particularly because travel companions are listed earlier in the 
policy with the same group of uninsured people in terms of the perils that will be covered (see page 
three; A1: if you are unable to go on your trip). 
Ref: DRN4870931

6
So – when considered in the overall context of the policy documentation – this ambiguity could give 
rise to different meanings with regards to what is and isn’t covered for travel companions. And 
according to section 69, the meaning that is most favourable to the consumer is to prevail, which in 
this context is that the pre-existing medical conditions of travelling companions will be covered if this 
is the cause of a trip being cancelled. 
So in summary, although I do believe that Mr and Mrs H’s trip was cancelled due to F’s pre-existing 
medical condition, I don’t consider that the travel companion exclusion satisfies the requirement for 
transparency under section 68 of the CRA 2015. So I do not think it would be fair for Union to rely on 
it. And given the ambiguous context surrounding the exclusion, I conclude that the more favourable 
meaning of the term is to prevail under section 69 of the CRA 2015 – i.e. that F’s pre-existing 
conditions will be covered – which means that Union should meet the cancellation claim subject to the 
remaining policy terms and conditions. 
my provisional decision
For the reasons outlined above, I’m currently minded to uphold this complaint and direct Union 
Reiseversicherung AG to meet Mr and Mrs H’s travel insurance claim, subject to the remaining terms 
and conditions of the policy. It follows that interest should be added to any settlement at the simple 
rate of 8% a year from the date of loss (i.e. cancellation) to the date of payment.
Jack Ferris
ombudsman

text:
K820x#11
complaint
Mr G has complained about the decision of UK Insurance Limited (“UKI”) to reject his claim 
for personal accident benefit under his travel insurance policy, saying that his pre-existing 
medical condition was notified to UKI and was not the cause of either the accident or the 
amputation.
background
Mr G had travel insurance underwritten by UKI as a benefit of his bank account for many 
years. Whilst on holiday, Mr G sustained serious injuries to his feet. UKI met the cost of his 
medical treatment overseas. After he returned to the UK, Mr G continued to receive 
treatment but it was unsuccessful and one foot had to be amputated. He submitted a claim 
for the personal accident benefit for loss of a limb.
UKI rejected the claim, giving a number of different reasons for concluding that it did not 
meet the policy terms. Mr G disputed each of those reasons and UKI paid a small amount of 
compensation for poor handling of the claim, but maintained the claim did not satisfy the 
policy conditions relating to “loss of limb”.
Mr G was aggrieved with UKI’s rejection of the claim. The complaint was investigated by an 
adjudicator who considered the medical evidence provided by Mr G’s GP showed that the 
claim was not covered under the policy. The GP stated that Mr G’s pre-existing medical 
conditions had caused the accident, made the injuries worse and affected his ability to heal. 
The adjudicator concluded that Mr G had not shown the loss of limb was due to an 
“accidental, bodily injury caused solely and directly by outward violent and visible means”. In 
his opinion, it was reasonable for UKI to reject the claim. 
Mr G disagreed. He said that the need for amputation was the result of the injuries he 
suffered whilst on holiday and had no other cause.
 
my findings
I have considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what is fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint. 
The issue for me to determine is whether it was fair and reasonable for UKI to reject Mr G’s 
claim for personal accident benefit.
I have considered the complaint as sympathetically as possible since I have no doubt that Mr 
G has had a terrible experience and the overall handling of his claim was not satisfactory.
UKI accepted that Mr G’s injury was a “personal accident”, despite a clear legal ruling by the 
Court of Appeal that a similar case could not be considered a personal accident; and 
contrary to the medical evidence that Mr G’s existing medical conditions caused the accident 
to occur. I have therefore treated the claim as arising from a personal accident.
I consider it significant that the policy states:
“In addition to anything in the general exclusions, we will not pay any claim, which 
arises from or is in connection with:
Ref: DRN4935201

2
1
Any sickness or disease, naturally occurring or degenerative condition …
3    A pre-existing medical condition …
5    Any complication following a bodily injury which is attributable to your death, loss 
of limb, loss of sight or total permanent disablement …”
In my judgment, Mr G’s claim is specifically excluded by clauses (1) and (3) because of his 
existing medical conditions. I note that Mr G stated that he disclosed his medical conditions 
to UKI. UKI denied any such knowledge. Mr G has no evidence that UKI agreed to cover any 
existing medical condition and I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that it covered 
any of those conditions.
Even if I am wrong to agree with UKI that it was entitled to rely on clauses (1) and (3) to 
reject the claim, it is clear from the medical evidence that clause (5) is also applicable. The 
overseas medical report states that the injury was infected at the date of treatment; and it 
was this infection which meant that Mr G did not recover properly and which led to 
amputation. Mr G’s GP stated that that his pre-existing medical conditions contributed to Mr 
G’s poor recovery and there is no medical evidence to question his professional opinion. 
I have also considered the handling of the claim. As explained above, UKI was entitled to 
reject the claim for medical expenses on the grounds that what happened was not an 
accidental bodily injury. I do not consider it should increase its offer of compensation. 
Despite my sympathy for Mr G’s predicament, I am satisfied that UKI was reasonably 
entitled to reject the claim. I am unable to agree it would be either fair or reasonable to 
require UKI to make any further payment to him.
my final decision
It is my final decision that UK Insurance Limited was entitled to reject Mr G’s claim.
I make no award against UK Insurance Limited.
Reidy Flynn
ombudsman
Ref: DRN4935201

text:
K821x#15
complaint
Mr and Mrs S complain that Allianz Insurance Plc won’t pay their pet insurance claim under 
their ‘Classic’ policy. My references to Allianz include its agents.
background
Mr and Mrs S took out a 4 week free policy with Allianz on 5 March. They converted the free 
policy to an ‘Essential’ 12 month policy starting 2 April and then upgraded to a ‘Classic’ 
cover for life policy on 13 April the same year. Later that day they took their puppy to a vet 
and he was treated for myositis (an inflammatory disease affecting jaw muscles). Mr and 
Mrs S claimed for the treatment costs.
Allianz wouldn’t pay the claim. Initially it said the dog showed symptoms of the condition 
before the Classic policy was taken out and the policy didn’t cover pre-existing conditions. It 
now accepts there was no pre-existing condition. But it still declined the claim under the 
Classic policy as the condition started within the first 14 days of that policy which is 
excluded from cover under that policy.
Allianz then said as a goodwill gesture Mr and Mrs S could revert to their Essential policy 
cover and have the claim considered under that policy instead (it told our investigator the 
claim should be payable under the Essential policy terms). Alternatively Mr and Mrs S 
could remain with the Classic policy but the claim wouldn’t be covered and it would apply 
exclusions in relation to the condition in line with its underwriting guidance.
Mr and Mrs S complained to us saying they upgraded to the Classic policy in good faith. 
They say they knew about the 14 day exclusion period when they upgraded but they weren’t 
aware of any health issues with their dog and didn’t expect to make a claim during that 
period. They thought guidance on our website supported their case. They want the claim 
paid and future claims for the condition covered under the Classic policy.
my provisional findings
I made a provisional decision explain why I was intending to partly uphold this complaint and 
say Allianz must give Mr and Mrs S two options, which I detailed. But as I thought Allianz 
acted fairly in rejecting the claim under the Classic policy those options didn’t include the 
option Mr and Mrs S wanted. I said:
‘Mr and Mrs S’ vet confirmed that at a vet puppy party on (date given) Mrs S was advised to 
get cover for life insurance. Mrs S upgraded to the Classic policy two days later and her 
puppy was seen with the claim condition that day. There’s no evidence to suggest Mrs S 
suspected her puppy was unwell when she upgraded. Allianz is no longer saying he had a 
pre-existing condition.
But the Classic policy, giving life cover for conditions, doesn’t cover any illness which starts 
in the first 14 days of the policy even when the policy is upgraded from the Essential policy. 
I’ve listened to the recording of the call when Mrs S phoned to upgrade and Allianz clearly 
told her about that exclusion. Mr and Mrs S accept they knew about the exclusion at the 
time of the upgrade.
Mr and Mrs S quoted our website to say that as they didn’t know about any signs of the 
illness or the need for treatment when they took the policy we think it's fair for an insurer to 
pay the claim. If Allianz was relying on the pre-existing condition to decline I'd look into 
those issues when deciding whether Allianz should pay, but Allianz isn’t relying on that 
Ref: DRN5047997

2
exclusion. If the puppy had been treated outside the first 14 days and Allianz was saying 
there were signs of the illness within the first 14 days I’d look at whether Mr and Mrs S 
would have reasonably known of a problem and the need for treatment in the first 14 days, 
but that’s not the situation.
In this case Mr and Mrs S’ puppy had symptoms, was treated and diagnosed within the first 
14 days of the policy starting. Allianz is entitled to decide the basis on which it’s prepared to 
offer an upgrade to the Classic policy and one element is that it wants the 14 day waiting 
period. As Allianz clearly told Mrs S about the 14 days exclusion when she was upgrading 
I think it can fairly rely on that exclusion.
This means Allianz doesn’t need to pay the claim under the Classic policy. It also means it 
can apply exclusions in relation to the condition in line with its underwriting guidance. 
Depending on what that guidance says it may be the exclusion/s will be wider than just 
myositis.
One option Allianz should give Mr and Mrs S is to continue with the Classic cover for life 
policy, but the claim won’t be paid and it can add the relevant condition exclusions/s to the 
policy. In response to my provisional decision Allianz needs to tell me what exclusion/s it 
would apply and send me the supporting underwriting guidance so Mr and Mrs S have that 
information when deciding which option to take.
The alternative option Allianz should give is for Mr and Mrs S to revert to the Essential 
policy. It’s told our investigator the claim would be payable under the terms of that policy. 
Mr S doubts that as Allianz told him the claim would be assessed under that policy’s terms 
and the Essential policy start date was less than 14 days before the start of the puppy’s 
illness. But their Essential policy schedule says ‘Any clause in the Terms and Conditions 
which refers to an 'illness which starts in the first 14 days of cover' does not apply to this 
pet under this policy’. I understand that’s because Allianz treats the Essential policy as an 
extension to the free policy. So subject to the policy excess and limit I see no reason why 
Allianz shouldn’t pay the claim under the Essential policy.
If Mr and Mrs S choose to revert to the Essential policy Allianz must pay the claim subject to 
the policy excess and limit. As they would then have 12 month cover for the myositis Allianz 
must pay any other claim for treatment in that period (if any). I also think it would fair for 
Allianz to refund the premium difference Mr and Mrs S paid for the more expensive Classic 
policy compared to what they would have paid for the Essential policy’.
responses to my provisional decision
Allianz said if Mr and Mrs S decided to continue with the Classic (cover for life policy) it 
wouldn’t be applying any specific exclusions relating to this claim to the policy. But it 
highlighted that the standard policy exclusions about pre-existing conditions and illnesses 
starting within 14 days of the start of the policy applied. It also said it couldn’t see a 
difference between the options I said it must give and what it had already offered to Mr and 
Mrs S and asked me to clarify.
Mr and Mrs S had no comments and said they would wait to see what exclusion Allianz 
would apply to the Classic policy.
Ref: DRN5047997

3
my findings
I’ve considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint.
In its offer Allianz told Mr and Mrs S it would apply exclusions in relation to the claim 
condition in line with its underwriting guidance if they chose to continue with the Classic 
policy. It’s now told me it wouldn’t apply any claim specific exclusion/s. It‘s reasonably said 
the standard policy exclusions for pre-existing conditions and illnesses within 14 days of the 
start of the policy would apply. For the reasons in my provisional decision Allianz doesn’t 
need to pay the claim for myositis under the Classic policy. If claims for other conditions 
arise in the future that Allianz decline on the basis of the standard exclusions Mr and Mrs S 
can ultimately complain to us about any future disputes.  
Allianz asked that I clarify how the options I said it must give differ from its original offer. The 
differences are it must:

tell Mr and Mrs S what specific claim exclusions it would apply if they took the Classic 
policy option. It’s now said none would apply and it should have reasonably given 
them that information before asking them to chose the options it gave

pay the myositis claim/s within the 12 month period subject to policy limits and 
excess, without assessment against remaining policy terms, if Mr and Mrs S chose 
the Essential policy option

pay Mr and Mrs S the difference in policy premiums if they choose the Essential 
policy option.
Neither party has made any objection to my provisional decision. So for the reasons in my 
provisional findings and these findings I partly uphold the complaint. Allianz acted 
reasonably in declining the myositis claim under the Classic policy but it must give Mr and 
Mrs S the options I’ve detailed below and they can tell it what they decide.
  
my final decision
I partly uphold this complaint.
I require Allianz Insurance Plc to give Mr and Mrs S the option to either:
1.
continue with the Classic policy. The claim for myositis won’t be covered. Allianz 
won’t add a specific exclusion to the policy in relation to the claim, or
2.
revert to the Essential policy. If Mr and Mrs S choose this option Allianz Insurance 
Plc must pay the myositis claim and any other claims for the condition within the 
12 month period, subject to the policy excess and limit. Allianz must refund the 
premium difference Mr and Mrs S paid for the Classic policy compared to what they 
would have paid for the Essential policy.
Under the rules of the Financial Ombudsman Service, I’m required to ask Mr and Mrs S to 
accept or reject my decision before 8 May 2018.
Nicola Sisk
ombudsman
Ref: DRN5047997

K820x#14
complaint
Mr J complains that AXA PPP Healthcare Limited has turned down a claim made under his 
daughter’s private medical insurance policy. He also complains the policy was mis-sold. 
background
In July 2017, Mr J took out a policy for his daughter as she was under 18. This was taken out 
on a moratorium basis, which meant any pre-existing conditions experienced in the previous 
five years wouldn’t be covered. 
In August 2017, Mr J made a claim under the policy on his daughter’s behalf. AXA turned 
down the claim because it thought that either Mr J’s daughter wasn’t experiencing 
symptoms, or if she was, then this was pre-existing. Mr J was unhappy about this. He said 
he’d been led to believe when taking out the policy that so long as there was no mention of 
any existing symptoms or conditions on his daughter’s GP record before the policy was 
taken out, then a claim would be paid. 
AXA maintained its decision to decline Mr J’s daughter claim. But it accepted it could have 
made it clearer to Mr J how the moratorium worked. It offered to cancel the policy and refund 
the premiums. Mr J didn’t accept this offer, and brought a complaint to this service instead. 
A few months later, Mr J wanted to make use of AXA’s own GP service for his daughter. 
He’d paid extra for this under the policy’s ‘extended cover’. However, he found he couldn’t 
make use of the GP service because it didn’t cover child-only policies. Mr J said he’d been 
led to believe his daughter could use the service when he was sold the policy. 
AXA accepted it had led Mr J to think his daughter could use its GP service. It said it would 
allow Mr J’s daughter (and his son who has a separate policy) to use the GP service until the 
first renewal. Also, it said the extended cover under the policy could be removed if Mr J 
wanted and a proportionate refund of premiums paid. It also offered £150 compensation. 
Unhappy with this, Mr J asked this service to also consider this new complaint. 
Our investigator didn’t uphold both aspects of the complaint. She didn’t think Mr J’s daughter 
was experiencing symptoms of a medical condition, and therefore in her opinion, the claim 
wouldn’t be covered. She accepted AXA hadn’t given Mr J correct information about the 
policy, but she thought the offers it had made to put things right had been reasonable. 
Mr J didn’t agree, so the matter’s been passed to me to consider. 
my findings
I’ve considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint. 
claim
The policy explains it covers eligible treatment, which doesn’t include preventative treatment. 
It then says:
“We do not pay for:
…
Ref: DRN5049854

2

any other preventative treatment or screening tests to see whether you have a 
medical condition if you do not have any symptoms.”
The policy defines ‘treatment’ as “surgical or medical services (including diagnostic tests) 
that are needed to diagnose, relieve or cure a disease, illness or injury”.
Mr J made a claim for his daughter to see a psychologist. She’d attended a drama class and 
her teacher had noticed she hadn’t spoken for the duration of the class. To make sure there 
wasn’t an underlying problem, a GP had referred his daughter to a psychologist.  
It isn’t the case that Mr J’s daughter can’t speak. I understand she’s attended nursery for two 
years and no concerns have been raised. Mr J says his daughter is shy, but being shy isn’t a 
medical condition and he wanted to understand if there was anything else medically wrong. 
He explains the GP had referred his daughter to a psychologist to rule out a medical 
condition.  
It seems to me that the only reported symptom is that of shyness. The investigator thought 
there was no reason for Mr J to believe his daughter’s shyness was a symptom of a medical 
condition. I’m minded to agree. Consequently, that means any treatment to see whether or 
not she has a medical condition would be considered preventative and therefore isn’t 
covered. 
Alternatively, as AXA has said, even if Mr J’s daughter’s shyness is found to be a symptom 
of a medical condition, it’s reasonable to say she was experiencing this before taking out the 
policy as the claim was made shortly after the policy was taken out. That would mean it 
would be considered pre-existing and fall under the moratorium. I haven’t included the full 
definition of ‘pre-existing condition’ here as I see AXA has previously included it in its 
response to Mr J. 
I’m therefore satisfied it was appropriate for AXA to turn down the claim.
sale of the policy
AXA accepts that when the policy was sold to Mr J, it should have made it clearer to him that 
any symptoms his daughter had experienced in the five years before taking out the policy 
would be considered pre-existing, regardless of whether or not those symptoms were 
mentioned on her medical records. I would agree. 
When a business has made an error, we think about what the consumer would have done, 
had they been given the correct information. Given that Mr J didn’t think his daughter was 
experiencing any symptoms when the policy was taken out, I think it’s likely he would have 
still gone ahead with the policy if the moratorium has been properly explained to him. 
However, AXA has offered to cancel the policy and return all premiums paid. I think this is a 
generous offer and not something that I would have required AXA to do. It’s up to Mr J if he 
wishes to accept this offer. 
Also, when Mr J took out the policy for his daughter, he paid for ‘extended cover’. That 
included (amongst other things) up to five consultations with a private GP by phone or 
online. When Mr J wanted to make use of this for his daughter, he discovered that AXA 
doesn’t provide this service for child-only policies. 
Ref: DRN5049854

3
I’ve listened to the relevant phone call, and unfortunately AXA let Mr J think his daughter 
could make use of the private GP service. The adviser failed to tell him his daughter couldn’t 
use it because it was a child-only policy.  
To put the matter right, AXA has offered to allow Mr J’s daughter (and son under another 
policy) to have up to five consultations with a private GP until the policy renewal. It also said 
that if Mr J wanted, it could remove the extended cover and refund the relevant proportion of 
premiums he’d paid for that cover. 
I can’t be sure what Mr J would have done if AXA had made it clear to him that his daughter 
couldn’t use its private GP service. He may have still wished to take out the extended cover 
because of the other benefits it provided. However, he may not have. That being the case, I 
think AXA’s offer here is reasonable as it allows him to cancel the extended cover if he 
wishes, but also allows his children to make use of the private GP service until renewal. 
I think Mr J has been caused some inconvenience by AXA failing to make it clear to him how 
the policy worked when it was sold. However, I see AXA has offered £150 compensation 
which I think is appropriate. 
Mr J is concerned that he can’t now change provider because his daughter has 
symptoms/conditions on her medical records since the AXA policy started. Mr J can change 
provider, though he may wish to seek independent advice from a broker about transferring to 
another provider and the type of underwriting that would be most appropriate for his 
daughter. 
Mr J also says his daughter hasn’t been able to use aspects of the policy (I assume he’s 
referring to the private GP service here) because it was mis-sold. Whilst I’ve accepted that 
AXA didn’t make it clear to Mr J that his daughter couldn’t use the private GP service, I’m 
satisfied this aspect of cover wasn’t the reason Mr J took out the policy in the first place. I’ve 
already explained why I think AXA’s offer to put the matter right is reasonable.   
my final decision
My final decision is that I don’t uphold this complaint. 
Under the rules of the Financial Ombudsman Service, I’m required to ask Mr J to accept or 
reject my decision before 8 May 2018.
Chantelle Hurn-Ryan
ombudsman
Ref: DRN5049854
quoted_clauses: We do not pay for: … Ref: DRN5049854 2  any other preventative treatment or screening tests to see whether you have a medical condition if you do not have any symptoms.
surgical or medical services (including diagnostic tests) that are needed to diagnose, relieve or cure a disease, illness or injury

text:
K820x#13
complaint
Miss D has complained about AXA PPP Healthcare Limited’s decision to decline her claim 
for treatment of thyroid cancer under her private medical insurance policy.
background
Miss D held private medical cover with an insurer (“Z”). 
In December 2013, Miss D visited her GP as she had noticed a cyst on her neck. Her GP 
referred her to a specialist (“Mr A”) who arranged for her to undergo investigations, including 
a fine needle aspiration procedure (“FNA”) during which the cyst was drained. The cost of 
these investigations was covered by Z. No definite problem was identified.
In February 2014, Miss D transferred her private medical insurance cover from Z to AXA. 
The policy was underwritten on a moratorium basis. This meant that anything Miss D 
suffered from in the three years before the policy started would be considered a ‘pre-existing 
condition’ and would not initially be covered under the policy.
In May 2014, Miss D again visited her GP as she had noticed that the cyst on her neck had 
re-appeared. Her GP referred her to a different specialist (“Mr S”). Miss D asked AXA to 
authorise the consultation and any investigations. After checking Miss D’s medical records, 
AXA advised Miss D that it wouldn’t do so because it thought that her condition was pre-
existing under the terms of the policy.
Miss D went ahead with the consultation in June 2014. Mr S recommended that she 
underwent further tests before he could properly diagnose her condition. Because AXA 
wouldn’t provide funding, Miss D had these through the NHS. In August 2014, Miss D was 
diagnosed as suffering from thyroid cancer and underwent surgery, again through the NHS. 
AXA continued to state that it had been correct to regard Miss D’s condition as pre-existing. 
Miss D was unhappy at this and referred her complaint to this service.  
Our adjudicator did not recommend that the complaint be upheld. She thought that the 
medical evidence suggested Miss D had symptoms of thyroid cancer before the policy start 
date. She concluded that AXA had acted fairly and reasonably when it decided to decline the 
claim.
Miss D did not agree with our adjudicator’s assessment. She maintained that she had been 
diagnosed with thyroid cancer only after the policy start date and therefore felt the treatment 
should be covered.
In view of the continued disagreement, the complaint has been passed to me for review. 
my findings
I have considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what is fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint. Having done so, although I recognise that 
Miss D will be disappointed, I do not uphold this complaint. I shall explain why.
The policy makes clear that cover is not initially provided for pre-existing conditions. The 
policy defines a pre-existing condition as follows:
Ref: DRN5165959

2
“any disease, illness or injury for which:

you have received medication, advice or treatment; or

you have experienced symptoms;
whether the condition has been diagnosed or not in the three years before the start of 
your cover.”
Shortly before taking out the policy, Miss D had undergone investigations into the cyst on her 
neck. The day before her policy started, Mr A had written to Miss D’s GP stating:
“Her recent histology raised the possibility of a lymphoma from the biopsy obtained 
from a neck node. Clinically there is no particular reason to suspect this.” 
Mr A nonetheless sent her for some blood tests but apparently later discharged her back to 
the care of her GP. Unfortunately, a few months later, after the cyst had returned, Miss D 
was diagnosed with thyroid cancer.
I accept that, at the time she took out the policy, Miss D had not been diagnosed with thyroid 
cancer and had no particular reason to worry about her neck. Indeed, if she had been 
worried, she would presumably not have transferred from Z as it had already provided cover 
for treatment of her neck condition.
However, I consider that the evidence suggests that the first appearance of the cyst was a 
symptom of her thyroid cancer. Given that this happened in the three years before taking out 
the policy and that she underwent treatment of the symptom at that time, I think it was 
reasonable for AXA to say that her condition was pre-existing under the terms of the policy 
and to decline the claim. 
my final decision
For the reasons given above, my final decision is that I do not uphold this complaint. I make 
no award against AXA PPP Healthcare Limited. 
Under the rules of the Financial Ombudsman Service, I am required to ask Miss D to accept 
or reject my decision before 20 July 2015. 
David Poley
ombudsman
Ref: DRN5165959

text:
K820x#14
complaint
Mr H has complained that Standard Life Assurance Limited has unfairly refused to pay his 
claim under his income protection policy.
background
Mr H had a personal income protection policy with Standard Life. In June 2015, Mr H was 
involved in a road traffic accident, which caused an injury to his knee. He said despite his 
injury he continued working until 5 October 2015 but then was absent from work due to pain. 
His contract as a risk and compliance consultant was terminated on 4 November 2015.
His policy has a 26-week ‘waiting period’ before benefit could be paid. So that meant if 
Standard Life accepted Mr H’s claim, benefit would only be payable from 4 April 2016.
On 4 May 2016, Standard Life refused to pay Mr H’s claim. He appealed and Standard Life 
reiterated its decision on 29 June 2016. Mr H then brought his complaint to us.
The adjudicator who investigated it didn’t think Standard Life had done anything wrong. Mr H 
didn’t agree, so his complaint has been passed to me to decide. 
my findings
I’ve considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint.  Having done so, I’m not upholding this 
complaint and I’ll now explain why.
In order for benefit to be paid under Mr H’s policy, he must show that he is ‘unable to carry 
out the material and substantive duties of his occupation because of illness or injury.’ 
In his occupational questionnaire, which Mr H completed for Standard Life in March 2016, he 
described himself as a compliance consultant. Mr H has told us that his job was a risk and 
compliance consultant and that his particular role encompassed sales. I don’t necessarily 
think this distinction would make any difference to the outcome of this complaint but, given 
that he wasn’t in that role at the time the waiting period ended, I think it was reasonable for 
Standard Life to assess his claim against a generic role of a compliance consultant. 
Mr H said that due to his road traffic accident in June 2015 where he injured his knee, he 
became unable to do his occupation in October 2015, as the pain had got worse. So from 
that point in October 2015, his ’26-week waiting period’ began. Benefit is only payable under 
Mr H’s policy if he is unable to do his occupation throughout the 26-week waiting period and 
remains so unable at the time the waiting period ended. Consequently, no benefit was due to 
be paid to Mr H by Standard Life before April 2016 in any event and so I don’t consider that 
Standard Life delayed in processing Mr H’s claim.
Mr H had an MRI scan in October 2015, which showed he had a lateral meniscal tear in his 
right knee. He had an arthroscopy in February 2016 and six weeks after this surgery he was 
referred to have physiotherapy and discharged from any further follow up by his surgeon. On 
the basis of this evidence, which didn’t show any further issues or that his recovery had been 
unusual, Standard Life told Mr H on 4 May 2015 that he hadn’t met the definition of 
incapacity in his policy, so it wouldn’t pay his claim. Given the lack of any evidence to the 
contrary, I don’t think Standard Life did anything wrong at this point.
Ref: DRN5241249

2
When Mr H appealed, he said he was still in a lot of pain, and unable to drive. So Standard 
Life obtained Mr H’s medical records from his GP. These notes said he was walking his dog 
in March 2016 and that he should give up playing rugby. And when Mr H saw his GP in April 
2016, his GP notes said Mr H had said his pain was decreasing. Standard Life also arranged 
some surveillance, which showed Mr H could drive during that time and walk without a 
crutch or walking stick. Additionally Standard Life had its Chief Medical Officer (CMO) review 
Mr H’s claim. In my view its CMO correctly asked himself (not whether Mr H had knee pain 
as he accepted Mr H had consistently reported it) but whether this knee pain would ensure 
Mr H wasn’t able to undertake a largely sedentary role. He believed there was no evidence 
to show why Mr H couldn’t undertake this role. It remains that there is no further evidence to 
contradict this CMO’s view for example from Mr H’s treating physicians. Consequently, I 
don’t consider that Standard Life did anything wrong in deciding that Mr H didn’t meet the 
policy conditions for payment of his claim.
Standard Life acknowledged there were some communications problems at the beginning of 
his claim and offered Mr H £200 for this. I think that’s appropriate and is of the amount I 
would normally award in these circumstances.
my final decision
So for the reasons I’ve discussed above, it’s my final decision that I don’t uphold this 
complaint.
Under the rules of the Financial Ombudsman Service, I’m required to ask Mr H to accept or 
reject my decision before 14 November 2016.
Rona Doyle
ombudsman
Ref: DRN5241249
quoted_clauses: unable to carry out the material and substantive duties of his occupation because of illness or injury.

text:
K821x#15
complaint
Mr and Mrs M are unhappy that Mapfre Asistencia, Compania Internacional De Seguros y 
Reaseguros, S.A. (“Mapfre”) didn’t cover private hospital costs under their travel insurance 
policy. They’re also unhappy with the way Mapfre handled their claim throughout, and its 
lack of support.
background
I issued a provisional decision on this complaint in July 2018. I asked everyone to send me 
any further comments and information before I reached a final decision. Mapfre said it 
accepted my decision. Mr and Mrs M were broadly in agreement with my decision, but they 
didn’t agree when I said that Mapfre’s actions didn’t cause significant delays.
Here’s what I said in my provisional decision:
“Mrs M was in an accident in February 2017 while travelling abroad. Mr M got in touch with 
Mapfre about this promptly. The next day he told Mapfre the doctor had said Mrs M needed 
an operation due to the accident – and this could either be carried out in the hospital they 
were at, or back in the UK.
Mr and Mrs M were understandably concerned about delaying the operation, and wanted 
this to be carried out as soon as possible. Mapfre confirmed that general expenses would be 
covered under the European Health Insurance Card (“EHIC”), but said it was still waiting 
confirmation from its medical team about the physician and private room costs. Mapfre’s 
agent also said during the call that his assumption was that the medical panel would cover 
the claim as medically justified.
Mr and Mrs M weren’t happy how long it was taking Mapfre to confirm everything was 
covered, so they decided to go ahead with the operation without Mapfre’s approval. Mrs M 
had already missed out on an operation slot, so this was carried out two days after the 
accident.  
Mrs M received a “fit to fly” note soon after the operation and Mr M got in touch with Mapfre 
about repatriation. He chased Mapfre about this several times, as he didn’t think it was doing 
enough to help. Mapfre got confirmation three days after the operation that Mrs M could be 
discharged – but Mapfre said it needed a full medical update before it could recommend 
repatriation. Mapfre received this and it arranged a return flight for Mr and Mrs M five days 
after the operation had taken place. 
Mr and Mrs M sent Mapfre all the invoices for their claim in March 2017, and Mapfre settled 
most of these by early April 2017. None of these costs are in dispute, so I haven’t 
considered them as part of my decision.
But Mr and Mrs M received a bill from the hospital in April 2017 for over €10,000 for the 
private treatment and private room costs. Mapfre says that as private medical treatment isn’t 
covered under the policy, it won’t cover these costs. It also says Mrs M signed a document 
agreeing to private care without first getting authorisation from Mapfre.
Mapfre agreed that the quality of its communication with Mr and Mrs M could’ve been better, 
so it offered them £200 in compensation for the trouble and upset caused. 
Ref: DRN5373024

2
One of our investigators looked into Mr and Mrs M’s complaint. She didn’t think Mapfre had 
done anything wrong by refusing to pay for the private treatment. This was excluded under 
the policy, and Mrs M had signed a document in the hospital confirming she accepted the 
costs for private care. This document said it was the responsibility of the patient to make 
sure these costs were covered by their insurer – otherwise she’d be liable for them.
She acknowledged that Mapfre hadn’t handled the claim as well as it should’ve, and there 
had been delays. But she thought the compensation Mapfre had already offered was fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances.
Our investigator also thought that Mapfre had delayed letting Mr and Mrs M know it wouldn’t 
be covering the hospital bill. So she thought Mapfre should cover the loss Mr and Mrs M 
suffered due to the change in exchange rate between April and June 2017.
Mapfre agreed with the investigator’s findings, but Mr and Mrs M didn’t. In summary, they 
said that when Mrs M signed the document, she was severely concussed and Mr M wasn’t 
aware of it until much later. And in any event, they said Mapfre should’ve given more helpful 
advice from the start.
They also said the amount of compensation wasn’t enough considering how distressing the 
whole situation had been, and the impact Mapfre’s lack of communication and delays had. 
Mr and Mrs M say they also incurred avoidable costs because of this.
Because no agreement was reached, the complaint has been passed to me.
my provisional findings
I’ve considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint.
Having done so, I’m intending to uphold the complaint in part. I’ll explain why.
Both parties have given detailed information and comments about the events. I’ve 
considered all the information available, but in my decision I’ve focused on the points that I 
think are most relevant.
Firstly, I accept that Mr and Mrs M’s travel insurance policy doesn’t cover private medical 
treatment unless it’s specifically authorised. So, I now need to decide if I think Mapfre has 
applied this exclusion in a fair and reasonable way, having taken into account the 
circumstances of the case. 
Mapfre says Mrs M signed a document accepting the private care – and she did that without 
telling Mapfre about it, or waiting for confirmation of what was or wasn’t covered. So it 
doesn’t think it should pay for any of the private costs.
But Mapfre’s notes show it was aware Mrs M was in a private room, and that there would be 
private professional fees from the doctors which wouldn’t be covered by EHIC, before Mrs M 
had the operation. So I think Mapfre had enough information to see it was likely Mrs M’s 
treatment would include private costs. 
Ref: DRN5373024

3
The only costs Mapfre did discuss at the time were the private room costs – albeit this was a 
day after the operation. And Mr M said they’d pay those costs themselves if Mapfre didn’t 
cover them. So, even if Mapfre had told Mr and Mrs M this earlier, I think they would’ve still 
chosen for Mrs M to stay in the private room. Because of this, I don’t think it would be fair or 
reasonable to ask Mapfre to pay the private room costs. 
But I can’t see that Mapfre discussed the private physician fees with Mr and Mrs M. It was 
only after it received the hospital bill a month later that it looked into those costs in detail, 
and decided not to cover them. 
If Mapfre wasn’t willing to cover the private treatment costs that it was aware of before the 
operation, I think it should’ve got in touch with Mr and Mrs M sooner to discuss options, and 
to explain what it wasn’t willing to cover. Instead, its notes show that it agreed to cover the 
claim.
If Mapfre had been clearer about the limits of cover earlier then I’m satisfied, based on what 
Mr and Mrs M have told us about the standard of care being given in the hospital, that it’s 
likely they wouldn’t have chosen to have the operation carried out privately. So I don’t 
therefore think it’s fair or reasonable for Mapfre to decline the claim for the private treatment 
costs. 
I can see that Mapfre feels strongly that it shouldn’t have to pay any of the costs. I’ve 
considered everything Mapfre has said – including that it assumed any additional costs 
would be minor and that Mr and Mrs M could’ve done more. But I don’t see why Mapfre 
didn’t contact the hospital directly if it had any questions or concerns about the private costs. 
And even if Mr and Mrs M had specifically told Mapfre there are private costs (rather than 
additional costs) – this is information Mapfre already had. So, the points Mapfre has raised 
don’t change my provisional findings. 
Mr M negotiated a reduction in the hospital bill with the hospital. He says he paid €7,000 in 
total, and he doesn’t have a breakdown of the final balance. Mr M should send Mapfre 
evidence of this payment – and the exchange rate used. But as Mr and Mrs M don’t have a 
breakdown of the final payment, I think the fair and reasonable outcome is for Mapfre to 
deduct the original cost of the private room from the amount Mr and Mrs M paid.
Mapfre accepts that the quality of its communication could’ve been better throughout 
Mr and Mrs M’s claim. It offered £200 in compensation for the trouble and upset caused. But 
its claims team also offered £50 for the delays – so the total offer is £250.
I’ve looked at everything that happened, and I’ve thought about what Mr and Mrs M have 
said. It’s clear that the situation was distressing for them both, considering the accident 
Mrs M had been in, and the injury she suffered. I agree that at times, Mapfre could’ve been 
more helpful to Mr and Mrs M, and there were delays during the claims process.
Ref: DRN5373024

4
Mr and Mrs M say that Mrs M could’ve been discharged from the hospital much earlier, had 
Mapfre done more. But while I agree Mapfre’s communications could’ve been better, I don’t 
think its actions caused significant delays here. I can see that Mapfre was regularly in touch 
with the hospital, but it needed to receive confirmation both that Mrs M was fit to fly and that 
she was ready to be discharged. Until Mapfre had this confirmation, there wasn’t anything 
more it could do. As soon as Mapfre had the information it needed, it arranged flights home 
within what I think was a reasonable period of time. 
So, taking everything into account, I think the compensation Mapfre has offered fairly reflects 
the overall trouble and upset it caused to Mr and Mrs M by its handling of the claim.”
my findings
I’ve reconsidered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint.
Mapfre hasn’t given me any further points to consider. Mr and Mrs M sent confirmation of 
the payment they made (€7,000). They also disagreed when I said that “while I agree 
Mapfre’s communications could’ve been better, I don’t think its actions caused significant 
delays here”. 
Mr and Mrs M said Mapfre didn’t contact the hospital when they said they would, or with any 
sense of urgency. And when a time was arranged when the doctor was available, Mapfre 
didn’t make the call at the appointed time.
Overall, Mr and Mrs M strongly believe that Mrs M could’ve been discharged earlier. As a 
result, they incurred unnecessary costs (including private room costs).
Mr and Mrs M already raised these points when they brought their complaint to us, and I 
considered them when I issued my provisional decision. And as I said in my decision, I can 
see that Mapfre was regularly in touch with the hospital, but it needed specific information 
before it could do anything else. As soon as it received that information, it arranged flights 
home within what I think was a reasonable period of time. So overall, I don’t think its actions 
caused significant delays here.
I agree that Mapfre’s communications could’ve been better. But I think £250 compensation 
fairly reflects the overall trouble and upset caused to Mr and Mrs M.
Taking everything into account, what Mr and Mrs M say doesn’t change my decision. So I’ve 
reached the same conclusions as I did in my provisional decision, and for the same reasons.
my final decision
For the reasons I’ve explained, I uphold Mr and Mrs M’s complaint in part. I direct 
Mapfre Asistencia, Compania Internacional De Seguros y Reaseguros, S.A.to
do the following:
Ref: DRN5373024

5
 
Pay Mr and Mrs M’s claim for private treatment in line with the remaining terms and 
conditions of the policy on production of an invoice – but it can deduct the cost of the 
private room;
 
Add interest at 8% simple per annum from the date the invoice was paid until the 
date of settlement*;
 
Pay Mr and Mrs M the total amount of £250 offered as compensation for the distress 
and inconvenience they suffered, if this hasn’t already been paid.
*HM Revenue & Customs requires Mapfre to take off tax from this interest. Mapfre must give
Mr and Mrs M a certificate showing how much tax it’s taken off if they ask for one.
Under the rules of the Financial Ombudsman Service, I’m required to ask Mr and Mrs M to 
accept or reject my decision before 20 September 2018.
Renja Anderson
ombudsman

The next day he told Mapfre the doctor had said Mrs M needed an operation due to the accident – and this could either be carried out in the hospital they were at, or back in the UK. Mr and Mrs M were understandably concerned about delaying the operation, and wanted this to be carried out as soon as possible. text:
K820x#11
complaint
Mrs G has complained about Friends Life Limited’s decision to decline her critical illness 
claim, made under a group critical illness insurance policy. 
background
Mrs G joined the group critical illness insurance scheme provided by her employer in 2009. 
She took the policy out online, through her employer’s staff intranet site. Under the terms of 
her employment, at each annual renewal she had the option to amend the level of critical 
illness cover that she required. The key information provided to her online through the 
intranet site, by her employer, at each renewal informed her “cover will be provided with no 
medical underwriting but pre-existing conditions are excluded”. The key information said the 
pre-existing conditions clause could be found in the schedule of insured conditions and a link 
was provided to it. 
 
In February 2012 Mrs G was diagnosed with metastatic malignant melanoma, which it was 
thought was related to a malignant melanoma she had had removed over ten years earlier.
Mrs G made a claim under the policy. 
As part of its assessment of the claim Friends Life wrote to Mrs G’s GP. Based on the GP’s 
reply it declined the claim, as it noted she had suffered with cancer in 2001, prior to joining 
the group scheme. It explained that there was no cover for any other cancer under the policy 
terms, if Mrs G had already suffered from cancer before taking out the policy, whether it was 
related to the previous cancer or not.
Mrs G did not accept Friends Life’s decision. She explained she had previously had a 
melanoma removed from her neck, which was then found to be malignant. However she had 
not thought this would affect her insurance when taking the policy out in 2009. 
As Friends Life maintained its position, Mrs G referred a complaint to this service. Our 
adjudicator did not uphold the complaint. She felt the policy terms and conditions specifically 
excluded cancer claims in these circumstances. 
The policy terms and conditions define cancer as:
 “Any malignant tumour positively diagnosed with histological confirmation and 
characterised by the uncontrolled growth of malignant cells and invasion of tissue…
For the above definition, the following are not covered:
- Any skin cancer other than malignant melanoma that has been histologically 
classified as having caused invasion beyond the epidermis (outer layer of skin).”
The policy excluded claims for cancer if the definition, above, had been met by Mrs G before 
she took out the policy.
The adjudicator noted that a histology report in 2001 said “the appearances are of a 
malignant melanoma of vertical growth phase. It is infiltrating the dermis to a depth of 
0.8mm”. Given this report, she was satisfied that the malignant tumour met the definition of 
Ref: DRN5739786

2
cancer and Mrs G had suffered from it before the policy was taken out. On that basis, she 
felt Mrs G’s claim was excluded under the policy terms and conditions. 
In relation to Mrs G’s other comment that the policy had been mis-sold and she had suffered 
prejudice, as she had not been made aware of the pre-existing condition exclusion, the 
adjudicator did not consider that the responsibility for this rested with Friends Life. Instead 
she considered that as Friends Life had provided information to Mrs G’s employer about the 
group cover it could offer, it was the employer’s responsibility to explain the key facts to its 
employees.  
Mrs G did not accept the adjudicator’s opinion. She maintained that the policy had been mis-
sold. She also said she was unaware of the diagnosis of cancer in 2001. As a result she said 
she would not have been able to make the business aware of the issue when she joined the 
group scheme. As a result of the disagreement between the parties the matter has been 
referred to me to review afresh.
my findings
I have included only a brief summary of the complaint (above) but I have considered all the 
available evidence and arguments from the outset, in order to decide what is fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances. Having done so, I do not uphold this complaint.
I agree with the adjudicator that Mrs G’s claim is excluded under the policy terms and 
conditions. Mrs G was not asked to disclose her previous medical history. Instead of full 
medical underwriting, this policy was offered with an exclusion for pre-existing medical 
conditions. Mrs G had suffered from cancer, as defined within the policy, before the policy 
started and any new claims for cancer were therefore excluded under the policy terms and 
conditions, for the reasons given by the adjudicator and set out above.
I think it likely Mrs G was aware of her previous diagnosis, because correspondence from 
her treating consultant surgeon from March 2002 says that he had talked to her about the 
implications of the diagnosis. 
I have considered Mrs G’s comments that she thinks the policy was mis-sold to her because 
the pre-existing conditions exclusion clause was not drawn to her attention.
Mrs G has provided copies of screen shots from her employer’s intranet site, which provide 
information about the policy. This indicates that the insurer provided her employer with 
information about the policy, for it to pass on to Mrs G and the other scheme members.
This key facts information explained that there was a pre-existing conditions exclusion which 
applied and further details could be found in the insured conditions schedule, a link to this 
was contained on the intranet.
This was a group policy, so Mrs G was not the policyholder, her employer was. Friends Life 
was obliged to provide her employer with appropriate information so the employer could 
provide details of cover to its staff members. The fact that there was a detailed intranet site, 
containing information about the policy suggests that Friends Life provided appropriate 
information to the employer. Friends Life was not responsible for running the intranet site, so 
if Mrs G feels the intranet site was misleading, this does not seem to be Friends Life’s 
responsibility. In any event, the information contained in the screen shots I have seen, did 
warn Mrs G that the policy contained exclusions for pre-existing conditions and provided her 
Ref: DRN5739786

3
with links to further information about those exclusions. It also encouraged her to read the 
policy terms and conditions, which were also available through the intranet site.  
Friends Life has also provided copies of its key features documents, which it indicates were 
sent to Mrs G’s employer. These contained detailed explanations of the pre-existing 
conditions exclusion. 
On balance, I am satisfied that Friends Life provided Mrs G’s employer with appropriate 
information for it to pass on to its members, so that they would be familiar with the features 
and benefits of the policy.
I am not persuaded that Friends Life mis-sold the policy, as it did not offer advice or a 
recommendation and provided Mrs G’s employer with sufficient and appropriate information 
to enable its staff members to make an informed decision about whether they wanted the 
insurance or not. 
my final decision
My final decision is that I do not uphold this complaint. I make no award against Friends Life.
Greg Barham
ombudsman 
Ref: DRN5739786

text:
K821x#12
complaint
Mr and Mrs A were on holiday abroad. Their daughter was taken ill and admitted to hospital. 
They complain that AGA International has declined to pay their medical expenses.
background
Mr and Mrs A’s two year old daughter was taken ill on the flight from the UK to their 
European holiday destination. Her illness continued and Mr and Mrs A consulted their hotel, 
who in turn contacted its on-call doctor. The doctor phoned Mr and Mrs A. Following this 
consultation the doctor recommended that the daughter be admitted to hospital. 
Mr and Mrs A say that the doctor asked for details of their travel insurance. Shortly 
afterwards the doctor called back and said he had arranged for a taxi to take Mr and Mrs A 
and their daughter to hospital.
The taxi took them to a nearby private hospital. Mr and Mrs A say that, after an initial 
consultation, the hospital took their insurance details. Mr and Mrs A also gave details of their 
European Health cards. Mr and Mrs A say that the hospital said it had contacted the insurer 
and everything was covered and their daughter could be admitted. 
The daughter was admitted and stayed for about 24 hours. When they left, the hospital 
asked Mr A to pay 70 Euros to cover the insurance excess. 
AGA says it was contacted by the hospital, but not until 9 days later. AGA declined to pay 
the expenses saying that Mr and Mrs A should have contacted it immediately. It would have 
advised them that private health facilities are not covered by the policy if there is a good 
state facility nearby, which there was in this case. It said the amount charged by the hospital 
was excessive for the short length of the stay.
Mr and Mrs A said that it was Good Friday in a very religious country. They had not been 
able to contact a general practice clinic or pharmacy as they were closed, and this is why 
they had contacted the hotel. The doctor, who referred them to hospital, later wrote a letter 
saying that this had been a factor in his decision to refer the daughter to hospital.
Mr and Mrs A complained to the Financial Ombudsman Service. Our adjudicator considered 
the case and recommended that AGA pay the claim. He said that it was reasonable for 
Mr and Mrs A to believe that they were covered in view of what the medical staff told them. 
Having reviewed the hospital’s stated policy in such situations; he considered it more likely 
than not that it had contacted the insurer.
AGA disagreed. It said that it had no record of the hospital contacting it until much later. It 
said Mr and Mrs A had failed to comply with the policy requirement to contact the insurer. It 
said it was not acceptable that the insurer should have to pay a bill if the hospital had misled 
Mr and Mrs A. It believed that the quality of care given to the daughter would not have been 
prejudiced if Mr and Mrs A had followed the correct procedures.
Because there is no agreement, the matter has come to me for a final decision. 
my findings
I have considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what is fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint.
Ref: DRN5874337

2
The policy document says, on page 4:
“SECTION 3 EMERGENCY MEDICAL EXPENSES
(not private health insurance)
NOTE: THIS IS NOT A PRIVATE MEDICAL HEALTH INSURANCE POLICY. WE 
WILL PAY FOR PRIVATE TREATMENT ONLY IF THERE IS NO APPROPRIATE 
RECIPROCAL HEALTH AGREEMENT IN EXISTENCE AND NO PUBLIC SERVICE 
AVAILABLE AND WE RESERVE THE RIGHT TO ORGANISE A TRANSFER FROM 
A PRIVATE MEDICAL FACILITY TO A PUBLIC MEDICAL FACILITY WHERE 
APPROPRIATE…” [Capitals as they appear in the policy]
In the following paragraph, on page 5, the policy says:
“If you are admitted to hospital as an in-patient, the Emergency Medical Assistance 
service must be notified immediately. They will deal direct with the hospital and 
arrange the payment of any bills. Repatriation by specially equipped air ambulance 
will be available where medically necessary…
Not covered...
3. any expenses or fees, for in-patient treatment or returning home early, which have 
not been reported to and authorised by the Emergency Medical Assistance service”.
I do not consider that the policy makes clear that the insurer would never pay for private 
medical care. The policy says “we reserve the right to organise a transfer from a private 
medical facility to a public medical facility where appropriate”. This could suggest that the 
initial private care would be covered in certain circumstances.
The front page of the policy has a table headed “we bring your particular attention to the 
following conditions and exclusions”. The table makes no mention of the exclusion of all 
claims involving private medical facilities if a public facility is available. This is in my view a 
significant exclusion that most customers would not expect. They might expect an insurer to 
reserve the right to lessen its costs by requiring a move after initial treatment. But many 
reasonable customers would not anticipate that, as happened with Mr and Mrs A, initial 
referrals made by first-responding medical staff would not be covered. The exclusion has 
not, in my view, been clearly and fairly highlighted.
I also consider that the requirement to contact the insurer “immediately” must be interpreted 
reasonably. The reasonableness of a delay must be interpreted according to the 
circumstances of the case. The very nature of medical emergency insurance means that it 
will be relevant in situations when customers will not think of immediately contacting the 
insurer.
The strict requirement to call the Emergency Medical Assistance service does not appear 
until page 5 of the policy document and is not highlighted. This is also where the emergency 
contact number appears. Reading the detailed wording of the policy document will not have 
been in the forefront of Mr and Mrs A’s mind during this worrying time. Their very young child 
had been ill for a period of time, and the doctor was recommending admission to hospital. 
Ref: DRN5874337

3
I believe Mr and Mrs A’s testimony that they put themselves in the hands of the doctor and 
hospital. In the circumstances I regard their actions as reasonable. I do not consider that 
they had any choice in the circumstances other than to accept the doctor’s recommendation.
I consider it significant that Mr and Mrs A’s daughter was in hospital for one day only. 
Mr and Mrs A have said that they believed that the hospital told them their insurance would 
cover the cost. AGA appears to have accepted that this happened. Mr and Mrs A also 
believed that the hospital had made contact with the insurer – which would have meant that 
the policy requirement that the assistance service “must be notified immediately” had been 
met. Even if Mr and Mrs A had contacted the insurer following the admission, I think it very 
unlikely that the insurer’s medical assistance company could have arranged for the young 
child to be transferred to a state facility within 24 hours before she was discharged from 
hospital. This is particularly bearing in mind the fact that most people were off work on 
account to the religious holidays.
my final decision
My final decision is that I uphold this complaint. I require AGA International to pay this claim. 
If the costs have already been paid by Mr and Mrs A, AGA should reimburse Mr and Mrs A 
and pay interest at the rate of 8% simple per annum from the date of payment to the date of 
settlement; or the interest Mr and Mrs A incurred if they show evidence of different charges.
I make no other award against AGA.
Timothy Bailey
ombudsman
