text:
K820x#11
complaint
Z has complained about the decision by The Society of Lloyd’s (“Lloyds”) to decline a claim 
under its group personal accident and illness policy, for benefit in respect of its employee, 
Mr Y.
background
The background to this complaint was set out in my provisional decision dated 5 August 
2014, a copy of which is attached and which forms part of this final decision.
Briefly, in November 2011, Mr Y was admitted to hospital suffering diabetic ketoacidosis 
(DKA) which was brought on by diarrhoea and vomiting. Although he was subsequently 
discharged, Mr Y continued to feel unwell and was readmitted to hospital on two further 
occasions suffering from DKA. Mr Y was discharged from hospital for the third time in March 
2012 but remained unable to return to work and consequently a claim was submitted by Z for 
benefits under its group personal accident and illness policy.
The claim was declined by Lloyds on the basis that Mr Y’s reason for being off work was 
directly related to his pre-existing diabetes and therefore excluded under the policy terms 
and conditions.
Z was unhappy with this outcome and brought its complaint to this service.
In my provisional decision, I explained that I considered Mr Y’s absence was attributable to 
his diabetes and that his ongoing self-administration of insulin for this diabetes constituted 
treatment. On this basis, I considered it was reasonable for Lloyds to exclude Z’s claim. I 
invited both parties to comment on my provisional decision.
Lloyds did not respond to my provisional decision.
Z responded to say it did not accept my provisional decision. Its comments can be 
summarised as follows:

Mr Y’s self-administration of insulin did not constitute the giving of treatment for his 
diabetes. The policy wording implied that such treatment had to be given by 
someone else, presumably a medical practitioner.

Although during his absence from work, Mr Y did suffer from diabetic ketoacidosis 
(DKA), his ongoing absence was because of a prolonged period of vomiting and 
diarrhoea. Lloyds had not shown that this was linked to his diabetes.

Even if Mr Y’s absence was related to his diabetes, and it was considered that he 
had received treatment for this, Lloyds should still accept the claim. This was 
because Lloyds had accepted a previous claim in respect of Mr Y that was related to 
his diabetes and by doing so it had waived its rights to apply this exclusion to future 
claims.
my findings
First, may I again apologise to the parties for the significant time it has taken to reach this 
stage of the investigation. However, I have now considered all the available evidence and 
Ref: DRN6007396

2
arguments to decide what is fair and reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint. 
Having done so, while I am sorry to disappoint Z, I am not persuaded to change my 
provisional decision. I shall explain why.
Z considers that Lloyds could not rely on the exclusion for pre-existing conditions because 
Mr Y’s self-administration of insulin did not constitute the “giving” of treatment for the 
purposes of the policy. However, I do not agree. Let me again state the policy wording:
“We will not pay for any claim:
2. Arising from or aggravated by any disease, sickness, disability or condition of a 
recurring or chronic nature of the Insured Person for which medical advice or 
treatment has been given during the 12 months immediately prior to the effective 
date of this insurance or the Insured Person’s date of addition to this insurance, 
whichever is later.”
Mr Y self-administers insulin medication which he receives on a repeat prescription. I am 
satisfied that this constitutes the “giving” of medical treatment for his condition. Furthermore, 
I have already explained in my provisional decision why I am satisfied that the giving of this 
treatment occurred during the 12 months immediately prior to the effective date of the policy.
Z, while it accepts Mr Y’s diabetes has played a part in his sickness absence, further 
considers that Lloyds has not adequately shown that it is the primary reason. It considers it 
plausible that Mr Y, even if he did not suffer from diabetes, would nonetheless have been 
absent from work for the period in question because of his vomiting and diarrhoea. However, 
while this is possible, I consider it unlikely and I note that the GP’s report confirms that, as a 
result of his vomiting and diarrhoea, Mr Y was suffering on a repeat basis from DKA and 
hyperglycaemia. These are conditions which are directly linked to diabetes. I consider it is 
reasonable to say not only that Mr Y’s diabetes “aggravated” his claim but also that this was 
the main reason he could not return to work. I therefore consider that Lloyds was entitled to 
apply the policy exclusion.
Finally, Z suggests that Lloyds had not applied the exclusion to a previous claim in respect of 
Mr Y which was also linked to his diabetes. Z considers that Lloyds has therefore created an 
expectation that this exclusion would not apply and that it is unfair to now apply it to this 
claim.
The previous claim was for an infection of Mr Y’s big toe. Z has provided evidence to 
suggest that this was related to Mr Y’s diabetes. Z has also provided an internal email from a 
Lloyds senior claims analyst which states:
“The previous claim … was paid as a gesture of goodwill. [Mr Y] had fallen and there 
was a slim margin for error over whether the amputation was necessary due to 
infection and/or as a natural consequence of diabetes. We took that decision in 
favour of TCF [Treating Customers Fairly] and without financial detriment to [Z or 
Mr Y]. This does not mean we have to adopt a similar stance again, especially as 
there is no such margin for error on this occasion.”
Z considers that, through its previous action. Lloyds has waived its right to apply the 
exclusion. However, I do not agree. I do not know whether the previous claim related to an 
accident or, as in the case of the current claim, an illness; if it were the former, the 
exclusions in the policy were worded differently. In any case, I consider that the above email 
Ref: DRN6007396

3
makes clear that it was a borderline decision as to whether the claim should be accepted but 
Lloyds decided to give Z the benefit of the doubt. I have already explained that I consider it is 
reasonable to apply the exclusion in the current claim. I am not persuaded to change my 
mind by virtue of Lloyds’ stance on the previous decision. 
my final decision
While I recognise it will come as a disappointment to Z, for the reasons given above, my final 
decision is that I do not uphold this complaint. I make no award against The Society of 
Lloyd’s.
David Poley
ombudsman
Ref: DRN6007396

4
COPY OF PROVISIONAL DECISION
complaint
Z has complained about the decision by The Society of Lloyd’s (“Lloyds”) to decline a claim under its 
group personal accident and illness policy, for benefit in respect of its employee, Mr Y.
background
In November 2011, Mr Y was admitted to hospital suffering from diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) which 
was brought on by diarrhoea and vomiting. Although he was subsequently discharged, Mr Y 
continued to feel unwell and was readmitted to hospital on two further occasions suffering from DKA. 
Mr Y was discharged from hospital for the third time in March 2012 but remained unable to return to 
work and consequently a claim was submitted by Z for benefits under its group personal accident and 
illness policy.
The claim was declined by Lloyds on the basis that Mr Y’s reason for being off work was directly 
related to his pre-existing diabetes and therefore excluded under the policy terms and conditions.
Z was unhappy with this outcome and brought its complaint to this service, where it was considered 
by one of our adjudicators. He considered that Lloyds had not provided sufficient medical evidence to 
justify excluding the claim and recommended that, in the absence of any further evidence, the 
complaint should be upheld.
Lloyds disagreed with the need for further medical evidence and felt that, by default, the treatment Mr 
Y received as a result of being a longstanding diabetic demonstrated this was a pre-existing condition 
that allowed for the application of the relevant policy exclusion.
The matter has therefore been passed to me to consider afresh.
my provisional findings
First, let me apologise to the parties for the significant delay in issuing a decision on this complaint. I 
recognise that it is over 18 months since Z referred its complaint to this service and over a year since 
the adjudicator issued his opinion on this matter. However, I have now considered all the available 
arguments and evidence to decide what is fair and reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint. 
Having done so, while I recognise it will come as a great disappointment to Z, I am provisionally 
minded to depart significantly from the findings of the adjudicator and to not uphold the complaint. I 
shall explain why.
Z was claiming under the “illness” section of the policy for temporary total disablement. The policy 
describes this as:
“Disablement which temporarily and totally prevents the Insured Person from attending to the 
duties of his usual business or occupation.”
There seems to be no dispute that Mr Y met this definition. The question is therefore whether Lloyds 
was entitled to exclude the claim.
Lloyds has sought to rely on the following exclusion:
“We will not pay for any claim:
2. Arising from or aggravated by any disease, sickness, disability or condition of a recurring or 
chronic nature of the Insured Person for which medical advice or treatment has been given 
during the 12 months immediately prior to the effective date of this insurance or the Insured 
Person’s date of addition to this insurance, whichever is later.”
Ref: DRN6007396

5
Lloyds says that Mr Y’s absence from work was due to his diabetes. In order for this exclusion to 
apply, Lloyds therefore needs to show that Mr Y had received treatment or advice for his diabetes in 
the 12 months prior to the effective date of Z’s policy. Lloyds says the effective date is 30 June 2011, 
though it started providing cover for Z on 30 June 2006.
The adjudicator recommended that the complaint be upheld because he considered that Lloyds had 
not provided medical evidence to show that Mr Y received treatment or advice for his diabetes in the 
twelve months before 30 June 2011. Lloyds, however, has pointed out that Mr Y is a type 1 diabetic, 
diagnosed in 1963, and is therefore insulin dependent. He receives his medication on repeat 
prescription and is subject to annual diabetic reviews.
Notwithstanding any review Mr Y may have had, I consider the self-administration of insulin 
constitutes “treatment” for the purposes of the policy exclusion set out above. Furthermore, he will 
have received this treatment during the relevant twelve month period regardless of whether I take the 
effective date of the policy to be in 2006 or 2011. Consequently, I consider that any “illness” claim as 
a result of a medical condition which can be attributed directly to Mr Y’s diabetes can reasonably be 
declined.
Let me therefore turn to the question of whether Mr Y’s absence can reasonably be attributed to his 
diabetes. In the GP’s medical report dated 27 March 2012, it is confirmed that Mr Y felt generally 
unwell over the three month period in which he was hospitalised three times. His illness was 
characterised by persistent diarrhoea and vomiting which led to DKA and hyperglycaemia.
It cannot be disputed that both DKA and hyperglycaemia are directly linked to Mr Y’s diabetes. While I 
accept that his period of ill-health may have started with gastroenteritis and that he continued to suffer 
from this, I would tend to agree with the insurer’s medical examiner who concluded this was a 
condition which would ordinarily resolve itself over several days, with the appropriate treatment.
I therefore consider that in the matter of Mr Y’s on-going ill health and his inability to return to work, 
the overriding factor is his diabetes. This is a pre-existing condition for which continuous treatment, in 
the form of self-administered insulin, is required and Lloyds has applied the relevant exclusion.
Z has suggested that it is paying for cover for an employee for whom it cannot successfully make a 
claim under its policy. However, it is clearly the case that illness or injury not related to Mr Y’s 
diabetes would still be covered.
my provisional decision
While I am sorry to disappoint Z, for the reasons given above, my provisional decision is that I do not 
uphold this complaint. I am not minded to make any award against The Society of Lloyd’s.
Both parties now have one month in which to respond before I issue my final determination.
David Poley
ombudsman

text:
K820x#11
summary of complaint
Mrs L’s complaint concerns Mapfre Asistencia, Compania Internacional De Seguros y 
Reaseguros, S.A.’s (“Mapfre”) decision to reject a cancellation claim she made under her 
travel insurance policy. 
background to complaint
Mrs L booked her trip in May 2012 and was due to travel in November 2012. She purchased 
her travel insurance in October 2012.
Shortly after buying the insurance policy her husband (who was not travelling with her) fell ill 
and as a result Mrs L had to cancel her trip. She made a claim under the policy for the 
cancellation costs that were incurred. 
Mapfre rejected her claim. It said that the policy she purchased did not include cover for any 
pre-existing conditions for her or a relative. The certificate completed by her husband’s GP 
said that the condition giving rise to the claim was pre-existing. It was therefore not covered 
under the policy. 
Mrs L was unhappy with Mapfre’s decision. She explained that her husband’s condition had 
been stable for around four years and she had no reason to think that this would deteriorate 
or that she would have to cancel her trip as a result. As Mapfre maintained its stance, she 
asked this service to consider her complaint. 
Our adjudicator did not recommend upholding the complaint. In summary, she was 
persuaded that the sales process clearly asked Mrs L to confirm that neither she nor anyone 
the trip may depend upon, such as a non-travelling close relative, had any pre-existing 
medical conditions. 
my findings
I have considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what is fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint. Having done so, I do not uphold this 
complaint. 
The issue I need to decide is whether Mapfre was reasonably entitled to reject Mrs L’s claim. 
Mrs L booked a trip in May 2012 and bought her insurance in October 2012 with travel 
departing in November 2012. 
Mrs L has said prior to Mr L’s deterioration in health in October 2012, his condition had been 
stable, so when the trip was booked she felt that she had no reason to believe this would 
change or cause her to cancel her trip. Whilst I appreciate Mrs L’s comments, the medical 
evidence shows that at the time the insurance was purchased, Mr L did have a pre-existing 
medical condition and had done so since 2010. He was, at the very least, under annual 
check-ups by a neurologist and the nature of his condition meant that it was on-going and 
potentially serious. Mr L’s GP confirmed that he was feeling unwell due to deterioration in his 
pre-existing medical condition. Several days after this, Mrs L was advised by the GP to 
cancel her trip. 
Ref: DRN6221571

2
The policy documents show that cover will not be provided for cancelling a trip because of a 
medical condition Mrs L, or any person her trip depended on, had which she knew about at 
the time of buying the insurance. Having reviewed the sales process, I can see that prior to 
making payment Mrs L was asked to confirm that “You, anyone else insured on this policy or 
any person on whose health this trip may depend (e.g. a non-travelling close relative) have 
no pre-existing medical conditions”. It goes on to say that “if you, anyone else insured on this 
policy or any person on whose health this trip may depend have any pre-existing medical 
conditions please click here”. I am persuaded the information on screen should have 
prompted Mrs L to click on this section of the page, or at least recognise that the policy she 
was buying did not cover any pre-existing medical conditions for her or Mr L. 
The type of policy Mrs L bought did not provide cover for any pre-existing conditions, so had 
Mrs L contacted the insurer as detailed at the point of sale, she would have been told that 
cover could not be provided for Mr L’s condition. The policy clearly confirms that no cover 
will be provided in Mrs L’s circumstances. I am satisfied that the sales process made it clear 
that Mrs L would need to disclose any pre-existing medical conditions for Mr L if she wanted 
cover for events arising due to his pre-existing medical condition. As Mrs L did not disclose 
such information, and purchased a policy clearly precluding pre-existing conditions, I am 
satisfied that Mapfre was reasonably entitled to reject her claim. 
my final decision
My final decision is that I do not uphold Mrs L’s complaint and I make no award against 
Mapfre Asistencia, Compania Internacional De Seguros y Reaseguros, S.A. 
Sean Hamilton
ombudsman
Ref: DRN6221571

text:
K820x#14
complaint
Mr and Mrs M have complained that UK Insurance Limited (UKI) turned down their travel 
insurance claim.
background
Mr and Mrs M have a travel policy as a benefit of their bank account. Whilst on a trip Mr M 
fell ill. He wasn't fit to fly so they had to extend their trip and make other arrangements to 
travel home. Mr M was aware that, because of pre-existing conditions, his extra costs 
wouldn't be covered but they claimed for Mrs M’s additional expenses. 
UKI turned down the claim. But it later said that some of its service could have been better 
and paid Mr and Mrs M £120 for their distress and inconvenience and to cover expenses 
associated with making their claim. 
Mr and Mrs M brought their complaint to us. The investigator thought that UKI had settled 
the claim fairly. Mr and Mrs M didn't agree so their complaint’s been passed to me to decide.
my findings
I’ve considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint. Having done so, I'm not going to uphold 
it. 
Mr and Mrs M’s policy says:
“This policy doesn’t cover any claims relating directly or indirectly to any pre-existing 
medical conditions relating to the insured person or anyone upon whom the trip 
depends.”
In this case the reason for the claim was because of Mr M’s pre-existing condition. And Mr M 
understands that he’s not covered because of that. But Mrs M’s claim also relates directly to 
Mr M’s pre-existing condition. And Mr M was clearly a person on whom the trip depended. In 
other words Mrs M incurred additional costs because of Mr M’s pre-existing condition. So I 
think her claim is caught by the above exclusion in the policy and it’s reasonable for UKI to 
turn it down.
Mr and Mrs M have said that they’re not sure what the policy would cover Mrs M for. I’ll 
explain that it’s not unusual for travel insurance policies to exclude claims that relate to 
pre-existing conditions of relatives. So I don't think there’s anything unusual in UKI turning 
down the claim in this instance.
I can see that UKI has given Mr and Mrs M different reasons for declining this claim. And I 
can understand they might find that confusing and unprofessional. But I don't think that any 
confusion in UKI’s handling means that it must pay the claim. 
my final decision
For the reasons set out above I don't uphold this complaint. 
Ref: DRN6293836

2
Under the rules of the Financial Ombudsman Service, I’m required to ask Mr and Mrs M to 
accept or reject my decision before 3 July 2017.
Joe Scott 
ombudsman

K820x#14
complaint
Mr D has complained that Simplyhealth Access mis-sold a personal accident insurance 
policy to him in 2011. 
background
Mr D took out a personal accident insurance policy with Simplyhealth in August 2011 during 
a phone call with one of their advisers. Policy documents were sent to Mr D after this call. Mr 
D paid a monthly premium for the policy until it was cancelled in May 2018. 
In 2018, Simplyhealth told Mr D they were no longer going to administer personal accident 
policies and gave him three months’ notice of their intention to cancel his plan. 
After receiving the notice of cancellation, Mr D complained and said he didn’t think he ever 
needed the policy as he always had this cover through work. And he was concerned that if 
he decided to go to another provider for the same insurance he would lose out due to the 3-6 
month waiting period to be eligible to claim. 
Our investigator didn’t feel Simplyhealth had done anything wrong as there was no evidence 
of the policy being mis-sold and he also had a 14 day cancellation period which was set out 
in the policy documents.
Mr D disagreed with the investigator. He says he doesn’t remember receiving the terms and 
conditions with the 14 day cancellation period and as there is no call recording of the initial 
call, there’s no proof of what happened at the time. He says he’s lost out because 
Simplyhealth have cancelled his policy but have kept all the profits. 
And so the complaint has been passed to me for a decision. 
my findings
I’ve considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint. Having done so, I don’t think Mr D’s 
complaint should be upheld. I’ll explain why.
Mr D says he doesn’t remember receiving the policy documents. But Simplyhealth have 
provided screenshots of their system notes to show that a phone call took place and that 
policy documents were sent to Mr D. I have no reason to doubt that Simplyhealth’s records 
are accurate. 
Both parties agree the policy was sold over the telephone. But unfortunately the call 
recording isn’t available. This isn’t surprising given the length of time that has passed since 
the call took place. So I can’t be certain of what was discussed at the time. 
However, Simplyhealth have provided a copy of the follow up letters which were sent to Mr D 
in August 2011. These included the policy terms and conditions as well as information on 
what Mr D should do if he wasn’t satisfied with the policy. The cover letter confirmed he had 
14 days to cancel the policy from 10 August 2011 if he wasn’t satisfied. 
I’ve seen the policy terms which were sent to Mr D in 2011. The policy terms say: “We 
exercise our right to cancel your policy if we make a commercial decision to stop providing 
Ref: DRN6581404

2
this policy or an equivalent policy. We will give you at least three months’ written notice of 
our decision.”
Simplyhealth confirmed they were cancelling these policies for all of their customers and as 
they’re allowed to do this under the terms of the policy, I don’t think they’ve treated Mr D 
unfairly. 
Mr D accepts he didn’t contact Simplyhealth to say he was dissatisfied until he received 
notice of the policy cancellation in 2018. He says he was persuaded by the adviser to take 
the policy in 2011 even though he didn’t need it as he had this cover through work.
I can’t be sure that Mr D told the adviser about this at the time but ultimately, it was up to Mr 
D if he wanted to take the policy. If Mr D did feel pressured to take the policy during the 
phone call, he had 14 days to reflect and cancel the policy but didn’t do so. For that reason, I 
can’t say Simplyhealth did anything wrong as they gave Mr D a chance to change his mind. 
In addition, under the terms of the policy, Mr D could have cancelled his policy at any time by 
giving Simplyhealth 1 months’ notice in writing. 
I’ve considered Mr D’s concerns about buying a similar policy with another provider. He says 
he may have to wait a 3-6 month qualifying period before being able to make a claim. But 
Simplyhealth explained that his current plan provided immediate benefit from the first day of 
cover. And it’s possible that other providers could provide similar cover. 
Qualifying periods with another provider will vary. But the policy with Simplyhealth didn’t 
provide indefinite cover so there was always a possibility that Mr D would need to find cover 
elsewhere. Whether or not similar cover is available elsewhere isn’t something I can hold 
Simplyhealth responsible for. And in addition, as Simplyhealth made this decision for all their 
personal accident plans, he hasn’t been treated differently to other policy holders with the 
same plan. 
Mr D has also raised concerns about Simplyhealth being able to provide a copy of the policy 
terms from August 2011 but not the call recording. A business will usually keep copies of 
terms and conditions to show any historic versions or changes. They won’t always keep 
copies of individual call recordings for long periods of time and this isn’t unusual.
Overall, I’m satisfied that Simplyhealth have treated Mr D fairly. Mr D is unhappy that they 
have kept the profits but have cancelled his policy. Mr D paid premiums for ongoing cover. 
And so he has been covered since 2011 until the cancellation of the policy. I don’t think the 
profits are relevant to the complaint made and I’ve seen no evidence that the policy was mis-
sold. 
my final decision
For the reasons set out above, my final decision is that I do not uphold this complaint.
Under the rules of the Financial Ombudsman Service, I’m required to ask Mr D to accept or 
reject my decision before 1 September 2018
Shamaila Hussain
ombudsman
Ref: DRN6581404

complaint
Mr and Mrs A have complained about the fact that Independent Sales Force Solutions Limited 
(trading as The Health Insurance Group, ‘THIG’) has said that Mr A should have disclosed his 
pre-existing medical conditions when he was applying for a group private medical insurance 
policy as recommended by THIG. As these conditions were not disclosed, the insurer has 
declined Mr A’s claim and cancelled Mr A’s group policy from the beginning.
Mr and Mrs A believe that it was due to THIG’s errors that the pre-existing medical conditions 
were not disclosed and they now find themselves without private medical insurance.
background
The circumstances leading to this complaint and my provisional conclusions are set out in my 
provisional decision dated 19 June 2014, a copy of which is attached and forms part of this 
decision. In that provisional decision I was minded to uphold Mr A’s complaint and require 
Independent Sales Force Solutions Limited (THIG) to do the following:

Once Mr and Mrs A have detailed out their costs in paying for medical treatment 
themselves to date, it should reimburse Mr and Mrs A for their costs of eligible treatment 
incurred to date less any premium they would have had to pay to insurer one.

Compensate Mr and Mrs A for any loss of comfort or other inconvenience they have 
suffered as a result of undergoing treatment through the NHS rather than privately under 
cover of their policy.

Instruct the services of an independent actuary to assess the likely financial loss to Mr and 
Mrs A of having to self-fund private healthcare for the rest of their lives, bearing in mind 
their age, health issues and any other factors which in the opinion of the actuary is 
appropriate, including any premium Mr and Mrs A would have had to pay to insurer one. 
On receipt of the actuary’s report, I was then minded to require Independent Sales Force 
Solutions to pay his or her recommended award to Mr and Mrs A.

Pay Mr and Mrs A the sum of £500 compensation for the distress and inconvenience 
caused by its and its representative’s (Mr H’s) actions.
I invited both parties to let me have any further representations and I have now heard from 
both parties. Mr and Mrs A through their representative accepted my provisional decision and 
THIG disagreed. It responded saying that:

It does not ask its agents to record case specific detail and therefore its agent, Mr H, had 
no way of knowing in 2009 what had been discussed with Mr and Mrs A previously by the 
first agent, Mr G.

Mr A never volunteered any information about his pre-existing medical conditions in his 
dealings with Mr H and as Mr A wished to remain covered by insurer one until 2012, Mr H 
had no reason to ask about these until then.

Mr H did inform Mr A of insurer two’s acceptance criteria in 2012 when he had expressed 
that he wanted to change insurers. Mr A did not, however, disclose any pre-existing 
conditions to Mr H.
Ref: DRN6640592

3

Mr A signed a declaration stating that he was not aware of any person being covered by 
the application receiving treatment relating to a heart or circulatory condition in the last two 
years.

THIG refutes that Mr H stated to Mr A that insurer two would accept his medical history 
without question. THIG has again referred to Mr H highlighting insurer two’s acceptance 
criteria to Mr A in relation to this point.

THIG does not accept that it should be liable for Mrs A’s medical costs going forward as 
both her previous insurer and insurer two had, through THIG, offered her continuing 
insurance which she refused; and

It is unlikely that Mr A would have maintained private medical insurance cover for the rest 
of his life, considering the likely costs of doing so. 
my findings
I have considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what is fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint. It should be noted that Mr A is now very 
seriously ill.
In my provisional decision I identified that I needed to consider who was responsible or likely to 
be responsible on the balance of probabilities for the non-disclosure of Mr A’s medical history 
that led to the voiding of the group policy providing cover for both Mr and Mrs A, by insurer two.
I was minded to find that as THIG had employed both Mr G (who clearly knew about Mr A’s 
medical issues) and Mr H, that any information that Mr G had would be retained on a file for 
any other agent of THIG to access, should Mr G not be available for whatever reason. 
However THIG has now said it does not do this. Consequently what I need to consider is 
whether or not this is reasonable from a customer’s point of view, such as Mr A’s, considering 
he had been a continuing customer of THIG’s for so many years.
I have not been presented with any evidence from THIG that it ensured that Mr A was aware 
that no file of his dealings with Mr G had been retained by THIG for the purposes of his 
dealings with Mr G’s successor, Mr H. Therefore I find that it was reasonable for Mr A to 
believe that his dealings with Mr G and their content would be available should Mr G be 
unavailable for whatever reason. Certainly I find that there is no doubt Mr G was fully aware of 
Mr A’s medical condition at that time, given the contents of his letter to Mr A as detailed in my 
provisional decision. Further Mr A is adamant that he did tell Mr H about his medical conditions 
in any event and certainly I find this is most probable, given Mr H was involved in the 
negotiations concerning the premium level with insurer one, on Mr A’s behalf. I find that it 
would be most unlikely that any advisor would be involved in such negotiations over premium 
costs if he or she was not at least also aware of any claims that may have been made in the 
previous year, which of course would be considered part of a medical history.
Further, as no evidence has been supplied to me concerning Mr H’s files or any detail of what 
he was apparently told or not told concerning Mr A’s medical conditions by Mr A or the extent 
of Mr A’s instructions to Mr H, I am not persuaded by the assertions put forward by THIG 
concerning its certainty that Mr A did not disclose any medical conditions to Mr H at any time 
whether through his negotiation with insurer one or through the application to insurer two. 
Ref: DRN6640592

4
I am far more persuaded by what Mr A has said concerning his disclosures to Mr H and 
therefore I find on the balance of probability that it is more likely than not that Mr A did disclose 
his medical conditions to Mr H as he has described and was also under the impression that as 
Mr G so obviously knew of them, there would also be no reason why that would not be on his 
file with THIG.
THIG has asserted that given Mr A signed the declaration confirming he had no pre-existing 
medical conditions that it is solely his responsibility. However as I detailed at some length in my 
provisional decision, I was not persuaded that this could be correct, most especially as it was 
Mr H who completed the answers to on the application form to insurer two on Mr A’s behalf.
Therefore I find that I have not been persuaded to depart from my provisional findings as to 
who I consider to be more likely to have been responsible for the non-disclosure of Mr A’s pre-
existing medical conditions to insurer two.
Consequently I find that I am more persuaded by Mr A’s account of what transpired in the 
application to insurer two and I find that THIG are responsible for the fact that Mr A’s medical 
history was not disclosed to insurer two and that consequently Mr and Mrs A now find 
themselves without any private medical cover.
As I have found that, I see no reason to depart from the redress I proposed in my provisional 
decision. I do acknowledge that THIG are of the view that Mr A would not have continued to 
maintain his private medical insurance given his issues with the costs of it. However I am not 
persuaded this is correct. Clearly Mr A wanted to have private medical insurance. Given his 
medical conditions he had clearly benefited from the comfort of having it up to this time. Further 
it is perfectly evident in my view that Mr A wished to retain this insurance and was simply 
attempting to minimise its costs as far as possible.
THIG has also said it does not accept that it should be liable for Mrs A’s medical costs going 
forward as both her previous insurer and insurer two had, through THIG, offered her continuing 
insurance which she refused. However in THIG’s letter to this service of 22 November 2012, in 
its attached note concerning this complaint, it said, following an entry for 9 June 2012, that as 
regards Mrs A,
‘it was agreed that as she was in good health she would join the group scheme [with 
insurer two] under Moratorium underwriting terms. It was then made apparent that 
because of Mr [A]’s non-disclosure the policy was cancelled from inception, which left 
Mrs [A] without insurance. As her broker we offered to obtain quotes for her own 
individual plan but [her representative] refused to let The Health Insurance Group deal 
with anything concerning her mother, and de-appointed us as her broker.’
I find that this is at odds with THIG’s present assertion that it provided Mrs A with alternative 
insurance and therefore I do not find that Mrs A had any alternative insurance provided for her 
by THIG. For the avoidance of doubt given the fact that this group scheme policy for Mr and 
Mrs A was cancelled in the circumstances it was, I do not find it unreasonable that their 
representative did not wish for THIG to attempt to find alternative insurance for Mrs A at that 
time.
Ref: DRN6640592

5
my final decision
For the reasons above and more fully detailed in my provisional decision attached, it is my final 
decision that I uphold this complaint. I now require Independent Sales Force Solutions Limited 
(THIG) to do the following:

Once Mr and Mrs A have detailed out their costs in paying for medical treatment 
themselves to date, it should reimburse Mr and Mrs A for their costs of all eligible 
treatment incurred to date, less any premium they would have had to pay to insurer one.

Compensate Mr and Mrs A for any loss of comfort or other inconvenience they have 
suffered as a result of undergoing treatment through the NHS rather than privately under 
cover of their policy. This means if Mr A or Mrs A or both have undergone treatment within 
the NHS, which would have been covered by insurer one, THIG should multiply the cost of 
the private bed to insurer one by the number of nights Mr A or Mrs A stayed in a NHS 
hospital and pay that amount to Mr and Mrs A.

Instruct the services of an independent actuary to assess the likely financial loss to Mr and 
Mrs A of having to self-fund private healthcare for the rest of their lives, bearing in mind 
their age, health issues and any other factors which in the opinion of the actuary is 
appropriate, including any premium Mr and Mrs A would have had to pay to insurer one. 
On receipt of the actuary’s report, I require Independent Sales Force Solutions to pay his 
or her recommended award to Mr and Mrs A. To avoid any dispute over the actuary to be 
instructed, I require THIG to find three actuaries and to allow Mr and Mrs A decide which 
they prefer to be instructed.

Pay Mr and Mrs A the sum of £500 compensation for the distress and inconvenience 
caused by its and its representative’s (Mr H’s) actions.
I make no other award against Independent Sales Force Solutions Limited.
Rona Doyle
ombudsman
Ref: DRN6640592

Copy of Provisional Decision
complaint
Mr and Mrs A have complained about the fact that Independent Sales Force Solutions 
Limited (trading as The Health Insurance Group, ‘THIG’) has said that Mr A should have 
disclosed his pre-existing medical conditions when he was applying for a group private 
medical insurance policy. As these conditions were not disclosed, the insurer has declined 
Mr A’s claim and cancelled Mr A’s group policy from the beginning.
Mr and Mrs A believe that it was due to THIG’s errors that the pre-existing medical 
conditions were not disclosed and they now find themselves without private medical 
insurance.
background
Mr and Mrs A have used the services of THIG for a number of years and more particularly 
had private medical insurance with a specific insurer (not the insurer who made the decision 
in this matter), insurer one, since 1975. In 2012, Mr and Mrs A and THIG discussed 
changing insurance providers to make the policies more cost effective. As a result, Mr and 
Mrs A proceeded to take out a group policy with insurer two.
Sometime later, Mr A made a claim against this group policy. Insurer two investigated his 
claim and ultimately declined the claim and decided to void Mr and Mrs A’s group policy due 
to the non-disclosure of pre-existing medical conditions from which Mr A appeared to have 
suffered for some years. This left Mr and Mrs A with no private medical insurance.
Mr and Mrs A then complained about the sale of the policy. They felt that THIG was aware of 
Mr A’s medical history and should not have sold them this new group policy if this had been a 
problem. THIG responded saying it had asked both Mr and Mrs A questions regarding their 
health and Mr A should have disclosed his medical conditions in response to these questions.
The adjudicator investigated the complaint but did not uphold it. She considered that the 
insurer had asked a clear question regarding any cardiac conditions, which should have 
prompted Mr A to disclose his condition.
Mr and Mrs A’s representative disagreed with the adjudicator’s assessment. She argued that, 
if the seller had no knowledge of Mr A’s medical history, therefore no proper fact-finding 
exercise had been carried out prior to THIG selling this policy to Mr and Mrs A.
The case has now been referred to me for determination.
my provisional findings
I have considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what is fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint.
The first issue I need to consider is who was responsible or likely to be responsible on the 
balance of probabilities for the non-disclosure of Mr A’s medical history that led to the 
voiding of this policy by insurer two.
Ref: DRN6640592

7
It is clear to me from Mr and Mrs A’s correspondence with THIG that Mr A was its customer 
from at least 2009. However despite repeated requests from the adjudicator, THIG was not 
able to disclose adequate documentation to demonstrate the extent of its relationship with 
Mr A or indeed the extent of Mr A’s instructions to it. Mr and Mrs A’s representative was 
finally able to locate letter from a THIG representative (Mr G) dated 15 January 2008 which 
appears to be both a letter introducing the services of THIG and more specifically detailing 
its advice following a meeting where Mr A is clearly told to stay with insurer one because of 
his medical history. It confirmed that no new ‘insurer will carry on cover for all of your pre-
existing conditions and all of them would exclude the overwhelming majority of the 
conditions you’ve experienced in the past. This would mean for instance, that any heart 
condition that should arise would be excluded from cover.’ THIG has said now to us that 
this is the first time it has seen this letter and that there is no copy of it on their file and it 
continues to maintain that nevertheless Mr and Mrs A became customers of THIG in 2009. I 
am not persuaded by this as clearly Mr G was representing THIG at this time and 
consequently it is evident that Mr and Mrs A were customers of THIG in January 2008. 
Further I am minded to find that it was reasonable for Mr and Mrs A to expect THIG to 
maintain its file on them so that any representative, to include any other representative than 
Mr G, would have knowledge of their relationship with THIG as their broker.
In 2009 there were various email discussions between Mr A and a further representative, (Mr 
H), of THIG because Mr A wished for better renewal terms with his then insurer, insurer one. 
The THIG representative, Mr H, confirms that if Mr A was willing to pay a higher excess, the 
premium amount would drop. Whilst Mr A is not wholly satisfied with this, Mr H says that that 
was the best he could do for this year. Mr A then renews his policy with insurer one in 2010 
and 2011. I am minded to find that given such negotiation to reduce an escalating premium, it 
would seem very probable indeed that Mr H would have had knowledge of Mr A’s medical 
conditions.
Mr A, himself, recounts that he appointed Mr H of THIG in October 2009 and that he 
negotiated the premium level with insurer one with the full knowledge of his medical history.
I am minded to find that is most probable. In January 2012 Mr A has said that at a meeting at 
his house, he and Mr H discussed his options in the light of his medical history and it was 
eventually decided that it might be better for Mr A to switch insurer and indeed set up a 
group scheme with insurer two so that his wife, Mrs A could be included too. Mr A says Mr H 
said the insurer two would accept his previous medical history without question. Mr A has said 
that Mr H completed the application for him and it is handwritten in what appears Mr H’s own 
handwriting (from other documents completed by Mr H) in the full knowledge of his medical 
history and consequently as he trusted him, he signed it.
Then Mr A received a letter from Mr H of THIG on 14 February 2012 which detailed out the 
recommendations of THIG. It said the requirements of Mr A were budget and benefits 
together with any existing cover for private medical insurance. On this basis it recommended 
the switch to the new insurer. That letter clearly sets out that pre-existing conditions (in the 
manner specifically detailed) would not be covered along with chronic or long-term medical 
conditions. Mr A says that this letter led him to speak with Mr H of THIG at some length on 
15 February 2012 querying with him that he had previously said Mr A’s previous medical 
history was unreservedly accepted by insurer two. Accordingly he received an email from 
Mr H on 22 February 2012 that this new policy with insurer two ‘had no exclusions’. I note 
that that email said nothing more about the actual conditions or moratorium which would be 
imposed by this new policy.
Ref: DRN6640592

8
Unfortunately when Mr A’s representative complained to THIG once Mr A’s claim had been 
declined and the group policy being cancelled from the beginning, Mr H then replied the 
policy was ‘subject to a declaration. [Insurer] have sent a letter explaining their actions. I 
have nothing further to add.’
It is my provisional finding that it is clear that Mr H knew Mr A relatively well and had visited 
him at home on several occasions to discuss his private medical insurance needs since 
2009. Therefore it seems to me on the balance of probabilities that he was well aware of Mr 
A’s medical history, most especially as he had been negotiating with Mr A’s previous insurer 
in relation to the premium level Mr A was being charged.
Furthermore it is clear to me by virtue of  the contents of the letter from the first 
representative of THIG that Mr A encountered, Mr G, dated 15 January 2008 to Mr and Mrs A 
that THIG through its representative Mr G, was fully aware of Mr A’s medical conditions.
Consequently as it is clear Mr H either was aware or reasonably ought to have been aware 
of Mr A’s medical history, (given Mr G’s previous involvement) it seems inconceivable and 
contrary to Mr H’s duty of care that he would have accepted a signed application from Mr A 
in which no disclosures were made concerning his medical history. The relevant declaration 
states the following:
‘Are you aware of person to be covered by this application who has received treatment or 
advice relating to;
any type of cancer – yes/no
any type of heart or circulatory condition – yes/no 
in the last 2 years?
Are you aware of any person to be covered by this application who has received treatment 
or advice relating to any:
Psychiatric or mental illness or condition in the last 2 years? Yes/No
OR
Knee problems
Back problems
Shoulder problems, or
Arthritis
In the last 6 months?’
In the light of this, I am minded to find that Mr A’s account of what occurred is the more 
persuasive and therefore I am minded to find that THIG is at fault for the fact that Mr A’s 
medical history was not disclosed to insurer two and that Mr and Mrs A now find themselves 
without any private medical cover.
Therefore the next issue I must consider is the appropriate redress. THIG has informed us 
that Mr and Mrs A’s previous insurer, insurer one, will not provide any cover for Mr and 
Mrs A. Clearly Mr A’s original claim to insurer two was not paid, however I have not been 
provided with any information from Mr A or his representative as to whether or not Mr A 
paid the costs of his treatment for this claim privately. If it the case that Mr A incurred the 
costs of his treatment himself, I would be minded to direct that THIG reimburse him the 
costs that would have been payable under the policy, taking into account the relevant 
excess that Mr A would have had to pay in any event.
Ref: DRN6640592

9
Whilst Mr A has said to us that he has since then paid for some private medical treatment, in 
order to consider the appropriate redress, I will require full details of what medical care he 
has required and which elements of it were paid for privately with the actual cost amounts 
along with which elements of that care or treatment were dealt with under the NHS. Likewise 
I will require full details of Mrs A’s recent health problems and what elements of her 
treatment were paid for privately and what elements were dealt with within the NHS, against 
the actual cost amounts incurred. Once I am in receipt of that information, then I am minded 
to require THIG to reimburse Mr and Mrs A for costs they have incurred which would have 
been borne by the policy along with an appropriate level of compensation for the elements 
which were covered under the NHS but which would have been eligible for private cover.
However it is Mr A and Mrs A’s future situation that is of primary concern to Mr and Mrs A. 
Both are now without private medical insurance and are in the likely position that any such 
insurance that they could now purchase would be relatively worthless to them given their 
age and indeed Mr A’s medical history and now Mrs A’s medical history. THIG has told us 
insurer one is no longer willing to cover Mr and Mrs A and given their age and collective 
health problems with Mrs A’s recent health issues too, it is unlikely that any other provider 
would be willing to offer any policy to Mr and Mrs A that covered these conditions.
Therefore I am minded to find that an actuary should be appointed whose fees are to be 
payable by THIG to assess the probable cost of Mr and Mrs A’s future private medical care 
having regard to their age and health issues. On receipt of the actuary’s views I am minded 
to require THIG to pay an appropriate amount to Mr and Mrs A to enable them to fund their 
own private medical care for the future. That amount would also take account of any 
premium Mr and Mrs A would have had to pay had they remained with insurer one.
Finally I need to consider the issue of distress and inconvenience as Mr A through his 
representative has clearly demonstrated to me that he has suffered considerable distress at 
finding himself and Mrs A without private medical insurance. I am minded to find that THIG 
caused this situation. Moreover it failed to accept it was at fault, instead implying that Mr A 
was to blame, which led to further significant distress to Mr A. Therefore I am minded to 
make an award of £500 compensation in relation to the distress and inconvenience caused 
to Mr and Mrs A.
my provisional decision
For the reasons above it is my provisional decision that I am minded to uphold this 
complaint.
I am minded to require Independent Sales Force Solutions Limited to do the following:

Once Mr and Mrs A have detailed out their costs in paying for medical treatment 
themselves to date, it should reimburse Mr and Mrs A for their costs of eligible 
treatment incurred to date less any premium they would have had to pay to insurer 
one.

Compensate Mr and Mrs A for any loss of comfort or other inconvenience they have 
suffered as a result of undergoing treatment through the NHS rather than privately 
under cover of their policy.

Instruct the services of an independent actuary to assess the likely financial loss to Mr 
and Mrs A of having to self-fund private healthcare for the rest of their lives, bearing in 
Ref: DRN6640592

10
mind their age, health issues and any other factors which in the opinion of the actuary is 
appropriate, including any premium Mr and Mrs A would have had to pay to insurer one.

On receipt of the actuary’s report, I am them minded to require Independent Sales

Force Solutions to pay his or her recommended award to Mr and Mrs A. 

Pay Mr and Mrs A the sum of £500 compensation for the distress and inconvenience 
caused by its and its representative’s (Mr H’s) actions. 
Rona Doyle
ombudsman

text:
K820x#14
complaint
Mrs H has complained that Union Reiseversicherung AG (“URV”) has refused to pay the 
costs of her medical treatment under her travel insurance policy.
Mrs H has a representative in this matter but I’ll only refer to ‘Mrs H’ in this decision, which 
may include things sent or said by her representative.
background
Mrs H had a travel insurance policy underwritten by URV. In October 2013 Mrs H was 
abroad in Europe when she became ill. Her hotel called an ambulance and Mrs H was taken 
to a private hospital. She had to undergo an emergency operation. 
Mrs H’s daughter was with her and so made a call to URV to open a claim. URV advised  
Mrs H’s daughter that the policy didn’t cover private treatment and that nothing should be 
signed or paid to the hospital.
URV declined to pay the costs for Mrs H’s medical treatment, but paid the additional travel 
and accommodation costs that had arisen from her illness.
Mrs H complained to URV. It asked about the circumstances surrounding Mrs H’s admission. 
Mrs H said that the exclusion of private medical care was a significant one and it should’ve 
appeared in the summary of cover. As it didn’t the exclusion was unfair and her medical 
costs should be covered. Mrs H didn’t think how she had been admitted to the hospital was 
relevant.
URV didn’t change its decision to refuse Mrs H’s claim and so she complained to this 
service.
Our adjudicator investigated the complaint. She didn’t recommend it should be upheld. The 
adjudicator thought that the policy was clear that the cost of private treatment wasn’t covered 
if there was “adequate state facilities available”. And that any private treatment had to be 
agreed in advance. The adjudicator said she didn’t think this exclusion was unusual in travel 
insurance policies. 
Mrs H disagreed so the complaint has been passed to me.
my findings
I’ve considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint.
Mrs H has asked about her legal relationship with the hospital, but this is outside my remit so 
I’m only dealing with the issue of whether URV‘s decision to apply the exclusion clause to 
Mrs H’s medical costs was fair and reasonable.
 
It’s agreed that the travel policy excludes the cost of private medical care if there is an 
adequate state hospital available. And that any private medical treatment has to be pre-
approved by URV. The policy also says that when travelling in Europe “you should carry a 
European Health insurance Card (EHIC)” to use at state hospitals so to save costs. Neither 
of these terms is unusual – they’re in most travel policies that I’ve seen.
Ref: DRN6731917

2
It’s also agreed that this limitation isn’t included in the ‘Summary of Cover’. Mrs H says that 
this is a breach of the FCA handbook as it’s a significant limitation of the cover offered. And 
it isn’t fair to a consumer if they aren’t clearly informed of such a significant limitation. She 
says without this information they aren’t able to make an informed choice about a policy. 
Mrs H has also provided extracts from three different policies from other insurance 
companies that don’t exclude private medical treatment to show it isn’t usual. But these 
policies say that treatment must be authorised by the insurer so I think it could depend on 
the circumstances whether private treatment would be agreed.
And I’m aware of a number of underwriters who have the same or similar clause as URV 
about private medical costs. So, I don’t think it’s an unusual or significant term. This is a 
travel insurance policy as opposed to a health insurance policy and I think its terms and 
conditions are clear about what is and isn’t covered. I also think the policy is clear that an 
insured person is expected to use reciprocal health arrangements when abroad, in particular 
to have an EHIC with them to reduce costs where possible. Again, this is also common in 
other travel policies. So I don’t agree that it has to be included in the summary.
Mrs H says that the maximum cover for medical costs is £5million, and a figure of that size 
must relate to private medical care. But the policy covers travellers to a large range of 
destinations all of which will have different medical costs and services available. I don’t think 
this amount on its own means private medical cover has to be covered.
Mrs H says that it’s for URV to show that the state hospital would’ve had adequate facilities 
to treat her. But I don’t agree. I think the policy was clear that private medical costs wouldn’t 
be covered, so it’s for Mrs H to show that this exclusion didn’t apply to her. I don’t think it’s 
reasonable to put the onus on URV. It’s for Mrs H to show evidence about why she had to be 
treated at the private hospital. I don’t have any evidence that the state hospital wouldn’t have 
been able to adequately treat her health condition.
Mrs H’s daughter rang URV just as her mother was going into theatre for her operation. URV 
clearly told her daughter that the policy wouldn’t cover private treatment. It said Mrs H had a 
choice of staying at that hospital “in the knowledge she may have to pay”. Mrs H’s daughter 
said it wasn’t possible to move her as she was about to be operated on and URV said “OK”.
But I don’t think this was an agreement by URV to meet the costs of Mrs H’s treatment. It 
went on to advise Mrs H’s daughter not to sign any financial papers, or pay anything to the 
hospital, and to keep their passports somewhere safe. URV said they should tell the hospital 
that their insurers were “making enquiries”.
Mrs H stayed in the private hospital up until she was discharged. I don’t have any evidence 
about why she wasn’t moved to a state hospital after her operation. But I’ve seen that when 
she was admitted Mrs H knew it was a private hospital, and that the hospital told her she 
may be liable for the costs.
So, looking at the evidence, I’m not upholding Mrs H’s complaint. I think URV acted fairly 
and reasonably in declining her claim for her medical costs.
my final decision
I’m not upholding Mrs H’s claim.
Ref: DRN6731917

3
Under the rules of the Financial Ombudsman Service, I’m required to ask Mrs H to accept or 
reject my decision before 1 August 2016.
Jocelyn Griffith
ombudsman
Ref: DRN6731917
quoted_clauses: you should carry a European Health insurance Card (EHIC)

text:
K821x#15
complaint
Mrs B has complained that Aviva Health UK Limited wrongly refused to cover her claim for 
her hand under her private medical insurance policy. 
background
Mrs B has had a private medical policy for around 30 years. In March 2014, she transferred 
to this policy with Aviva on the advice of a broker. The transfer was on what is called 
‘continued moratorium’ underwriting terms. This means in Mrs B’s case that as she had 
continued cover for private medical insurance since 1982, only conditions, which she 
suffered from in the five years before the start of her first policy wouldn’t be covered. This 
was also restricted to not providing cover for the treatment of chronic conditions unless it 
was an acute flare up of that chronic condition.
In November 2014, Mrs B asked Aviva to cover her claim to have an operation to treat her 
trigger finger. During the call she confirmed to Aviva that she’d an injection to this finger in 
March 2013, so before this policy started. Aviva said that because she had symptoms prior 
to one year before this policy started her operation and treatment wouldn’t be covered under 
this policy. It said cover was only extended to conditions or symptoms that started from 1 
April 2013 under its continued ‘moratorium’ condition.
Mrs B didn’t agree and so she brought her complaint to us. The adjudicator who investigated 
her complaint thought Aviva’s term was unclear. He felt the term said cover would continue 
from the date Mrs B first had private medical insurance which meant from 1982 so that 
would mean her claim for her finger would be covered.
As Mrs B had had her finger operation and treatment on the NHS, he felt that Aviva should 
pay Mrs B £50 compensation for the delay in having to wait for her operation and a further 
£250 compensation for her inconvenience in not having her claim met.
Aviva didn’t agree and so Mrs B’s complaint has been passed to me to decide.
my findings
I’ve considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint.
Aviva said that although a policyholder may have had cover for many years, its term is clear 
that it only provided cover for pre-existing conditions for one year before its policy started, 
namely 1 April 2013. It explained that when it accepted her, it only accepted her on the same 
underwriting terms she had held with her previous insurer not the same policy terms and 
conditions.
The term says:
“Continued moratorium
For members who were insured on a moratorium basis on another policy and then 
transferred….
We do not cover treatment of any pre-existing condition, or any related conditions if 
you had symptoms of; medication for; diagnostic tests for; treatment for or; advice 
about that condition in the five years before your initial date of cover. Your initial date 
Ref: DRN6823517

2
of cover is the date you started cover with your first insurer (provided there has been 
no break in cover since then).”
It goes on to explain cover is provided for a pre-existing condition if no treatment or advice 
has been received for that condition for a two year period after your initial date of cover. 
Crucially in my view, it further explains that its application form explains when the “continued 
moratorium” underwriting has been chosen no benefits will be available if the condition was 
pre-existing for five years from the date of the existing policy and there wasn’t a clear two 
period of no symptoms or treatment.
I think that if Aviva thinks this means her immediate previous policy, then this term is too 
unclear and confusing because it said its moratorium is only related to one year before her 
previous policy started and this term talks of an “initial date”, which in Mrs B’s case was 
1982. So I don’t think this term makes sense with reference to that stance. Clearly, to me, it 
seems written to mean the five-year period before Mrs B’s cover first began which would 
have been 1982.
As I think the term is too unclear and confusing then it follows it should be construed Mrs B’s 
favour. So I consider that Mrs B complaint should succeed. Therefore, as Mrs B had her 
operation on the NHS and couldn’t avail of the comfort of her private medical policy with 
Aviva I agree it should pay her a total of £250 compensation for the delay and inconvenience 
she suffered in having her operation and treatment for her finger. 
It appears there was another issue with a further pre-existing condition, which has now been 
sorted out so I won’t deal with that in this decision.
my final decision
For the reasons I’ve discussed above, it’s my final decision that I uphold this complaint. I 
now require Aviva Health UK Limited to pay Mrs B £250 compensation.
Under the rules of the Financial Ombudsman Service, I’m required to ask Mrs B to accept or 
reject my decision before 12 February 2016.
Rona Doyle
ombudsman
Ref: DRN6823517

We do not cover treatment of any pre-existing condition, or any related conditions if you had symptoms of; medication for; diagnostic tests for; treatment for or; advice about that condition in the five years before your initial date of cover. Your initial date Ref: DRN6823517 2 of cover is the date you started cover with your first insurer (provided there has been no break in cover since then).

text:
K820x#13
complaint
Mr and Mrs W have complained about the level of payment offered by ACE European Group 
Limited in settlement of a claim under their personal accident policy.
background
The background to this decision was set out in my provisional decision dated 17 October 
2014, a copy of which is attached and which forms part of this provisional decision.  
Briefly, in November 2007, Mrs W fell and injured her knee. In April 2008, she underwent 
knee replacement surgery. She submitted a claim under her personal accident policy. ACE 
considered that any disability from which Mrs W suffered was primarily due to pre-existing 
osteoarthritis, rather than the accident. However, it eventually paid Mrs W £1,000 in an effort 
to settle the complaint. Mr and Mrs W considered that they were entitled to more benefit 
under the policy and referred a complaint to this service.
In my provisional decision, I noted that ACE had previously settled a claim by Mrs W in 
respect of permanent disability she said she had suffered following an accident in 2002. In 
light of the restrictions that had already been placed on her leisure activities by virtue of her 
2002 accident, and for which she had already received benefit, I considered that Mrs W had 
not shown that the 2007 accident had entirely prevented her from carrying out her usual 
interests and pursuits. I therefore did not consider that she had demonstrated her entitlement 
to benefit for permanent total disablement. I further considered that while Mrs W might be 
entitled to benefit for loss of use of her knee, the most that she could reasonably expect to 
be paid under the policy was £768. Given that ACE had already paid in excess of this, I did 
not consider it reasonable for me to ask it to pay anything further.
I invited both parties to comment on my provisional decision.
ACE has offered no comment.
Mr and Mrs W have responded to say that they do not accept my provisional decision. They 
say that the benefit paid for the 2002 accident represented only 22% of the full insured 
amount for permanent total disability. They say that this was because Mrs W’s level of 
disablement at the time was assessed as being only 22%. They say that, contrary to 
expectations, she had undergone improvement since that time but that the 2007 accident 
has now set her back so that she fully meets the policy definition of permanent total 
disability. They therefore consider that further benefit should be awarded.
my findings
I have considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what is fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint. Having done so, while I am sorry to 
disappoint Mr and Mrs W, I see no reason to change my provisional decision.
Mr and Mrs W say that the reason that Mrs W received only 22% of the full amount of total 
permanent disability benefit for her 2002 accident was because her level of disability was 
assessed as being 22%. I have re-examined the evidence from the time of this claim and I 
disagree that this was the case. Mrs W was claiming to be totally disabled under the terms of 
the policy. In my opinion, the reason that ACE reduced her benefit to 22% of the full amount 
was because it considered that this was the extent to which her disablement could be 
Ref: DRN6894396

2
attributed to the accident; it considered that the remainder was due to her pre-existing 
medical conditions. ACE’s decision was accepted by Mr and Mrs W at the time.
Given that Mrs W received benefit for total permanent disability for an accident in 2002, it 
follows that she cannot claim for such benefit again. If the disability was total, she cannot 
claim to have become even more disabled at some later stage. In any case, as noted in my 
provisional decision, I am not persuaded that Mr and Mrs W have shown that the 2007 
accident has impacted to any significant extent on her ability to carry out her interests and 
pursuits, given that these had already been severely curtailed by the earlier accident.
I have already explained why I think that the most that Mrs W could reasonably expect to 
receive under the policy was £768 in respect of a proportional payment for loss of use of her 
knee. Given that ACE has already paid her benefit of £1,000 in respect of this, I consider 
that it would not be reasonable for me to require it to pay anything further.
my final decision
Under the rules of the Financial Ombudsman Service, I am required to ask Mr and Mrs W to 
accept or reject my decision before 6 January 2015.
David Poley
ombudsman
Ref: DRN6894396

3
COPY OF PROVISIONAL DECISION
 
complaint
Mr and Mrs W have complained about the level of payment offered by ACE European Group Limited 
in settlement of a claim under their personal accident policy.
background
Mr and Mrs W held a personal accident insurance policy with ACE. The policy offered various benefits 
in the event of either of them suffering bodily injury following an accident.
In November 2007, Mrs W fell and injured her knee. In April 2008, she underwent knee replacement 
surgery. She submitted a claim under the policy.
After considering the medical evidence, including a report from Mrs W’s treating orthopaedic 
consultant (“Doctor B”), ACE decided that any disability suffered by Mrs W was primarily due to pre-
existing osteoarthritis, rather than the accident. It therefore offered a settlement of £240, which was 
equivalent to 2% of the benefit payable under the policy for total loss of use of a knee (£12,000). Mr 
and Mrs W were unhappy at this offer and brought a complaint to this service.
In February 2011, the ombudsman issued a decision directing ACE to arrange an independent 
medical examination (“IME”) to assess the level of Mrs W’s disability and the extent to which this 
could be attributed to the accident as opposed to any pre-existing condition. The ombudsman further 
directed ACE to consider Mrs W’s claim against the range of benefits available under the policy, 
including permanent total disability, rather than simply total loss of use of a knee. The ombudsman 
said that if benefit was payable under more than one benefit heading, the benefit offering the highest 
payment should apply.
In June 2011, Doctor B carried out an IME of Mrs W on behalf of ACE. In August 2011, based on 
Doctor B’s report, ACE continued to state that Mrs W’s disability was primarily due to her pre-existing 
osteoarthritis but increased its previous offer of settlement to £1,000 as a gesture of goodwill. Mr and 
Mrs W still did not accept this offer and referred a further complaint to this service.
In October 2012, the adjudicator who investigated the second complaint recommended that it be 
upheld in part. She considered that the medical evidence suggested that Mrs W met the criteria for 
permanent total disability benefit to be paid. However, she considered that ACE still had not 
established the extent to which this disability could be attributed to the accident. She therefore 
considered that ACE should seek a further report to establish this information and to settle Mrs W’s 
claim accordingly. She also considered that ACE should pay Mrs W £300 compensation for the 
distress and inconvenience she had suffered as a result of the significant delays caused by its 
handling of her claim. 
ACE wrote to Doctor B to ask further questions about Mrs W. Doctor B responded in February 2013. 
In March 2013, based on Doctor B’s response, ACE wrote to Mrs W to explain that it considered that, 
because her disability was primarily due to her pre-existing condition rather than her accident, Mrs W 
was entitled to only 4% of the benefit payable under the policy for total loss of knee, meaning she was 
entitled to £480. Because this was less than the £1,000 it had already paid, it said it would pay no 
further benefit. Mr and Mrs W still did not accept ACE’s offer and therefore referred the matter to this 
service for a third time.  
The adjudicator recommended that their complaint be upheld. She considered that Mrs W’s claim 
should have been considered against the benefit heading of permanent total disability (which offered 
benefit of £60,000) rather than total loss of use of a knee. She further considered that Mrs W was 
entitled to 13% of this benefit, meaning that she should receive £7,800 plus interest.
ACE did not accept the adjudicator’s recommendation.
Ref: DRN6894396

4
my provisional findings
I have considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what is fair and reasonable in 
the circumstances of this complaint. Having done so, I am minded to depart significantly from the 
findings of the adjudicator and to not uphold this complaint. I shall explain why.
The policy defines permanent total disability as:
 “A permanent disability caused other than by loss of limb or eye, which entirely prevents:
-
any other person insured over statutory retirement age from following or attending to their 
usual interests, pursuits or other avocations for the rest of their life.“
Mrs W has explained that her usual interests and pursuits were golf, gardening and sewing. In Doctor 
B’s report of June 2011 he states:
“… she is unable to complete her golf game due to discomfort and pain after long walk. She is unable 
to enjoy her gardening due to inability to kneel on the ground.”
However, ACE has provided evidence to show that Mrs W made a claim for benefit under the policy in 
2003 in respect of an accident suffered in 2002. At that time, Mr and Mrs W stated as follows:
“Sewing with two small groups of ladies who meet weekly and work on projects for church and other 
charities … She has had to completely give these up.
Gardening … She is now unable to do anything except supervise others working on the land.
Golf … This is now totally impossible.
We have delayed sending this claim in the hope that the problems would get less ... it would now 
seem that the damage is permanent.” 
On the basis of the reported impact on Mrs W’s leisure activities, ACE agreed to pay permanent 
disability benefit of £13,200 under the policy.
In light of the restrictions that had already been placed on her leisure activities by virtue of her 2002 
accident, and for which she has already received benefit, I do not consider that Mrs W has shown that 
the 2007 accident has entirely prevented her from carrying out her usual interests and pursuits. I 
therefore do not consider that she has demonstrated her entitlement to benefit for permanent total 
disablement.
ACE has also considered her entitlement to benefit for loss of, or total loss of use of, a knee. The 
maximum benefit payable under this category was £12,000. However, I note that in Doctor B’s report 
of June 2011, he states:
“[Mrs W] has satisfactory range of movement of her left knee as expected after total knee 
replacement.” 
ACE calculated that Mrs W had suffered, at most, 40% loss of use of the knee, and furthermore, on 
the basis of Doctor B’s February 2013 report, considered that her accident had contributed no more 
than 10% to her disability (the remainder being accounted for by her pre-existing osteoarthritis). ACE 
therefore calculated that she was entitled to £480 benefit under the policy, which was 4% of the 
maximum benefit payable. Given that this was less than the £1,000 it had already paid to Mrs W, it 
declined to make any further payment.
Ref: DRN6894396

5
I consider that, given Mrs W has almost a full range of movement in her left knee, ACE’s estimate that 
she had suffered 40% loss of use is reasonable. I further consider that Doctor B’s February 2013 
report suggests that Mrs W’s 2007 accident resulted in her needing a knee operation between six and 
ten years sooner than she otherwise would. Assuming that the average person might expect to carry 
out their leisure activities for a period of about 60 years, I therefore consider it reasonable to say that 
Mrs W’s accident has contributed approximately 10-16% to her disability. I therefore consider that the 
most that Mrs W could reasonably expect to be paid under the policy was 6.4% of £12,000, or £768. 
Given that ACE has already paid in excess of this, I do not consider it reasonable for me to ask it to 
pay anything further.
my provisional decision
For the reasons above, while I recognise it will come as a disappointment to Mr and Mrs W, my 
provisional decision is that I do not uphold this complaint. I am minded to make no award against ACE 
European Group Limited.
David Poley
ombudsman

In Doctor B’s report of June 2011 he states: “… she is unable to complete her golf game due to discomfort and pain after long walk. Sewing with two small groups of ladies who meet weekly and work on projects for church and other charities … She has had to completely give these up.
