text:
K821x#15
complaint
Mr and Mrs S complain that Europaische Reiseversicherung AG (‘ERV’) hasn’t paid a 
cancellation claim under their travel insurance policy. 
background
Mr and Mrs S held an annual travel insurance policy, underwritten by ERV. The policy was 
taken out in May 2017. 
The day before Mr and Mrs S were due to travel, their daughter (Miss S) was unfortunately 
taken to hospital. Mr and Mrs S ended up cancelling their trip, and made a claim under their 
policy with ERV. 
ERV said the claim wasn’t covered because Miss S had been under treatment and 
investigation for a medical condition since 2016, which was connected to the condition 
leading to the cancellation claim. 
Unhappy, Mr and Mrs S brought their complaint to this service. 
Our investigator recommended that the complaint should be upheld. 
Mr and Mrs S accepted our investigator’s opinion but ERV didn’t, so the complaint has been 
passed to me to decide. 
my findings
I’ve considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint.
The terms and conditions of Mr and Mrs S’s policy say:
‘What is not covered….
4) any claim arising directly or indirectly from a pre-existing medical condition, 
known to you prior to the commencement of the period of cover, affecting any 
close relative, travelling companion whether insured under this policy or not, a 
non travelling relative…..if:

a terminal prognosis has been received prior to the commencement of the 
period of cover;

they were on a waiting-list, or had knowledge of the need for, surgery, 
inpatient treatment, or investigation at any hospital or clinic at the 
commencement of the period of cover;

or during the 90 days immediately prior to the commencement of the period 
of cover they had:
-
required surgery, inpatient treatment or hospital consultations; or
-
required any form of treatment or prescribed medication;’.
Ref: DRN7442755

2
I’ve considered the two medical certificates which Mr and Mrs S sent to ERV in connection 
with their claim. 
The first medical certificate looks to me as if it has been completed by Mr and Mrs S and 
signed by a GP. This medical certificate says the illness leading to the cancellation of the trip 
was unknown, and refers to a doctor’s letter which confirms Miss S was admitted to hospital 
as an emergency. 
It appears the second medical certificate has had some additional information inserted by 
Miss S’s GP. This medical certificate says the illness leading to cancellation was a ‘flare-up 
of inflammatory arthritis...’. 
The second medical certificate goes on to ask ‘has the patient suffered from the same or 
similar condition in the past? If yes, is the present illness, in your opinion, related in any way 
to the past condition?’. The GP has answered ‘no’ to this question. 
Finally, the second medical certificate says Miss S had been under supervision of a 
consultant for a particular medical condition – and was being given infusions in the previous 
six months. 
Our investigator didn’t think ERV had demonstrated that Miss S met any of the bullet points 
under the exclusion I’ve set out above. And, I agree there isn’t any confirmation in any of the 
medical evidence I’ve seen from her GP that Miss S does fall within the exclusion.
ERV replied to our investigator’s opinion with some information about the type of infusions 
Miss S was receiving. ERV says this information indicates Miss S would definitely have had 
treatment in the 90 days before the policy was taken out. ERV has also said it’s prepared to 
request a copy of Miss S’s medical history to confirm this. 
I’d generally expect an insurer to request any medical information it thinks is necessary in 
order to fully assess a claim as soon as possible. This would usually be at the point a claim 
is first being considered by the insurer – rather than waiting until when a complaint has been 
brought to this service. 
But, in any event, I don’t think it’s necessary for ERV to ask for this medical information now. 
Even if I accept Miss S was receiving treatment for a pre-existing medical condition in the 90 
days before Mr and Mrs S bought their policy, I’d still recommend that this complaint should 
be upheld.  
This is because – even if I were satisfied that Mr and Mrs S’s claim was excluded under a 
strict interpretation of the policy terms and conditions – I don’t think it’s fair or reasonable for 
ERV to decline their claim in the circumstances. 
I’ve thought about what I consider to be the purpose and intention of the policy exclusion I’ve 
quoted above. And I think this is to protect ERV from the risk of claims which are more likely 
to arise because of a pre-existing medical condition, and to protect ERV from claims which 
could be said to be foreseeable by the policyholder.  
Ref: DRN7442755

3
Mr and Mrs S say their daughter has suffered with her back since 2000 – but, in 17 years, 
she has never experienced anything like the situation that led to them having to cancel their 
holiday. 
Based on what Mr and Mrs S have told us, I’m satisfied this incident was – from their point of 
view – a completely unexpected and unanticipated event. And I think it was an incident 
which they are reasonably entitled to expect their travel insurance policy with ERV to provide 
them with cover for. 
 
So, this means I don’t think it’s fair or reasonable for ERV to apply the above policy 
exclusion to reject Mr and Mrs S’s claim.  
my final decision
My final decision is that I uphold Mr and Mrs S’s complaint. 
Europaische Reiseversicherung AG must accept Mr and Mrs S’s claim, in line with the 
remaining terms and conditions of their policy. Interest should be added to the settlement at 
8% simple per year from the date of the claim until the date the settlement is paid1. 
Under the rules of the Financial Ombudsman Service, I’m required to ask Mr and Mrs S to 
accept or reject my decision before 23 December 2018.
Leah Nagle
ombudsman
1 If Europaische Reiseversicherung AG considers that it’s required by HM Revenue & Customs to 
take off income tax from that interest, it should tell Mr and Mrs S how much it’s taken off. It should 
also give Mr and Mrs S a certificate showing this if they ask for once, so they can reclaim the tax from 
HM Revenue & Customs if appropriate

text:
K820x#14
complaint
Mr P and Miss L have complained about AXA PPP Healthcare Limited’s decision to decline 
Miss L’s claim under their private medical insurance policy. AXA PPP declined the claim on 
the grounds that Miss L’s condition existed before the policy started. 
background
In August 2015, Mr P took out a private medical insurance policy with AXA PPP. The policy 
also covered his wife (Miss L) and their children. The policy was underwritten on a 
moratorium basis. This meant no cover was provided for at least the first two years of the 
policy for any condition which had existed in the three years before the policy began.
In November 2015, Miss L asked AXA PPP to authorise a consultation with a specialist in 
relation to abdominal pain from which she’d been suffering. After getting Miss L’s medical 
records, AXA PPP declined to authorise the consultation. It said Miss L had suffered 
abdominal pain in the three years before taking out the policy for which she’d seen 
specialists and undergone investigations. It therefore considered her condition was pre-
existing and excluded under the terms of the moratorium.
Mr P and Miss L complained to AXA PPP about its decision. They said the pain which Miss L 
was now experiencing was different to that she’d previously experienced. When AXA PPP 
wouldn’t change its position, they referred their complaint to this service. They said the policy 
wording was difficult to understand and that it had been unfair for AXA to decline their claim. 
They thought that AXA PPP’s employees were inadequately trained to make decisions about 
the nature of Miss L’s condition.
Our adjudicator didn’t recommend that the complaint be upheld. In her opinion, the terms of 
the policy were clear and AXA PPP had acted fairly in declining the claim. She didn’t think 
Mr P and Miss L had shown that AXA PPP’s employees were inadequately trained.
Mr P and Miss L didn’t accept the adjudicator’s findings. They said the policy was not easily 
understandable by a layperson. They said that while Miss L had pre-existing symptoms of 
abdominal pain, these hadn’t been diagnosed and she therefore couldn’t be said to have a 
pre-existing condition. They understood that AXA PPP’s underwriters weren’t medically 
trained and they considered this to be unacceptable. 
  
In view of the continued disagreement, the matter has been passed to me for a decision.
my findings
I’ve considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint. Having done so, I do not uphold this 
complaint. I shall explain why.
The policy states clearly that no cover will be available during the first two years for any 
pre-existing condition. The policy describes a pre-existing condition as:
“any disease, illness or injury for which:

You have received medication, advice or treatment; or

You have experienced symptoms;
Ref: DRN7917160

2
whether the condition has been diagnosed or not in the three years … before the start of 
your cover”
I think this is clear and understandable. The definition of a pre-existing condition also clearly 
extends to symptoms of undiagnosed conditions which I think is reasonable. The policy is 
intended to provide cover for unexpected health events. AXA PPP doesn’t want to provide 
cover for medical problems which the insured person knew about before taking out the 
policy, regardless of whether that problem has yet been diagnosed.
Miss L wanted to have cover for a consultation about abdominal pain she’d been suffering. 
But her medical records show she’d suffered pain in this region since February 2014 for 
which she had been referred to specialists and had undergone investigations. Indeed, her 
GP’s referral letter of October 2015 told the specialist that the reason for the consultation 
was “episodes of severe abdominal pain she has been experiencing for over 2 years.” I think 
it was reasonable for AXA PPP to conclude her current pain was likely to be related to the 
pain she’d previously experienced and for which a cause had yet to be established. 
I therefore think it was reasonable for AXA PPP to decline her claim.
I’m not aware of any requirement that underwriters of private medical insurance policies 
need to be medically trained. I’ve seen no evidence that AXA PPP’s employees were 
inadequately trained to deal with Miss L’s claim or the subsequent complaint.
Finally, Mr P and Miss L have also raised concerns over the sale of the policy. However, as 
the adjudicator has explained, they need to raise these concerns in the first instance with the 
business which sold them the policy.
my final decision
For the reasons given above, my final decision is that I do not uphold this complaint.
Under the rules of the Financial Ombudsman Service, I’m required to ask Mr P and Miss L to 
accept or reject my decision before 9 June 2016.
David Poley
ombudsman

text:
K820x#13
complaint
Mr M has complained about Canada Life Limited’s decision to decline a critical illness claim. 
It was made under Mr M’s policy after his partner, Ms T, was diagnosed with multiple 
sclerosis (‘MS’). Mr M says the claim should be paid. 
background
Mr M is a member of a group critical illness scheme provided by his employer since 2010. 
On 1 July 2013, he added Ms T to the scheme.  
Sadly, Ms T was first suspected to have MS in September 2013. Mr M made a claim to 
Canada Life at that time, but this was rejected since there wasn’t a clear diagnosis. After a 
confirmation of MS, Mr M made another claim in March 2014.   
Canada Life said the claim couldn’t be paid. That was because Ms T was suffering from a 
related condition prior to her joining the scheme. 
Mr M didn’t agree and made a complaint. Canada Life made a payment of £500 to 
acknowledge its mistake in its reasoning for declining the claim the first time. This is because 
it could’ve told Mr M about the pre-existing condition clause sooner. But it told Mr M it still 
couldn’t pay the claim because of the clause.  
The complaint was brought to this service.  
Our adjudicator reviewed the complaint. He found Ms T’s medical evidence showed she had 
been suffering from a related condition. The policy defined that this was excluded. So, he 
couldn’t say a claim ought to be paid.  
Mr M didn’t accept our adjudicator’s view. He said it couldn’t have been certain that Ms T 
was suffering from the related condition prior to being added to the policy. A formal diagnosis 
of the condition wasn’t given until after 1 July 2013.  
As the matter remains unresolved, it’s been passed to me. 
my findings
I’ve considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint.
I’m very sorry to learn of Ms T’s diagnosis. I appreciate that holding critical illness cover is 
valuable to her and Mr M. Businesses are able to consider what terms to offer policyholders 
or members of their insurance schemes. In Mr M’s case, his policy comes with exclusions in 
respect of pre-existing conditions. 
The policy says that:
“No benefit is payable for an insured illness in respect of which any related condition 
existed at any time prior to the entry to the scheme by the insured person, unless at 
least two consecutive years had elapsed since the person concerned last had 
symptoms of, or received treatment or advice in respect of, the related condition.
Ref: DRN8212835

2
A related condition is defined in the policy as:

any previous occurrence of an insured illness and

any other medical condition which, in the opinion of our Medical Officer, is either 
directly or indirectly associated with, or is likely to have led to, the occurrence of 
that insured illness.”
 
Under the definition of MS, the policy sets out a list of excluded related conditions for MS. 
One of these is optic neuritis (I’ll call this ‘ON’ from here). 
I realise the parties dispute when Ms T was diagnosed with ON. Canada Life says one of 
Ms T’s doctors tested Ms T’s sight in June 2013. He said at that time showed indicators of 
MS.  
As part of Ms T’s first claim, a report was sought from her treating neurologist. Regarding the 
ON, he said:
“in May [2013] she developed a right [ON]".
A differing consultant neurologist (who also gave Ms T’s MS diagnosis) wrote to Ms T’s GP 
in March 2014. He noted ON had been identified in April 2013.  
I understand there are differing dates of diagnosis for the former condition. Mr M has 
explained he doesn’t agree with our adjudicator because the final diagnosis that Ms T had 
suffered ON was after she joined his policy. 
Despite a definite date, I still don’t believe that the clause can be avoided, to say that a claim 
is payable. The policy terms set out above note no claim will be payable in respect of MS if 
ON existed at any time prior to entry to the scheme.
Though the diagnosis didn’t take place until some (disputed) time later, the evidence shows 
that ON likely existed before 1 July 2013. Though the cause for this could’ve been some 
condition other than MS, the policy wording includes ON as a related condition. Though ON 
can occur for other reasons, I understand it is most commonly caused by MS. So I can’t say 
that the policy wording is unfair by including this as a related condition.  
I know my decision will be disappointing to Ms T and Mr M, but I don’t think Canada Life is 
wrong in declining the claim. That’s because the pre-existing condition clause does apply. 
I realise Mr M is unhappy that rather than allow an appeal (in the stated three month 
window) to his first claim, Canada Life chose to start a second claim. Though this may have 
been a differing procedure, the effect is the same. Canada Life conducted the same 
assessment it would have made upon receipt of new evidence, either as an appeal or as a 
second claim.  
Had Canada Life told Mr M sooner of the pre-existing condition clause, it may have affected 
his and Ms T’s actions with the second claim. Like our adjudicator, I think it’s addressed its 
mistake by paying them £500 for the additional trouble caused to them. But I don’t think the 
claim is payable in any event. 
my final decision
I don’t uphold this complaint or make any award.  
Ref: DRN8212835

3
Jo Storey
ombudsman

complaint
Mr and Mrs B complain about an exclusion in their private medical insurance policy with AIG 
Europe Ltd. They are also unhappy about AIG’s initial decision to refuse Mrs B’s claim.
our initial conclusions
Our adjudicator noted that there had been some delay as AIG had initially refused the claim, but he 
thought the £200 offered by AIG was fair compensation. He thought the decision to have the 
exclusion in the policy was an appropriate use of AIG’s commercial judgment. 
my final decision
I have considered all the evidence from both parties, in order to decide what is fair and reasonable 
in the circumstances. 
The policy doesn’t cover private treatment if this is needed within 30 days of emergency treatment. 
Although AIG initially told Mr B that his wife couldn’t claim under the policy because of this 
exclusion, it later accepted the claim was payable. It offered to pay the claim plus £200 
compensation. 
I think it’s arguable whether or not Mrs B’s claim fell within the 30 day exclusion. But in any event, 
AIG has now accepted the claim is payable. I understand that Mrs B has received some treatment 
under the NHS. Mr B argues that his wife’s health would be far better if she had received treatment 
privately, but I haven’t seen any evidence that this would be the case. I think £200 is appropriate 
compensation for the inconvenience caused by AIG’s delay in accepting the claim. If Mr and Mrs B 
want to accept this, they should contact AIG directly. 
I note that when Mrs B was admitted to an NHS hospital, Mr B wanted his wife transferred to a 
private hospital for in-patient care. But the policy doesn’t cover a transfer from an NHS hospital to 
a private hospital, nor does it cover in-patient treatment. AIG told Mr B that if his wife still needed 
the private treatment after she had been discharged from hospital, it would still cover this. I find 
this to be reasonable. 
My final decision is that I don’t uphold this complaint. I make no award against AIG Europe Ltd.
Under the rules of the Financial Ombudsman Service, I am required to ask Mr and Mrs B either to 
accept or reject my decision before 28 May 2015.
Chantelle Hurn
ombudsman at the Financial Ombudsman Service

explanations of particular relevance to the case. 
ombudsman notes 
Ref: DRN8406049

The policy says
“What this policy does not cover
1. We will not pay for:
Emergency treatment or any claim for treatment carried out within 30 days of receiving 
emergency treatment for a medical condition or any related medical condition in any country.” 
Although Mr and Mrs B think this exclusion is unreasonable, the adjudicator correctly explained 
that it is up to AIG which exclusions it includes in its policy. Mr and Mrs B say they want a 
reason for AIG using the exclusion, but AIG has already explained that this policy does not offer 
full private medical cover and is designed to complement treatment available on the NHS. I 
therefore don’t require AIG to provide further explanation. 
what is a final decision?

A final decision by an ombudsman is our last word on a complaint. We send the final decision 
at the same time to both sides – the consumer and the financial business.  

Our complaints process involves various stages. It gives both parties to the complaint the 
opportunity to tell us their side of the story, provide further information, and disagree with 
our earlier findings – before the ombudsman reviews the case and makes a final decision. 

A final decision is the end of our complaints process. This means the ombudsman will not be 
able to deal with any further correspondence about the merits of the complaint. 
what happens next? 

A final decision only becomes legally binding on the financial business if the consumer 
accepts it. To do this, the consumer should sign and date the acceptance card we send with 
the final decision – and return it to us before the date set out in the decision. 

If the consumer accepts a final decision before the date set out in the decision we will tell the 
financial business – it will then have to comply promptly with any instructions set out by the 
ombudsman in the decision. 

If the consumer does not accept a final decision before the date set out in the decision, neither 
side will be legally bound by it.

text:
K820x#14
complaint
Mr S made a sickness claim under his income protection policy and is unhappy Ageas 
Insurance Limited (Ageas) won’t pay this. 
background
In August last year Mr S’s father sadly died. Because of this he was unable to work for some 
months. Sick notes from the time record the cause as “anxiety / depression”. In December 
Mr S made a phased return to work and took out an income protection policy. This started on 
10 December and covered him for accident, sickness and unemployment. The following 
month Mr S stopped working because he was affected by work related stress. He made a 
claim under his policy. 
Ageas said his policy excluded cover where accident and sickness occurred within 12 
months of the start date and was caused by a pre-existing condition. In this case although 
the medical information did refer to work related stress it also talked about “anxiety / 
depression”. So it thought the exclusion applied here and it turned down Mr S’s claim. 
Our investigator thought Mr S was suffering from anxiety / depression before he took the 
policy out and still had that when he made his claim. So he thought it was fair of Ageas to 
turn this down. Mr S doesn’t agree so I need to reach a final decision. 
my findings
I’ve considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint.
Mr S has clearly been through a really difficult time and I was very sorry to learn about the 
issues that have affected him. But I think it was fair for Ageas to turn down his claim. That’s 
because:

Under the ‘what is not covered’ section of the policy it says “accident and/or sickness 
which is caused by a pre-existing condition”. And it doesn’t seem to be in dispute Mr S 
had received treatment for anxiety / depression in the 12 months before the policy start 
date. Looking at the policy terms I think that meets the definition of a pre-existing 
condition;

So I need to think about whether Mr S couldn’t work from January onwards because of 
this condition (or something caused by it) or because of something else. I appreciate 
Mr S was initially off work because of a bereavement and his subsequent time off was 
due to work related stress. But the medical evidence suggests the underlying cause was 
“anxiety / depression” because sick notes from the earlier and later periods both make 
reference to this; 
Ref: DRN8649179

2

Mr S says there’s no reference to work related stress in his medical notes prior to 
January of this year. I think that’s right. But, as I’ve said, I think the underlying issue here 
is anxiety / depression – and this is referenced before and after January. I can also see 
that when Mr S spoke to his psychologist in April 2016 he said his problems at work had 
been ongoing for the last 12 months. But it doesn’t look like that caused him to have any 
time off prior to his bereavement. I think that also suggests that while work related stress 
may have been the trigger for his absence from January onwards the underlying cause 
was anxiety / depression; 

I can also see that when Mr S submitted his claim he included a report from his GP 
which referred to a moderate depressive episode (and linked this to work related stress). 
But in answer to a question about whether Mr S had suffered from this condition in the 
three years prior to this incident his GP referenced the stress and anxiety he’d previously 
been treated for. That suggests there was a link between these episodes rather than 
them being unrelated events. I think that’s supported by the relatively short period of time 
between Mr S’s phased return to work and his subsequent absence; 

Mr S has highlighted an exclusion in the policy terms which excludes cover in some 
circumstances for mental health conditions. I understand he believes this doesn’t apply 
in his case. I think that’s right – and Ageas has acknowledged this. But I think the key 
issue here is that it’s turned down his claim for other reasons. I think it’s acted fairly in 
doing so. 

Mr S has also suggested that the policy wasn’t properly explained to him when he took it 
out. But I understand the policy was sold by a broker and Ageas wouldn’t be responsible 
for what they said. It’s open to Mr S to raise this issue with the broker if he wants.
my final decision
I’ve decided not to uphold this complaint. Under the rules of the Financial Ombudsman 
Service, I’m required to ask Mr S to accept or reject my decision before 7 October 2016.
James Park
ombudsman

text:
K820x#11
complaint
Mr H has complained about ACE European Group Limited’s decision to decline his claims 
under his personal accident policy.
background
Mr H holds a personal accident policy which provides a lump sum for permanent disabling 
injuries and weekly payments for temporary total disablement.
He submitted a claim form to ACE in January 2012 disclosing a knee injury. He had also 
previously asked ACE to consider a claim for an injury to his back whilst at work. ACE 
declined the claim, as it had no evidence that Mr H’s injuries were a result of an accident, as 
defined in the policy.
Mr H did not agree and brought his complaint to us. The adjudicator who investigated his 
complaint did not recommend that his complaint should be upheld. He also concluded that 
there was no evidence Mr H’s injuries were as a result of an accident and that they were 
more likely to be due to pre-existing conditions. 
Mr H did not agree and asked for the case to be reviewed. The matter has therefore been 
passed to me to determine. As ACE has not had the opportunity to consider Mr H’s further 
claims in respect of hearing loss and cancer, I will not comment on these in this decision. 
Mr H has been advised to raise these concerns with ACE in the first instance. 
my findings
I have considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what is fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint. Mr H bought an ACE Business class 
Express, Directors Injury Insurance policy. In the schedule he opted for the following 
benefits:

Accidental Death for £250,000 benefit;

Permanent Total Disablement for ‘usual’ or ‘any’ occupation – not insured;

Permanent Disabling Injuries for ‘any injury’ and ‘specific injury’ for £250,000 benefit;

Temporary Total Disablement (per week) for a benefit of £500;

Temporary Partial Disablement (per week) – not insured.
This policy only pays benefit if its very specific criteria for a valid claim are met by Mr H. In 
order for any benefit to be payable to Mr H, he must satisfy these conditions entirely.  
For any injury to meet the policy conditions it must have occurred as a result of an accident. 
The relevant term in the policy booklet details that an accident is the following:
“Accident shall mean a sudden, external and identifiable event that happens by chance 
and could not have been expected.”
The accident in question must then cause a bodily injury and the policy defines bodily injury 
as follows:
“Bodily Injury shall mean injury which is caused solely by Accidental means and 
which independently of illness or any other cause results in the Insured Person’s 
death or disablement, within twenty-four calendar months from the date of the 
Accident.”
Ref: DRN9050769

2
As Mr H is also claiming that he is disabled, he must satisfy the following conditions:
‘Permanent Disabling Injury shall mean disablement which has lasted for at least 12 
months and which in ACE’s opinion is beyond hope of recovery and will in all probability 
continue for the remainder of the Insured Person’s life.’
Also relevant is the following:
Temporary Total Disablement shall mean temporary disablement which entirely 
prevents the Insured Person from engaging in their usual occupation.’
Mr H made a claim in January 2012 stating that he hit his knee against a computer desk and 
damaged his knee cap. Prior to this in October 2011, he also made a claim for his back.
Unfortunately Mr H’s medical notes and records do not record that he sustained any 
accident to his back. Indeed in November 2011 his medical notes state he has long standing 
back pain. The notes at this time also record that there has been no recent change in his 
back pain.
Further in January 2012 his medical notes confirm that his knee pain is as a result of 
osteoarthritis and his notes do not mention he sustained any accidental injury or record that 
any accident occurred.
As I result whilst I do not doubt Mr H has various problems with his knee and back, I find that 
ACE correctly assessed Mr H’s claims by examining his medical notes and records and I find 
that Mr H’s claims do not meet the relevant policy definitions in order that benefit is payable 
for these conditions under this policy.
my final decision
For the reasons above it is my final decision that I do not uphold the complaint and I make 
no award against ACE European Group Limited.
Rona Doyle
ombudsman
Ref: DRN9050769

Bodily Injury shall mean injury which is caused solely by Accidental means and which independently of illness or any other cause results in the Insured Person’s death or disablement, within twenty-four calendar months from the date of the Accident.

Permanent Disabling Injury shall mean disablement which has lasted for at least 12 months and which in ACE’s opinion is beyond hope of recovery and will in all probability continue for the remainder of the Insured Person’s life.

text:
K821x#15
complaint
Mr G complains that Vitality Health Limited refused his private medical insurance claim.
background
Mr G had cover through his employer with an insurer (that I’ll call ‘Insurer A’). Insurer A 
applied the following exclusion for Mr G:
“Benefits will not be payable for any investigation or treatment arising from; Any disease or 
disorder of the cervical and thoracic spine, its intervertebral discs, facet joints, spinal cord,
nerve roots, supporting musculature and ligaments."
His employer then changed to a new insurer (that I’ll call ‘Insurer B’) on a Continued 
Personal Medical Exclusions (CPME) basis. In other words, any existing exclusions would 
be transferred to the new insurer. Insurer B transferred across Mr G’s exclusion but worded 
it differently. The new exclusion said:
“No benefit is payable for any investigations and treatment related to your spinal trouble.”
In December 2016, Mr G’s employer again changed insurer, this time to Vitality (again on a 
CPME basis). Vitality transferred across a similar exclusion for Mr G that said:
“No benefit is payable under this plan for any further investigations or treatment due to spinal 
trouble and related conditions”
In January 2017, Mr G made a claim as he’d been experiencing back and leg pain. Vitality 
thought his claim fell under the exclusion so it turned it down. Mr G didn’t agree but Vitality 
maintained its position. Mr G arranged a private consultation himself in March 2017 and was 
told to obtain a GP referral so he could see a specialist on the NHS. He did this, and 
following an NHS consultation in May 2017 he had an MRI scan and surgery was carried out 
on 5 June 2017 under the NHS. Unhappy with Vitality’s refusal of his claim, Mr G brought a 
complaint to this service. 
Our investigator recommended the complaint be upheld. He said the original exclusion 
hadn’t included the lumbar spine, and so Vitality had been wrong to turn down the claim. He 
thought Mr G had been in a significant amount of pain for a long time as a result of Vitality’s 
wrong claims decision. He also thought that if Mr G had had treatment sooner then he would 
have needed a less invasive procedure with a shorter recovery time. The investigator 
recommended Vitality pay £5,000 compensation. He also thought Vitality should reimburse 
Mr G for any costs he incurred from private consultations he’d paid for himself, plus interest. 
I issued a provisional decision on 10 November 2017. My provisional findings said:
“Mr G’s claim was for lumbar canal stenosis at L4-5. This affected the lumbar spine rather 
than the cervical and thoracic spine. I therefore agree with the investigator that this didn’t fall 
under the original exclusion wording with Insurer A, which should have transferred to 
Insurer B and then Vitality. 
Insurer B confirmed to our investigator that it applied the exclusion it did because it didn’t 
have the wording to match the previous exclusion that had been applied by Insurer A. It 
explained that when it uses the word ‘your’ in an exclusion, this will always be specific to 
Ref: DRN9199887

2
something rather than a broad exclusion. It confirmed its exclusion didn’t affect any claims 
relating to the lower spine, which is why a previous claim made by Mr G relating to his 
lumbar spine in 2016 was accepted. 
Whilst Vitality wasn’t responsible for the exclusion wording that Insurer B applied, it seems to 
me that Vitality’s removal of the word ‘your’ when it took over the cover changed the 
meaning of the exclusion. This meant that the exclusion became a broad exclusion for any 
spinal trouble rather than specifically for the spinal trouble Mr G had previously experienced 
(ie related to his cervical and thoracic spine).  
I see that on 1 March 2017, Vitality became aware of the different exclusions that had been 
applied by Insurer A and Insurer B. Insurer B had told Vitality that although the wording of 
the exclusion it had applied to Mr G’s cover differed slightly from that of Insurer A, it thought 
the meaning remained the same. I think Vitality should have changed its exclusion wording 
at this time to the original applied by Insurer A and accepted Mr G’s claim.
Mr G didn’t have his surgery until 5 June 2017. That means his treatment was delayed as a 
result of Vitality slightly changing his exclusion, and then continuing to refuse the claim even 
when it became aware of the different wordings. I agree Mr G should be paid compensation 
for this, but I disagree with the investigator’s recommendation that Vitality pay £5,000. I say 
that because I haven’t seen any evidence that if Mr G had received treatment earlier he 
would have needed a less invasive procedure with a shorter recovery time. An MRI scan 
wasn’t carried out at Mr G’s March 2017 consultation so the specialist couldn’t have known 
what treatment was needed until this took place. Once the MRI scan was done in May 2017, 
surgery was booked soon after. 
Having said that, Mr G has explained the amount he was pain in, and I’ve also seen the 
emails he wrote to his specialist at the time which confirm this. It’s apparent that Mr G was in 
a lot of pain whilst he was waiting for his surgery. When I’m considering compensation to 
award for pain and suffering, I take into account the amount of pain someone was in but I 
also need to consider how their daily activities were impacted. I see that Mr G was able to 
continue to work, though I understand he wasn’t able to travel as much as he usually would 
for work. Taking this into consideration, I think fair compensation would be £2,000.
 
As Mr G’s claim was payable but he instead had treatment in an NHS hospital, he was 
denied the comforts of private accommodation. I think Vitality should pay Mr G the daily rate 
for a private bed for the number of nights he spent in an NHS hospital. I also think it should 
reimburse him for the private consultation he paid for in March 2017, plus interest.” 
I asked both parties for any further comments they wished to make. Neither party had any 
substantial comments to make about my provisional findings, however Mr G did want to 
know how Vitality would work out the cost of a private bed. 
my findings
I’ve reconsidered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint. Having done so, I see no reason to 
change my decision given that neither party had any substantial comments about my 
provisional findings. 
However, Mr G did want to know how Vitality would work out the cost of a private bed. 
Ref: DRN9199887

3
To confirm, I’d expect Vitality to pay the sum it would have incurred for accommodation at 
the private hospital where Mr G would have most likely undergone the treatment. Therefore, 
if Mr G would have received treatment at a particular private hospital because that’s where 
his treating consultant worked, then I’d expect Vitality to pay the rates charged for 
accommodation at that hospital. If Mr G doesn’t know where he would have had the 
treatment if his claim had been accepted, then I’d expect Vitality to pay the rates charged for 
accommodation at a private hospital local to him. 
my final decision
My final decision is that I uphold this complaint and require Vitality Health Limited to do the 
following:
-
pay Mr G compensation equivalent to the amount it would have paid for a private 
bed, multiplied by the number of nights Mr G spent in an NHS hospital; 
-
pay Mr G additional compensation of £2,000;
-
reimburse Mr G for the cost of his March 2017 private consultation. *Interest should 
be added at the rate of 8% simple per annum from the date the invoice was paid to 
the date of settlement; and
-
change the exclusion wording to the original applied by Insurer A.
*If Vitality considers that it’s required by HM Revenue & Customs to take off income tax from 
the interest, it should tell Mr G how much it’s taken off. It should also give Mr G a certificate 
showing this if he asks for one, so he can reclaim the tax from HM Revenue & Customs if 
appropriate. 
Under the rules of the Financial Ombudsman Service, I’m required to ask Mr G to accept or 
reject my decision before 2 January 2018.
 
Chantelle Hurn-Ryan
ombudsman

text:
K820x#14
complaint
Mr W complains about the sale of his Income Insurance policy by Barclays Bank Plc.
background
In 2010, Mr W took out the policy. This provided a monthly benefit in the event he wasn’t 
able to work because of accident, sickness or unemployment. 
In 2016, Mr W complained about the sale of the policy. He thought he’d taken out the policy 
at the same time as a loan. He said he wasn’t told how the policy worked, or how much it 
would cost. He thought a pre-existing condition meant the policy hadn’t been suitable for 
him. Also, he was unhappy that his policy continued after his loan had been paid off. 
Our investigator recommended the complaint be upheld. She noted Mr W had taken out a 
standalone policy, therefore it wasn’t linked to a loan. But she accepted he had a pre-
existing condition which may have affected his ability to make a claim. She didn’t think 
Barclays had shown that the pre-existing condition exclusion had been brought to Mr W’s 
attention. She therefore recommended it refund the premiums Mr W had paid, plus interest. 
I issued a provisional decision on 4 December 2017. My provisional findings were:
“Mr W took out the policy at a branch in November 2010. Barclays has explained the policy 
was sold on a non-advised basis, so it didn’t give Mr W any advice about the suitability of the 
policy. 
There isn’t much information available from the time of sale, but that isn’t surprising given 
the policy was taken out over seven years ago. There is a brief record of a customer 
discussion which has been recorded on Barclays’ computer system. This says Mr W wanted 
to review his protection needs and would have a quote for the Income Insurance policy as 
well as life cover. 
As I understand it, in 2009 Mr W had taken out a loan through Barclays with payment 
protection insurance (PPI). He says he wasn’t happy with the cost of the PPI, and this was 
only reduced when he queried this in a branch in 2010. Mr W’s PPI policy was cancelled the 
day he visited the branch in November 2010 and took out the Income Insurance policy. 
It therefore seems that Mr W visited the branch because he was unhappy about the cost of 
his PPI cover, and the adviser in the branch gave him a quote for the Income Insurance 
cover. This was cheaper than what Mr W had been paying for his PPI, but provided the 
same cover (yet it wasn’t linked to his loan). 
I can’t be sure what information Mr W was given about the policy when he was given the 
quote. However, I see Mr W agreed to take out the policy. Barclays then sent him a copy of 
his policy document, together with the policy schedule. 
I’m satisfied these documents made it clear what the policy covered and how much it would 
cost. There was no mention of it being linked to Mr W’s loan. As it was a standalone policy, it 
continued after Mr W had paid off his loan. 
Ref: DRN9313956

2
Mr W says he had a pre-existing condition of depression, and he doesn’t think the policy was 
suitable for him, as he wouldn’t have been able to make a successful claim if he stopped 
work because of depression. 
The policy contains the following exclusion:
“Accident and sickness in any of the following circumstances:

If it is caused by a pre-existing medical condition i.e. any condition, injury, illness, 
disease or sickness for which you had symptoms, consulted a doctor/consultant or 
received treatment or medication during the 12 months immediately before the start 
date.
This exclusion will not apply if at the time of a claim, you have not had any symptoms 
or consulted a doctor/consultant or received treatment in the two years before the 
claim.”
Mr W has shown that he was taking anti-depressant medication when the policy was taken 
out, and that he continued taking this until January 2013. 
I therefore accept that when Mr W took out the policy, he had a pre-existing condition. But 
that doesn’t necessarily mean the policy wasn’t suitable for him. I say that because if he 
stopped work because of an accident or a medical condition (other than depression), the 
policy would have responded. Also, even if a claim were made for depression, this would 
only be refused if he continued to experience symptoms or receive treatment in the two 
years before a claim was made. Furthermore, a valid claim for unemployment would have 
been paid.
However, the issue for me to consider is whether or not Barclays told Mr W about the 
exclusion. The policy was sold on a non-advised basis which means Barclays didn’t give 
Mr W any advice about the suitability of the cover. It would have been up to Mr W to decide 
whether or not the policy was suitable for him. But Barclays was still obliged to provide Mr W 
with information about the policy, including significant exclusions such as the one above. 
The difficulty with this case is that there isn’t much information from the time of sale, so I 
can’t determine what Mr W was told about the policy or the exclusion. However, I see that 
Barclays did send Mr W an annual review of his policy. I’ve seen the 2012 annual review 
letter, and I’ve also seen another letter sent to Mr W in 2012 about an increase to his 
monthly premium. Both of those letters gave a summary of the policy’s key benefits and 
exclusions, and included the pre-existing condition exclusion I’ve referred to above.
On balance, whilst I can’t be sure that Mr W was told of the relevant exclusion before he 
agreed to take out the policy, I see that this was brought to his attention in 2012. If Mr W 
thought this exclusion meant the policy hadn’t been suitable for him, I’d have expected him 
to have brought this to Barclays’ attention at the time. However, he didn’t make a complaint 
until 2016 and continued paying for the cover until 2017. That suggests to me that despite 
the exclusion, he still wanted the cover. 
I therefore don’t find that the policy was mis-sold.”
I asked both parties to provide me with any further comments they wished to make. 
Ref: DRN9313956

3
Barclays confirmed it didn’t have anything further to add. 
Mr W responded and made the following points:

he didn’t go into the branch to complain about the cost of his PPI. He says he was 
quoted a lower monthly amount but it wasn’t explained to him that it was a completely 
different product to PPI and wasn’t linked to his loan. 

if he’d understood he was being sold a policy that only protected the cost of his loan 
and not his monthly income, he wouldn’t have taken it out. 

his pre-existing medical condition meant the policy was mis-sold to him.
my findings
I’ve reconsidered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint. 
Mr W says he didn’t go into the branch to complain about the cost of his PPI cover. Although 
he was quoted a lower monthly amount for the Income Insurance cover, he says it wasn’t 
explained to him that it wasn’t PPI and was a standalone product. 
When Mr W brought his complaint to this service, he explained that he decided to take out 
the earlier PPI policy because he wanted unemployment cover in case he lost his job and 
couldn’t keep up his loan repayments. He further explains that he wasn’t happy with the 
amount he was paying for his PPI (he says this was £32.65 per month) and this was only 
reduced when he visited the branch in 2010.
I don’t for certain what happened. But given that Mr W’s PPI policy was cancelled the day he 
went into the branch and took out the Income Insurance cover, it does seem likely that he 
told staff at the branch he wasn’t happy with the amount he was paying for his PPI. A quote 
was carried out for the Income Insurance policy, which provided him with the same benefit 
amount that he’d had under his PPI policy and gave him the same cover – the only 
differences being that it was cheaper and wasn’t linked to his loan. 
I can’t be sure that Mr W was told in the branch that his policy wasn’t linked to his loan. But 
the documents I’ve seen don’t mention anything about being linked to a loan. Instead, they 
make it clear that the policy could be cancelled at any time. 
As the policy was sold on a non-advised basis, it would have been up to Mr W whether or 
not he took it out. Mr W says if he’d understood the policy protected his loan amount rather 
than his monthly income, he wouldn’t have taken it out. But the policy schedule made it clear 
how much benefit the policy provided.  
Mr W again says that he thinks his pre-existing medical condition meant the policy was mis-
sold to him. I’ve already addressed this in my provisional decision, and Mr W hasn’t provided 
me with any new information or evidence that I need to consider. So I remain satisfied the 
policy wasn’t mis-sold to Mr W, and for the same reasons that I’ve explained in my 
provisional decision. 
my final decision
My final decision is that I don’t uphold this complaint.
Ref: DRN9313956

4
Under the rules of the Financial Ombudsman Service, I’m required to ask Mr W to accept or 
reject my decision before 22 January 2018.
Chantelle Hurn-Ryan
ombudsman

This exclusion will not apply if at the time of a claim, you have not had any symptoms or consulted a doctor/consultant or received treatment in the two years before the claim.

text:
K822x
complaint
Mr W has complained about Friends Life Limited’s decision to limit the amount it paid in 
respect of a claim he made under his employer’s group critical illness insurance scheme.
background 
Mr W joined his employer’s group critical illness insurance scheme in September 2001. In 
2011 Mr W made a claim under the policy, having been diagnosed with Rheumatoid Arthritis. 
But this was turned down as Mr W didn’t meet the policy definition. In June 2012, Mr W 
chose to increase his benefit from £125,000 to £200,000.
Mr W’s condition worsened and he made another claim in 2013. The claim was accepted, 
but Friends Life said that only £125,000 would be paid. This was because policy exclusions 
applied to the extra benefit he’d taken in 2012, specifically the pre-existing medical condition 
and associated conditions exclusion.
Mr W was unhappy with the decision. He said he didn’t have a pre-existing medical condition 
as per the policy terms he’d seen. He also didn’t think he could be said to be suffering from 
an associated condition as he was claiming for the same illness in 2013 as he had in 2011. 
Mr W also complained about some service issues, including a cheque issued with the wrong 
amount and the mishandling of his subject access request.
Friends Life apologised for the poor service but didn’t change its decision regarding the 
amount paid to him in settlement of his claim. So, Mr W brought his complaint here.
Our adjudicator thought Mr W’s complaint should be partly upheld. She thought Friends Life 
had applied the terms of the policy fairly and so agreed that the right amount had been paid 
to Mr W. But the adjudicator felt that Friends Life had made some mistakes when handling 
the complaint, so she recommended that it pay Mr W £250 for the trouble and upset it had 
caused. Friends Life agreed to settle the complaint as per the adjudicator’s recommendation. 
Mr W didn’t agree with the adjudicator’s opinion. He didn’t think the exclusions, read literally, 
could be applied to the circumstances of his claim. The adjudicator maintained her view of 
the complaint so Mr W asked for an ombudsman to make a final decision.
my findings
I’ve considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint. Having done so, I think this complaint 
should be upheld in part for much the same reasons as the adjudicator has given.
In order to work out whether Friends Life’s decision was fair, I’ve looked at the full policy 
terms and conditions that were applicable to Mr W’s claim. In the ‘Exclusions’ section, it 
says:
‘Friends Life will not be liable for any claim for member benefit or child benefit which directly 
or indirectly in whole or in part arises out of or relates to a pre-existing condition. A pre-
existing condition for a member is any critical illness or operation covered by the policy 
which the member has suffered or undergone at any time prior to the member's cover start 
date...’
Ref: DRN9444262

2
It also says:
‘Friends Life will not be liable for any claim for member benefit for any member, or child 
benefit for any child, for any critical illness or operation in respect of which any associated 
condition existed (whether diagnosed or not) at any time prior to the cover start date.’
In order to understand the full effect of these exclusions, I’ve referred to the ‘Definitions’ 
section at the beginning of the terms and conditions document.
It says that in respect of an increase in member benefit, the ‘cover start date’ is the ‘date on 
which that increase takes effect’. So, this means that both the pre-existing medical condition 
exclusion and the associated condition exclusion would apply to the extra £75,000 Mr W 
took in June 2012.
A ‘pre-existing condition’ is defined as ‘any critical illness or operation covered by the policy 
which that member has suffered or undergone at any time prior to the member's cover start 
date.’ Mr W says that this doesn’t apply to him, as by Friends Life’s own admission, he 
wasn’t suffering from a critical illness in 2011 because he didn’t meet the policy definition. 
I agree with Mr W that if read literally, the exclusion doesn’t apply to his circumstances.
But an ‘associated condition’ is defined as ‘any medical condition, which is…in the 
reasonable opinion of Friends Life's chief medical officer directly or indirectly linked with, or 
is likely to have led to the occurrence of a critical illness or operation…’ 
It’s not in dispute that Mr W had Rheumatoid Arthritis before he increased his benefit in 
2012. So, I think it falls within the definition of an associated condition because it has led to 
the occurrence of a critical illness, as defined within the terms. Because of this, I think it was 
reasonable for Friends Life to apply this exclusion to Mr W’s claim, and limit his payment to 
£125,000.
I appreciate that Mr W would’ve received several different documents explaining how his 
cover worked. And I think that some of the documents could’ve been clearer in explaining 
this point. It also seems that Mr W hadn’t seen a copy of the full policy terms. But Mr W’s 
employer was responsible for making these documents available to Mr W. And, when the 
documents are read as a whole, I think it’s clear how the exclusions affect increases made to 
the benefit.
I understand Mr W experienced some service issues when he claimed and when he 
complained. The adjudicator explained that complaints about how a business has dealt with 
a subject access request are handled by the Information Commissioner’s Office. But she 
recommended that Mr W should receive £250 for the trouble and upset caused by the other 
issues. Friends Life agreed. Like the adjudicator, I think this sum represents fair 
compensation for the issues Mr W experienced. So, I think it should be accepted in full and 
final settlement of this complaint.
Ref: DRN9444262

3
my final decision
For the reasons set out above, I uphold Mr W’s complaint in part.
Friends Life Limited should pay Mr W £250 for the service issues he experienced.
Under the rules of the Financial Ombudsman Service, I’m required to ask Mr W to accept or 
reject my decision before 17 December 2015. 
Hannah Wise
ombudsman

text:
K821x#9
complaint
Mr G has complained about the sale of an accident, sickness and unemployment (“ASU”) 
policy purchased through PMI Partners, a trading name of Assured Futures Limited.
background
In 2010 Mr G made two online applications for ASU insurance – one to cover a percentage 
of his income and the other to cover his mortgage. However, as the cover that Mr G wanted 
was higher than the benefit levels available to him under the two policies, he was contacted 
by PMI Partners by telephone about his application. As a result of the discussion, Mr G took 
out an ASU policy which provided a monthly benefit of 90% of his net salary, subject to him 
having regular monthly bills of this amount. 
In 2011 Mr G attempted to claim under the policy after suffering an accident which prevented 
him from working. The claim was declined by the underwriters of the policy, as Mr G had not 
been prevented from working for more than 60 days and as such, did not satisfy the policy 
waiting period. Mr G made a complaint to PMI Partners as he was under the impression he 
had taken out a policy with a 30 day excess, which he understood to mean that he would 
receive benefit after 30 days of being unable to work. He also complained that he had been 
sold a policy where he had to demonstrate his monthly commitments if he wanted to claim, 
but said he had required a standard income protection policy.
PMI Partners did not uphold the complaint. It explained that Mr G had taken out a policy with 
a 30 day excess which included a 60 day waiting period. It felt this was adequately explained 
within the policy summary that Mr G was required to read online before initially selecting the 
cover. PMI Partners said that Mr G had agreed to take out the commitments based policy 
after being told that he could achieve a greater level of cover than the two separate policies 
he had initially wanted. Mr G remained unhappy so he referred a complaint to this service.
Our adjudicator considered the complaint should be upheld in part. She was persuaded that 
Mr G had wanted the higher level of cover the commitments-based policy provided, but was 
not satisfied that the policy excess and waiting periods had been adequately explained to 
him. The adjudicator recommended that PMI Partners liaise with the policy underwriter to 
establish whether Mr G’s claim would have been payable if he had been provided with ‘back 
to day one’ cover, as this had a waiting period of 30 days. If the claim was payable, the 
adjudicator recommended that PMI Partners should pay compensation equivalent to the 
benefit owing plus interest. Neither Mr G nor PMI Partners agreed so the matter has been 
passed to me to consider afresh.
my findings
I have considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what is fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint. Having done so, I uphold this complaint in 
part for largely the same reasons as the adjudicator.
PMI Partners believes that the meaning of the excess and waiting periods were adequately 
described within the policy summary document, which it says Mr G was required to read 
when he initially made his online application. I therefore assume that one of Mr G’s online 
applications was for the commitments-based ASU policy (which Mr G refers to as ‘income 
Ref: DRN9457601

2
protection’). Having reviewed the policy summary, there is no explanation as to the 
difference between the excess and the waiting period. I would therefore not have expected 
Mr G to know that by selecting a 30 day excess, he would have to be off work for 60 days 
before being eligible to make a claim under the policy.
In any event, after Mr G made his online applications, he spoke to a PMI Partners 
representative over the telephone, and I consider it reasonable for him to rely on the 
information given to him at this time. PMI Partners asserts that Mr G’s policy was sold on a 
non-advised basis and as such, it does not accept that Mr G was given any advice by its 
representative over the telephone. When a sale is non-advised, a business is required under 
the Insurance Conduct of Business Sourcebook (‘ICOBS’) to provide customers with 
sufficient information about the product, so that they are able to make an informed decision 
as to whether it meets their demands and needs. Therefore, even though this was a non-
advised sale, I need to consider whether the information given by the representative over the 
telephone allowed Mr G to make an informed choice about the particulars of his policy.
Having listened to the telephone call, I am not satisfied that it was made clear to Mr G how 
the policy excess operated. Moreover, there was no mention of the excess being subject to 
an additional waiting period. The representative asked Mr G if he was looking at a 30 day 
excess and he replied that he was. The representative then stated:
“30 day excess just means supporting yourself for the first month and then the policy would 
pay out in the second month for you.”
Mr G said that he understood this to mean he would receive benefit after 30 days and I do 
not think this is an unreasonable interpretation of what he was told. Certainly, he was not 
made aware that he would not receive any benefit unless he had been unable to work for 
more than 60 days. I understand that after finding out he could not make a claim in 2011 
because of the 60 day waiting period, Mr G amended his policy so that he had ‘back to day 
one’ cover, which had a waiting period of 30 days. To my mind, this further demonstrates 
that Mr G had always intended to take out ‘back to day one’ cover.
In light of the above, I consider that the policy was mis-sold in this regard. I agree with the 
adjudicator’s recommendation that PMI Partners should ascertain whether Mr G’s claim in 
2011 would have been payable if he had been provided with ‘back to day one’ cover from 
the outset. I further agree that if the claim would have been payable, PMI Partners should 
pay compensation equivalent to the benefit amount that would have been paid.
Mr G has objected to the adjudicator’s opinion that he wanted the regular commitments-
based policy. Mr G says that he asked for an income protection policy but after attempting to 
claim, he was told that he would need to provide evidence of his commitments. Mr G says 
that he did not want this type of policy and was unaware that he would need to evidence his 
commitments if he needed to claim. 
Having listened to the sales call, it was explained to Mr G that if he wished to proceed with 
the two policies he had selected online, the maximum cover he could obtain was 50% of his 
gross income. Alternatively, he was told that if he took out the commitments based policy on 
its own, he could cover 90% of his net income – so long as he had regular monthly bills of 
this amount. Mr G was happy to proceed on this basis so that he could achieve a higher 
level of cover. Mr G confirmed he had regular monthly commitments that were greater than 
90% of his net income. The representative made Mr G aware that he should contact the 
Ref: DRN9457601

3
policy provider if any of his commitments changed. I further note that the policy summary 
stated:
‘If you have a claim you will be required to prove the amounts of all of the commitments you 
have covered. Any claim payment will be limited to the value of commitments you can prove 
you normally pay…’
In light of this evidence, I am satisfied that Mr G was made aware that the policy only 
provided the benefit level of 90% of his net income if he had regular monthly commitments of 
this amount, and he was happy to take out the policy on this basis. I am therefore unable to 
uphold this aspect of Mr G’s complaint.
my final decision
For the reasons set out above I uphold this complaint in part. I require Assured Futures 
Limited to liaise with the policy underwriter to establish whether Mr G’s claim in 2011 would 
have been payable if he had been provided with ‘back to day one’ cover. If the claim was 
otherwise payable, I require Assured Futures Limited to pay compensation equivalent to the 
benefit that would have been paid to Mr G if he had had this cover.
i
Chantelle Hurn
ombudsman
i 
Ref: DRN9457601

If you have a claim you will be required to prove the amounts of all of the commitments you have covered. Any claim payment will be limited to the value of commitments you can prove you normally pay…

text:
K821x#14
complaint
This complaint concerns B.I.B. Underwriters Limited’s decision to decline a claim by Mr O
under his BIB Underwriters Farm & State plan.
background
The background to this complaint was set out in my provisional decision dated 11 May 2015, 
a copy of which is attached and which forms part of this final decision.
In summary, I was not provisionally minded to conclude that Mr O’s claim under the policy 
succeeded. B.I.B Underwriters Limited accepted the provisional decision. Mr O disagreed 
and submitted further evidence.
Mr O believes he responded to the medical questions in good faith. In his view the relevant 
question is unclear. To illustrate this point he has provided a copy of another businesses 
proposal form. Mr O also submitted medical evidence in support of his argument that he was 
unaware of the fracture until diagnosed by the consultant trauma and hand surgeon. 
my findings
I have reconsidered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what is fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint. Having done so I see no reason to 
change my provisional findings. 
I agree with Mr O that the question asked in April 2012 is widely phrased. I do not find that 
he deliberately answered the question incorrectly.
However, although I can accept that Mr O was not aware that he had a fracture until he was 
told some months after the fall - this evidence was contained in the business file - it is clear 
from the medical evidence that he had been getting pain in his wrist for five years. I 
understand that Mr O has had similar cover for many years and feels that his claim should 
be met. The issue here though is that the policy under which he is claiming only started in 
April 2012. At that time the evidence indicates he was already suffering from a problem with 
his wrist.
my final decision
For the reasons given in my provisional decision and above, my final decision is that I do not 
uphold this complaint. I make no award against B.I.B. Underwriters Limited.
Under the rules of the Financial Ombudsman Service, I am required to ask Mr O to accept or 
reject my decision before 15 July 2015.
Lindsey Woloski
Ombudsman
Ref: DRN9494420

2
COPY OF PROVISIONAL DECISION
complaint
This complaint concerns B.I.B. Underwriters Limited’s decision to decline a claim by Mr O under his 
BIB Underwriters Farm & State plan. 
background
Mr O applied for the policy in April 2012 and cover started in the same month. His policy included 
personal accident and sickness benefits. It specifically covered temporary total and temporary partial 
disablement if the insured person was prevented from undertaking a substantial part of their usual 
occupation.
Ref: DRN9494420

3
In December 2012 Mr O submitted a claim under the policy’s personal accident provision. He said 
that he had slipped over in June 2012, had noticed some pain but ‘strapped hand up and carried on’ 
but that he had now been told to have an operation.
B.I.B. Underwriters reviewed the claim but said that there were discrepancies between this and what 
he had disclosed on the application form. It said that Mr O had visited his surgery over a period of 5 
years with complaints of wrist joint pain. It felt that these should have been disclosed by Mr O when 
he applied for the policy. It said that if it had been aware of the true nature of his wrist problem, it 
would have excluded any problems associated with his wrist from cover.
Mr O did not agree with this decision and referred the matter here. Our adjudicator considered the 
complaint and concluded Mr O’s  response to the question on the application form was made honestly 
and in good faith. He felt that Mr O had a valid claim. He recommended that B.I.B. Underwriters 
assessed it and made a proportionate settlement taking into account Mr O’s pre-existing condition.
B.I.B. Underwriters Ltd disagreed with the adjudicator’s conclusions. In its opinion the medical 
evidence suggested that the operation Mr O had in December 2012 was to fuse an old un-united 
fracture of the scaphoid and not following any accident he may have suffered in June 2012.
As no agreement has been reached, the matter has therefore been passed to me to consider afresh.
my findings
I have considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what is fair and reasonable in 
the circumstances of this complaint.
When Mr O applied for the policy In April 2012 he was asked the following question:
“Are all persons proposed for Personal Accident Insurance in good health, not had or do not have any 
physical or mental defect or infirmity?”
Mr O answered ‘yes’ to this question. It is clear from the medical evidence that Mr O had a history of 
wrist joint pain. I won’t summarise all the evidence, but Mr O went to see Dr H, a consultant trauma 
and hand surgeon, in July 2012. Dr H reported that Mr O had been getting increasing pain in his non-
dominant wrist for the past five years. He said that Mr O could not recall any injury but that he worked 
on a farm which was a demanding job. His GP also wrote in July 2013 that Mr O had started getting 
pain and symptoms in his wrist in the last five to six years. So I think it is fair to say that Mr O did have 
a wrist condition that was in existence before the policy started.
Nevertheless I find that the application question was widely phrased and I don’t consider that Mr O’s 
answer was deliberately misleading. I think that the answer was inaccurate, but I accept that Mr O did 
not consider he had a physical infirmity that he needed to disclose.
That said, Mr O’s policy does not cover pre-existing conditions. I think that the policy is clear about 
that. The medical evidence shows that Mr O had an underlying condition and that any injury in June 
2012 simply aggravated this. I don’t think Mr O could have formed the impression from his policy that 
a claim would be payable in these circumstances. I recognise he will be disappointed by my decision 
but I don’t presently think that B.I.B. Underwriters treated Mr O unfairly by not paying his claim.
my provisional decision
My provisional decision is that I don’t uphold this complaint. 
Lindsey Woloski
ombudsman
Ref: DRN9494420

4
Ref: DRN9494420
