text:
K820x#14
complaint
Ms M (via her representative) complains that Zurich Assurance Ltd mis-sold three insurance 
policies. 
background
In 1996, Zurich sold Ms M an income protection policy. The aim of this policy was to pay 
monthly benefit after a waiting period of 12 months if she couldn’t work because of accident 
or illness. The policy lapsed in 1999.
In 2002, Zurich sold Ms M a whole of life policy. The aim of this policy was to pay a lump 
sum in the event of her death. The policy lapsed in 2003. 
In 2003, Zurich sold Ms M a life and critical illness policy. The aim of this policy was to pay a 
lump sum if she died or was diagnosed with a listed critical illness. The policy lapsed in 
2004.
In August 2014, Ms M complained to Zurich about the sale of all three policies. Zurich didn’t 
uphold the complaint and issued its final response on 2 October 2014. 
Ms M initially brought her complaint to this service on 26 March 2015. She didn’t proceed 
with the complaint at that time, but came back to us in January 2017. 
Zurich objected to this service considering Ms M’s complaint. It thought her complaint had 
been brought outside our time limits. 
Our adjudicator noted that Ms M’s complaint was about the affordability of the policies, as 
well as the suitability. He thought Ms M would have known the policies weren’t affordable for 
her before they lapsed. Because of that, he concluded that her concerns about affordability 
fell outside our time limits. 
However, he thought we could consider Ms M’s concerns about suitability, as she didn’t 
know she had cause for complaint about this until 2014. After doing so, he found that the 
policies were suitable and hadn’t been mis-sold. 
Ms M didn’t agree with our adjudicator’s findings, so the matter has been passed to me to 
consider. 
my findings
Our rules (the DISP Rules of the Financial Conduct Authority Handbook, which is available 
online) set out the complaints we can consider.
DISP rule 2.8.2R says:
“The Ombudsman cannot consider a complaint if the complainant refers it to the Financial 
Ombudsman Service: 
…
(2) more than: 
(a) six years after the event complained of; or (if later)
Ref: DRN9691306

2
(b) three years from the date on which the complainant became aware (or 
ought reasonably to have become aware) that he had cause for complaint…”
The event complained about is the sale of the policies. Ms M brought her complaint here 
more than six years after the dates all three policies had been sold. 
I therefore need to consider when Ms M ought reasonably to have become aware she had 
cause for complaint. 
Ms M’s representative has explained that all three policies lapsed because Ms M couldn’t 
afford them. As such, I think Ms M ought reasonably to have known that the policies hadn’t 
been affordable for her sometime between the dates they were sold, and the dates they 
lapsed. As her complaint was brought here more than three years after the dates all three 
policies lapsed, I agree with the adjudicator that we can’t consider Ms M’s concerns about 
affordability, as this aspect of her complaint falls outside our time limits.  
Our rules do allow us to waive the time limits in exceptional circumstances. Ms M’s 
representative says she only knew she couldn’t afford to pay the premiums, and didn’t 
realise she shouldn’t have been sold the policies in the first place because they were 
unaffordable. 
I think that if someone is sold an insurance policy they can’t afford to pay for, it’s not 
unreasonable to expect them to realise that perhaps they shouldn’t have been sold the 
policy. So I don’t think exceptional circumstances prevented Ms M from bringing her 
complaint to this service (or our predecessor scheme) within the relevant time limits. 
Ms M has also complained about the suitability of the policies. It seems she didn’t think the 
policies may not have been suitable for her until she received advice from her representative 
about this in 2014. As her complaint was referred here within three years of that date, I’m 
satisfied that this aspect of her complaint falls within our time limits. I’ll therefore consider the 
suitability of each policy in turn (without considering whether or not the policies were 
affordable for her). 
income protection policy
Ms M was employed and was entitled to six months sick pay from her employer. She was 
sold a policy that provided benefit within the policy’s maximum limit after a 12 month waiting 
period. Her representative thinks the waiting period should have been shorter. 
I agree with Ms M’s representative that ideally, the waiting period would have coincided with 
the end of Ms M’s sick pay arrangements. However, I see the fact-find says the policy was 
budget driven and so Ms M wanted to take out a 12 month waiting period, rather than six 
months. 
As the adjudicator has explained, the shorter the deferred period, the higher the cost of the 
policy. Therefore, whilst I appreciate the 12 month waiting period wasn’t ideal, I think it was 
probably better for Ms M to have some income protection cover in the event of long-term 
sickness, than none at all.
Ref: DRN9691306

3
whole of life policy
In 2002, Ms M met with a Zurich adviser. He noted in his recommendations letter (which was 
sent to Ms M) that her objective was to protect her family if she died. He said that her life 
assurance need, after taking her existing arrangements into account, was £103,000.
The adviser recommended a whole of life policy that provided an initial lump sum benefit of 
£103,000. He explained to Ms M that he recommended she take out the indexation option, 
so that the premiums and benefit would automatically increase each year.
The adviser then confirmed that they’d discussed the alternative, which was term assurance. 
The adviser explained this was cheaper and provides life cover for a specific term. He then 
said “This is not suitable as it is important to have protection for the whole of your life 
because you want the reassurance that the plan will always be available and are prepared to 
pay a little extra for this peace of mind rather than having a higher level of cover today.”
Ms M’s representative thinks she should have been sold term assurance rather than whole 
of life cover, as this would have been cheaper. 
I think this is quite balanced. Term assurance can be set up to provide decreasing cover 
over its term (usually appropriate to protect a decreasing debt, such as a mortgage). 
Alternatively, it can provide level cover over its term (this may be appropriate for someone 
wanting a specific amount of cover until, say, their children have grown up). 
Whole of life cover on the other hand, isn’t limited to a specific term. Instead it provides 
cover for the whole of someone’s life and a claim is inevitable. Because of that, the cost of 
whole of life cover is more expensive than term assurance. Some people take out whole of 
life cover for inheritance tax purposes. But others take it out because they like knowing that 
there is a lump sum available for their family whenever they die.
Ms M wanted to protect her family in the event of her death. I understand she was single 
with one dependant. Her son was aged 14 at the time. There is an argument that if she 
wanted the policy to protect her son, she would only need this until he was no longer 
dependent on her. In that case, a term assurance policy of say, 10 years, would have been 
appropriate, and far cheaper.
However, I can’t ignore that Ms M and the adviser discussed the option of taking out the 
cheaper option of term assurance. But Ms M was apparently willing to pay more for whole of 
life cover, as she wanted the reassurance of having cover that would always be available.
That being the case, on balance, I don’t think I can reasonably say the adviser sold her the 
wrong type of policy.
Ms M’s representative makes the point that she had £197,000 of existing life insurance 
cover. Because of that, he says she didn’t have a need at all for life cover. 
I see it was recorded that Ms M had life cover from four sources. Two of them covered her 
interest-only mortgage of £62,300. The third provided her with £14,500 cover. The fourth 
was death-in-service benefit provided by her employer of £120,000.
Ref: DRN9691306

4
The adviser then recorded that Ms M wanted £300,000 life cover. He rounded up her 
existing cover to £197,000, which left her with £103,000 shortfall. This was the level of 
benefit he recommended under her whole of life policy.
I see that Ms M was earning £30,000 before bonuses. It’s quite typical for advisers to 
estimate someone’s life cover need as being around 10 times their salary. That is what 
happened here. I don’t think Ms M probably needed this amount of life cover. Having said 
that, I don’t think it’s appropriate for advisers to rely on someone’s death-in-service benefit 
when making recommendations for life cover. I say that because if that person’s employment 
were to end, they would no longer have that death-in-service benefit. 
Therefore, excluding Ms M’s existing cover that protected her mortgage and her death-in-
service benefit, she only had £14,500 worth of life cover. I don’t think it was entirely 
unreasonable for the adviser to recommend she increase this. 
Overall, I don’t find this policy was mis-sold.  
life and critical illness policy
On 13 November 2003, Ms M applied for life and critical illness cover. The policy had a lump 
sum benefit of £44,000, over a 15 year term. Although Ms M already had a whole of life 
policy that provided her with life cover, it seems she decided to let that policy lapse in 
November 2003 and take out this policy instead. So she didn’t have duplicate life cover. 
There isn’t much information from the time of sale, but I see the application form refers to an 
exchange of contracts taking place on 1 December 2003, which is the same date that the 
policy started. It would therefore seem that Ms M was taking out the cover to protect a 
mortgage. 
I haven’t seen any information relating to the mortgage, so I don’t know if the benefit amount 
and term matched the mortgage. But given that Ms M had a dependant, I think that life cover 
and critical illness cover was appropriate for her. 
conclusions
Overall, I’m satisfied that the three policies weren’t mis-sold. 
my final decision
For the reasons given above, my final decision is that I don’t uphold this complaint.
Under the rules of the Financial Ombudsman Service, I’m required to ask Ms M to accept or 
reject my decision before 14 July 2017.
Chantelle Hurn-Ryan
ombudsman
Ref: DRN9691306
quoted_clauses: The Ombudsman cannot consider a complaint if the complainant refers it to the Financial Ombudsman Service: … (2) more than: (a) six years after the event complained of; or (if later) Ref: DRN9691306 2 (b) three years from the date on which the complainant became aware (or ought reasonably to have become aware) that he had cause for complaint…

This is not suitable as it is important to have protection for the whole of your life because you want the reassurance that the plan will always be available and are prepared to pay a little extra for this peace of mind rather than having a higher level of cover today.

text:
K820x#14
complaint
Mr H complains that Unum Ltd turned down a claim made under his previous employer’s 
group income protection scheme. 
background
Mr H was covered under his employer’s income protection scheme. This paid benefit after a 
waiting period (also known as a ‘deferred period’) of 26 weeks in the event Mr H couldn’t 
work because of accident or illness. 
Mr H made a claim. His employer said he was first absent on 3 October 2016. Mr H 
explained on the claim form that he’d stopped work because of lower back pain, aching 
through his hips, legs and knees, as well as fatigue. But as Mr H returned to work in 
December 2016, before the waiting period had ended, Unum found the claim wasn’t valid. 
Mr H’s employer told Unum about previous absences he’d had for back pain, and asked if it 
could link them together (if those absences exceeded 26 weeks, then the claim might be 
payable). Absences can be linked under the policy if they are for the same condition and last 
two weeks or more. Unum therefore looked at the medical evidence during those previous 
absences to see if it supported that Mr H wasn’t able to work for a total of 26 weeks. 
After doing so, Unum turned down the claim. It didn’t think Mr H’s back problems would have 
prevented him from being able to work. Unhappy with this, Mr H brought a complaint to this 
service. 
Our investigator didn’t recommend the complaint be upheld. He thought Unum’s claims 
decision was reasonable, given the evidence. 
Mr H didn’t accept our investigator’s findings, so the matter’s been passed to me.  
my findings
I’ve considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint. 
The policy definition of incapacity is:
“(a)…the member is unable, by reason of his illness or injury, to perform the material and 
substantial duties of his insured occupation, and
(b) the member is not following any occupation…”
Mr H’s employer chose a 26 week waiting period for the scheme. That meant Mr H would 
need to be off for 26 consecutive weeks before a claim could be considered. Mr H’s first date 
of absence was 3 October 2016 but he returned to work in December 2016, before the 26 
week waiting period had ended. So I agree that Unum couldn’t consider the claim based on 
these dates. 
But Mr H had been off work previously for lower back pain. So his employer asked Unum to 
consider linking these absences. 
Ref: DRN9825143

2
The policy says “Although the deferred period is normally a period of continuous absence 
Unum will link periods of absence of at least 2 weeks duration through incapacity arising 
from the same cause provided the deferred period is completed within twice the length of the 
deferred period.”
As the normal deferred period is 26 weeks, that means the linked absences of two weeks or 
more for the same cause would need to total 26 weeks over a 52 week period. 
I’ve looked at the medical evidence from the dates of Mr H’s absences that exceeded two 
weeks. 
Mr H’s first absence was 26 August 2015 to 16 October 2015. 
In August 2015, Mr H saw a consultant spinal neurosurgeon. An MRI scan showed that Mr H 
had degenerative changes around a previously operated disc, which his consultant thought 
would account for his back pain. He recommended that Mr H have further physio.
Mr H has explained that his recommended physio treatment was delayed because of a 
problem with his private medical insurer. He says he funded treatment with an osteopath 
himself, and this allowed him to return to work in October. 
Although Mr H’s specialist reported that he was experiencing pain during this period, there’s 
no mention of how this impaired him. I haven’t seen any of the osteopath treatment notes.
Overall, I think it’s arguable whether or not Mr H was unable to work during this period. 
Mr H next period of absence was 9 December 2015 to 3 April 2016. 
Mr H had some physio sessions during this period but didn’t find them to be of any help. He 
says he was also seeing a chiropractor during this period and had found some benefit 
through this, though I haven’t seen his chiropractor’s notes. I’ve checked Mr H’s medical 
records but the first appointment relating to his back pain during this period was on 18 March 
2016, which was shortly before he returned to work. Although Mr H was given sick notes by 
his GP for low back pain throughout the period of absence, I see that he was requesting 
them by email. There’s therefore little medical evidence to support that Mr H’s back 
problems were preventing him from working.
During this period of absence, Mr H had surgery for another medical problem. Mr H says this 
other medical problem wasn’t the reason for his absence from work, and that he’d recovered 
from the operation before he’d recovered from the back pain that was preventing him from 
working. 
When Mr H met with his consultant about that other medical problem in January 2016, he 
mentioned his intention to go on holiday. It seems unusual for someone who’s been signed 
off work with back pain for around a month to feel fit enough to go on holiday, particularly 
one that would be considered a long-haul destination. Mr H says he was only considering 
this holiday and in the end, he didn’t book the trip because of his back pain. I don’t know if 
that’s the case. I see that he emailed his GP in February 2016 to explain that he was 
travelling to this particular destination (six days later) for ten days and wanted a letter to 
show what prescription medication he would be carrying. Also, I understand that Mr H 
posted pictures on his social media account of a trip to this particular destination, though I 
don’t know when it took place. 
Ref: DRN9825143

3
I see that Mr H spoke with an occupational health adviser in March 2015 (around three 
weeks before he returned to work) and he told her he could walk for up to two hours and sit 
for an hour. He thought his main problems were back pain, as well as alack of focus and 
concentration. 
On balance, I don’t think I can reasonably conclude that Mr H was incapacitated because of 
his back problems during this period. That’s not to say that he wasn’t experiencing back pain 
during this time (as well as his other medical problem). But I don’t think the evidence 
supports that his back problems caused him a level of impairment that prevented him from 
working. 
I think Unum makes a valid point that Mr H’s back pain has remained largely unchanged 
since 2015, yet despite his ongoing pain and fatigue, he’s been able to work for significant 
periods of time since then. Unum’s company medical officer thought that Mr H would be able 
to work, so long as he had an ergonomic workstation and got up regularly to walk around. I 
think that’s a reasonable conclusion.
Mr H had further periods of absence because of his back problems but, even in combination 
with the absence between August and October 2015, they don’t total 26 weeks. So I haven’t 
considered whether those absences are medically supported.
Whilst I recognise my decision will disappoint Mr H, I think it was appropriate for Unum to 
turn down the claim. 
Mr H is also unhappy about Unum’s handling of the claim. He says Unum made some 
slanderous statements about him to his employer, and refused to talk to him about the claim. 
Overall, I think Unum handled Mr H’s claim fairly well. I appreciate it took some months for 
Unum to reach a claims decision, but that’s not unusual when an insurer needs to wait for 
medical evidence and then consider it. I don’t agree that Unum made slanderous statements 
about Mr H to his employer - it was entitled to give an opinion on whether it thought his 
absences were medically supported. And the reason Unum didn’t correspond with Mr H 
about the claim is because it corresponded about the matter with the policyholder, his 
employer. I don’t think there was anything wrong with that. 
Mr H has also complained about what he sees as the intrusiveness of Unum’s investigation 
into his claim. 
Unum has explained that during its assessment of the claim, it found that Mr H was the 
owner and director of a company. It asked him to provide details of any earnings during the 
linked periods of absence. I think this was appropriate because for a claim to be payable, 
Mr H couldn’t be following another occupation. I appreciate Unum didn’t ask for this 
information at the outset, but that was because it didn’t know about the company at that 
time. 
my final decision
For the reasons set out above, my final decision is that I don’t uphold this complaint. 
Ref: DRN9825143

4
Under the rules of the Financial Ombudsman Service, I’m required to ask Mr H to let me 
know whether he accepts or rejects my decision before 16 October 2017.
Chantelle Hurn-Ryan
ombudsman
Ref: DRN9825143

Although the deferred period is normally a period of continuous absence Unum will link periods of absence of at least 2 weeks duration through incapacity arising from the same cause provided the deferred period is completed within twice the length of the deferred period.

text:
K820x#14
complaint
Mr G has complained about the amount offered by Chubb European Group SE in settlement 
of a claim for permanent disablement under his personal accident insurance policy.
background
Mr G held a personal accident insurance policy underwritten by Chubb. The policy would pay 
various types of benefit if Mr G were to suffer an accidental injury. These benefits included 
temporary disablement which was a regular benefit payable for up to 52 weeks in the event 
that Mr G was temporarily unable to work due to his injury. The policy also offered a lump 
sum payment of up to £20,000 if Mr G were to suffer permanent disability, the actual amount 
being dependent on the severity of that disability.
In December 2015, Mr G unfortunately suffered an accident in which he injured his back. He 
initially stopped working. He later attempted a return to work. However, he found he was 
unable to continue due to his ongoing back pain and his employer eventually informed him 
that his contract would be terminated in June 2018 due to his ill-health.
Mr G made a claim to Chubb. It accepted the claim under the temporary disablement benefit 
heading and paid him £2,297.
Mr G went back to Chubb. He said it should pay him more to reflect that he was suffering 
from a permanent disability.
Chubb agreed to seek further medical information to enable it to assess Mr G’s claim.
In October 2018, Chubb wrote to Mr G explaining that while he may be permanently 
prevented from following his previous occupation, it didn’t consider that his injury prevented 
him from following any and every occupation. It further noted that he was suffering from a 
degenerative back condition. On this basis, it offered Mr G a further £5,000 (25% of the 
maximum amount payable under the policy) in settlement of his claim.
Mr G was unhappy at Chubb’s offer and its overall handling of his claim. He referred his 
complaint to us.
   
In February 2019, our investigator issued a view recommending that the complaint should be 
upheld. While he considered that Mr G hadn’t shown he was entitled to the maximum benefit 
payable of £20,000, he also considered that Chubb had failed to provide adequate 
justification for why it considered the 25% settlement to be appropriate. The investigator 
recommended that Chubb should ask Mr G’s treating specialists for advice on the extent to 
which Mr G’s current level of disability was attributable to the accident and should use this as 
the basis of its settlement offer. The investigator further recommended that Chubb should 
pay Mr G £300 compensation for the poor way it had handled his claim.
Both Mr G and Chubb agreed to the investigator’s findings.
Chubb sought the views of Mr G’s treating specialists on the extent to which his current level 
of disability was attributable to the accident but was unable to elicit their opinions. The 
investigator and Mr G therefore agreed to Chubb’s suggestion that it should instead arrange 
for Mr G to undergo an independent medical examination (IME) with Dr L, a consultant 
orthopaedic surgeon.
Ref: DRN9835461

2
The IME took place in March 2019. Dr L concluded that Mr G’s accident aggravated an 
existing back condition and brought forward by twelve months a level of disability which 
would have occurred even without the accident.
Based on Dr L’s report, Chubb was satisfied its settlement offer of £5,000 was fair. Our 
investigator agreed. Mr G, however, disagreed. He considered that Dr L hadn’t taken full 
account of his treatment history since the accident and that his findings were inconsistent 
with the findings of his treating specialists. He pointed out that he was in constant pain since 
the accident and was unable to perform the physical occupation he used to perform. He 
considered he should be entitled to a benefit payment of £18,000 under the policy.
In view of the continued disagreement, the matter has been passed to me for a decision.
my findings
I’ve considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and 
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint. Having done so, I don’t uphold this 
complaint. I shall explain why.
The investigator recommended in his view of February 2019 that Chubb should pay Mr G 
£300 compensation for its poor handling of the claim. This was accepted by both parties and 
the money has been paid. I therefore don’t need to consider this matter in this decision. 
Instead, I just need to determine whether it was fair for Chubb to pay £5,000 in settlement of 
Mr G’s claim for permanent disability.
The policy states:
“If you or any other eligible person (Insured Person) suffer Bodily Injury as a direct result of 
an Accident which within 24 months of the Accident results in Permanent Disability, Facial 
Disfigurement or Death, or requires treatment within 12 months of Dental Trauma occurring, 
the following will be paid:”
The policy then has a list of disabilities such as “loss of hearing in both ears” and “loss of use 
of a thumb”, along with the corresponding amount which will be paid for that disability. This 
list includes “permanent total disablement” which in Mr G’s case has a benefit level of 
£20,000, and “temporary disablement” which has a benefit level of £60 per week.
The policy defines “permanent total disablement” as:
“… disablement caused other than by loss of limb or Sight which, having lasted for at least 
12 months, will in all probability entirely prevent the Insured Person from engaging in or 
giving attention to a profession or occupation of any and every kind for the remainder of his / 
her life.”
The policy defines “temporary disablement” as 
“… disablement which prevents the Insured Person from engaging in or giving attention to 
his / her normal, gainful occupation or which confines the Insured Person to his / her home 
on medical grounds.”
Ref: DRN9835461

3
At the top of the policy’s list of disabilities and associated benefit is “permanent disability” 
with a benefit level of “up to £20,000”. Under this heading, the policy states:
“A proportion of this sum will be paid depending upon the degree of permanent disability in 
accordance with the following scale:”
The policy later on states:
“Payment for any Permanent Disability not shown in the table on page 11 will be based on a 
medical assessment of the disability in relation to the table and not in relation to the Insured 
Person’s ability to work.
If the Insured Person was already disabled before an Accident or already had a condition 
which is gradually deteriorating, the payment will be reduced. The reduced payment will be 
based on a medical assessment of the difference between:
a) the Permanent Disability after the Accident; and
b) the extent to which the Permanent Disability is affected by the disability or condition 
before the Accident. …
The most an Insured Person can receive for Permanent Disability resulting from any one 
Accident is the amount specified for Permanent Total Disablement.”
When Mr G first made his claim, Chubb assessed it against the heading of temporary 
disablement and calculated that Mr G was entitled to benefit of £2,297. I’m satisfied this was 
a fair assessment of the benefit to which he was entitled under this heading due to his 
inability at certain times to perform his normal occupation during the first 24 months following 
his accident. 
Mr G considered he should also be entitled to benefit for permanent disability. Chubb 
therefore agreed to seek further medical information. However, while Mr G was medically 
unable to continue in his previous role, which was a manual occupation, it did not seem from 
the medical evidence that he was medically prevented from performing any occupation 
whatsoever, which was the eligibility requirement under the policy for Mr G to receive 
permanent total disablement benefit. I’m therefore satisfied that it was fair for Chubb to 
refuse to pay Mr G this benefit which, if Mr G’s accident had been entirely responsible for his 
disability, would have been £20,000.
Mr G may nonetheless have been eligible for permanent disability benefit. However, the 
amount of this would depend on the degree of his permanent disability compared to those 
listed in the policy. It should be remembered that this assessment should not be in relation to 
his capacity to work and, given the medical records indicated that Mr G was suffering from a 
degenerative back condition, it should also take into account the extent to which his disability 
might be due to factors other than the accident.
Chubb had difficulty in getting information about the extent to which Mr G’s disability was 
due to his accident. It offered a settlement of £5,000 which was 25% of the maximum 
permanent disability benefit payable under the policy. However, Mr G objected to this and 
the investigator considered the figure had been chosen arbitrarily. Both parties therefore 
agreed to the investigator’s recommendation that an expert view should be sought from 
Mr G’s treating physicians. I’m satisfied that this was an appropriate course of action.
Ref: DRN9835461

4
Unfortunately, these physicians appeared reluctant to express an opinion. Both parties 
therefore agreed that Mr G should undergo an IME with Dr L. Again, I’m satisfied that this 
was an appropriate course of action.
After reviewing the medical evidence and examining Mr G, Dr L concluded:
“I acknowledge that [Mr G] has undergone radiological imaging of the lumbar spine which 
has identified the presence of degenerative intervertebral disc disease but no previous 
history of fracture or trauma. To that end, it is my clinical opinion that the claimant has 
aggravated this pre-existing complaint. It is my clinical opinion that the incident accelerated 
the development of pain that would have occurred irrespective of trauma by the order of 
twelve months. Although the incident may have advanced symptom onset, I do not believe it 
has worsened his overall condition nor altered his prognosis in the long term.”
In other words, Dr L considered that even if he hadn’t had the accident, Mr G would have 
suffered the same level of disability due to a pre-existing condition, albeit he wouldn’t have 
done so until twelve months later.
I note that Mr G disputes Dr L’s opinion and considers he hasn’t taken full account of all the 
evidence. However, Dr L had access to all the relevant information. He is an expert in the 
relevant field. I see no reason to dispute his opinion. While he has gone further in his 
comments than Mr G’s treating specialists, who were reluctant to express views on the 
extent to which the accident contributed to his level of disability, I don’t find that he has said 
anything which is inconsistent with the opinions of those specialists.
If Mr G had suffered an accidental injury which, by itself, left him permanently unable to 
perform any occupation whatsoever, he would have received £20,000 benefit under the 
policy. As it is, he has suffered an accidental injury which meant he was unable to perform 
his own occupation a year sooner than would otherwise would have happened. I appreciate 
this is still a very significant blow to Mr G but nonetheless, in insurance terms, there is a big 
difference between the two situations.
Mr G says that if it were not for his disability, he would have expected to work in his previous 
occupation for a further eight years. But according to Dr L, Mr G’s accident, by itself, simply 
brought forward his disability by one year. This means the accident has therefore deprived 
him of only one eighth, or 12.5%, of his anticipated future earnings; the remaining 87.5% is 
accounted for by his degenerative back condition. Therefore, even if Mr G had been eligible 
for permanent total disability benefit, I would have expected Chubb to reduce this to 12.5% 
of £20,000, in other words £2,500, to reflect the limited contribution of the accident to his 
disablement. And of course, because Mr G wasn’t eligible for permanent total disability 
benefit, for reasons I have previously explained, I consider that Chubb could reasonably 
have paid 12.5% of a lower figure than £20,000 to reflect that Mr G’s disability was not as 
severe as permanent total disablement.
In view of the above, and despite my sympathy for Mr G, I am satisfied that Chubb’s 
settlement of £5,000 is fair. I don’t consider that he could reasonably claim he was entitled to 
more than this under the terms of the policy. 
my final decision
For the reasons given above, my final decision is that I don’t uphold this complaint.
Ref: DRN9835461

5
Under the rules of the Financial Ombudsman Service, I’m required to ask Mr G to accept or 
reject my decision before 17 July 2020.
David Poley
ombudsman
Ref: DRN9835461
